Whilst it’s not as gritty as 1988’s Thy Kingdom Come demo, the performances are recorded live with little to no audible overdubbing, and the whole thing has a very primitive, “scratchy” sound. This is a very, very formative era of Morbid Angel, and for this reason it’s thoroughly impressive how well written the songs are already at this point. Structurally, the songs are mostly the same to how we all know and love them - Chapel, Angel, Azagthoth (later known on Blessed as The Ancient Ones), Hellspawn and Abominations are practically the exact same arrangements here as they are later, albeit with some sonic differences that are impossible to ignore (we’ll get to that later). Unholy Blasphemies, Lord Of All Fevers and Welcome To Hell (Not a Venom cover - this is Evil Spells from Altars) are a bit different with a slower riff here and there that there wasn’t later, but you’re not going to hear any incredible reimagining of ideas from this album’s material à la Prototype to Monotheist. The songs could be already considered fully formed at this point - had Abominations actually been released in 1986, it could’ve perhaps given pre-established extreme bands such as Bathory or Sodom (if those seem like odd comparisons, just know that some would even consider Abominations’s satanic speed metal tendencies to be adjacent to first wave black metal) a serious run for their money, and even in the following years, cult favourites such as Necrovore’s Divus De Mortus and Nihilist’s trilogy of demos were scoring serious cred amongst the underground with noticeably less refined material. So what’s the catch with Abominations? Was it shelved for no apparent reason?

Well, the most obvious spanner in the works is Browning’s drumming. Whilst the vocal work on this album is not strictly inferior to that which succeeded it, the kit work leaves a lot (Sandoval) to be desired. The drum patterns and beats are repetitive and mostly indistinguishable from each other from song to song, with strictly rudimentary fills and a very noticeable limitation on the overall BPM of the songs. There aren’t any of the iconic blasts nor double bass pedalling that help define Morbid Angel’s sound. This is the biggest factor that makes the songs sound arguably incomplete; additionally, there are few to none of the incredible guitar effects Azagthoth was to use in his psychedelic soloing style later on, from univibe to delay to the unorthodox micing techniques. The rhythm guitar doesn’t sound tight enough to stand alongside Seven Churches or Reign In Blood despite the obvious proficiency demonstrated by Azagthoth and the late, great Richard Brunelle, partially due to the slapdash drumming and partially due to what can maybe be attributed to inexperience. Short-term bassist John Ortega occasionally offers up a bass solo or embellishment worthy of note, but it doesn’t tighten up an already loose and slightly sloppy sounding album. These sonic imperfections are why the album was shelved and the band spent 3 more years shuffling around the lineup and refining their sound, and it paid dividends. For all the atmosphere and spooky first wave vibes this album has to offer, songs such as Chapel Of Ghouls and Lord Of All Fevers sound much more punishing and unforgiving on Altars, and the material that wound up on Blessed received the same upgrade, despite whatever production gripes can be had about that album. The album is excellently written; the EXECUTION and performance of the material is what was deemed unfit for release, and it’s easy to see why considering how much better the band made these songs later on. After all, for as fun as Hellspawn is on Abominations, the version on Formulas Fatal to the Flesh - Hellspawn: The Rebirth - is so much tighter, sonically varied in its guitar attack and generally better performed (whilst retaining a raw edge) that it makes Hellspawn: The Original sound almost laughably amateurish by comparison. 

In conclusion, Abominations Of Desolation is not a bad album, or even a bad album by Morbid Angel’s standards. It could’ve been released at the time of recording and blown the mind of many an extreme headbanger in the same way Altars did. However, it is an INFERIOR, IMPROVABLE album. It’s easy to make an argument that this less-praised release has an “unique vibe” compared to Morbid Angel’s main catalogue of ABCDFGHIK albums, and the intros to Chapel and Lord are very atmospheric and unique, they’re significantly less mind-blowing than the later versions which proved to be enduring genre classics, to the point where you could reasonably skip it in a discography run - you’d only be missing out on Demon Seed, which is far from essential anyway. 

I’d recommend this album to anyone who’s heard all the Morbid Angel albums (except Illud, you really don’t need to do that one), people who are really into their death metal history, and people who like raw black/death demo material. Abominations Of Desolation is a great album - better than many other death metal debuts that were released - but not essential.

It had been a long time since I checked in on Shaman, so this 2022 release completely passed me by. Given that it was their first record in twelve years, it’s no great shock, but I was glad to have them back, even if their resurrection was brief. Despite the oft-fellated ‘Ritual’, I think this band got much better when Andre Matos left, and 2007’s ‘Immortal’ is still my favourite album by them. The only reason I knew ‘Rescue’ existed was I’d been spinning the first two Age Of Artemis albums a lot, and discovered vocalist Alirio Netto ended up joining Shaman later on. 

As it turned out, this was the fifth and final release from the Brazilians, despite original brothers Luis and Hugo Mariutti returning to the fold, and it’s a real shame, as it’s easily better than ‘Origins’ was. For one thing, the production is rich and textured, and the band are on top form throughout, pulling from a mixed bag of songwriting tricks to produce a varied, surprising set of songs. Netto is a perfect fit, given that Age Of Artemis are one of the best Angra clones out there, and he’s absolute fire behind the mic, giving a smooth, soaring performance. All Angra-related albums follow a set of strict guidelines, and ‘Rescue’ is no different. You get uplifting power metal scorchers, multifarious prog workouts, and tender ballads, all dusted with that authentic tribal atmosphere we know so well. Truthfully, there’s not much of the latter here; native instruments pepper some of the atmospheric sections, but that’s it. The album is mostly divided into high-wire double kickers and more melodic mid-paced tracks that flirt with prog and a touch of hard rock, but it’s all held together with rock solid writing.

Things kick off with the fast, pelting ‘Time Is Running Out’, one of the best songs here, before jumping straight into ‘The I Inside’, a prog-power cut with more double kicking from Ricardo Confessori and one of the catchiest choruses on the album. ‘Don’t Let It Rain’ is a very whimsical rock song with a vague anime vibe about it, whereas ‘The Spirit’ is another power metal barnstormer. The middle section of this album really reminds me of Karevik-era Kamelot, as tunes like ‘Boundaries Of Heaven’ are sort of gothic and romantic, very synthy and all about the chorus. That one is a good example of it, but ‘Brand New Me’ gets kind of dull, and after that, we’re just in ballad territory until the end of the album. Shaman play with restraint throughout most of this, so while there are fret board pyrotechnics, it’s nowhere near as self-indulgent as some of Angra’s work. So, this is another quality album from Shaman, probably about as good as we were going to get as a final send off, but it’s still a shame to see them go.

This record is insanely straight out to its target customers. What can you probably say about a debut record that is entitled “I Am Satan”  with good old Baphomet and his old pal Grim Reaper trying to outgrin each other on its cover? It is certainly not a feature-length review you should expect. To put the essence in a nutshell: these nine black/death metal tracks leave a trace of devastation. Period. Not.

These Peruvian underground warriors eventually released their long-awaited debut in February 2015, fifteen years into its existence. It is well known that one only reaches the stars after wandering a quite rough territory. In Goat Semen´s case we are talking about numerous lineup changes and chronic lack of money, that hindered a full-length album, but not a long list of split releases with bands such as Krieg, Naxzul, Sabbat or Anal Vomit.

What we hear is truly traditional and uncompromising blackened death metal. The quartet does not lose any time confronting us with the tracks Holocausto and Genocidio that both go like a bull at a goat, erm, gate. It is always nice when there is no need for a dictionary for the song titles. South American outfits such as Sarcofago, Krisiun or Anal Vomit are coming to your mind in no time, when the drumming bludgeons into your auditory canals like jackhammers wresting new caverns for dead bodies from a mountain. The Spanish vocals yelp like a dog with rabies and swim in reverb trapped inside a cavern of blasphemy. 

After serving a shitload of cliches Ego Svm Satana invites you to a ten minute Odyssee entitled Hambre, Peste, Guerra y Muerte. We, as devotees of cavernous black/death metal, probably start to wonder if anything more interesting is hidden somewhere on this record. The answer is “no.” After 40 bludgeoning minutes, once more the good old-fashioned in-out, in-out proves itself reliable in a musical way. Even if you did not ejaculate gallons of black seed listening to this debut there is undeniably a strange sensation of satisfaction. The overall production is well-made. A reasonable compromise between the rust of early '80s Venom and the power that sounds good on more recent opuses by Inquisition.

It is good to see and hear the goat semen finally coming to fruition. The chimera evolving from it  will certainly not become a new Lucifer, but without any doubt one of his henchmen. Ego Svm Satana causes fun at a devilish velocity.

Because this is a compilation of several demo's by a band that does not believe in clean and tidy sound mixing, you will understand that the stuff on offer here is going to be on the unsophisticated side of things, to put it mildly. And if we also consider that this is also a band that does not believe in friendly and accessible music, you can damn well bet your sweet little behind that this CD is one abrasive blow to the face.

Martyrvore hocks up a glob of relentless black/death metal in the way of forebearers like Beherit, Naked Whipper, Von, Blasphemy and Impaled Nazarene circa "Tol Cormpt Norz Norz Norz" did in those dark days passed, with some early Krieg added here and there too. The riffing more resembles the sound of a rusty chainsaw than it does that of a guitar, while a battering percussionist goes at it with the slime-caked growls of the vocalist. The songs are short, primarily fast, and in the straight forward execution there is a definite influence of grindcore bands like Blood or Agathocles present. There's little to no melody and a near total lack of any nuance whatsoever, with the overall execution being kinda rough around the edges. Every now and then, the guitar scrape does give way for a short blackened thrash riff that has a somewhat passing resemblance to actual music, but these never last that long. Pretty much nothing lasts long here, honestly, and you know what? I can totally get behind this. Sure, it's sloppy and primitive and these guys wipe their ass with anything that is subtle and sophisticated, while some might even say that probably any moron could conjure up something like this any day, but dammit, this is just great stuff! It's fast, aggressive and simply oozes a vile, blackened atmosphere throughout, sounding absolutely unhinged while doing it.

As mentioned above, the sound quality is raw, especially in the second half of the disc, where it practically reaches basement level. Where the first half of this comp has me thinking of what those early Beherit recordings sounded, which still wasn't pretty but got the job done, the second half has a thin, gritty sound to it. For any other band more concerned with polish and shine to their music, this would be a nightmare scenario, but for Martyrvore it works. It adds that last demented touch to the already disturbed aggression at play, adding even more menace to the whole. These tracks are only suited for the most hardened noisemongers among us, but for most, this is absolutey inaccessible. And while I kinda agree that in parts the sound is rough indeed, I can't imagine the band wanting it any other way.

So yeah, this is one of those releases that is only suited for the most niche crowd out there. It might not be perfect, and is probably far from it, but I dig this stuff for sure. It oozes unhinged aggression and menacing atmosphere, and that is just about all that I want from a release like this.

So far "From Light to Darkness" is Saevitia Monumentum's only release and already the band has stamped a distinct if very deranged identity all over the music. The actual music itself is uncomplicated raw aggressive BM but it's the way the trio - I'm assuming the band is a trio, to judge from its MA photo but at present there's not much other information on SM I can find - play and the crazed zest the guys put into everything they do that makes it stand out like a thumb just begging for a hammer to smash it down, if that thumb could talk. 

Right from the start listeners can guess they're going to be in for a wild ride with this loony flight crew, crashing and crash-landing their way through raging BM that aspires to the epic and the bombastic. Along the journey death, doom and crushing sludge elements embellish the music and background synthesiser adds a space ambient layer that adds a sense of high opera. Listeners will realise quickly that the album is aimed at an audience straddling the edges of underground and commercial mainstream metal, with all songs heavily lyrics-based and not much attention being paid to generating and sustaining particular atmospheres or moods, but the roller-coaster ride is so exhilarating with the multi-voiced SM crew at the flight controls that you want to stay with them right to the end just to see what barmy thing they get up to next.

The music is rock-solid and usually fast in delivery, and the musicians have a great time playing and singing, as much to one another as to listeners, to judge from the way the lyrics bounce from one vocalist to the next. The only criticism I'd offer is that the songs aren't all that different from one another and it's only when the band reaches the halfway point in the album that the music starts to vary more in style and mood. The cold-space ambience hardly changes for the album's length and for some songs doesn't enhance them at all but rather detracts from their aggression. The highlight of the album is the wild and deranged singing which can border on cartoonish and is sometimes a little excessive especially when the lads are taking turns in singing.

As it is, the album serves mainly to introduce Saevitia Monumentum and their particular style of energetic and demented BM, and a good and consistent introduction it is too.

Up until this point, Overkill had noticeably been evolving and experimenting with their sound ever since they released, in my eyes, their magnum opus “Horrorscope”. “I Hear Black” was a step into a slower and dreary landscape of more conventional heavy metal concepts with a dash of rock, their thrashier side on a few songs, and some pieces of the already emerged groove metal genre. “W.F.O.” was a leap back into their thrash metal side while still maintaining more groove metal elements than they have done before. “The Killing Kind” though is a very much different beast compared to the last few releases. This is where those groove metal elements really take the wheel and drive home the listener on two pairs of tires that mix in their thrash roots and a few other elements spread out on a couple of tracks such as their sabbath-esque doom influenced side, dipping their fingers into a rock-esque ballad, and D.D. getting a little funky on a pretty well rounded instrumental. 

This is the point where I think the band really got “experimental” with their sound and began mixing up their rhythm section and Blitz began approaching different melodies and doing some crazy, and at times strange, things with his voice. “The Killing Kind” also signifies the beginning of their “groove phase”, for a trilogy of groove metal focused albums with “From Underground And Below'' and “Necroshine '' being the next two to follow. Even with groove metal taking the center focus on these albums, the band never truly let go of their thrash metal roots as they integrate thrashy and speedy parts within sections of some songs or having a few songs harken back to their roots with a different coat of paint. Out of the three, “The Killing Kind” is probably the closest to having the most “traditional'' thrash elements within the album, which interestingly enough is mostly found in the front half of the record while the second half is much more focused on slower and mid-paced groovers.

In between the release of this record and their last LP and first live album, “Wrecking Your Neck Live” (a review I may get to some day), both Merritt Gant and Rob Cannavino had been replaced by ex-Anvil guitarist Sebastian Marino and former Liege Lord (and now current) vocalist Joe Cameau on guitars. Both Joe and Sebastian are very competent guitarists in their own right and, in retrospect to this era of the band, fit very well with the more groove metal orientated sound the band was messing around with at this time. Writing wise, the music can be fairly repetitive and simple, an issue that I agree persists the most out of the whole of this trilogy of albums, but the riffs themselves for the most part are fairly catchy and the songs do offer changes in tempo, melody, and riff structure so the songs aren’t completely brain dead repetitive. Joe and Sebastian both put on solid performances and showcasing that they can thrash out on some of the speedier songs such as “Battle”, “God-Like”, and “Certifiable” while still being able to slow it down to a steady groove in “The Cleansing” or “Bold Face Pagan Stomp”. Besides the rhythmic and lead sections on this album, I’ve always liked the solos on here despite them not being anything groundbreaking as the music builds up to the solos. Stylistically, the solos themselves are less on the shredding side and more “groovy” and melodical. 

Tim Mallare still remains on the drum kit and he really gives it his all on this record as he offers a varied performance ranging from quick tempo shifts to throwing in organic fills that help build and release tension. D.D. Verni keeps toe to toe with both Joe and Sebastian on the bass as he keeps the rhythmic section in check. There’s actually plenty of depth from D.D. to be found on this album, as his bass acts as the backbone to most of the melodies on these songs as the guitars play a specific part of the medley, the bass fills in the rest with “Let Me Shut That For You” being a good example showcasing this. He also is given much more room to shine on the overly bass driven instrumental “Feeding Frenzy”, as big sections have this funky underlying feeling mixed with the thrashier sections that have the guitars and drums joining in. Now the best thing about this album, and really any Overkill album, is Blitz himself. Blitz just down right sounds pissed off here which adds more to that groove metal sound they’ve pushed here. Everything identifiable with Blitz's vocals is still here, that raunchy, sleazy, shrill voice is still all put together but Blitz does harken back to his cleaner vocals, noticeably in the sabbath inspired doom / groove metal mix “Burn You Down / To Ashes'' as he practically whispers to the listener throughout most of the run time, the rock inspired ballad “The Morning After / Private Bleeding”, and towards the end of the grooving “The Cleansing”. Joe Comeau, a vocalist himself, does backing vocals on this record and if there’s another positive element to be found in this era, it’s Joe adding another dynamic alongside Blitz and plays off with his vocals very well. 

One of the things I love about this album though is its production. This album sounds heavy as hell and probably one of my favorite production jobs in their career. The guitars are thick and crunchy, the bass audible and groovy, the drums slams but doesn’t dominate the mix, and Blitz in all of his nasally glory spitting out every enunciation is heard. But if there’s really any gripes to be had with “The Killing Kind” it would be some of the lyrical writing, some of the simplicity of the songs, and some odd parts in the opener “Battle”. So first, some of the lyrics have the shortcomings of the “pissed off, edgy, macho man metal head” type of lyrics found on your typical groove metal record. Lots of mother fuckers thrown around in some songs and aggressive lyrics relating to fighting people. Luckily there’s not much of that as one would think but there are some fairly silly lyrics to be found, with “Bold Face Pagan Stomp” being the clearest example, like just out that song title out loud. The overall simplicity of the songs isn’t a major issue but compared to what came before, it feels a little lacking. Luckily the song's time lengths aren’t long so they don’t feel like repetitive slogs and there’s enough added to keep the flow going.

Now I bring this all the way back to some of the….choices Blitz made for his voice on “Battle” including the lyrics. To start, I really like the instrumentation and the writing for the song. It’s a basic thrasher with groove metal type riffs being the core DNA. My main issue is Blitz’s oddly performed “yeahs” spliced into a good portion of its runtime. I remember as a young teen being annoyed with “Battle” because of this choice and I would usually skip it into the better conceived “God-Like”. Of course now I’m used to Blitz's performance here and can appreciate all the other elements found on the song, even the cameo of Catwoman and Christopher Walken themselves, but the choice to just have Blitz oddly squeeze out a bunch of “yeahs” throughout the song really hinders it. If they just had Joe, who’s already provided backing vocals throughout this record, do those parts and sing them normally, I believe it would have been a much better choice. Some have brought up Blitz’s performance on the “The Morning After / Private Bleeding” and while I relent that it isn’t his strongest performance on a ballad, he still performs well and when he goes from his softer clear vocals to his normal vocals it helps lend more strength to the whole of the song as it builds up the emotion. Also yeah, the “Jesus cleanse me” lyrics at the end of “The Cleansing” are a little hooky and cheesy but fuck it I like it, I like the epic feel of the song that’s established at the beginning and overlaying those vocal lines as if it’s a choir full of Blitz clones pays it off. So yeah, fuck you. 

And you know what, surprisingly to my memory, “The Killing Kind” has a little more variety than I originally thought. I always remembered it was the first album from the band to be groove metal focused but there are enough elements here to keep myself interested. As I’ve said, writing wise those groove elements are the driving force behind most of the riffs but you still got your thrashing types in songs like “Battle”, “God-Like”, “Certifiable”, and “Let Me Shut That For You”, down right groovers in “Bold Face Pagan Stomp”, “The Cleansing”, and “Cold, Hard Fact”, a doomy / sabbathy type song found in “Burn You Down / To Ashes”, a more traditionally and rock inspired ballad in “The Mourning After / Private Bleeding”, and the funky, thrashy, groovy mix in the instrumental “Feeding Frenzy”. While the thrash based songs aren’t as super fast, the songs may be a little more simplified, and maybe a little repetitive at times, I think as a whole these songs are a lot stronger than some reviewers may want to admit. 

There’s still a nice mix of tempos between songs and within songs when the riffs change up and pretty solid soloing work and solid performances all around. I still hold the opinion that Overkill did the whole “groove metal phase” fairly well and I’m someone who doesn’t even really like groove metal much as a genre, hell I dislike it most of the time. But Overkill was one of the few that, to me, did it really well and was just another avenue to allow them to evolve and experiment, as we’ll see bigger experimentation on the next two in this so-called trilogy. “The Killing Kind” in my eyes is a very good album, a flawed album for sure but nowhere close to being bad. Some of the artistic choices found throughout the album hold it back a little but regardless, it’s a solid record on it’s own and do have some standout tracks, such as “God-Like”, “Certifiable”, “Burn You Down / To Ashes”, and “Feeding Frenzy”. If you didn’t care for this album at first listen of if the odd choices in “Battle” may have turned you off, I recommend giving this another go, it may surprise you how much you’ll enjoy it this time.

Another in the seemingly endless barrage of blackened speed metal bands from Brazil, Cult of Horror is a three piece from the wildlands of Rio de Janeiro. Featuring prominent members of the underground scene who have spend time with Whipstriker, Apocalyptic Raids, Comando Nuclear and Bordel Inferno, among others. Cult of Horror revels in the bloodiness of cult horror films and the grittiness of first wave black metal, combining the two into a wretched slab of writhing, blackened heavy metal.

Babalon Working is the band’s debut album, released in April of 2016. Led by the distinctive snarls of Sister Jeanne (aka William Nadler), the band charges forth with a rabid attack of rollicking double kick percussion, thumping bass lines and scorching speed metal riffing. The entire offering is slathered with a grimy layer of blackened foulness, yet the band primarily sticks to first wave black metal and Motörocking speed metal coalesced with punk-fueled d-beat rhythms.

Some of the members have spent time in doom and stoner metal bands, and this influence shines through in more than a few spots, like the trippy, almost Trouble-tinged ending of “The New Flesh”. These doom-laden moments offer something quite unique in the blackened speed metal arena, as most bands tend to focus on full out speed and groove for the entirety. It’s a nice touch and one that certainly sees these guys carving out a niche all their own right from the start.

Babalon Working is a pretty cool album that fans of the first wave should enjoy to no end: the doomy passages and cult horror imagery just serve as an unexpected bonus. It’s rough and rabid, much like most of the stuff coming out of the Rio scene these days, but that makes it no less enjoyable, seeming more like a vintage horror flick than a Hollywood blockbuster. Fans of first wave black metal merged with metalpunk should look no further for their next listen.

Written for The Metal Observer.

album: Monstrous Manoeuvres in the Mushroom Maze
texto:
How have the years treated Woburn House? Well, time seems to have made them far more mellow than they used to be and perhaps a little more politically in tune. Not that they were extremely aggressive to begin with, but Woburn House have calmed their music down a notch and formed the perfect experience to relax to on a mild evening in the middle of Autumn with a fine glass of whiskey for company. This season seems to be a good representation of the changes in Woburn House’s appearance, oddly enough. From the fiery season of Summer, with its vibrant colour schemes at sunset to the delicate season of a full-flavoured Autumn whereby the leaves are changing their colours and the winds are beginning to howl once more in preparation for the oncoming winter, which is bound to be bleak. I must say, I’m reasonably fond of the debut, even to this day. I may have given it a somewhat borderline average rating, but it has stood the test of time within my extensive collection and every so often, I do whip it out for a listen or two. ‘Monstrous Manoeuvres In The Mushroom Maze’, a true mouthful of a title, is a definite step up from the problematic debut. 

It would seem that the finer details which held Woburn House back have been addressed and replaced, instead of simply being dealt with. The German trio have opted for a new sound, of sorts, so instead of being an evolved state of the debut, the sophomore has learned to adapt into something else in order to achieve its full potential and purpose in life. There are aspects of this piece which still cause me to raise an eyebrow, but there is more in the way of material to praise than criticise on this crucial record that has been billed as a make-or-break situation for the Germans. I personally didn’t think they had more time in which to adapt to life in the limelight. They were either going to sort out their issues, or they were going to lose a listener as far as I was concerned. As harsh as that may be, consider the debut was by no means a lost cause, I felt it generous enough to give them one more opportunity to prove their worth and, thankfully, that golden opportunity has mostly been taken. This record sees a number of changes, some subtle, some not so. This is a much more thought provoking record and, in some areas, seems to be a fairly political and personal viewpoint on the part of the band themselves. 

The feeling of being personal doesn’t just stretch to the lyrics, or even the stirring sample on ‘Oil’, taken from the very successful movie ‘Network’, but the softer approach makes this seem more inviting, whereas a lot of the guitar work seemed rather disengaging on the previous effort, though the guitar work was amongst the best elements on the record. Even from the sample we can see that Woburn House have detected their issues and are steadily working on becoming a more accessible unit through a more mellifluous sound, which is no longer just supplied by the guitars, but the bass, the drums and even the vocals, which are mostly clean. Although not a fan of the movie ‘Network’, I do love the quote they use, ending with the iconic words of the character Howard Beale, “I’m a human being, goddamnit! My life has value!”. There are a number of things about this record which strike me as hints as to what has occurred here, even before hitting the play button. The final song, a twenty-three minute epic, is entitled ‘Transformer’ and is a wonderful chance at seeing, and hearing, the numerous alterations made by the musicians in order to secure their endangered future. 

The title itself hints at a new sound and that is precisely what has been delivered on a plate to us. From the clean vocals to the softer guitar work, there are elements present here even in the samples of singing birds that makes this record a far more soothing one to listen to. The production isn’t exactly inspiring. It’s a bit flat, but does a sufficient enough job to make the material seem as if it has a stable enough basis to work upon. The guitars still sound rather lacking in emotion and considering how much softer Woburn House have become, perhaps the emotional vulnerability of some aspects, and the hopeful bursts of others should be highlighted better by the production. There are some unnecessary elements, such as the long period of nothingness on the final song, which could have been nothing short of amazing if it had continued to lull the listener with a clean guitar section and a rumbling bass section. Unfortunately the singing bird samples go on for a bit too long, though when the instrumentation does resume, it does so well enough for me to forget this brief hopeful burst of bird singing and distant voices. All in all, this is a much improved sophomore with more heart and passion. Liking the mellow direction.

I personally think that Japan has a touch for creating awesome thrash metal bands. Clearly, all of you must agree after such a great legacy of bands like Sabbat, Abigail, (although black/thrash but still it's thrash), Casbah, Outrage, Jurrasic Jade, Gargoyle etc. and also the newest and fucking awesome band Tiger Junkies. And Fastkill follows in their footsteps closely. It's raw, it's fast, it's kill.

Guitars are fucking awesome here, they are not much innovative, but just a good mixture of plain raw hardcore punk mixed with speed metal. Every song, from start till the end, thanks to riffage, is extremely head-bangable, and absolutely moshable. It's like a frenzy of little ear explosions that cascade through every riff you hear. Awesome thrashy ingenuity. So guitars get 17%, being close to perfect for this kind of thrash.

To fill in a hole in this thrash experience, there are the vocals. Some would say annoying, but I say they are epic. That unique shrieking is fascinating in some ways, and really it adds up to the whole thrashy sound of the songs. The vocals are just what they're supposed to be the "I don't give a fuck I can't sing falsettos". It's thrash, and it's called thrash for a reason. Not every singer must sound like Rob. So the whole vocal idea is pretty interesting incorporated in this whole thrash orgy mixture. So vocals get 15% for being an enhancer of this thrashness.
Lyrics on the other hand, are standard satanic thrash, being just what they are, nothing less than perfect enough. They're not poetic, they're not pretty, they're plain thrash. So they get 15% for following the consistency of the thrash experience.

Last but not least, drumming and bass line are a good and well oiled rhythm machine. Oiled enough to withstand a fucking zunami of fucking fast and raw metallic riffage. Drumming being the whole circle pit coordinator and bass line adding that fast hardcore punk bum-bum-bum bass gun-machine. So drumming gets 13% being just a 7% away from perfection and bass line gets 16% for being moshy and straight-to-the point.

Fastkill is really a good quality thrash, if you like bands like Abigail and Sabbat, that is. It's definitely worth listening to, because it's really good good thrash and you should treat your ears with the awesomness of this thrash metal chainsaw.

Verdunkeln are one of the most interesting black metal acts currently operating out of Germany. After the sweeping success of their self-titled demo in 2005 and their monstrous 2007 full-length debut, the band had positioned themselves to compete with top-tier contemporaries such as The Ruins of Beverast and Lunar Aurora in a major way. However, the band went silent for almost exactly five years, releasing this, their sophomore effort, only last year. 

The band picks up right where they left off. For long-time fans, rest assured that some of the band's most defining elements: those chorus-heavy clean guitar lines, the hypnotic repetition and the dark, post-punk inflected grooves are all alive and strong on Weder Licht noch Schatten. As with their previous album, frontman Gnarl and drummer Ratatyske choose to open with a relatively short track before jumping into the meaty, 10 minute + epics that make up the majority of the album. “Das Antlitz des Himmels” is a fairly energetic tune, but it's close-in production and only brief use of those chorus heavy clean guitars gives this a song both a more immediate feel and a sense of claustrophobia that's not usually a major element of the band's approach. My guess is that the choice was made to smack you across the face and get your attention ready for the headier songs that follow.

“Am Ende des Abgrunds” exemplifies Verdunkeln's unique approach to black metal. Thunderous mid-paced beats, sometimes busier and full of double bass and toms and sometimes more sparse, yet always heavy, serve as the rhythmic anchor. Two or three guitars play at any given time: a pair in more traditional roles, playing either crunchy powerchord riffs or tremolo melodies, another continuing with that distinctive clean chorus pedal sound, echoing off with arpeggios, giving a watery, subterranean feel to the proceedings. I keep mentioning this guitar, but it's really probably the most distinctive thing about Verdunkeln. I encourage you to look it up on YouTube or, for those familiar, give Nirvana's “Come As You Are” a listen as that's probably the most well-known example of the effect in modern pop music. Anyway, it adds an unusual presence to the band's music, not quite occupying the same role as a traditional, distorted guitar would but not really acting like keyboards would, either. 

The song also uses exclusively clean vocals, a technique continued throughout much of the album, double-tracked and also given a healthy dose of reverb. This makes Verdunkeln somewhat comparable to bands like Urfaust (their labelmates, probably not coincidentally), though the vocals here are more abrupt and deeper, more foreboding than theatrical. Harsh vocals are used on subsequent tracks, and sometimes even occupy some middle-ground, using mid-range singing tones made somewhat harsher in Gnarl's throat. I really enjoy this technique, as it blends together the clean vocal lines and harsh rasps into what's clearly the performance of a single vocalist. It lends the whole thing a lot more weight, as the harsh vocal sections are much more easily read as more intense than those that favor clean vocals.

For the most part, the material here is just as spellbinding as anything on their past two releases. However, there are a couple of guitar melodies used here and there that are a little less than stellar – see the repeating figure about 2/3 through “Unsre Richter” for an example. In fact, that particular flavor of vaguely circus-y, highly repetitive figure pops up several times on Weder Licht noch Schatten. They're fairly aggravating, as they're so unlike the rest of the band's guitar work (not to mention so fundamentally annoying) that they yank you out of the moment, something that's entirely unacceptable when listening to music that's so reliant on building an atmosphere and keeping you there through the use of the band's usually hypnotic riffing. The songs also seem to get lost sometimes, something that never happened on the last album even though it had two tracks longer than anything on this release. Whether it's a symptom of the band being out of practice or out of ideas is up for debate.

The more severe problem that prevents this album from being on the same plane as their previous works is the production. Though the guitars sound like they're using the same lower-than-standard tuning as before, the mixing is entirely different – here the rhythm guitar gets a crunchier, mid-heavy tone and is mixed out quite dry and in pretty wide stereo. Before the guitars had a wetter, bassier tone and were mixed quite distant. Somehow, though they took up less of the real estate in previous mixes, the guitars actually sounded like they were being played louder. The drums suffer, too, with far less reverb this time around than before, especially on the snare. That echoing snare was apparently more of an essential element of the band's sound than I thought. Lastly, the vocals are also much drier this time, again with less echo. Combined with a little less ferocity in the harsh vocals, it makes for a more direct, human approach – not exactly the most fitting style for such an otherwordly band. Verdunkeln has never been a band about ultra-catchy riffs or triumphant melodies; they're a band that drags you into their vast caverns and convinces you that you never want to leave. In contrast to The Ruins of Beverast, who suffocate you with their oppressive weight, Verdunkeln's lethality is in the space between their instruments, letting the mind fill those voids with dark things conjured up by the band's endless atmosphere. This time around things are a little too close, a little too comforting. A simple remix might be all it takes to bring this album back to the glories of Verdunkeln past, but for now we'll just have to take what we can get. Maybe the next one will come around quicker than this one did.

In the murky world of pure, unadulterated death metal originality is a commodity that is priceless until the second album drops. It is at this time that the very new hangers-on decide to drop off in favor of something more static (or trve as those misguided densians of mediocrity have named it). Of course, Faxed Head is the kind of band that never got ANY attention to begin with. I first heard about them from the biography on the Mimicry website. Shortly thereafter I began to hear their name shouted aloud every so often, always followed by "What are they like?" Unappealing frankly. This band has gone to every conceivable length to ensure that even those who worship the cum-and-lung-butter festooned floors of death metal have a hard time listening let alone enjoying. And of course that's the point. That's the point of so much these days. It's hardly an original purpose or argument anymore if it ever really was, but Faxed Head is much closer to being a brilliant success than any other would-be brilliant success.

Where most folks stray when making an effort like this is to get too cought up in the immediatly gratifying sense of stupidity that can overwhelm those not studiously familiar with death metal's more sheepishly stringent cliches. It's very clear that the guys behind the masks of Faxed Head grew up with that shit and it's easy to imagine that somewhere in that mess of a group is a large collection of Slayer merchendise. And maybe it's appropriate that the most overt metal tendencies are in full force on the first track. Rest Stop Cleaing is all fast beats and angular riffs, equal parts frenzy and spitted reproach. The central emotion driving this whole affair is anger though, not rage. This lends the myth of the band to truth which is fine by me. Everything on the record works better if you actually think the members of the band are vastly deformed, suicidal mental patients. Ain't this what metal is really all about?

Perhaps. It must be said that most of the record is not so easily recognized as metal. The Four Freshman, a song about lost youth or possibly geriatric care, mixes metal and lounge evenly but neither ends up being distinct. Mr. Bus Driver could have been an ordinary song (never a radio hit though) if it wasn't sung in the McPatrick head croak.

The best songs on the album are those that weave in black metal fury into understated (if a little frantic) avant jazz. But all this genre talk is making me hungry. Demon's Chills is the best song on the record for depicting Valkyre flight, the din of battle, and the closing gats of hell all in a minute. It's safe to say that had the rest of the record been this strong the band would have had one hell of a monster on their hands. On the other hand, it's really for the best that they only leave this structure in two places. The other is Farmer Ferdinand Hudson, which is infinitely more melancholy and is more satisfying in a less head banging fashion.

What's odd is how the most advanced and Bungle-like material is ultimately lost here. In this environment songs like Chiropractic and Bring the Dead Boy Peace are lost in favor of the I'm-clevor grinning of Coalinga Love, a direct parody of the Tupac Shakur song, California Love. The difference might be in the number of ring modulators they use, or how many references to Taco Bell. Regardless, it's all vastly entertaining even if it's somewhat inferior as a parody. And yes, that can describe the whole record right there.

A lot of preconceived notions fill one's head when you hear about a drum machine-driven brutal death metal band.  I imagine a lot of people immediately think of Mortician's absurdly fast grinding, Putrid Pile-style 'bree' vocals, or the trillion bizarre, sloppy goregrind bands out there.  Bloodsoaked is one of the few bands that is simply using the machine out of necessity rather than desire: the music here is pure oldschool brutal death, with no grind influence or impossibly fast drumming in sight.

The one-man project of Peter Hasslebrack, Bloodsoaked concentrates on purely oldschool brutal death metal.  There are no breakdowns, no pig squeals, no arpeggios; simply classic brutal death in the style of the great legends of old such as Cannibal Corpse and Suffocation.  The closest 'modern' influence I can find is in Insidious Decrepancy, which even then is a stretch.  The music here isn't as rhythmic as newschool death metal; instead, the riffs are almighty.  Despite not being terribly original, it's certainly refreshing in an age more concentrated with eye-roll inducing bass drops than talent.  The music here is more speedy and tremolo-picked than slow and chugging; perfect for those of us who are looking for the zombie resurrection of oldschool DM.

Opening with 'Killing You', Bloodsoaked shows what it's all about: sick, guttural death metal that doesn't sacrifice talent for extremity.  The guitar playing here is surprisingly technical at times, but not overbearingly so: the more complex riffs always make sense and never seem to be there to prove something.  Hasselback's vocals are a very low, traditional growl, like a less ridiculous version of Mortician, which compliment the music nicely.  The occasional double-tracking is used sparingly, and rightfully so: such a technique is getting very overused, and the discretion presented here makes its instances (such as on the title track) that much more powerful.

If there's one thing that would really turn people off of this album, it's the general lack of originality.  Bloodsoaked is obviously not breaking tremendous new ground with 'Brutally Butchered', but I'm sure that Hasselback never wrote this album with the intention to do so.  The whole purpose here is to make solid, enjoyable brutal death that will appeal to all fans of the subgenre.  And honestly, when I'm listening to a song like 'Grinding Your Guts' and banging me head with the ending groove riff, who am I to complain about such a goal?

'Brutally Butchered', while not mind-blowing, is a highly respectable entry into the brutal death scene.  Tasteful, intelligent, and heavy as hell, I have no doubt that there are many who would be wise to give this LP a try.

Gehenna's 'First Spell' is the band's initial major offering and the pinnacle of their early unique sound. 'First Spell' is a fusion of simple, almost passive, melodic black metal, melded with a strong gothic overtone.

Two basic, yet very important elements push 'First Spell' out of the crowd and into its own personal niche. The raspy, choked near-whispers that comprise the vocal work lurch out of the speakers like a ghostly fog to give a doomy, death-like feel to the whole release. The keyboard work here is crucial as well, as it is the loudest, most musically driving element of the mix both leading and anchoring tracks as they form, expand and die away. Without such a strong relationship between the vocals and keyboards, and their respective sounds and roles individually, this disc would be a let-down.

The guitar work is very simple and does not represent a strong presence in the mix and is lacking in drive and power, both in form and feel, which is one of the only real weaknesses of 'First Spell'. There are minor leads and harmonies scattered about 'First Spell' and the clean, somewhat brittle, arpeggios in "Unearthly Loose Palace" are a nice accent, but otherwise the fretwork sticks to basic formulated power chords running through simple song structures, either backing or being backed by the essential keyboards. Dirge Rep's percussion work feels passive and weak as well. Most of the time, the drums are very straightforward double-bass rhythms with little to no variety aside from the occasional stint into double-time. The keyboards are the most important musical object in this release, giving 'First Spell' its emotional substance and wide, cavernous, ghostly atmosphere. The keyboards add the necessary element of variety, sometimes serving as the lead (such as the vibrant church organ in the album opener "Shivering Voice of the Ghost", with it's center-stage performance coming just after two minutes into the track) and other times serving as a well-executed backdrop to an already formed theme or idea, such as the simple, but very effective chords in 'The Conquering of Hirsir". The album's tracks all play through at a slow to moderate pace, so if you're expecting some of the intensity and speed of more modern Gehenna releases...this isn't it.

The production of 'First Spell' lacks a significant low-end presence, but wraps itself tightly in a blanket of warm, analog mids and highs, with an ambient, spacey atmosphere which works to give the album it's veiled, ghost-like emotion. As previously stated, drums and guitars could have been a bit louder to enforce their sound and roles, but because of that the vocals and keyboards (again, the best part of 'First Spell') take the forefront, it's a near-even tradeoff. As for Bass? No. You'd really probably have to EQ your stereo system to even begin to goad it out of the mix.

The lyrics are pretty simple, and the song titles are effective at summarizing the lyrical content within. There is nothing extravagant, nor anything standoffish in terms of written prowess, with most songs dealing with a worldly sense of dread and that therein. The best lyrics on the album come from the opener, "Shivering Voice of the Ghost", in which a better title could not have been picked with it's combination of lyrics, death-like rasps for vocals, and crisp, haunting keyboard work.

'First Spell' is ultimately going to appeal to fans of slower, more laid-back melodic black metal and fans of dirge-like goth metal. Maybe even a few 'part-time' Doom metal fans would appreciate this. Fans of newer, modern Gehenna actually may not be so interested, as this is Gehenna's unique release before this particular sound began to dwindle away with future albums, opting for a more modernized combination of moderate paced black and death metal. This is definitely worth a listen from any of the above groups, and for being nearly a decade and a half old, 'First Spell' is still pretty easy to find at a reasonable price. The only drawback is that the album is less than half an hour in length, spread across only five songs. 

Outside of 'First Spell's weak spots in terms of some frail production values and short running time, this disc is one of the only albums I've come to appreciate with this type of 'doom and gloom' style of metal. If all of the above fits into your tastes, then invest your time and money into it.

Wow.  Where to start?  Their first effort, "The Sprit of Ukko," is a complete masterpiece.  Kiuas is definitely one of those bands that comes around once every thousand years.  Now why does such a one-in-a-thousand band feel so compelled to release an album that lacks as much inspiration as the first one reveled in?

     I don't feel the need to break this review down song by song as all you have to do is listen to "The Spirit of Ukko," then remove all the devotion to truly energetic songwriting and delivery.  Don't forget to also take away a good number of riffs and replace them with unnecessary keyboard retardation.  This is what kills extended listening of this album for me.

     Undoubtedly though, the best track in my opinion off of this album is Race With the Falcons.  What can I say, it's the one song that might still, in any way, embody what Kiuas sought to do with the first album, expand upon it, and still maintain a certain level of sincerity.  This song is quite armed and ready to strike.

     Try to stay clear of Through the Ice Age though (unless you're a pretentious prog fabrication who loves to off-time shit because you like the stares).  This song is a good representation of where Kiuas went wrong.  Repetitious to the extreme with only enough riffs to keep the keyboards and monotone vocals from overpowering your sense of integrity.

     Everything else is pretty much middle of the road in that it's nothing new, and not that creative (although there are some growls that can raise eyebrows). A good formula works for a long time.  Look at 50 caliber rifles for an example.  No sense in changing it up prematurely.

     Overall, a 75/100 I give this album for not being bad, but not being that good.  Come on Kiuas, you couldn't have burned all that creativity off in one go, get your shit together.

A good showing here from Scandinavian newcomers Rexoria, already onto their second album after putting out the first a year earlier, racking up another solid release for Pride & Joy, who I suspect will become one of the frontrunner labels for new power metal in coming years. Rexoria are one of those female-fronted bands eschewing the symphonic scene for something meatier, but that’s not to say this is a spike-studded fist to the face. Keys are still in residence, and there’s the occasional nod to more commercial styles scattered about, but mainly they are here to rock you with catchy choruses, trem-picked riffs, and the powerful vocals of Frida Ohlin, a softer version of Noora Louhimo who can rasp it up with the best of them, but gives a dignified, stately performance that keeps everything locked in. 

Battle Beast are a pretty good comparison, but Rexoria aren’t much into 80s pop, and remember the metal must come first, no matter how catchy your refrains are. The mid-paced cuts are very much in line with the stuff Battle Beast were doing on ‘Unholy Savior’, the good tracks, anyway, except Rexoria keep hacking away with hooky riffs laced with delicious duel harmonies, an old school mentality that comes out in almost every track. ‘Velvet Heroes’ blasts out of the gate with a Celesty-style strike of melodic power metal, morphing as it goes on into a killer fist-pumping anthem Noora and chums would give the thumbs-up to. Later tune ‘Roaring’ is a classic up-tempo HammerFall jaunt with another shiny chorus, and I have to say, Rexoria do better when they infuse their formula with speed metal drumming. Best track here by a wide yard, the shimmering ‘Reach For The Heavens In Time’, begins with a lost Tolkki lead before Frida drips her vocal honey all over it, her lines taken straight out of an 80s power ballad, then kicks up some dust with a chorus that sounds like it was written to please Kai Hansen. Rexoria vary the pace nicely, often within the tunes themselves, and it keeps things fresh. The title track begins with some annoying narration, and never really takes off, despite a decent Falconer lick, and ballad ‘Endless Nights’ comes way too early as track three, messing up the momentum delivered by the first two digs. I wish they’d ditched that one. 

The production is icy smooth, giving a nice rounded feel to things, and with more experience Frida Ohlin could be a real asset to the female-fronted world. There’s nothing here that will surprise you, but it’s a cool power metal romp, and I sense good things coming their way.

Mikko Aspa has long since been a force in the Finnish metal scene. With projects like Clandestine Blaze and Deathspell Omega under his belt, he was always going to be subject to much attention from the media, as well as the fans. I’ve followed his career closely in regards to Clandestine Blaze and, to a lesser extent, two of his other projects, Deathspell Omega and Fleshpress, all of which differ from each other in some way or other. Although the beginning of Mikko’s career with bands like Clandestine Blaze seems to be marred by a mediocrity he couldn’t shake off, time has been kind to him. Deathspell Omega are highly thought of in black metal circles, though I myself have never taken to the sound that particular act projects. In terms of the Clandestine Blaze’s illustrious full-length career, the records keep getting stronger and stronger as Mikko gains experience. ‘Church of Atrocity’, for example, has a number of stellar moments which any black metal musician would be proud of. I don’t consider him an artist who pushes the envelop in terms of his individual sounds with his respective projects but, when judging his career in general, he definitely serves up a tasty dish of experimentation to his audience and Stabat Mater are no different.

He is a man who has his finger in many flavoursome pies, each offering a different taste and texture from the previous. Not only is he in MANY different bands, usually spearheading them too, but he is the proprietor of a few established labels, particularly Northern Heritage, who often have a decent streamline of material on offer, whilst generally specialising in Mikko’s preferred field of black metal. Although I hear a few ties to his other projects on this self-titled piece, I still believe Stabat Mater to be somewhat unique to the field of funeral doom. Having released several splits, occasionally alongside his other projects, such as A.M., a doom/sludge hybrid, and one demo, this is the first full-length outing from our man from Finland. Working alongside iconic bands such as Mournful Congregation and Worship has surely given Mikko the experience and knowledge with which to successfully portray a funeral doom band. He has learned and been skilled by the very best the sub-genre has to offer, so it’s no surprise to me that this debut is outstanding amongst its peers. Reminding me, although not overwhelming, of Australia’s Disembowelment, Mikko gradually builds up his tentative atmospherics before occasionally unleashing faster tempos. These are cleverly melded into the songs and do not feel out of place.

These cold, harsh landscapes details grim stories of death, rape and general misery (two of which you definitely get the feeling for during the music itself as it is very bleak) and remind me somewhat of Clandestine Blaze, particularly in terms of the distorted guitar tone, which emphasises a monotony akin to that of the earlier works of the aforementioned act. The production for this piece is perfect. Not too dark, but certainly not light. It maintains a bleak feel throughout with slow, sombre passages of monotonous guitar riffs and varied drum patterns, but Stabat Mater are not limited to the slow style in which most funeral doom bands pertain to and worship with every ounce of strength they can muster. Consisting of three nonsensical filler tracks does force me to down-rate this record, but only slightly. Some people complain about the length of the record and it is short. However, funeral doom is a sub-genre which can easily become tedious when bands employ tactics such as too many long songs and a duration which exceeds the hour mark. In terms of this self-titled piece,  the duration feels right and doesn’t allow for boredom to become a factor since there are only three songs to hear and two of those are modest in length (with the third almost being a twenty minute epic).

I would consider black metal to be very dark, pitch black in fact, but funeral doom is very grey in essence. It reminds me of oncoming storms with their grey clouds, distant thunder and sprinkling of rain. Black metal is the center of the storm and funeral doom is what occurs just before it, when you can sense something in the air changing and the atmosphere growing bleaker by the second. Stabat Mater combine those two feelings in me well, using slowed down black metal vocals (which sound akin to his vocals for Clandestine Blaze, though elongated ). Having viewed this record as, essentially, a dissonant, slower version of Clandestine Blaze, the final song changes my perception and adds a splicing of adventure in the atmosphere as a sample of an operatic singer eases its way into the limelight and shunts the harsh dissonance out of the way, replacing it with a much softer, yet equally sullen side to the projection. Normally I would consider this long passage of eerie ambiance and accompanying sample obsolete, but it’s generally very soothing, so much so it seems warranted, even though Mikko does eventually draw the funeral doom instrumentation back into the state of play, albeit with cleaner vocals provided by himself, added a spiritual feel to the content which seems to make sense when considering the album art. A strong debut and definitely deserving of praise.

Okay, so I found these guys on Metal Archives a few weeks ago, went on their Myspace and was quite surprised by what I heard. Hailing from Illinois they are a home grown U.S. thrash band. Let me start off by saying I love (heavier) prog,  thrash & death metal. However, not being a fan (in any way, shape or form) of anything 'core -I have strong reservations about the vocals, more on that in a minute.

The music is solid "modern" thrash, the riffs are pretty decent -the guitar tone has nice thick tone to it and plenty of that razor sharp thrash sound. The soloing is good -nothing gratuitous or unnecessary but solidly fitting the songs  (ex. "Fool's Paradise" "Waste of Life" "At the Mountains of Madness"). The bass does what it should for this type of thrash: stays on the bottom providing low end for the guitars and a cushion for the drums to ride on -nothing overly special but you can make it out in the mix. 

The drumming is solid thrash drumming -the kit was well recording. If triggers or even (puke) an electric kit was used you'd never know -they sound refreshingly real in a time where everything is over triggered or compressed. He does some solid double-kick work on the title track, "At the Mountains of Madness", "Waste of Live" -nothing to write home about but solid. His fills are nicely timed -i.e. tasty, not overblown or "round house" but he plays to the music (*gasp!).

Now my complaint: the vocals. Why can't anyone in metal today get this right? If you're gonna play 'core crap -fine then play Trivium drivel. But if you play thrash either try at least to listen to Steve Reynolds of Demolition Hammer fame or Pat Lind of Morbid Saint -two good examples of badass thrash vocals.  Jon Macak is a good bass player but vocally he sounds like all the other "modern" thrash bands. Which is the problem. Musically this album isn't gonna win any awards but it's solid -the vocals just tear it down. He uses that raspy -'core-ish vocal style that grates on my nerves. Try something new -get a fifth guy to sing -whatever- but stop the vocals! They (for me) killed this album. 

I recommend this album for those looking for solid, if not tried and true thrash. I don't believe rating albums perfectly but for a debut this showcases great musicianship -but any vocalist in Illinois who loves thrash and can do it RIGHT -please audition for these guys.

Lo and behold, Vomitory are back in business again in order to celebrate their 30th birthday. Many live dates have already been confirmed for 2019, a new album is still uncertain, but, as a German proverb says: "Die Hoffnung stirbt zuletzt" (hope is the last to day). However, even if the band decides to add no further album to its voluminous catalogue, death metal freaks, vandals and all kinds of aggressors have the possibility to go wild to the old works of the Swedes. "Raped in Their Own Blood", the debut, has only one major flaw. The artwork sucks. But in terms of the main content, the music, the band shows its muscles. The experience of the band's first seven years from 1989 to 1996 shines through the individual tracks. There are absolutely no immature sequences, the album is basically on a par with the later works and everything is death metal as f**k: the sound of the guitars, the barking voice, the general brutality.

Moreover, the ten songs don't suffer from incoherent patterns. The listener does not get lost in a continuum of noise, there is always a certain structure that guides him or her through the wasteland of terror. The main riff of "Inferno", to mention but one example, serves as point of orientation, because it adds a very dynamic touch to the song. It is exactly this type of riff that saves death metal formations from monotony. The limited genre needs such a feature to avoid boredom and the debutants are aware of this challenge (and, better still, they are able to manage it). They also do not shy way from a few catchy elements. The chorus of the title track keeps sticking in the mind in a matter of seconds. Finally, Vomitory vary the pace more or less successfully. The average velocity is not too high and so they also create some nearly melancholic sections. Bolt Thrower hail from the distance every now and then, but they are no obvious influence.

From the air raid sirens which introduce the songs until the last chord, Vomitory do not show a sign of weakness. Highlights such as the title track embody exactly the kind of violence death metal is known for, while "Dark Grey Epoch" offers, among other things, lines that almost remind me of Candlemass. But the doom-compatible sections remain exceptional on an album that does not head for new shores. The brutal production as well as the music focus on purity and therefore any alien elements do not show up. The magnificently titled (joke, joke!) "Raped in Their Own Blood" is exactly what it wants to be: a clear statement, a representative record of the genre for an explicitly defined target group, even though the closer reveals a certain, black painted Celtic Frost inspiration. So love it or hate it, but don't fear you will be left in uncertainty. And now I wait for a new album of the dudes. I am curious to see what will happen in 2019, not only in relation to Swedish death metal returnees.

Because American Line Productions is the label that brought the world less than subtle acts such as Kabak, Disgorge and Domain, I immediately thought that Cangrena would be a band of the same mold, but (in part) because of the production they have going on this album, there isn't a whole lot of resemblance. Let me tell you all about it.

Cangrena plays death/grind alright, but in a way more old school style than the remorseless brutality their label mates have on offer. In a big part this is because of the rather peculiar production on this album. The kinda muffled sound mix reminded me of the first albums of South American bands such as Sepultura, Psychic Possessor and Sarcofago, with the latter being pretty similar in style to Cangrena as well. Frantic blast beats and aggressively tremelo picked riffing fight it out with gargling down-pitched vocals, immediately bringing to mind what bands such as Sextrash, Holocausto and the already mentioned Sarcofago did on their debut releases. The riffing has a Possessed edge to it as well, upping the old school factor even more, but the influence of the 80's output of Carcass and Napalm Death should be mentioned as well. At times I even hear a faint crossover thrash influence (think Cryptic Slaughter or even Righteous Pigs) in the riffing as well. The music sounds awfully familiar throughout the whole album, and if someone would have told me that this was a lost South American death metal album from 1988, I would have readily believed them.

As mentioned before, the production sounds pretty odd here. Even by 1999 standards this sounds hopelessly dated, with its dry sounding drums, thin guitars and effect vocals, but lo and behold, it works for them! Yes, it does sound dated as hell, but at the same time it (unintentionally?) gives the music an old school vibe that a lot of throwback bands nowadays would kill for. I certainly dig this cd a lot, despite the peculiar production and the mistakes the band makes throughout the album's runtime. It all makes this album ooze a certain underground charm, and that is something that I am particularly susceptible for.

This is not a release that I'd say is recommended or a must-hear, but I would say that this is an interesting oddity for sure, a kind of insider tip for all who are into old school death metal or 80's South American thrash/death metal for sure. It won't fill some kind of gaping hole in your collection, but if you find it for cheap (or download it), it sure is an enjoyable rarity worthy of your time.

Rolf has offered us yet another example of his extremely reliable, consistent ability to write catchy traditional metal/rock songs complete with his own brand of unmistakable and catcy riffs, hooks, and choruses. Resilient offers nothing "new" to the seasoned fan per se, and yet we are able to once again restore our confidence in the man who's delivered decades of worthy and classic albums throughout his long career.

Running Wild's earnest sound has always provided a unique inspiration to metal fans, and "Resilient" reinforces my belief that Rolf is among the most sincere and consistent metal songwriters in the history of the genre.

A possible complaint with this album could  be that the tempo hasn't picked up much since The Rivalry. Speed metal isn't what you'll find here, but neither will you find the lack of energy and "hard rock" flavor of Rolf's post-2000 catalog. Instead, the listener will immediately take notice of the true metal vibes throughout the record. And while there is certainly an arena-rock element to Rolf's songwriting, "Resilient" seemlessly incorporates the catchiness and bombastic qualities of that aesthetic without compromising the hard edge that Running Wild's fans expect.

Given the "studio project" status that Running Wild has maintained for the past decade or so, it's somewhat disappointing to note that these songs can't possibly be backed by a highly-anticipated tour since the two core members mostly rely on hired hands for festival gigs and other large venues. On the other hand, this record seems to suggest a revitalized band, a renewal of Rolf's natural role in the metal community, and a strong feeling that the "Final Jolly Roger" came too soon to be taken seriously. Retirement should not be considered at this point, because this record's strength clearly indicates that Rolf and company are still able to deliver the goods with style and confidence.

"Shadowmaker" 's shortcomings as an album will seem less significant now that "Resilient" has emerged - a stronger, truer reflection of Rolf's metal vision that even casual fans will recognize immediately. HAILS!

Hardly a reviews miniseries – only a threesome of albums which, coincidentally, happened to fit well under the same umbrella, as part of the June 2023 Metal-Archives Reviews Challenge.

What was, exactly, Galadriel's initial influence on Orkrist? On the first side, an Elven queen, on the other side, an Elven sword; on both sides, 'dark' metal bands hailing from Bratislava, Slovakia, lyrically influenced by J.R.R. Tolkien's writings though both also extended their lyrical content, the former to... pretty much anything, including erotica and environmentalism, the latter to folktales in the broadest sense. Add that Orkrist's female singer Lýdia Lacová once worked as a one-off replacement for Galadriel's Sona Kozakova on the awkward World Under World, add further that in the 2020s Orkrist, after a long break, seem to be blooming again while Galadriel, they again played a show with earlier this year, is progressively waning, and the parallel will be complete.

So, after having discussed Galadriel's 2015 (temporary?) studio swansong, enter Luea, Orkrist's brand new album from six months ago. A slow grower indeed, that will take several listens to really get into; blame weird production choices for it mainly. The drums, thin and plastic, are the biggest offenders; another of these too many cases where one seriously doubts of the reality of the human drummer credited, given how much mechanical and lifeless the beat overall appears. Electronic kit, perhaps; heavy triggering and post-processing, otherwise; in any case, coming to that point, and considering the fantasy theme, they could have borrowed Summoning's unmistakable machine for a similar, or probably better result. Furthermore the keyboards often sound unnecessarily loud, the prime example appearing as early as the first bars of the opening track. By contrast the mix shows a strong tendency to smother the vocals, the male growled parts especially. And not the less bizarre is this shrill distortion, à la low-fi black metal demo, which punctually affects the guitars (Salt not More than Gold).
          
Still, to those daring enough, Luea will progressively reveal its secrets, and make the journey eventually rewarding, if not totally without hurts. Keep in mind we're once again treading a realm of legends here, and as such the songs, of complex structures and substantial lengths, are hard to classify in a well-defined genre, the whole work being thought more as a vast fantasy-folk soundscape than as a tight, coherent metal album. The backbone may be identified as mid-paced melodic / symphonic black metal, still that tag describes but imperfectly the various alien organisms which intermingle with it, including folk, electro and Baroque music inspirations. The flute is very present, most of the time as a melancholic backing murmur; exceptionally, it will take the lead, as in Black Bird's Beard, making that last song bascule wholly into folk metal territory – of the serious kind. In the distance, a synthetic harpsichord reinforces the antique touch (Twelve of Everything, or Black Bird's Beard again). Mark violins and celli, too, and even whole orchestral breaks, equally synthetic we guess. The list could go on. Still, always the metal will have the last word, launching a precise riffing attack or improvising a guitar solo whenever its survival is at risk. The more surprising, in the lot, being perhaps the fact the whole edifice never degenerates into the undistinguishable mess it seemed promised to.

If the vocals were on par with the compositional research, and if in turn the production was doing justice to the music overall, we'd certainly get a potential album-of-the-year, powerful, original, inspired. But about the latter we already wrote all the wrong there was to write, and the former too appear somehow lacking, mixing issues notwithstanding. Lýdia Lacová is a competent singer who knows her scales, but lacks a truly distinctive vocal colour to be in complete symbiosis with the music she's fronting. The male counterpart she's interplaying with, Grom is his name(!), grumbles and creaks alright from the depths of the venerable myths-laden forest, still again his performance sounds wise, too wise for this world of adventure and mystery.

Galadriel or Orkrist? The question is open now. Never mind – the more tales we hear, the better. Thus speaks the eternal child in you.

Highlights: Raven of Revenge; Salt not More than Gold; Twelve of Everything; Love and Stone.

I know a lot about Iron Savior, their legacy, and the amount of work accomplished by Piet Sielck in the power metal scene, but I really don't know jack about Iron Savior's music, their finest offering, or anything related to Piet Sielck. I'm lame like that. I put off this semi-legendary group for really no reason at all, until I found "The Landing." It was as if destiny wanted a date: a free promotional copy, my hunger for power metal, their metallic reputation and supposed consistency were exploding in my face all at once. I took the opportunity to finally give these guys a shot, and I am certainly not disappointed. It's pretty much a traditional slab of beefy, consistent power metal spiced with some excellent tunes scattered throughout Iron Savior's steel-covered gospel.

With the faction's many connections underneath the German power metal niche, it's really no surprise they have influence from some of their counterparts—Kai Hansen and other veterans were members at times, in fact. "The Landing," though, goes through a number of tempos and patterns which all represent the general theme of power metal, such as the rousing nodding of the "The Savior" or speedy melodies and riffs blessing a decent portion of the album's material. I get a vibe that these dudes really put the 'power' back in power metal, just the way I like. Simply put, there's a really impressive knack that allows Iron Savior to produce awesome ironclad anthems which sound fun and catchy, heavy and memorable. Really can't ask for anything more.

I'm personally fond of the album's rapid numbers, particularly the opening burst of ecliptic speed that baptizes the near-perfect "Starlight" and the uplifting bombardment that is "Faster Than All." A lot of the band's mid-paced numbers are really compelling too, with all the epic sing-a-long choruses and fiery songwriting that anthems of this nature should demonstrate. Most of “The Landing” is pretty good, but "Before the Pain" comes along as this 80s ballad that sucks the fun right out of the experience, and the not-so-grand finale of "No Guts, No Glory" serves as a slice of filler to end the record, strangely. Both tunes stick up the air, but not enough to make "The Landing" a disposable listen, and I'm fairly impressed with the overall effort provided by these stern veterans of German power metal. "The Landing" worked as an enjoyable introduction into the world of Iron Savior, so give it a shot too if you haven't jumped aboard the cosmic quest with Sielck and friends.
