"Deeds, not words" is the title of British BM band Deitus' debut album, though without very much information about these guys at my finger-tips I can't say how much they live up to that motto. This is straightforward no-frills / no-nonsense 1990s-styled raw BM that stresses hard-edged martial riffing, outbreaks of blast-beat drumming and plenty of melodies in songs with occult and Satanic themes. All songs show thought and care in their construction and each track stands as a flowing self-contained unit in its own right with a lot of drama, aggression and energy. The weakest element here is the spidery BM vocals which are all but swamped by the energetic music, which is a bit unfortunate as most songs feature singing and the music accommodates it, never fighting it. While the guitars have a distorted sound, the band's overall style is actually clean and polished enough for all instruments to be heard clearly and the general sound is more steely and spacious than grinding.

All songs are played well and consistently though if they had fewer and more distinctive riffs and melodies they might all emerge as potential singles. Trying to pack in as many riffs as possible into each and every song has the unfortunate effect of robbing them all of their own identities. As they are, the longer tracks "Ladder of Divine Ascent" and "Todestrieb" coming at the end of the album stick out more, probably because they also feature some lead guitar playing, pay more attention to creating mood and ambience than the other earlier pieces or experiment a bit with the band's style and sound.

While the album is technically good and these Deitus guys have considerable ability and song-writing skills, they need to develop a more distinctive style and sound. At present they sound very much like 1,001 other generic raw black metal bands drawing on 1990s black metal influences and inspirations. The vocals very definitely need to improve beyond raspy spider chant and incorporating a second vocalist (with perhaps some death metal influence) probably wouldn't go astray. There are indications on the later tracks, especially "Todestrieb", that suggest that what I'm hearing here is just a small part of what Deitus are capable of and they could certainly incorporate more ambience and non-BM elements than they do here. 

C'mon guys, we're looking forward to your second album where deeds not words are what we want you to live up to!

Skullfist, those Canadian metal-minded misfits, blast into 2014 with their new full length Chasing the Dream on Noise Art Records.  Their 2011 offering, Head of the Pack was a great stripped down, straight-ahead metal assault that hearkened back to the halcyon days of metal; channeling the arts of such acts as Iron Maiden, Judas Priest and Motörhead.  The anticipation of this beast should be no small matter and should provide an ample supply of no false metal.

Not wasting anytime the album is kick started by “Hour to Live”. Skullfist masterfully picks up right where they left off with blueprint fully enabled: blazing guitars, frantic drum work from new member Chris Steve (ex-Cauldron) and an over-the-top vocal display.  However, it sounds like a bit of studio tampering has pushed Jackie Slaughter’s vocals back in the mix—not entirely bad, but slightly diminishing the frenetic quality heard on past efforts.  “Call of the Wild” has an especially solid groove along with chorus guitar fills that emulate Iron Maiden; always a sound choice.  Lots of serious fret work here from Jackie and Johnny Exciter.  Title track “Chasing the Dream” however, sees the tarnish that over production can leave; riddled with a generic disposition and easily overlooked.

There are several surprises thrown into Chasing the Dream that break the album up perfectly.  The first of which is a re-recording of “Sign of the Warrior” that appeared on their 2010 Heavier than Metal EP.  While it was probably not necessary for a redo, this is clearly the superior version as the original is rather murky and unpolished.  The second little nugget comes in the form of “Shred’s not Dead”, an instrumental track that is devastatingly unique.  This one runs the gamut from soaring guitar riffs to Casey Slade’s cranked up bass fills and finally precise drum breaks. Quite an unexpected little treat right there.  “Mean Street Rider” warrants mention as it opens with a soundbite of Jackie Slaughter breaking his neck skateboarding—sometimes you have to pay to play.  None-the-less this is a rocking, no-nonsense way to close out the album.

After several spins of Chasing the Dream a gradual immersion began to occur; though there is a part of me that just wasn’t quite sold at first.  This album continued to crawl back into the CD player, even after repeated spins.  Deep down the hesitancy to embrace this album probably stemmed from a longing for that raw, primal sound heard on Head of the Pack as opposed to a more modern, highly produced album.  In any case, all of the negative noise is easily silenced by beholding the phenomenal material within.  If you are already a fan, I would venture a guess you own this already… shred is most certainly not dead!

Eulogy are a band that was lost in the mix.  Between great mainstream acts like Morbid Angel and Obituary, and underground acts like Massacre and Brutality, Eulogy were overlooked in the Florida Death Metal scene.

This CD is the only CD they put out that can be compared to a full length.  It was actually recorded at the Ritz (surprise!) in Tampa, but the sound quality is exceptional for a live recording. Save for a little bit when you can tell that the sound guy is trying to level everything out (in the first song, "to Perish the Screams").

Now as for the music, imagine Morbid Angel sped up, with a better vocalist.  Jason Avery is unargueably the most underrated vocalist.  The guitars are quite technical, and the drumming is a nice mix of blast beats and unusual changeups, with Mr. Gore uses the Tom Tom drums more than normal, which is great.  More bands should give the Tom Toms more attentions.  The bass holds its own, although it doesn't bring anything exceptional to the table.

Another bonus is that Jason mentions the now defunct Ace Records, which was (is?) a legendery metal record shop in Tampa.

Although this album doesn't bring anything new or fresh to the field, it is still a great look back at what death metal used to be.  Imagine if all the underground bands today put as much heart into their music as these guys did.  Imagine if the underground today was full of the intensity that Eulogy had.  Just imagine.  Then listen to their masterpiece, "Dismal", and cream yourself.  Eulogy deserve all the praise that Morbid Angel gets, and this album proves their diversity and uniqueness.

To perish the screams, indeed!

Malefic is to the black metal genre what Paul Cezanne is to impressionist painting; he comes after the initial movement and is not directly related to the pool of creative minds behind said movement. Calling him a “post-black metal” musician however would likely only earn me the scorn of black metal fans. He is sometimes labeled “suicidal black metal,” or “suicidal/depressive black metal.” More often, he is labeled as “ambient” or “atmospheric.” While crushingly depressive, Malefic’s Xasthur has little else in common with bands that prominently showcase self-mutilation or feature explicit references to suicide: Malefic’s style is significantly more reserved (reclusively private as a rule of thumb) and uses mostly abstract language.  

Your typical Xasthur album has a fairly constant, repetitive drum beat and the same is true with the riffs. Vocals are used only sparingly and cannot be understood without a lyric print off. Synthesizers are used frequently, though emphasis is given to the rhythmic repetition of dissonant chords. Melodic passages are featured maddeningly low in the mix, so low that if one were to casually listen to the album only once then practically every song would seem to be merely the same distorted drum-loop repeated over and over again. Listening to a Xasthur album many many times however eventually does reward the listener with a rich musical variation which was not immediately apparent. This is because of a conscious effort on the part of the musician to diminish the overall contrast to a point of near grey-on-grey: distinguishing the ideas within will require you to strain your ears and demands repeated listenings. If you don’t have the patience to sit down and give your undivided attention to these songs, or if you find this sort of presentation off-putting then you will never EVER like Xasthur. Simply put, this music is one hell of an acquired taste. I’ve heard that the sound quality is markedly more accessible on vinyl but getting your mits on a vinyl copy so long after the initial release means you’ll likely be paying a small fortune on ebay just to fund some aging misfit's drug habit. Pirated MP3’s are probably the worst place to start since you’ve got to contend with the loss of even more detail from the data compression in addition to the original low fidelity. The quality of your recording isn’t likely to make or break your opinion of Xasthur, just know that you’re not making it any easier on yourself by going with a low bit rate audio file.  

Compared to other Xasthur releases Nocturnal Poisoning is probably the weakest if for no other reason than the whole trajectory of the Xasthur project is more-or-less an unending revision of the ideas showcased on this album and the demos which preceded it. The recoding quality of all the releases has been purposely lo-fi, but this initial release has a distinctly tinny aspect to the sound quality which disappears all-together on subsequent albums. Its difficult to give this album a percent review by comparison to “classic” black metal albums (one will invariably fail the album on the basis that it doesn’t adhere to those expectations) but it is also difficult to compare this album with the whole of the Xasthur library: anyone familiar with later releases inevitably comes to see the original songs differently after hearing so many subsequent revisions and variations on similar themes. 75% is probably the fairest approximation of this album’s worth, which while lower than I’d like to rate the album at least gives the reader some sense of the room that exists for improvement on subsequent releases.

Ah, RHAPSODY…uh, I mean, RHAPSODY OF FIRE…the finest example of Dungeons and Dragons metal the musical world has ever seen.  Taking the power in power metal to an nth degree of pomposity, symphomania, and patience-stretching, it’s no secret that these Italian whack-jobs are adept masters of instrumentation and compositional ability, albeit drowned in miles-thick layers of cheese.  Thankfully, though, those skills and added bouts of heaviness keep them from becoming TOO laughed-at, and on my end I’d consider them one of my biggest guilty pleasures, worth the occasional listen but too crazy for me to enjoy whole-heartedly.

And after being screwed by two different labels (shame on you, Joey DeMaio…I thought you were one of us!), their first release under their newly-inked Nuclear Blast contract is upon us…so, we have to ask, is it any good?

As the last part of an epic trilogy of events that started with “Symphony of Enchanted Lands 2: The Dark Secret”, it’s no surprise that this new album’s sound is very much akin to the overtly symphonic madness that’s given the orchestral movements top billing lo the past few albums, which took some getting used to.  I’d always felt that the increase of the string usage and the downplay of the core band’s metal elements was detrimental, as though the guitars, drums, and bass were tossed in with no other reason than to keep these guys within the metal spectrum, but thankfully such a feeling isn’t as flamboyant this time around.  “The Frozen Tears of Angels”, while keeping the orchestral sound fully in check, puts more emphasis on the central band, where the crazily melodic solos/leads of guitar, keyboards, and (surprisingly) bass, Luca Turilli’s crushing metal riffs, double-bassing-to-hell percussion and Fabio Leone’s tropospheric operatic wailings poke out through the thick fog of strings, brass, and woodwinds with a thankfully necessary increase in speed, while at the same time working with them to evoke that “Hollywood Metal” sound they’d been shooting for.  It’s hard to ignore the obvious compositional ability and playing skill these guys have, as they’re able to cram so many ideas into singular songs with arrangements that make them flow seamlessly, making for a more-than-simply enjoyable listen.  So good are they that you’re able to ignore all those cheesy-as-shit lyrical themes of dragons, trolls, mystical battles, and the like (Luca may have a vivid imagination but I can’t say he’s the best lyricist out there, not by a long shot) and take in the complete scope of the musical work, as the likes of the straight-forward rocker “Crystal Moonlight”, the dark and epic “Reign of Terror”, and the powerful “Lost in Cold Dreams” shine as the brightest crimson flames, illuminating charred and bloody battlefields via the mirrored edges of so many tempered, holy blades…oh dear god, they’re getting to me!

In the end RHAPSODY OF FIRE again unleash a platter of fantastic metal tunes disguised as pure orchestral music.  Maybe as a result I’ll be more well-versed in their Italian wares and pick up all those earlier works should I feel that completes urge.  Guilty pleasures ahoy!

Most are only familiar with Burden of Grief under the guise of "That one decent band that was on a lot of melodeath compilations around the turn of the century." To their credit, they haven't necessarily lost a step in the decade-plus since then. They are still a decent band, churning out decent albums that break absolutely no new ground but contain a few rippers alongside a morass of ho-hum numbers that maintain interest but quickly vacate the cerebrum after listening. Follow the Flames is for all intents and purposes an identical precursor to Unchained, upon which I leveled some acclaim a couple of months back. A solid album in that late '90s In Flames/Eucharist mold which inherently puts nearly all of its eggs in one basket, that being the classy leads that are obviously the primary allure for the style.

So in that regard, Follow the Flames delivers all of what is expected, along with a tiny bit more. Just like its successor, the band squeezes out a few grimy, rocking grooves that help homogenize proceedings, along with very (very) few keyboards. An example of the latter would be "Fallen," which opens with that massive flange and segues into backing organs that remind me very much of Colony. Verses tend to drag as much as they enthrall, featuring that typical staccato melodeath riffing style intermingled with tremolo trappings. The band never fully blew me away in this regard, but came close during the second half of the title track and virtually all of "Born in Fire," which is a face-melter of relatively high order. Really digging the vocal cadence as well, which helps add some variety to an otherwise standard and unexciting death growl. Anyway, the leads totally kill it and it stands as the highlight of the album as a result.

The production values are strong as well; not unappealingly modern and polished. The only issue I have is with "Disruption of a Confused Mind," which sounds like a demo track compared to the rest of the album. I'm not sure if this was an older song interjected to fill space at the eleventh hour, but it sounds like this was the case. In any event, Follow the Flames keeps itself stoked for nearly all of its duration, even if the final couple of tracks fail to evoke the same sense of tense authority as "Born of Fire" or the chunky and rollicking "Doomed to Fail." Sometimes it feels as if the band is fast-tracking through the verses to get to the next luscious lead interval, but I wasn't necessarily bored by the album at any point. Just like Unchained, this will satiate most appetites, as even a veteran such as I was able to get a few spins out of it without pause.

At the risk of sounding redundant, I do recommend this band to newcomers of the style. Burden of Grief can serve as a potent stepping stone to more challenging fare, and have maintained what is now a pseudo-throwback allure in the present. This band sounds straight out of '99, and for those of us who dug that style then and miss it now, these guys have their place. Full of melancholic melodies that come nowhere near sounding sappy and pontifical, Follow the Flames works just well enough.

This band seemed to float around on obscure labels before getting picked up by Black Mark, who usually has a pretty good ear for talent. This appears to be a rerecording of the album they released the year before also called Metaphors. The style here is good 80's-influenced thrash metal that attempts a more prog or technical approach at times, but the musicians, while fairly tight, aren't necessarily fully fit for it. This makes it end up sounding a bit unique.

I guess Voivod could be be a comparison, especially in the opener which is to me clearly the best tune on the album. Mystik is another band that is similar, especially in the vocal department, and just the half-tech sound of it really reminds me of Megadeth, especially in tracks like Imposed Silence. It feels a bit more North American in its influence than Euro. Sprinkled through the album are some sound bites. They are tasteful and the production as a whole is pretty nice.

One noticeable thing about this album is the band never races into full-out thrash aggression. It focuses more on attempts to be clever in riff delivery rather than relying on speed. An especially slower track is the finisher, Messiah. It is a good song, dark and gloomy with an almost doom-like delivery which breaks into thrash a few times. 

The whole album is listenable. It isn't gonna blow your mind, but the riffage here is well and varied even if it isn't extremely exciting. I believe I found it for a few bucks on Amazon or somewhere, it might be worth it for thrash collectors.

Recommended tracks: Destiny Eternity, Perpetual, The Messiah.

It's my firm belief that Primal Fear's glory days were the early 2000s, the years that gave us gems like Nuclear Fire and Black Sun. Even though they've never peaked quite like that again (2016's Rulebreaker being quite a low point), the Germans are definitely on an upward spiral right now. 2018's Apocalypse showcased the grittier, riffier side of the band in short spurts, but fell down on its mid-to-slow paced softer numbers. Here in 2020, with the release of Metal Commando, I'm happy to declare that this has been rectified and the new album shows off all the positive aspects of post-2010 Primal Fear reasonably well. The weighty heaviness has been diluted a little, but the songwriting has definitely improved. As far as speed/power metal has gone in 2020, Ralf & co. are definitely in the upper echelons, where an act as prolific as them should be.

Let me just get something off my chest first: the artwork and album title are pretty awful and totally unsuited to the quality of metal contained within. I mean, a skull with wings? Metal Commando?! This doesn't do justice to the well-crafted songwriting displayed on tracks like "Hear Me Calling" and especially the epic "Infinity". That minor nitpick aside, there's something about this record that keeps me coming back for more. The album kicks things off damn well with a one-two-three combo of mid-paced 'n' punchy, slow 'n' rocking, and fast 'n' melodic Primal Fear classics. Opener "I Am Alive" has a super headbangable main riff; follow up "Along Came The Devil" oozes swagger; and track 3, "Halo" is pure soaring power metal goodness done the way only Germans know how. At this point, it's worth mentioning the impactful production quality which packs the drums full of power, gives the strings a metallic crunch and puts a shine to Ralf Scheepers' iconic vocals. It sounds great, if not quite as heavy as moments like "Cannonball" or "The End Is Near".

After the first three numbers, things start to get interesting as the Germans fire all sorts of different moods at the listener. "Hear Me Calling" goes for a cheesy, crooning vibe and its wonderfully theatrical chorus succeeds in being far more emotive than its Apocalypse equivalent ("Supernova"). "The Lost & The Forgotten" is the pedal-to-the-metal ball-buster of the variety that wrecks necks; easily my favourite cut on the whole disc. "I Will Be Gone" is a full-on acoustic power ballad which is bound to be the main point of controversy among naysayers. It's utterly gorgeous and surprisingly moving, serious kudos to the sextet for pulling off the obligatory 'soft song' with such aplomb. Unfortunately, the energy doesn't quite pick up the way I want it to. Both "Raise Your Fists" and "Howl Of The Banshee" are quite run-of-the-mill and forgettable. This whole album would've been more concise had these been left on the cutting room floor, leaving the hard-hitting "Afterlife" to kick things back into gear after the ballad.

The grand finale, "Infinity," certainly deserves a special mention for actually holding my attention for its entire duration upon initial listening. We already know Primal Fear are capable of writing brilliant long-players thanks to 2016's phenomenal "We Walk Without Fear". This 13-minute epic doesn't quite earn its duration - it could definitely cut off the pointless outro - but the main theme is so triumphantly melancholy, the result is addictive. Ralf is also really giving it everything he's got on this track: what a beautiful anthemic chorus. Metal Commando will definitely give both newcomers and die-hard fans the wrong idea upon first glance, but there's so many points of intrigue, exhibitions of great musicianship and sections of pure fucking metal, that it makes a worthy addition to the great Primal Fear discography. Still don't think they need three guitarists, though...

The Faceless belong in a very exclusive group of deathcore bands that actually transcend the typical mediocrity that plagues the genre, and have even moved in a direction more like technical death metal. Their core roots are not all gone, but have diminished for the most part. Gone are the ridiculously simplistic breakdowns that occasionally popped up on their previous effort, Akeldama, now replaced by slightly more complex rhythms in chug-chug fashion. 

The album seems to have a space and science fiction theme (as hinted by the title), which is more interesting than the lyrical content of Akeldama. The atmosphere of the songs successfully reflect the main theme, with spacey solos, jazzy, bizarre sounding chords, and the presence of alien-esque samples and keys. I have always enjoyed the keyboards in the Faceless' work, so I was disappointed to hear their keyboardist had left. But there's still keys, just not in a prominent way as with Akeldama. As for the sample in Hideous Revelation, it was well done, but not very original. I'm pretty sure the exact quote appears on Tool's 10,000 Days album, but I digress.

The production is pretty good. The drums are very clicky, but it's not so over the top that it becomes unbearable. The guitar tone is decent, especially in comparison with other tech death bands (Necrophagist comes to mind....). The vocals are well done, varying in appropriate parts, and even throwing in clean singing in some instances. Personally, I enjoyed the singing thoroughly, and it would have been cool to hear it implemented more frequently throughout the album. The bass isn't completely drowned out by the other instruments, and even gets to shine on occasion, particularly for the incredible sweep intro to the Ancient Covenant.

While this album is worthy of praise, it also has its downfalls. For an album with nine tracks, it is inexcusably short. Prison Born could have been 3 minutes longer, Shape Shifters was a complete waste, and Hideous Revelation is the most blatant breakdown exercise I've ever heard. The songwriting is also very choppy in some places, with a lot of riffs lacking flow in their transitions. We get it, you're technical, but that's no excuse for a lack of song structure. The solos were excellent in some songs, such as Coldly Calculated Design, but others did not stand out, and even sounded very much like others on the album. Lastly, I hate "Sons of Belial." It's too slow, too chug-chug, too boring and out of place on the album. 

Overall, this band has great potential, and could very well put out an album that would become a classic example of good technical death metal. This album is nowhere near close. This band needs to grow musically, particularly in their songwriting skills. Also, I have seen them live and watched many live videos, and their lead guitarist, Michael Keene, needs to practice, because he is sloppy as shit. Recording an album full of technical tricks doesn't mean anything if you can't recreate it live.

Although I adore the Gothic/melodic death metal evolution that Sweden's Tribulation has undergone, I was first introduced to the band on their 2009 opus The Horror, which was a much more explosive, energetic sound that felt like your trademark Swedish death metal getting a nasty, awesome thrashing kick in the pants. I would argue that that full-length debut remains their best overall album, a masterpiece of feral ferocity, though I take no issue with their later explorations whatsoever, it's almost as if they've given us at LEAST two good bands to worship over their career thus far (three if we include Formulas of Death as its own weird, psyche/death metal thing). Though I've reviewed a bunch by the Swedes, somehow it evaded my brain me to cover the band's EP PRIOR to The Horror, Putrid Rebirth.

So here I remedy this oversight, and to the surprise of none, this earlier material has the same propulsive and almost spastic energy to it that The Horror perfected later. This is some ghoulish death/thrash with a clear 80s ancestry, a blend of evil grooves circa Death and then the dizzying speed rhythms of a band like Morbid Angel. You can tell that the band was already adept at creating this shit, the only thing that Putrid Rebirth is really missing is a production as memorable as the debut, and to an extent the songs just aren't quite as catchy as what would come later. But it's all here, from the skilled drumming to the effective leads to the rabid barking. There's a bit of a jam room aesthetic to the mix, which is otherwise dry but fluidly captures all the instruments, it's not quite demo level (they have one before this I think), but on the level of some earlier 90s straightforward death metal records. There's not a lot of atmosphere for your imagination to work with, but the central thrust of the riffing and beats won't give you much time to notice.

The two sides of the EP have slightly different production, with the first more blunt and straight to your face, and the second a bit more atmospheric, kind of a bridge to The Horror but again, just not as skin peelingly amazing as that album sounds. Even if you have no interest whatsoever in the more dramatic style the band is exploring now, this and the debut are both fairly easy to recommend to anyone on the hunt for well wrought old school death metal. Putrid Rebirth is frantic and fun, especially if you've got no patience for bullshit and just want everything to sound like your buds' demos in 1991-92 that they were passing out before opening up for something like the Grind Crusher tour. There's nothing atypical about this, but if you like splatter, you like vintage death metal, get a copy.

Solo-project after solo-project, some individuals die off and are cannibalized by the rest. A one-man band should provide a world of isolation and an air of being the last lamb at the slaughter. Yet, some can’t grasp their own essence and produce nothing but another rusty machine. Pestilent Grave’s “Esoteric Blasphemy” swings the cage doors open to liberate a primitive mindset for black metal, without falling into a plastic sound. Vith uses misanthropic inspiration thrown against an austere production to lead himself along a path of black metal blight. Forming in 2008, releasing a demo entitled “Black Majesty Invoked,” a full-length has arrived. “Esoteric Blasphemy” is a short 15 minute CD that goes by fast and leaves you violated, begging for more through a veil of tears and blood.

First on the chopping block, “Gut Rot” spills forth a web of rotting blur. Dry production and a dry throat, Vith composes repetitive riffs and drumming to underline his dusty screams. “Bloody Release” enters in with a shuddering slowness, morphing from the rapidity of “Gut Rot” and the filthy fusillade of “Virtuous Selfmutilation.” Next, “Fucked Up and Insane/Invoking the Lost Goddess” reaches five minutes and is the longest trip into psychosis. Lumbering on until the end, its loathsome message is carried through a somniferous spray of music, changing so little it all gets bunched up and completely confuses you, in a good way. The last track, “Esoteric Blasphemy” is a mound of more confusion that ensures your experience will end in more confusion and mind-numbing.

Pestilent Grave is the definition of rawness, just like the 90’s. Without care for an easy listening experience, bands like this understand that the vilest of attitudes and the evilest of music is often better played through production that mirrors those ideas. Limited to 50 copies, order “Esoteric Blasphemy” and expect to turn up the volume more and more with each song. 

- Written for Tanin'iver Zine

I had been completely charmed by Category VI's debut record a few years back, so I was pleased for the chance to write about their sophomore effort. If you've yet to hear the band, then we're looking at some prime U.S. power metal with an old school slant.

"Strike of the Axe" delivers unto us Category VI's brand of metal circa 2017, with a godly guitar tone breaking through some atmospheric foreshadowing for a fist-banging anthem. Amanda Gosse's vocals command the punchy arrangements contained with a powerful, reverb kissed below, which absolutely does the job. I love the crooning adorning "Full Metal Jacket", giving me some sweet nostalgic vibes, though I can't pinpoint on what it may remind of. Nonetheless the vocals are a highlight throughout, and I'd say a step up from Fireborn.

Musically this is for the most part blazing, and performed in stellar fashion. There's plenty of riffs to sink your teeth into, complete with tasteful battery, and some raunchy bass lines although on the subject of bass I did feel some of the more flamboyant, effect-powered parts to be detrimental. but give me out their bass over inaudible bass any day. Rippers like "Mirror" and the aforementioned "Full Metal Jacket" outclass anything on the last album, so I'd say Category VI succeeded in writing a superior follow up.

If you dig acts like Seven Kingdoms, Mindmaze, or Helion Prime, then I'd call this a no brainer although Category VI do separate themselves from their contemporaries with a more pugilistic edge, and a lethal injection of classic metal attitude which would call to mind Judas Priest or Mercyful Fate. Overall a solid record. You could do far worse than check this out.

Sweden's Rimfrost take a different approach to the frozen north than many of their thematic peers, in that they sacrifice a lot of the brazen folk melodies, pomp & circumstance to provide a solid black/thrashing. The glory here is delivered straight through the band's energetic discharge...and there is a huge influence of German thrash metal here that truly works with the subject material. Perhaps the best comparison is to Immortal, who also have a very punchy style to these rhythms which Rimfrost excel at. Veraldar Nagli, the band's second full-length effort, has a cool tone to it which feels very authentic but well balanced. The guitars are boxy and the drums crash about, while Hravn's vocals unsettle through a powerful, emotional snarling.

A good band, and another good pickup for Season of Mist. Title track "Veraldar Nagli" provides for an immediate confrontation, hostile and thrashy and ready to punch your kidney in with the hilt of an oak hewn battleaxe, before reversing direction to cut your head clean off. The riffing is like Immortal meets Witchery, a frigid and diabolical slew of palm muted frenzy. "The Black Death" reveals a bit more of the band's Norse glory, a galloping mid-paced rhythm which rolls into black chords and double bass. "The Raventhrone" is right back to the thrashing, thick guitars (here they sound like Iced Earth, sans mediocrity). "Legacy Through Blood" has 3 minutes of acoustics, percussion and atmosphere delivered through a synthesizer, before the war drums pick up. It's about 9 minutes in length, and mostly slower thrash rhythms. "I Stand My Ground" and "Mountains of Mána" pick the pace back up, both solid throttlings, and "Scandinavium" is another of the longer tracks (8+ minutes) with slower riffs and acoustics. The closer, "Void of Time", has a glorious, charging gait, and you can subliminally feel the winds of old howling through the silence above its spread of punching rhythm.

I enjoyed my time with this, and would recommend it to fans of Immortal or the late 90s material from Enslaved (in particular Blodhemn). It offers further proof that not all Viking metal must be laden in synthesizers and excess folk instrumentation to succeed, and the thrash-like influence is welcome. Not every riff is great, and to be honest there are times where some of the excitement lapses off (in particular the longer tracks), but certainly enough meat on the tired bones.

Highlights: The Black Death, The Raventhrone, Mountains of Mána, Void of Time

Among the many ways that the 2010s crop of traditional metal revivalists mirrored their NWOBHM inspirations was a sizable collection of projects with a lot of potential that just didn't end up going much of anywhere. The only noteworthy difference seems to be the various countries that have produced these undiscovered studio gems, as the scarcity of metal behind the iron curtain left little opportunity for aspiring bands to be crowded out of the scene. Nevertheless, the advent of the internet and various social media accounts focused exclusively on promoting various metal subgenres has afforded even the most obscure of outfits the opportunity to reach an audience, though even in this more advantageous disposition an outfit like Polish heavy metal upstarts Savager seemed destined from humble returns when their 2017 debut EP Casus Belli finally became available on cassette.

But for what this quintet may have lacked in notoriety during their brief run in the late 2010s, they all but made up for in iron grit and sheer determination, at least insofar as what they managed to commit to recording. In the same tradition inherited from the likes of Manilla Road, Manowar and Cirith Ungol, then transmitted to faithful adherents like Ironsword and Eternal Champion, Savager dabbles in low-fi, blood and guts territory that is not for the faint of heart nor the operatic Prima Donna. Tempos tend towards the swift side and flirt heavily with speed and thrash metal stylings, the visual of steel clad barbarians cutting their foes limb from limb and spilling blood upon some snow-covered battle field hangs in the listener's head. Yet while the resulting battery of rage constructed by this outfit's instrumentalists is truly impressive, the berserker growl and Eric Adams-like falcon cries of lead vocalist Bartek Koniuszewski is what ultimately sells this EP.

The auditory carnage arrives with no need of an elaborate introduction with a double kick-steeped, driving speed anthem right out of the early 80s Manowar example, spearheaded by a thunderous riff set and a bear-like roar from Bartek that culminates in the most off the hook offering of the pack. That being said, the similarly forceful and speedy sonic assault of "Evil" and the nimble riff work of the quick paced "Might Of The Thunder God" are similarly primed to leave an entire regiment of decapitated bodies in their respective wakes, the latter seeing some rock solid, Ross The Boss-inspired lead guitar passages to bring it all home. The instrumental romp "Leviathan" turns the tables towards more of a pummeling Omen vibe meets Iron Maiden's "Transylvania" for an interesting contrast point. But the most compelling contrast point amid all the speed and fury is the down tempo metallic stomp of "Call Of The Savage", channeling that more epic side of the Manowar coin, only minus the bloated interlude segments and voice overs.

On paper, this 20 minute slab of old school heavy metal in a comparably analog-like production package had all the right elements to be a major contender in the still bustling NWOTHM craze circa 2017. Sadly, little came of this apart from a few thousand listens on YouTube and 50 hand numbered cassette copies being dispersed to the four winds. It was almost to be expected given the large number of outfits still active and sporting this same exact sound, be it the aforementioned Ironsword and Eternal Champion, or the dozens of other lesser known projects spread about Europe and the Americas. It doesn't really push the envelope as hard as the aforementioned outfits, nor does go too far beyond the stylistic norms that go with an early 80s epic approach, but it's not without a clear sense of charm and is definitely worth a spin by any self-respecting true metal trustee.

"Reunion", although perhaps not very spectacular - is a more than worthy attempt at capturing a Black Sabbath concert on cd in the original line-up (and imo certainly tons better than the "Live At Last" release).

Of course you can hardly say that musically this is "the best" Sabbath line-up but it's a nice, nostalgic look back on the Ozzy era and it has to be said that all of the band-members give it their utmost best, resulting in a fairly decent live album with practically all of the "classics" featured. 

Couple this with 2 very decent new (!) tracks, which although perhaps not as strong as some of the bands other tracks, did make me curious as to what the "reunited" line-up could come up with album-wise (as it seems now - nothing - the reunion has turned out to be a complete disgrace and only interesting for nostalgia's sake - thank you very much guys but perhaps it's time to lay Sabbath to rest once and for all) and a very nice booklet and you get a release which is well worth buying (and certainly more so than the xxxth "best off" compilation).

Not bad at all...

First wave black metal is not dead at all. It still resists, brutal, often rough and unmistakably attractive. Among its top representatives, in Italy, there are the classics Necrodeath, which after twenty years of career released their eleventh album. Keeping to the dark and violent themes typical of the band, this album presents a concept that is all but original, but always maintains its charm: the seven deadly sins.

Following the classic canon of the genre, there is nothing delicate about the opening song, Sloth. Very fast, with a buzzing and particularly hypnotic riff and lyrics as graceless in their execution as they are fascinating to listen to. Interestingly, the lyrics are half in Italian and half in English, in a mix that is more successful than one would expect, and all describe the sins to which they refer quite well. There is a very nice change of tempo in the second half, slower and with a ferocious solo. Lust starts with a crackling arpeggio and then reveals itself in Flegias's deadly and dirty scream. The main riff is slow and threatening, effectively alternating with moments of frenzy. The female voices and laughter that interrupt the song are an excellent, however short, atmospheric addition. Envy is even faster and searing than Sloth, perhaps too devastating at first, but then improves by becoming more varied. The slightly more melodic arpeggios that appear for very little during the chorus are perfect. Guitars are particularly creative and changeable. The infernal scream also alternates a deep and threatening growl. 

Pride is a fierce and creeping mid-tempo, in which from time to time the classical guitar is introduced to bring restlessness and ambiguity, helping to make the atmosphere particularly dark. The sustained rhythm makes this song strangely catchy. The ending is perhaps too abrupt, but does not penalize that much. Wrath is very short and overwhelming. It very heavy and, when it slows down, it does very little. The short duration does not prevent from putting an expressive solo high in acidity, which combined with the growl reveals to the maximum degree the atrocious power of wrath. Gluttony is the worst song, too inconsistent with tempo and with boring lyrics (it is also true that it is a sin difficult to define and less intriguing and titanic than the others), although the guitar picks up malignant and desperate notes. Fortunately, halfway, the acoustic guitar is back in the background while a whisper lists the seven sins. The solos in the last part, very clear and screaming, and the slowing down of the guitar, which are the background to the suddenly echoing voice, are very evocative. 

Greed begins in beauty with, apparently, the words of Satan himself. Certainly the voice is particularly demonic, stratified and supported by screams and laughter, the instrumental apparatus starts slowly and then accelerates as normal. After the first two minutes there is a short interlude with chanting in clear voice (but with an echo in scream) and black mass bells, a bass solo and then a guitar solo. The next part keeps the clean backing vocals and the slow rhythm, adding choirs and finally an organ. Of course, of all the songs, it is the one that best conveys the atmosphere of hell. Thanatoid accentuates the dark and poisonous shades. The instrumental part is constant and enthralling, and the verses, so fast as to go almost out of tempo, in truth perfectly reflect the anguish and fury that permeate the album. The refrain, shouted with desperation, is perfect. This is also one of the songs that best shows the group's technical skills. Graveyard of the innocents is slower and at a much smoother pace. The voice is particularly varied in the techniques, as is the instrumentation in the melodies. After all the previous ones, however, it is underwhelming.

So The seven deadly sins is a great job. It is not a milestone of its kind and in the long run it's tiring, also because the songs are all quite similar anyway, but the artistic ability behind it is undeniable. For lovers of classic black metal it is essential.

Together since 2020 when they put out their debut release ""Zagovor" ("Charm"), Russian trio Ikotka have been busy refining their style of raw occult atmospheric black metal with several EP releases and two more albums. "Raspad" ("Disintegration" or "Decay") is the band's third album and, if you don't count a compilation and two singles, ninth release. As with earlier releases, "Raspad" revolves around the musicians' interest in protective charms and spells, this time to protect against the decay and disintegration of a past world of war and chaos and the damage this world is doing to them physically and psychologically. The lyrics of four of the five songs on the album are based on old Russian spells.

Once out of its starting gates, the album charges ahead like an angry wounded bull with an extremely raw and noisy guitar sound and thudding percussion, topped by harsh stentorian vocals that almost sound like throat singing and which enhance the majesty of the music in opening track "Немирье (Притча)" ("Wartime (Parable)"). The tremolo guitars exert a hypnotic effect in their metallic judder and the voices command attention with lyrics of the penetration of the evil of conflict and war into one's soul. The second track is just as harsh and severe in its style as the first track, though slower and brooding in parts. The melodies can be very stirring in their gloom and melancholy, strange though that might seem, but there is an aggressive force from within the musicians that is driving the music onwards and infusing it with power and a vision of where to go and how.

The songs might appear similar on first listen, but repeated spins reveal differences among the five tracks, with each one having a different mood and outlook than the others. The tracks trace a journey from a place of relative light in a mostly dark world into levels of greater darkness and sadness, with all the risks of torment and possible derangement that might go with them. The third track has a sense of tragic grandeur in its riffs and pounding drums. 

Track 4, "Оттерпеться от Пытки (Покаяние)" ("Stop Endure the Torment (Repentance)") starts out as a meditative drone ambient that steadily works itself into blasting melodic BM with clear and distinct lead guitar riffs in later parts of the long track. Compared to the previous tracks, this one is even more sombre and sorrowful in its aggression, even as the riffs ring out loudly and clearly. A surprising slow solo guitar passage suggesting inner mental torment and sadness comes near the end of the song. The final track, also the title track, has a triumphal air as the musicians complete the occult ritual and escape the fate of the damned.

Though Ikotka's sound is very raw and noisy, at the same time the music is clear enough that riffs and melodies can be heard and the moods they bring can be felt and absorbed by listeners. The trio play with a limited instrumental set-up – guitars, bass, percussion, synthesisers – but deliver a powerful and sometimes droning doom style of raw BM. That the songs trace a narrative through the changing moods of the music and the lyrics demonstrates the thought and care the musicians took in recording and presenting the songs in the order they appear. Though some tracks could have been edited for length and tightened up a little so that the music could have been even more forceful, there's hardly any filler on the recording. Every moment on the album has feeling, force and power. 

When it all ends, as it must, you have been swept up so much in the album's embrace that you can feel rather lost and alone, especially after that last track which has built up to a mighty sonic tower of raw tremolo-guitar noise and droning lead guitar.

album: Seagulls Insane and Swans Deceased Mining Out the Void
texto:
Short of dropping their daks and going Full Monty for the obligatory group photograph on their MA entry, what's a band like Seagulls Insane and Swans Deceased Mining Out The Void to do to get any attention around here?! Why - hope for a kind person to upload their debut album in full to Youtube.com, that's what! Which deed a very nice person called XOdiumNostrumX (thank you very much!) did nearly two years ago. Yes, it took Yours Truly a long while to find this - I was distracted by many other things - but now at long last, the band's one (and so far, only) release will get a full hearing worthy of a Metal Archives review!

Appropriately for a band with a name that's far out but not really that extreme, the music is out-there but not so that even the two band members can't listen to it. It's a mix of industrial, noise and straight-out melodic blackened doom / post-metal with a hardcore skull-crushing edge. The melodic metal / hardcore elements and strained growling vocals are done very well and can be pretty terrifying and often sneeringly malevolent. The more experimental aspects are not quite so well done, in part because they include a lot of special effects that we've all heard before on similar fusions so they sound generic and not very original at times.

The album is divided into five long parts with the longest at about 16 minutes in length, so it's possible this was all meant to be one long continuous work with track divisions inserted at particular moments to allow for the usual tea-n-cigarette breaks. On the other hand, each part does boast individual melodic and rhythmic grooves that actually do rock so the five tracks are almost like full-fledged songs. Their in-between status - are they or aren't they proper "songs"? - might frustrate listeners but give SIASDMOTV the opportunity to explore melody, texture and mood in their own way. As the guys advise in the lyrics to Part 1, the album is akin to " ... a circle not a segment / No end and no beginning / No use to seek the sense yet still one can not be misled". Some of the more interesting sections of music occur near the beginning and ends of most tracks where most instruments drop away leaving just the guitars to undergo textural and tonal deconstruction which can immerse and concentrate the mind quite wonderfully in a dark sound realm. As the album progresses, the band veers into the epic and bombastic with heavy pounding percussion, thunderous riffs and a decadent ambience reeking of decay and corruption. There is quite a lot of repetition which sometimes works and sometimes doesn't, depending on how good the melodies, riffs and layering of textures and mood are originally.

The best parts of the album are not so much the actual music itself but aspects of the band's style: the heavy grinding bass, the vocals which labour under immense concrete-slab pressures and the rock grooves. Occasionally the experimental and the rock-oriented sides of the band come together really well as in the bass lines of Part III where the grinding rhythm is augmented by sinister sound effects that sound like a demon didgeridoo. Guitar feedback on Part III and other tracks that sounds like the after-effects of a passenger jet flying off into the distance get the thumbs-up from me, even when it resembles fingernails screeching up and down the blackboard like forever. (Well this is supposed to be an extreme and chaotic album after all so what are you complaining about?) The start of Part V is a glorious moment of unhealthy black doom wallowing, guitar drone howl and sickly acid space ambience.

There's a fair bit to criticise but also quite a lot to praise: sure, the album isn't quite as original and right out on a limb as I'd like it to be but those black metal and other metal elements that the musicians bring in are done very well. The overwrought bombastic aspect might be excessive and sometimes I think SIASDMOTV could have pulled back on this in favour of developing particular atmospheres more. In the album's favour though are long extended instrumental passages of sheer guitar feedback torture bliss and (depending on what listeners can tolerate) these more than make up for the recording's shortcomings.

Bound Hands is (or was) a small death metal band straight from the underground metal scene of Aarhus. Although they have been around since the turn of the decade, it wouldn’t be until early 2023 before they released their self-titled EP. This would also come to be their only release with their original line-up, as the vocalist and one of the guitarists left the band in December of the same year.

With this EP, Bound Hands deliver some bone crushing old school death metal. It never disappoints you throughout the 18 minute runtime, giving you exactly what you’d expect. The release is heavy, groovy and has great production. The EP never really ventures into the incredibly fast territory that death metal has come to be associated with, but stays as a medium tempo record. This makes the grooves that much groovier, and generally fits the album quite well. The production is clear, but in no way overproduced, and what you’d come to expect from any modern death metal release.

The same quality is held up throughout all four tracks, making this a very solid record, and a great first release. Much of the energy brought to the table is due to vocalist Andreas Truelsen. His vocals aren’t anything incredibly noteworthy, and falls well within the death metal standard, but he has a sort of presence in the music and his live performances that is hard to match, and makes him very hard to replace. So with him gone, and without them having found a replacement yet, I don’t know what to expect from future releases, but my hopes are high.

Overall, while this EP doesn’t bring anything new to the table when it comes to death metal, Bound Hands’ self-titled work is still a very solid release worthy of giving a listen.

The band idea takes its origins away back in 1997, when the guitar player Alessandro Pace, former member of avant-garde rock group Klimt 1918, thought of creating different music. Sadly, The Foreshadowing was formed only in 2005, when Alessandro found perfect band members for all of the instruments. Honestly, i didn't expect much from this album. Italian gothic based metal usually is full of Über-Mega-Cheesy moments. Macbeth, Mandragora Scream, Lacuna Coil or Theatres des Vampires could be considered "masters"...

This album contains none! It's also very solid, all tracks "touch" you emotionally and the riffs are rarely repeated, so getting bored while listening isn't possible. There are many powerful moments in the songs that give you feelings of melancholy that only expressive music like Anathema's "Angelica", "Far Away" or "Fragile Dreams" can create. You are probably guessing the album is gothic metal, but the almost omnipresent irksome-doomy guitar work and almost omnipresent depressing keyboard makes it gothic-doom metal. The emotional "Anathema" moments are usually obtained when the lead guitar becomes more melodic and the keyboard gets more intense, but it's important to say that nothing would be possible without Marco Benevento's incredibly soothing baritone (the only type of vocals on DoN). Such flavors are frequent ("Cold Waste", "The Wandering", "The Fall", "Days of Nothing"). The song "Last Minute Train" has a ballad-like structure. The drumming is decent but non-spectacular as in any album that lacks much dynamism. I have listened to this album for many times and the only catchy song is the more upbeat "The Departure". The only song that doesn't follow the same gothic-doom metal pattern with stylistic differences is "Into the Lips of the Earth", which is a minimalist ambient. 

Lyrically, the album deals with an imaginary apocalypse, the "opera" of an insane man that is fed up with the world. Some monologue can be found in "Ladykiller" and "Last Minute Train". The album cover is well realized and it's related to the theme (man in despair, apocalyptic red sky, ravens). To get the best album experience, you must listen to it from start to finish and follow the lyrics. Everything is good, but there are no standout songs.  

"The Foreshadowing aim is to bring you into an atom-sphere of apocalyptic tragedy and alienation from humanity and everyday life with a moody and powerful music."

That's a quote from one of their official internet pages and i think they transposed their ideas really well into this album. "Days of Nothing" is with nothing inferior to works of more well-known bands such as My Dying Bride, Paradise Lost, Moonspell or Anathema. I really hope the second album won't disappoint my now big expectations.

I've kind of been listening to tracks from this album for quite a while, but never really sat down and thought to review it. Sludge isn't where my heart is, but I'm not going to lie, this album is still pretty good even if it's not my taste in music.

The cover art is slightly disturbing, what with it being a picture of John Gacy (known as the Killer Clown) who was a serial killer and rapist. That pretty much sums up the band's work: disturbing. The titles and topics of the songs show this ('Dr. Seuss Is Dead' and 'Cassie Eats Cockroaches' showing the former, 'Scream of the Butterfly' the latter as it tells the story of a woman performing an abortion on herself - really, who comes up with that?), and really this is some messed up shit. If you like to understand lyrics, I'd suggest keeping away from this album.

There is a great variety in terms of how the music is played on this album. 'Cheap Vodka' and 'Toubabo Koomi' take a fast (for sludge anyway) approach to the music with heavy guitars and pounding drums while 'Dr. Seuss Is Dead' is far slower, although it is still heavy. Then there are a couple of songs that are hardly metal at all, and focus on largely sending a creepy feeling up your spine. Although the vocals vary like the music does though, I just don't really like them. They're not bad as such, but they're far from being the best I've ever heard.

'Dr. Seuss Is Dead' is the track that sticks in my mind the most, I'm not sure why. It's long, slow and repetitive - exactly the kind of music that I don't like - and yet it somehow manages to capture my attention every time. It's a bit of a weird feeling really. The pace actually changes quite a lot throughout, speeding up and slowing down a lot a various points. It never gets too fast, but it does get to a decent speed at some bits. Really, I don't know why I like it. The vocals aren't the reason, neither are the guitars or the drumming. And let's face it, the bass isn't going to do it either. It just comes together very well.

The song 'Cheap Vodka' is one of the ones I like best because it feels slightly more thrash-like than the other tracks, although it is still more along the lines of doom than thrash metal. The song is short but sweet, a mere two minutes coupled with the faster pace meaning that it passes much quicker than the other songs do. It does feel a little out of place, but with an album so varied it isn't quite as obvious as it otherwise would be.

I'm also drawn to 'Toubabo Koomi' more than the other songs, again because it is faster and has a feel to it that I'm more comfortable with. Unlike 'Cheap Vodka', this track lasts five minutes. As a result it pretty much hides itself from discovery if you're looking at the length of all the songs, but it doesn't feel as long because it's faster than the other tracks. The drumming on this track is pretty fast like the rest of the music, but at some parts you just think how insane it is that people can play like that. It's not fast the whole way through, but for the most part it is and it does sound very, very good.

If you can deal with how messed up the meanings behind the songs on this are (as well as the actual lyrics) and you don't mind slow headbangers rather than rapid double bass on your drums, you will enjoy this to at least some extent. I'm not saying it's perfect, because it isn't. There are plenty of other artists that I like better and I didn't love every song on this album. However, no matter what your stance on sludge metal is you will enjoy this album, simply because there is something for everyone on this record.

album: Where I Am the Chalice, Be Thou the Blood
texto:
A band name like Devilpriest playing a blackened death metal style is a fast way to catch my attention, especially when the album art looks as cosmic as their latest. The Polish outfit has been around for roughly a decade at this point, but it was this third release that put them on my radar. Titled Where I Am The Chalice, Be Thou The Blood, one can assume it opts for a weird blend of predictable Satanic cheese and leveled-up intensity.

Make no mistake, such a combination is not a bad thing. The general vibe of hellish worship and evil incarnate is carried through means of longer tunes that cover intricate rhythms in thick, machine-gun drums and burning hot blackened shrieks. Devilpriest casts not only the themes, but the intensity of death metal masterminds Deicide in their later years, flattening the sharp surface with a dense atmosphere helped with tremolos and blasting. If nothing else, this forces the stronger leads to stand out when needed.

A good example is "Channeling Into The Peerless Transgressiveness" with its unwavering intensity in the drum and rhythm department, letting the simmering bridges and guitar work pop out all the better in the beginning. To the opposite end, opener "He Is In Me" uses a slow crawl to establish mood, working in suspense to reach our climax, and I may even say the following "Dragon Of Blasphemy" even fixes us with a catchier chorus. As the titles suggest, this is pretty on the nose, but I imagine the Poles are self-aware, and this one-two punch was a nice hook.

Ultimately, Where I Am The Chalice, Be Thou The Blood doesn’t offer anything we’ve not encountered before, but it was a rather fulfilling listen. It strikes that perfect balance of being over the top in many ways while also maintaining a respectable foundation, and that’s sometimes all we can ask for.

Originally written for Metalegion Magazine

Finland’s malevolent black-thrash metal mob Urn are back with their 6th full length album. Having been active since 1994, this remains a cult name in the underground that continues to put out ferocious records. This new opus will be unleashed by Osmose Productions on March 28th.

Thunderous guitars and drums come into life with a chiming bell as demonic vocals join the mix, instantly conjuring a majestic and epic black-thrash attack. Mixing tough rhythms with melodic leads, the classic heavy metal feeling is very prevalent in the beginning moments of this record, something I am always grateful for. Their barbaric high-speed assault kicks in with that savage edge to it that made their last album so killer. Keeping the precise picking and varied drum performance from before, the band feels full of energy and a strong hunger for destruction. Pounding with fury, the low end rattle of the bass comes through gloriously while the potently mixed guitars have so much body, a stunning mix indeed. Equally impressive are the magnificent solos which are packed with melodics and shredding mayhem in equal measure. There is no denying the refined talents of these seasoned maniacs and it is a pleasure to hear them back in such fantastic form. “Demon Steel” is off to a stellar start.

Although it’s always fiercely ripping away at you, this record definitely knows how to use dynamics. From those soaring melodics to the blasting hellfire; there is no resting or laziness in the songwriting. While remaining true to the formula that the band set out with (at least the more thrashy records of their career), we hear the strength they have developed coming closer than ever to perfection. There has always been an impressive ability with this band to sound totally extreme and yet retain a very 80s anthemic quality in their music, a balance that is just right to my ear and sounds very Finnish. From Tarot to Archgoat to Rippikoulu; Finland has always had a strong mix of heavy metal bands. Urn are another part of this legacy which sits in the darker side while upholding the earlier roots.

Staying true until the end, this belligerent band keeps the faith with no remorse and no mercy for the wimps bastardising the modern era. The old school is alive and well with no compromise being shown by these stalwarts of savagery. Their metallic flame burns bright and remains ablaze until the end with a stunning array of songs that all show strength. With a primal energy that is so damn contagious, Urn command you with an impressive presence through the speakers. Harkening back to the likes of Desaster, Nifelheim, Sodom and Destruction; Urn know how to wield the blade of black-thrash metal and cause the most havoc and mayhem possible with it, slicing through posers without hesitation. You will be bewitched by the venomous excellence of their new album and its adrenaline-pumping fury that will spellbind you until the end.

“Demon Steel” is indeed a perfect title for this metallic offering of total viciousness. Sharp, refined and ready to brawl; this Finnish horde shows no sign of rusting yet with their sixth album a total triumph worthy of their unwavering discography. Violent, impactful and intense with a ton of 80s grandiosity, this is a superb follow up to “Iron Will Of Power”.
