Dismember have always been a band to try new things with each album that they put together; this one is no exception to that claim.  Their ability to merge heavy riffs with melody and not overdue either section of their song structures is truly a wonder to behold.  Bands like Dismember are the ones that define the real meaning of what melodic death metal is all about.  Dismember focus first on constructing death metal while the melody is simply the icing on the cake.  Possessing jaw-dropping breakdowns through storms of lava-like melodies that show that this band does not fuck around when it comes to playing melo-death for true bastards.

Unlike many death metal bands that keep the connotation running that everything has to be chaotic and fast, Dismember break away from that trend and decide to use their sense of rhythm instead; making for unlimited compositional options as well as some solid hooks.  While the breaks sometimes lead into pure rage and chaos of blast beats and heavy strumming, the entire entity of their music offers more of a sense of clarity in a way that the music is actually going somewhere, instead of just throwing in random speed riffs to hold the songs together.  Differing from “Like an Ever Flowing Stream” and “Indecent and Obscene,” the production is significantly grimier and has more of a rusty feel.  Despite the somewhat different mix style, I happen to like the change for this album, and I can not imagine listening to it any other way.  The part that really stands out to me about this is Matti’s vocals – they sound as if they’re performed in more of a belching manner, rather than growling.

The guitars churn with unique metallic growls of their own, similar to a tag-team of killers brandishing rusty chainsaws.  For the majority, this is a pretty aggressive album; it flows with the anger and sorrow of a soldier in a war as he frantically searches about for means to stay alive in a living Hell.  Aside from the adrenaline that the aggressive parts pump this album with, there is a definite sad point in this album, which is a reminder that no war is fought without casualties or sacrifice.  Listen to “Life - Another Shape of Sorrow,” and tell me that’s not one of the most coherent representations of the word ‘sorrow’ in death metal.  God damn that is something else!

Could it be the epic climax of the album?  You’re damn right it is.  Are you bored of all of the endless death metal remakes which sound like copy bands of Morbid Angel?  If you want real death metal that makes In Flames look like pussies and makes Deicide look like a bunch of newbies, then go for a Dismember album closest to you.  This is awesome and prudent work on behalf of the kings of Swedeath.  Check it out some time.

A year after the still very successful, yet nowhere near as out-of-this-world record as 1984's Victim of Chains, Back to Attack, 1986 brought about what would, unfortunately, be Gravestone's last studio album to date, and it looks like it will remain to be the last one. The Teutonic Masters saw multiple lineup changes during that one year since the previous album, most notably, they saw Mathias Dieth go and be replaced with newcomer Jürgen Metko. If you know the first two releases, and you've seen them being played by the band live on YouTube (or perhaps if you were super lucky, even live), you know that Mathias Dieth is probably the second most essential member of Gravestone after Berti Majdan, so it is rather difficult to try to recreate what he would do to the band's sound. Did Gravestone stand a chance without him, or was this a futile attempt?

Surprisingly, Gravestone did a great job at carrying on without him. Sure, Creating a Monster won't sound the same as when the Reinelt-Dieth duo was still in the band, but the outcome of this release is the best imaginable handling of the situation by the rest of Gravestone. The mean, scratchy and ballsy attitude remained, however, they certainly soaked the sound itself in more refinement and sophistication as opposed to the roaring, blaring guitars and drums that we heard on the previous two releases. The production is clearer and smoother, the overall sound is less ferocious and more accessible. The direction and the slight change fit the band's evolution after the two predecessors. The only thing that suffered was the shredding, which would not have been a big deal in any other band's case, for the most part. But the Reinelt-Dieth duo created some of the most incredible dual-guitar shred-offs in German metal history, and while Metko and Reinelt try to save what's saveable, it's just not the same. The leads became less significant, and it is more about the moderated, nearly radio-friendly choruses and riffs. 

Though slightly softer, this album is still an excellent piece of Teutonic heavy metal. Two of the strongest songs on here are to be found right in the middle of the release, with the title song being the greatest song on here, and "The End of Our Love" being the second best. The former features one of Berti Majdan's most memorable vocal lines in the chorus, supported by absolutely menacing, razor-sharp riffs that follow the vocal melody with great precision and discipline. The latter carries on the band's excellent ability and habit of writing excellent love-disappointment pieces, and this one might be the second best after "So Sad". The smooth, fluid acoustic chords work remarkably well with the consistent, silky bass guitar during the verses. The opener "Masters of the Earth" is also worth a mention, as it's one of the only speed metal songs by this band, by a band that's known for mid-paced and slow-paced heavy metal masterpieces. Despite that, the opener is magnificently energetic and fierce, with a very respectable solo, which manages to recreate (true, only distantly) the solos from the last two releases.

The rest is not bad at all, but the balance of the disc is certainly not as outstanding as the mentioned standouts. "Dirty City" is a bit pointless with its strange, unintuitive instrumental arrangements in the verses, horrible lyrics, and Majdan's exaggerated shrieking at certain times. I've heard several people call the vocalist the reason why they aren't into Gravestone, and this is the first time in history in which even I agree with them, who loves his work on Victim of Chains and Back to Attack. "Illusions" is much better, though the melodies start to sound slightly unnatural and forced. At 1:48, that hook would not be bad, but with Majdan yet again going above and beyond what would fit the music, and the less-than-powerful chord progression, it's all rather discardable.

All in all, Creating a Monster is an honorable final effort by a band that a couple of years earlier was one of the most incredible forces in the Teutonic metal scene. It is hard to recommend a record like this when all I could tell you is "Check out Gravestone's third-best album!", which would not get a lot of people excited to listen to this. If you like heavy metal, particularly Teutonic heavy metal, with all of its quirky characteristics, such as the strong accent and at times, grammatically disastrous lyrics, then you should check this out. The fact that it's slightly weaker than Back to Attack and significantly weaker than Victim of Chains does not mean much, as you could say that about most heavy metal albums out there. That does not mean this record does not fall well above the average, even slightly above the group of merely "good" albums.

Powerful, fast & charismatic will be a few words to describe this great effort by “Krof”, yes it is a one man black metal band. Krof has been playing in quite a few bands but he wanted something that he could say that belongs to him & so Aigro Mucifelam was formed.

On this album we’ve 38 minutes of insanely fast drumming, blackish guitar riffs, scary atmosphere and strong & extremely harsh vocals with few & only few strange sound effects. All songs can be related with each other because the upcoming song catches on from where the last song finished and develops continuity & maintains the whole mood. The music is for real black metal fans and is really toxic for newbies & mallcore kids to digest. The production is really immaculate as it gives the raw & primitive feeling while at the same time every instrument except the bass can be heard clearly.

There’s not a single dull or weak moment in the whole album, each & every minute is bliss. All instruments have been played with great musicianship, the drums are as brutal as hell, they cast such a spell that you cannot lose concentration for even a second, the guitars give you something new in every song, the riffs are superb, very blackish & very fast. When combined together the guitars & the drums create such an atmosphere in all songs that is cold & grim as hell and you can feel it. How can we miss out the vocals, because the vocals are brilliant, very powerful, full of anger & hate just like we want them to be.

Aigro Mucifelam has the potential to reach a cult status & it’ll sooner or later, I am really impressed and I’d recommend it to every black metal fan.

The mega-prolific Ced is at it again with yet another project. After expanding his flagship Rocka Rollas to a full-band lineup and shifting to a broader heavy/power metal sound rather than focusing exclusively on Running Wild worship, then in turn reviving that same nautical speed/power glory in Blazon Stone, Ced has gone somewhat back to his old ways of doing everything himself, vocals included, an approach he hasn't taken in any of his numerous projects since the very early days of Rocka Rollas (though he is back behind the mic in that band). This time he's opted to broaden his palette to pull from other German power/speed metal influences like Blind Guardian, Helloween and Gamma Ray.

Ced's vocals in Breitenhold just ooze exuberance and youthful vigor, more than effective enough to serve as the focal point for Breitenhold's galloping fantasy-fueled riff fests. Though the lyrics are, as is usual in Ced's projects, sort of generic/uninspired, they're not totally embarrassing or anything, just standard metal anthems of fantasy, battle and adventures. He has clearly put tons of effort into his vocal training though, as his ability to create those totally necessary high-pitched wails is really convincing. He really belts it out in songs like "Thunderstorm Arise." His skill with layering voices for those fist-pumping dude-choir bits has carried over from his other projects as well, if not relied on quite as heavily as the technique is in either Blazon Stone or Rocka Rollas.

Compared to those other two bands, the riffs in Breitenhold are a bit more subtle, letting more of the dynamics and attention-grabbing fall to the vocals. Riffs are mostly speedy affairs but are fairly often not a lot more than galloping palm muted riffs or series of strummed chords while the real fireworks happen in the leads or vocal lines. Sometimes the riffs do steal the thunder, though, like the speed demon that opens up "The Battle Far Beyond." The leads are mostly as glorious as they need to be and sometimes are downright great. The soloing throughout is spot on and is injected with heaps of emotion, like in instrumental interlude "Neverwaking Sleep," but some of the longer stretches of lead work seem a little directionless, like in the lead-in to the central solo of the title track. 

That's not to say things ever sound even remotely unprofessional. By now Ced's accomplishments as both an instrumentalist and producer are well-documented. Bass lines are fluid and immaculately captured, drums are played authoritatively and captured with plenty of crack and rumble, and the guitar playing is ridiculously tight throughout. There's also obvious confidence in his own singing prowess as the vocals are pushed right up front in the mix. The problem with this approach is that the big sing-along choruses in Breiteinhold just don't quite grab me the same way they do in Rocka Rollas or Blazon Stone especially. There are some winners, but the consistency just isn't quite there.

Coupled with the relative de-emphasis on riffs carrying the weight of the album, I just can't quite muster the same excitement for this album as I did for the Blazon Stone debut especially. I was also a bit misled by the album, as I thought it would be a pretty major departure from Ced's old Running Wild tricks, but not only does that band's influence still make a strong showing here, the other major influences he's taking from are still stalwarts of classic German power/speed so it's not like he started playing old Swedish heavy metal or USPM or something. I should also mention that I definitely prefer Running Wild to just about any other of those other bands, so the disappointment with this album is something of a paradox: I lament that it didn't quite move far enough away from the Rolfisms of Ced material of the past, yet I also prefer those Rolfisms to what he's reaching for with Breitenhold in the first place. 

That said, I can't help but enjoy a lot of the music on Secret Worlds. "Thunderstorm Arise" is just a ripping track and "Legions of Breitenhold" has a chorus that's sure to get your blood pumping. There's also a little more attention given to little things like track sequencing, intros, outros and interlude tracks that seem to indicate that Ced has started to reign in his unending fount of power/speed metal and focus a bit harder on refining his approaches and emphasizing quality. Though this album just came out in November 2015, there's already another Breitenhold album just over the horizon and the snippets I've heard from that seem to address my issues with this debut - the music is a bit riffier but has moved further from the Running Wild territory. I suppose we'll see what Ced has done with the band sooner rather than later, as was probably your expectation from the prolific musician at this point anyway.

Sinister as fuck. I mean, what good could eloquence serve here ? That's right: if you're looking for punishingly grim music, relentless in its seething hostility, surely this is it. Screw Chopin's 'Funeral march'. Incantation's notorious mixture of pure death metal with gruesome doom dirges is the way to go if you're looking to grin til you pull a freaking stroke. 

But it's not all brutish agitation for the sake of it. This isn't some common sludge-fest that puts the listener to sleep after the second track. The death metal is hectic and lively, with a throbbing vehemence to it. There's such a concentrated blackness to it - an urgent, corrosive intensity, animated by an underlying sense of horror, at times bordering on the apocalyptic. And the doom stuff pulls the audience into its near-nauseating state of indignation towards existence - well, that doesn't sound too great to go through when put that way, but, the point is it's convincing for what it's attempting to do. I think this is basically Six Feet Under if they were good (OK, didn't mean it that way).

The absolutely cavernous, subterranean howls stick so well to those disturbingly abyssal dirge sections. They're sort of like if an extreme metal band got a grizzly bear to sing for them. Generally this sort of lower-than-ground vocal frequency style shits all over the instrumental and stalls the tracks with monotonous boredom, but in this case, they bring a sort of "voice from beyond" type of presence. They're just as threatening and ominous as the composition. All in all this album's just got this massive weight to it. It feels genuinely immovable, and intimidating. A bit like a 'Symphonies of Sickness' (Carcass), it's got this lucid, nearly repulsive macabre quality to it  - an unforgiving brutality at its core.

Of course the production sucks from a purely mixing point of view, this being made before death metal's decent production era. It's appreciable in that within its aesthetic it reproduces the album cover art in musical form, mirroring that weirdness and organic realism. But obviously it's far from optimal with the entire drum set too far at the back and in particular the masked kicks and the neglected overheads that can't supply their dramatic splash and crash to the monstrous guitars, and the toms have a hard time getting head above water at all. It sounds giant and mighty, though, in spite of the material/technical shortcomings. It's big, gritty...and a bit filthy.

What's always been really cool with these guys is they don't give a shit about intros. So, where other bands like to play it cute and often spend an unnecessary amount of time and effort establishing foreplay with the listener, Incantation just bust the door down and give it to you whether you wanted it or not - although this sentence now accidentally sounds like an innuendo. Hear Track 3 'Iconoclasm of Catholicism'. That tremolo picked, pure death metal goodness. Mmm. Chocolate ice-cream with roasted nuts. Come to think of it, I'd love to see these guys work as brutal dairy farmers. Oh yes, and they're very, very angry at Christendom of course. That had to appear here, somewhere. I think every single song title makes a reference to that, so. They're satanic brutal dairy farming bears.

Xenomorphic Contamination is an Italian 2-man brutal death project formed by drummer/(backing) vocalist Davide Billia of Hour of Penance, Septycal Gorge & guitarist/bassist/vocalist Max Criminal Exhaler of Fecal God.

Xenomorphic Contamination bases their subject matter on...you guessed it: aliens. Also that album art is fucking fantastic; a refreshing deviation from the overdone try hard gore that (dis)graces many a brutal/slam death albums. Colonized from the Inside paints a picture of an extraterrestrial invasion that ends in the downfall of humanity and absolute triumph for our otherworldly masters. The concept is nothing really new but I dunno...I just like that creepy alien fucker!

The album starts off with a fitting alien-sounding intro (that reminds me of films like District 9, Battle: LA etc.) and progresses into brutal death assault. The guitar tone heard is satisfyingly crushing and noticeably distinct. Then the deep, monstrous guttural growls (no ridiculous pig squeals or -core highs to be heard) violently carve their way in, backed by the relentless blasting. The guitar work at certain parts hints influence from Nile. Some of this said influence carries into the next track as the double bass frenzies add another layer of percussive intensity. Then this track shifts into a slow to mid-tempo crushing stomp that almost resembles a deathcore breakdown but twice as effective. So far, so good.

Biomechanical Retaliation offers more gurgled vocals and a cool blackened riff that isn't utilized fully. Martyrs follows, creative percussion work with wonky riffage accompanied, fucking crushing slams and a bass drop among other things. This track goes all out and is arguably the most enjoyable on this album. The frustrating thing here is that XC, rarely for the most part, settles into a definitive groove, a skull-crushing interlude busts in and hypes one up and before you know it the aforementioned groove is lost blue balling the listener. Also XC fail to capitalize on the massive riffs they manage to churn out. The music is constantly shifting and turning chaotically that it starts to miss the point at times. However, when they let it breathe especially towards the last two tracks, the results are quite pleasing. Maybe just a smidgen of restraint next time guys?

The playing has a  tech death vibe to it but doesn't embrace it fully and that is perfectly fine. The drummer is a beast with multiple appendages and his performance here is bewildering. However, I wished if he could pull back at a certain moments but I guess then it wouldn't be br00tal death now, would it? Apart from that, the samples were a fantastic touch. They are used moderately and integrated rarely but I am eager to see if the duo are willing to expand on that front in order to grant their music a more unique and um...alien atmosphere.

Good? Sure. Great? Not quite there...yet. I'm sensing massive potential here but tends to falter in some aspects despite possessing plenty of great riffs, powerful vocals and interesting drum beats. Hints of innovation are to be found but they are just that...hints. Overall though a cool release that will more than satisfy (& slightly annoy!) anyone who craves extraterrestrial themed brutal death chaos. As for those looking for something with a bit more depth & subtlety, too much blastbeats & rawr.

Much has already been written about bands who figure things out as they go. A shaky but promising first release, a minor change in sound in a spare demo or EP, and boom, a new record that showcases the direction that was previously hinted upon in a fully realised manner, which is then met with praise or derision by critics and fanbase. Tale as old as time. While there are many who are content simply refining their sound over the course of their career, I find the aforementioned approach to be far more interesting to observe as a reviewer and music fan. Really, that’s what makes Nihilism’s sophomore, Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance so fascinating to me, because not only does it give us something entirely different to what preceded it, it came about in the span of a mere two years, during which the band was radio silent.

From the moment “I” breaks out, you’d almost be forgiven for thinking an entirely different band worked on this. Gone is the prolonged introduction, we’re immediately met with cacophonous blasting and ringing dissonant notes that possess a near-mathy character. Hell, even Chris Bonos seems to have found his place, his previously shy screeching at the front, injected with a much needed shot of adrenaline. Sure, Obscurite Noir wasn’t necessarily lacking in intensity, but it was nowhere near as lively. The choppy riffing presented here is equal parts brain-bending and pummelling, and things remain unpredictable throughout the song’s 4 minute length. It’s genuinely astounding how much they manage to cram in without losing the plot. Music this shifty requires everyone involved to be in lockstep, not only in terms of playing, but also in terms of vision. I hate to repeatedly draw comparisons to previous works in my reviews, but I really can’t wrap my head around how they managed to invert their writing approach of “3 minutes’ worth of ideas stretched to 5”, and keep it cohesive.

“II” sees the duo further spread their wings, with a slightly greater emphasis on atmosphere, without necessarily sacrificing intensity. Wrenching grooves are offset by rampant percussion coursing underneath them, the slight disagreement in tempo keeping the listener guessing, while also giving them a trail to follow. The whole thing is a roller coaster really, as Nihilism also manages to inject some slower parts into the mix without robbing the piece of its tension. Guitar breaks uphold an equilibrium of tension and tranquillity, and always escalate towards something, be it one of the band’s majestic tremolo streams, or a lopsided arpeggiated groove. Radical as their transformation might have been, the fact that they knew what they should keep from the debut is reassuring, as the aforementioned tremolos do a lot to help mix things up, in addition to providing a foil to the discordant jangling that permeates the music.

Unfortunately, it doesn’t take long for things to start feeling more and more scatterbrained. “III” is a dour and sludgy instrumental, that, despite its quality, comes much too early in the album and kneecaps the momentum that was built up to that point, and after all my listens, I am not quite sure if it ever manages to recover from that. The album begins to move in fits and starts, more akin to a sputtering car engine than a black metal onslaught, “IV” also featuring brass and choir breaks alongside the bursts of dissonant black metal. Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance makes an attempt to course-correct through that song, but things come to a screeching halt IMMEDIATELY AFTER with “V”, an ambient composition that contents itself with droning and groaning around for longer than it has any business to. I understand that an element of the avant-garde is unpredictability, but given that we’re talking about a conceptual work, especially one that lasts a mere 34 minutes, it’s hard not to feel the whiplash from one moment to the next.

Even though the last third of Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance manages to bring things back with “VI”’s labyrinthine and grandiose finale (awkward clean vocals included), and a denouement that actually means something in “VII”, with its female-vocal driven post-cataclysmic bliss, it doesn’t pass muster. It’s the equivalent of plummeting down a cliff and having your fall interrupted multiple times over by stopping on another cliff and needing someone to push you so that you can keep going down. In brief, the density of ideas per song is pretty solid, but when you take a wider lens to look at the entirety of the album it falls out of whack because it’s doing too much on a track-by-track basis. Sure, the concept of “an apocalypse brings about a new world that allows us to transcend” is there, but it feels like I’m watching it unfold at x2 speed, and it deserves better than feeling like a sped-up YouTube video.

Ironically enough, it feels like Nihilism were tempering their ambitions on this one. Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance is beholden to the same constraints their debut was in terms of its duration and track listing, when in reality its leaps in style and technique deserved so much more. Looking at individual parts under a microscope shows us a band that has fully come into its own, creating erratic and contorting music that suffocates and elevates the listener in equal measure, but I can’t help but feel like they don’t let us absorb the vistas we see in the journey they created. Even then, despite its hectic nature, it continues to be a commendable effort, and a bold step forward for what had started as a merely vicious black metal band with little else to help it stand out. I can only hope we get to see something new from them in the future, perhaps another great leap forward, one that actually gets the time it deserves.
