"Convulsive, shuddering, rotten, and grim. Some of the gnarliest death metal around. That bass tone..." Those words were my initial reaction to Your End after purchasing the Deathcamp EP and I stand by them. Here is a band treading on semi-unique sonic ground with gusto, unafraid to experiment within the parameters of genre confinement. This is death metal to be sure, leaning heavily on the well-worn template of Asphyx-ian death-doom, with lots of slow-crawl agony and smoky battlefield atmospherics; juxtaposing that is a grind element that really ratchets up the torque and tension between the blast-and-crawl. Other bands have trod here before but something about Your End's songwriting chops and the force of its execution really elevate this material. Part of it is the baleful, morose atmosphere engendered by perhaps the harshest bass tone this side of early Godflesh. The bass carries this beast. The guitars, more of a standard HM-2 tone, struggle to surface over the bass and that battle for dominance is quite dynamic and engaging. The drumming is also snug, with a tight snare sound that echoes through the aural mire. The vocalist shifts between heaving, belching gutturals and harsh shrieking rasps in an effective fashion, not overplayed.

"Opium" opens with four minutes of well-crafted dark ambient, layering ominous synths, hazy guitar riffs, and pitch-shifted vocals into a maisma of atmospheric over-indulgence (at four minutes plus, it is a shade too long) before launching into "Lucifer's Chariot," whose opening death-doom riff is comfortingly familiar in light of the startling powerviolence-esque grind parts that intersect it. "Pierced With The Horn Of The Ram" is my favorite, sounding like early Grave with the bass cranked all-the-way into the red. This is Swe-death at its most maxed-out, blown-out, in the red and yet beneath all that abrasive noise are catchy-as-hell riffs anchoring the song in tradition. The title track wraps up the EP with a sullen death-doom epic. Color me a fan who can't wait to hear the rest of Your End's releases. There is a lot of potential to mined from the ideas on just this EP alone.

This is the first full-length work of Dizziness, after 3 demos and a split. It includes 5 new tracks and 3 that have been released in the past. The demo of 2010, "Evocation of Ancestral Grandeur", really got my attention so I wanted to see the potential of the band in their first complete attempt.

After a short intro which puts the listener in the proper mood, a storm of riffs breaks out and it clearly pays homage to the Greek black metal scene that flourished in the early 90s. With the exception of "Polemos" all tracks have medium to long duration, with repeated riffs but because of their quality they do not sound boring to the least. The familiar tremolo picking is present and the musical ideas brim with nostalgia and admiration for the forgotten past. Drums keep the rhythm firmly with a fair amount of blastbeats and some sparse slow parts, while I would like the bass to sound just a bit louder. Regarding the voice, it differs from the standard high-pitched one that we usually find in black metal. On the contrary, Gareth chooses a deeper vocal approach that blends very well with the music content.

At this point I would like to share a thought. I have the impression that when Dizziness write more melancholic melodies they really thrive. Don't get me wrong, the whole album is decent and all the songs are above average. But tracks like "For Glory and Pride" and "Nyx" create very strong emotions and big expectations from them. Finally, it would be an omission not to mention the production, which is good but at the same time as raw as it should be for this particular genre.

It is always nice to see that the local scene continues to consist of new bands that have dedication and passion for what they do. When this happens, the musical result rarely disappoints. Dizziness show some very good elements in their first attempt and are worth a careful listen. They will take you several years back.

Originally written for: The Lair of Storfeth

Like my title states, I believe that this album is underappreciated. 

Yes, most fans dislike this album. Yes, the members of this band (especially Ozzy, if you need proof, read his autobiography) do not look back on this album/period fondly. Regardless, this album does not sound bad.

I will admit that the album may not be as good as the band's previous work, but it still sounds like a Black Sabbath production and album. The addition of keyboard synthesizers do seem to expand on the bands sound while adding to Sabbath's "darker" sound that they are known for. Also, let us not forget how the band had experimented and even used some synthesizer work on their previous albums. Looking back, one could also view the addition of the synthesizers as "being ahead of their time" or even "pioneers", since much of the next decades work (including metal and even Ozzy Osbourne's solo work) included keyboard synthesizers.

Also, the bands performance is still great. There is still the signature "dark" guitar work of Iommi throughout the album. Geezer's ant-establishment lyrics (which they have had in all of their albums) is well-represented, along with his bass. Ozzy's vocals, even though he was losing interest in the band, and was looking to form a new one, are actually just as good on this album as the earlier ones. Bill Ward's drums keep perfect time, cause the album to sound great (as always), and even his vocals, as represented in the track, "It's Alright", are rather good. Lastly, as stated before, the addition of the keyboard synthesizer work complements and adds to the overall feel and sound of the album.

There are also other reasons as to why this album is underappreciated. First for many fans, they did not care for the direction that the band seemed to be going. This is understood, for it is of personal taste. Second, it is well known that all of the band members (not only Mr. Osbourne) have admitted to having addiction problems, and at this time in their career led to many difficulties in this (and especially the next- Never Say Die!) album. Again as stated before, there is also Ozzy Osbourne's lack of interest in making this album due to his addiction problems, and looking to start another band with other musicians. Therefore, it only makes sense why some fans, and the band do not look at this album favourably.

Regardless of the problems stated above, the expansion on the sound and solid work from the band's members still make this an album worth listening to and an underappreciated work by Black Sabbath. This is especially evident in the fact that regardless of the problems that the band was going through, they were still able to come together and make a decent album together. This is proof of true talent, and one of the reasons why this band is considered on of the greatest in rock and roll. Even at their worst they were still better than others.

While basically a various artist driven answer by AFM Records to the longstanding success that Frontiers Records and Magnus Karlsson have enjoyed of late, Wolfpakk has proven a tenacious beast that rivals and even surpasses both parties' various projects in terms of output and gathering up an impressive who is who of vocalists and guitarists to project their music into the proverbial stratosphere. The only area in which they've lagged a bit behind their rivals has been in terms of converting the wide array of guest talent into a unified sound that can pass for a veritable full length album rather than a de fact VA compilation under another name. However, with the recent unleashing of their fourth studio effort, Voss, Sweeney and all the rest have managed to hit pay dirt in the unified sound department with Wolves Reign, largely by anchoring the core stylistic inclination of the whole into something a bit more of a consistently power metal mold. To be clear, the variety of elements that are employed to cater to the respective strengths of each vocalist are still present, but from one song to the next, the balance of atmosphere and impact has hit that consistent sweet spot needed to have a unified whole.

In essence, what Michael Voss has accomplished with his songwriting and his guitar/bass contributions to the lion's share of these songs is emulate the strict stylistic template of Karlsson, complete with a consistent keyboard backdrop on the entirety of the album and a generally faster pace, all while putting a bit more of a traditional heavy metal twist on it to keep it from being a full on carbon copy of either Free Fall or The Ferrymen. The massive opening fanfare of a power metal anthem "Falling", featuring the smooth melodic vocal handiwork of one of Germany's less remembered 80s icons Claus Lessmann of Bonfire fame, could almost be an outtake from one of Free Fall's album save for the riff work being a bit more rocking and stripped down. The faster driving brilliance of "No Remorse" takes things into more overt power metal territory, a fitting context for former At Vance powerhouse Oliver Hartmann, who sadly has been out of the metal world in favor of hard rock for quite a while, yet also starts on a lullaby-like keyboard note during the intro, yet another unsubtle nod to Magnus' handiwork. Even the anthem featuring ex-Grim Reaper front man Steve Grimmet "Scream Of The Hawk" ventures dangerously close to Free Fall territory, sporting some fancy riff work and a strongly Helloween-tinged speeder of a chorus section.

The same brand of occasional world music gimmickry that occasionally reared its head on the previous studio album is not absent from this album either, though given the more atmospheric character and driving melodic brilliance of the arrangement, fits into the equation a lot more smoothly. The cruising, rock-infused beast of a nod to Native American history "Blood Brothers", featuring the iconic pipes of Saxon's Biff Byford no less, see occasional chants indicative of a jamboree dance mixed in with the crunchy riff work, yet also manages to sound pretty close to something that Saxon could have thrown onto one of their last 4 or 5 albums. Similarly, the guitar solo segment handled by Night Ranger and ex-Ozzy shred master Brad Gillis is nothing sort of riveting, going so far as to rival a typical Jon Petrucci excursion. Not to be outdone, rival 80s icon and Pretty Maids vocalist Ronnie Atkins ends up lending his talents to this album's token epic "Mother Earth", which is among the more mellow and vocally oriented numbers to come in an 8 minute package. It has more of a semi-ballad rooted rock anthem feel to it, which is further accented by some sugary melodic lead work courtesy of Jen Majura, and fleeting hints of Egyptian/Middle-Eastern inspired music that hints at a slight Rainbow/Axel Rudi Pell influence.

Though this style of album has become a dime a dozen between the ever-expanding number of projects hiring auspicious vocal and guitar mercenaries to lend their respective credibility, not to mention an ongoing fascination with rock-infused heavy metal that has been heightened by a number of prominent projects such as The Unity and Serious Black due to the ongoing game of musical chairs in the European metal scene, this is a strong offering that definitely deserves at least as much consideration as the rest. It's a slight cut above what Wolfpakk has fielded in the past, not to mention a boon for guitar enthusiasts who wonder what it would sound like to hear the likes of Brad Gillis, Chris Holmes and George Lynch lending their shredding skills to something more along the lines of a power metal album. There are few in the way of dull moments apart from maybe the sappy ballad "Tomorrowland", and despite relying upon a very orthodox songwriting formula that only occasionally breaks out of the typical verse/chorus mold, is a highly entertaining and engaging listen that will definitely have staying power beyond the first and second time through.

Angel Sword's debut Rebels Beyond the Pale was a diamond-studded masterpiece, blustering onto the scene with the oft claimed and seldom delivered boast that they sounded like an 80's metal band. They did the unthinkable by not only penning an authentic treatise on the subject, but in an astoundingly unique way. Vocal harmonies sounded like a barbershop quartet of biker demons, guitar solos gushed with emotion despite their inherent simplicity; it was like Motörhead and Manilla Road wedded in unholy matrimony. Could Neon City possibly improve upon this formula?

...I personally don't think so, but keep in mind I'm a helplessly addicted speed freak. Try as I might, I never found Neon City quite as captivating as Rebels Beyond the Pale, due primarily to its more weighty, pensive approach to songwriting. Sure, there are a few hot tamales like 'Evil Eye' thrown in, but overall this album seems a bit shy to flex their muscles anywhere but their own mirror. I think Cirith Ungol's One Foot in Hell is an apt comparison, though one that fails to paint the complete picture due to the friggin' werewolf behind the microphone.

Jerry Razors is a baritone beast as always: there's so much grizzled machismo in his voice, I can almost smell the bacon on his breath. It's a raspy howl that may at first may seem a bit austere and one-dimensional, but the notes he's able to reach and harmonies he's able to effectively spearhead sound like Solid Snake after opera lessons. 'Starlight Shadow' begins with a fairly humdrum bass-driven gallop, though it's quickly dominated by dazzlingly high alto registers from Jerry. Before you know it, he's delved into an aphotic baritone that reaches lower pitches than most locomotive engines.

This infernal bellow leads the charge for most every layered chorus; a technique strikingly similar to what's used throughout Heavy Load's Stronger than Evil, not to mention countless unsung USPM greats like Glacier's self-titled EP. But for those of us who have shamelessly air guitared to 'Run with the Devil' or 'Devil in Disguise' (that was unintentional), you may be a bit disappointed to find how inert Neon City can seem sometimes. (Get it? Because neon is an inert gas. That one was intentional). 

This goes back to my previous point: It's clear Angel Sword have a real knack for enchanting melodies far more effusive and emotional than they have any right to be. It seems to me they have intentionally distanced themselves from bloodthirsty speed metal in order to explore the full potential of these slower, artsier avenues. Which may remind you, almost uncertainly unfavorably, of Enforcer's Zenith. The moseying harmonies of Neon City feels significantly less contrived than Zenith, yet in a contextual sense, the similarity is almost uncanny. If you yearned for another high voltage onslaught like Rebels Beyond the Pale could offer you with 'Lords of Thunder' or 'Lightning Runners', you may be a teensy bit underwhelmed by the mid-tempo grooves of Neon City.

However, these grooves are still tremendously well-written, and the caked-on mood and atmosphere are very much carried over from previous affairs. If it seemed like I was unusually hard on this album, it's only because Rebels Beyond the Pale was such a goddamn masterpiece. You should listen to it, you should listen to this album too, and you should ignore how abruptly this review ends.

Still cold, still old, but that doesn’t stop Catamenia from throwing another one at us the very next year. I think they’re realizing now that keyboards are quickly becoming an old tactic, but this time they’re actually handling it with stronger leads (as opposed to sticking with the formula and hoping for the best like on the last album). What I dislike the most about this album is how messy it sounds – like a blizzard in a land where everything was just cold, not attacked by a snowstorm.

This is the last album with the original vocalist, who does the same high shrieks and tired growls. His shrieks / screams always sound great, and here I’d say they’re at their peak since it sounds like someone slit his throat. His growls aren’t really all that great, but they’re still a nice addition. Sometimes he’ll do some pretty lame yelling with a back-up clean vocalist – please excuse this vocal style because it has no place here. 

There are considerably less keys, which means no more abundant enchanting background notes or magical keyboard solos. Nay, the album comprises of more refined riffs; they take on a very melodic and optimistic approach, much like Eternal Tears Of Sorrow (but less focused sounding). The guitar tone is chilly as ice in your very hand, and while the rupturing tenor isn’t completely back, it does give off this bright mind-set. The older albums were dark and rather gothic, but these new ones, like I foretold in the earlier reviews, really aim more towards power metal-esque leads, rising to the challenge of evildoers and poseurs alike. It’s trait that hasn’t yet been refined, but will characterize Catamenia’s music to come.

Bass still manages to grumble along unopposed, though it may have a harder time doing it. For one, everything sounds very loud; from the eclectic leads to Mika’s banshee screams to the cymbals crashing – its just one big chaotic blizzard. Regardless, the drum kit is fucked sideways – it must have been a production balance fuck-up, because the crash cymbal is way too loud. It has the ability to drown out nearly everything, and hear it does so to a good half of the instruments taking part. Awkward, since the toms are relatively quieter and the drum bass is much quieter. I won’t doubt the man’s bashful playing, but the drummers of Catamenia haven’t had a damn good production job since Morning Crimson.

Here is where I start to get confused calling Catamenia black metal, even if they are a “melodic” variant of such. This sounds more like straight up power metal with harsh vocals than it does melodic black metal. The screams fit well with the black metal, but go tell that to Kalmah and Eternal Tears Of Sorrow while you’re at it. Shit, they’re all Finnish bands, so why not group them all together anyway. Anyway, this marks the end of the band’s second phase, and isn’t it lovely that they ended on a positive note?

Get ready for a power groove extravaganza as Dagoba shoves the gates of the abyss open wide on their second full-length album, "What Hell Is About", offering up a churning, wicked mass of volatile Metal Armageddon. This French quartet impresses as being monstrously heavy, with the twelve tracks that make up the record bearing a steely, industrial edge. From the first note of the roaring title cut to the gunshot climax of "The White Guy (Suicide)", Dagoba delivers everything that a headbanger could expect from this style of music and then some. 

After forming in 2000, Dagoba focused on crafting material for their debut EP for a solid year, honing their all-out assault to a fine edge. Their six song introductory EP, "Release The Fury"saw the light of day in November of 2001 to wide critical acclaim. Hitting the studio in early 2003 with producer Doug Chang, Dagoba formulated their full-length, self-titled debut record which saw the light of day later that summer, that precursor setting the stage for heavy touring and a buildup of experience culminating in the factually substantial sounds that you will find on "What Hell Is About". 

Although influences such as Fear Factory, Pantera and Machine Head may be culled from the group’s enormous, powerful sound, Dagoba has taken these inspirations as their own and in doing so, tracks such as the violent yet tuneful "Die Tomorrow (...What If You Should?)" and the infectiously slamming cut, "The Fall Of Men" rage with an abundantly savage, bitter aggression. 

Launching into a harsh, resonating bark during "The Man You’re Not", vocalist Shawter proves that he can stand toe to toe with vocalists such as Anselmo and Bell. The frontman also provides the programming and samples that do much to enhance the band’s poignant Metal attack, rounding out the overall sound of the music without taking away one ounce of its brutal, muscular persuasion. 

Meanwhile, "Cancer" displays a different face of the group, being no less intense but coming across in a manner that would make Rob Flynn blush. Here we can ascertain that the sound of Dagoba is certainly multifaceted, and the shifting of gears makes for an alluring diversion. Elsewhere, the interlude "042104" makes for a great segue into the hammering, in-your-face anxiety of "Morphine - The Apostle Of Your Last War", an inventive and well-arranged foray into brash aural architecture. 

In the final analysis, "What Hell Is About" is a domineering, mammoth slab of twisted steel that deserves both high praise as well as substantial recognition as being a distinct advancement of this particular style of heavy Metal.

Katatonia is my favorite band and it’s always fun to examine their releases in depth. 1993’s “Dance of December Souls” is the band’s debut, a raw piece of music somewhere between death/doom metal and black/doom metal. It’s a highly regarded and influential album in both subgenres.

At this point, Katatonia was a band that relied a lot on its youthful vigor and passion. The sorrow on “Dance of December Souls” is extremely apparent in every aspect, from the heartwrenching guitar melodies to Jonas Renkse’s tortured screams. Masterminds Jonas and Anders were not even in their 20's at this point and do their best to create a dismal feeling of sorrow.

And Katatonia certainly succeeds. After a short intro, the album opens up with “Gateways of Bereavement”, which goes for the throat right away. Slow, brooding power chords linger and support the vocals. Jonas screams his guts out, and with this approach it’s not surprising that his voice couldn’t take extreme vocals in the long run. Much of the music is what became Scandinavian extreme doom metal; a mix of early melodic death metal sounds and the heaviness from traditional-sounding doom metal.

The Scandinavian scene was arguably at its most creative at this point, forming genre blueprints still valid to this day. "Dance of December Souls" is extremely important in that sense. Just like 1996's "Brave Murder Day", this laid down many foundations for future death/doom metal bands. I believe this album was also very instrumental in shaping the more depressive forms of black metal. The way Jonas spews out the lyric lines on this album reminds me quite a lot of what was to come in the more negative forms of black metal.

But beyond its importance, how does this fit into the Katatonia discography? Well, it certainly has many recognizable traits. A Katatonia trademark already present on “Dance of December Souls” are the guitar melodies. Just like on most of their material, there are many guitar moves that are as memorable and emotional as they are simple. “Without God” and “In Silence Enshrined” have especially brilliant lines.

It really is the guitars that drive everything on this album. The mood and execution of the guitars range from darkly nihilistic to absolutely dreamy. The strong shoegaze influences hadn't quite become a part of their sound yet, but there are some very moody acoustic and clean guitar sections on here. Frontman Jonas Renkse plays the drums, and as a result the beats are extremely simple and mere support to the guitars.

However, an album as youthful and passionate is almost bound to have its downsides. And it does. Some of the compositions are massive and not that fluently written. There are many epic sections and shifts between distorted and clean guitars. Some of the transitions are not particularly smooth. The shorter songs, like “Without God”, feel more fluent and compact. It stands in strong contrast to Katatonia’s clean vocal material where the songwriting is central and absolutely meticulous.

There are also some stylistic jumps that don't mold all too well. The album has traces of death metal, black metal, doom metal and even traditional metal. Sometimes it sounds angry, sometimes dreamy, sometimes almost triumphant. There's not really enough consistency, beyond the main objective of being very depressive. I think the ambitions were simply set a bit too high, considering how new Katatonia was at the time.

Despite its flaws, it’s hard to overstate how important this album is for the extreme side of the doom metal genre. It paved the way for death/doom and later developments like depressive black metal and blackgaze. It’s my least favorite full-length from my favorite band, but still a damn solid piece of early death/doom metal. I am very impressed by how they could achieve something like this so early. You can already tell that Katatonia was going places.

Originally written for deathdoom.com

Black metal is highly influenced and inspired by nature. The Norwegian scene played a significant role in setting the association of black metal with frozen landscapes, forests, and mountains. Aridus, which literally means “dry” or “parched,” breaks this stereotype and shows that the genre can take as much inspiration from dark, barren deserts as the snowy winters of Scandinavia. 

This is the first full-length from Wolves in the Throne Room bassist Galen, and he does an impressive performance here by being the sole writer and instrumentalist behind this album. Fans of Wolves should not expect a mimicry of that band. Interestingly enough, Wolves in the Throne Room is from the Pacific Northwest of America, and it seems that they too are influenced by the natural beauty of their surroundings. Aridus, though, is much different. It’s clear that Galen is summoning the desert environment of New Mexico (where he is from) to create this music. The tracks mostly feature the tremolo-picked guitar power chords that is typical of black metal, but Galen also layers eerie melodies on top of these riffs in many places. While the songwriting is not totally unique, the songs create a dark atmosphere that makes the album enjoyable during a solitary night. Additionally, I find myself drawn in by the several drum-beat changes that occur throughout. The songs “Aridus” and “Serpent Moon” demonstrate this well through their use of alternating kick and snare type drumming that refreshes the song and encourages the listener to headbang along. On the other hand, “The Infinite Corridor” is the most unique since it is comprised primarily of acoustic/clean guitar picking while a bass guitar and drums create a background melody. Some kind of flute or wind instrument can be heard faintly here as well, lending the track an almost Native American vibe. Perhaps Galen can incorporate this more in future recordings to give Aridus a more unique or original sound.

All in all, this album is worth the chance for any black metal fans who want to hear something inspired by desert, as opposed to snowy, landscapes. Even though the album doesn’t stray too far from the usual black metal formula, it’s still a good listen and shows promise for what Aridus has to offer in the future.

Good evening thrash fans and welcome to what should prove to be another notch in the spike studded thrash metal leather belt of sincerity.  Tommy Victor and co. are back with a vengeance and the Power of the Damager is their newest testament to add to the already obvious resurgence of thrash metal.

After hearing the dreaded Scorpio Rising nearly 3 years agao, I was somewhat reluctant to believe that Prong were ever going to "ge it right" ever again.  Wondering, if they would simply fade away and be remembered for their late eighties and early nineties calssics such as Beg To Differ and Prove You Wrong.  Then from out of nowhere Prong re-emrge with this pulse pounding, stripped down, raw, bare-boned, in your face NY styled thrash metal album ala POTD!

Right from the get-go, the first obvious improvement is the stellar production, which gives this album a bottom end which to me sounds similar to the crunchy bottom end of the newest Exodus album.  That's a good thing...Tommy Victor has obviously picked up a few tips from Al Jourgensen over the last few years.  Another immediate improvement is the riffs.  Tommy has finally gone back to his roots and penned some classic styled riffs that will leave all thrash enthusiasts alike with a smirk of contention on their faces when listening to this album.  The bass guitar is now being handled by former touring guitar player Monte Pitman, and although not extemely prominent in the mix, the bottom is heard and the effectiveness shines through beautifully.  As for the drumming, well, no one will ever be able to outplay Ted Parsons as a Prong skinsman, but at least were back to the double bass runs and some pretty kick as fills from time to time.  The drumming is also back up to par.

Songwise, Tommy hasn't re-invented himself in my opinion, but rather simply reverted back to the old faithful formula that worked so gracefully back in the thrash metal hayday.  This  album has no real weak tracks and nothing that will really standout as being plodding or boring, but I will say that Looking For Them, the title track, and The Banishment are by far my favorites and will most definately be heralded as classic thrash metal efforts by critics alike.

Overall, this may not be the best release of  2007, but it certainly is a sign of positive things to come in the near future, not only for Prong, but to the thrash metal scene as a whole.  Thrash Metal is back with a vengeance and Prong have carved their niche.

Here we are at a classic when it comes to Bucketheadland, Pike number 5 - Look Up There, a fan favorite.  When it comes to Buckethead's Pike series, there are three that you'll see the fans raving about:  Pike 51 - Claymation Courtyard, Pike 65 - Hold Me Forever, and this one.  In my opinion, this is the weakest of those three by a massive margin.  This album contains two long songs that are both big, involved and relaxing guitar solos.  I totally understand why this album is so adored.  It is a very soothing and relaxing album, but that is really all it is.  The simplicity and repetition of the album hurts it rather than helps it in the long run.  All that being said, this is still a great Pike.  Those who enjoy long and freely moving guitar solos are in for a treat.  

The first song of this album is dubbed "Golden Eyes".  This track is a ten minute long number with sweet, melodic leads circling about on top of a set of electronic drums.  The electronic drums are quite foreign upon first listen, but they actually give a little bit of additional pizzazz to the song that sets it outside of the box.  The soloing is calm and active, with a subtle wah effect to make things a little more interesting.  Occasionally Buckethead engages a phaser that gives that classic jet engine sound.  The solo feels improvised, rarely ever repeating the same lick twice.  Those who love long and thought-evoking guitar solos will like this track, and love the album.  "Golden Eyes" is inferior to the title track, however, but it is still a very enjoyable song.

The other song on this Pike is the title track that clocks in at a whopping twenty one minutes in length.  This song features more natural sounding drums, and a softer feel than the first song.  It begins with soft, gently strummed melodies and chords that go through a few different progressions.  The song picks up to carry on for about 19 more minutes of guitar soloing with the same soft chord progression going on underneath it.  The soloing is beautiful, and it ranges from loud and aggressive to soft and passionate.  The drums will change intensity to match the aggression of the guitar, making for a more diverse track than it would seem.  Overall, the song is a great and soothing listen.  I still, however, find it to be too long.  I don't know how many people can take a 21 minute guitar solo, thankfully it is a really beautiful one.  

The musical realm that Big B achieves on this Pike is quite unique when compared to a lot of his others.  Even though Buckethead is no stranger to long guitar solos and peaceful melodies, the album has a rather down-to-earth and mellow feel that makes it a soothing experience.  Even though it is not one of my favorite Pikes, I find myself coming back to it a lot, as it is very calming and sometimes genuinely beautiful.  Those who enjoy losing themselves in long, thoughtful, expressive passages of music must check this out.  It is easy to see why some Buckethead fans consider this to be the very best.   

Once the title track finishes, that's really it.  The album is nice and relaxing, but it lacks any dynamics beyond this.  This is best taken as a simple set of guitar soloing, those who are expecting wacky experimentation of some of his other efforts or the serene heavenly beauty of A Real Diamond in the Rough won't get that here.  This is one of Buckethead's more simplistic releases, and it is a great album to calm you down.  Those who are interested in hearing Buckethead's work should consider giving this a try, it is a great introduction to his mastery as a guitar player.  Do keep in mind that he has way better stuff than this.

Sit down children, it’s time to explore myth and legend galore in the brand new collection of tales from eclectic prog bassist Mike LePond of Symphony X. Silent Assassins, the outfit usually linked with LePond’s name releases their sophomore full length album, Pawn And Prophecy, to follow up the immense self titled debut that came in 2014. One might call the outfit a supergroup, consisting of four talented veterans to semi-veterans within the American heavy metal scene.

Aside from LePond, there is fellow Symphony X alumni Michael Romeo on guitars and keys, vocalist Alan Tecchio of Hades and Watchtower fame and guitarist “Metal” Mike Chlasciak known for his time with Halford and his own band Metal Mike. Obviously with two quarters of the band stemming from Symphony X, including the dominant sounding LePond himself, the sound will be reminiscent, yet still different in approach. Perhaps not as prone to progressive elements, the music rather sticks to the Manowar school of heavy power metal, with progressive touches strewn as icing on the already formidable power cake. 

The album basically picks up where its predecessor left off, but also cranks everything up the scale in terms of intensity, power and songwriting. Everything just feels like more, and in an entirely good sense. The heavy riff style turned up a notch, Tecchio’s vocal lines and delivery turned up a notch, and the pummeling bass? Forget about it. LePond bulldozers right over everything in his path, delivering heaviness with precise marksmanship in tracks like massive opener 'Masters Of The Hall', and tender emotion with great passion in surprisingly potent ballad 'The Mulberry Tree', which with a few listens rises to the top of the litter in terms of favorite tracks, with its slight folky tunes and rhythmic flow to go with the innate power of the vocals.

Tecchio carries great power in his vocal chords, and a very American style to his singing, and manages to sound completely his own and highly versatile to fit the various moods and styles present on 'Pawn And Prophecy' as he belts out high pitched screams to contrast the rhythmic mid range vocals that span the album. 

Unlike the previous album, not a track on here feels like filler; everything holds a high standard and every minute is justified. The only ‘perhaps’ to that would be the epic title track, closing the album off. Don’t get me wrong, the song is epic in every sense of the word, blending everything decent on the rest of the album and making it great; the prog elements, the intricate riffs and the heavy bass presence, along with lyrics evoking misty dawn on the highlands.

With a length spanning 20 minutes it sets the tone to beat for the next album, and the expectations high, as it marks the same kind of versatility that has spanned the entire album; 'I Am The Bull' begins with a lengthy bass solo that just screams of Joey DeMaio (Manowar), and the song picks up into something like Manowar meets Black Sabbath, straight out of the eighties. Then there are speedier numbers in 'Avengers Of Eden' and 'Hordes Of Fire' that shatter all resistance with simple, yet massive guitar licks and intricate bass lines. With Pawn And Prophecy, Silent Assassins have released an unexpectedly strong and varied album, one that is sure to be remembered, and for the foreseeable future, is likely to set the tone for American power metal.

Standout tracks: Hordes Of Fire, The Mulberry Tree, Pawn And Prophecy

Got to admit I hadn’t ever really paid attention to the later Metal Church albums. I’d heard some songs here and there and thought they were fine but not really that great. But in the wake of Mike Howe’s passing, I felt like I wanted to give ‘em more of a chance and I’m pretty glad I did.

Damned If You Do is Howe’s swansong, I guess – the most recent album the band has put out back in 2018. It’s pretty much a stodgy, meat and potatoes listen, without much to really make it stand out from the pack save for the fact that this is a legendary fucking band and Howe’s pipes grace it like molten goddamn steel. There aren’t really any surprises here, from the chugging riffage and militaristic rhythms and the bitter, biting lyrical spewings. It’s as straightforward a metal album as you’ll ever hear – maybe more conservative than I usually go for. But as I hadn’t really been listening to their albums prior to this one, it doesn’t seem too worn out to me. And the band attacks the material with conviction, which makes it worth hearing.

Maybe Howe’s vocals are part of it. Dude was out of the music business for decades and I guess this preserved his soulful, raging howls like in cryogenic technology, awakened now as if no time had passed. He just has a shitload of conviction and sells these songs like the most talented and wily door to door salesman of all time, never deviating from his patented gritty sneer but packing a surprising amount of emotion into it. I can believe he means it.

The songs are all fairly consistent with no weak points, and the shorter runtime overall makes it a punchy, digestible listen as compared to the preceding album. The title track is a classic-style riff ‘n chorus barn burner and “The Black Things” is a cool tune too. My favorites come in the middle of the album with the three-song run of the thrashy “Guillotine,” the hammering “Rot Away” and the somber epic “Into the Fold” – these are all just fucking solid songs.

If the album has a failure it’s just that there’s nothing on here to live up to the epic songs they used to do like “Anthem to the Estranged,” “Badlands” or “Waiting for a Savior.” This album just drives steadily down the middle. It could have really been elevated if they’d thrown in something more epic and experimental. It's a failure purely of expectation and legacy, so I'm not really sure it's even much of one at the end of the day. But as an AC/DC-level consistent rocking listen, Damned If You Do is worth a listen.

He's burning through the distant mist of Earth
To find what's missing in his soul
Into the blinding light, eternity
The rim of hell he will control

RIP, Mike.

album: Loot, Shoot, Electrocute / The Temple of Set
texto:
As reviews of split releases are only posted on the bands site of your choice, I will of course only review the Pungent Stench side here.  There is only one complaint, namely that if you’re collecting Pungent Stench, there’s nothing rare here. This is a just a song from their album “Masters Of Moral”.

The whole artistic concept behind  “Masters Of Moral” was superb but I will refrain myself for now (elaboration will follow in my review of the full length) and focus on this song. When Pungent Stench reunited I was afraid the band would focus on their last previous album “Club Mondo Bizarre” and write some groovy stuff. I was in for a surprise! 

“Loot, Shoot, Electrocute” is nothing less than fast & furious death metal. Most notible are the tighness of the drums compared to their early works and the (slightly) more complex riffs. Not that they’re a technical death metal band here. Far from it! The main ingredient still is brutal death metal. The song is fast, catchy and simply said pure death metal fun.

The lyrics are rather generic for a band of their reputation but the song and vocal performance are so good, it doesn’t actually matter for a change. No use getting this release though. Just get off your ass and go get “Masters Of Moral”!

So, 90 points for the song, 20 points deduction for lacking ‘rare’ material and 10 points bonus for that briliant band photo!

I'm going to start by saying that if you were expecting Demons & Wizards to one-up their first album with this, you're going to be disappointed. With that out of the way... this is a damn good album.

This is a Power Metal album more or less in the vein of the previous one, and what it lacks in originality, it makes up for in sheer ass-kickingness. It is generally not as heavy, featuring much more acoustic guitar, but the softness is used to great effect, and the heavy songs seem even heavier by contrast. There is a noticeable lean toward older Blind Guardian and Iced Earth in the musical style.

Lyrically, the first album just blows this out of the water. There's no "Gallows Pole" here, there are really no lyrically outstanding songs at all. This is pretty much on par with most Power Metal. The vocals are the same as they were on the first release, which is definitely not a bad thing.

Standout tracks include Beneath These Waves, a reasonably heavy and mid-to-slow -paced song that brings to mind Blind Guardian's early releases; Wicked Witch, a ballad that actually knows when to end, as well as having good music, lyrics, and vocals throughout; and Dorian, which is relatively fast-paced and quite heavy, sounding like a cross between early Iced Earth and early Blind Guardian. The cover of the Immigrant Song does the original song justice, if it is not slightly better.

I would recommend this album to anyone who liked the first album, as well as anyone else who likes any non-Italian/Finnish Power Metal at all.

Germany's Purgatory have been around since 1993, and in all those years they have unleashed various full lengths that were not always consistent in style. On their first albums they were your typical mid 90's death/grind band, Deicide meets Impetigo meets Morbid Angel, a recipe they held on until 2004's "Luciferianism". On that album the grindcore influence had to make place for more sturdy, traditional death metal, kinda Vader meets later Behemoth, and this until the album I'm reviewing here.

Here the band's sound has taken on a darker, slightly more atmospheric edge and it actually really suits them. Sound wise Purgatory have gone deeper into the Behemoth/Belphegor realms of extreme metal (with dashes of Nile thrown in) but they also reference the more underground breed of black/death metal bands like Nexul or Lvcifyre. The band has pulled up a utterly massive wall of sound here, where the percussion collides with the menacing guitar tone and the brutish vocals to earth shattering effect. Sporadic slower, heavier parts have been worked into the compositions while swathes of haunting keyboards and spoken word parts help establish the atmosphere where the band without doubt was aiming for. Unfortunately, sometimes even to undesired comical effect. The words "let my people go", spoken not entirely without accent, in "The Curse of Samhain, pt. II" brought back memories of an episode of "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air". The malevolent nature of the music let's you forget such minor flaws in an instant though.

Please allow me to make a mention of the stark black and white artwork and layout as well. It supplements the music well and the engravings in the booklet set the mood perfectly for the pulverizing music contained within. 

With this album, the band have reinvented themselves and fit effortlessly into the current state of underground extreme metal and this without coming across as forced in any way. That's no mean feat and there are plenty of other bands of Purgatory's generation that can not make that same claim. Hell, there's even way younger bands that can't even make that claim!

Malvery's first demo is similar to their only full-length release, "Mortal Entrenchment in Requiem". It still contains the very desperate and sad emotions, and it's no surprise Amer LeChâtier committed suicide shortly after the first album.

The first song is just an intro to set the tone, and it's very desperate as usual, with threathening keyboard melodies and so on. Délectation Morose starts off with Amer taking out all his thoughts, and they're soon accompanied by a guitar riff and some brutal drums. The next 3 songs are still as hateful, accompanied by excellent riffs, agressive drums and growled vocals, and trust me, they're probably the harshest vocals you'll ever hear. It also contains a live song, D'Illusion En Suicide. The demo ends with the same threatening keyboards melodies as the intro - giving a very melancholic, sad, and desperate tone. 

Very raw black metal - a keeper.

Clownhammer is a groove metal band that incorporates nu metal elements in their sound.  You might think that it’s a bad thing.  It actually isn’t a bad thing.  They are surprisingly not bad.  I expected them to be a lousy band.  Their self-titled album is actually good.  Clownhammer has a lot of potential.  They sound like they’re influenced by groove metal and Korn.  There’s no over the top songs on this album.  The songs are pretty much mid-paced.  The songs aren’t really explosive on this album.

This album starts off with a music box playing Pop Goes The Weasel.  Then the actual music starts.  Sean Baker and Alfred Riojas do some fantastic guitar work on the first track titled Eastside Story.  It’s a pretty solid song.  It features a solid guitar solo.  I didn’t expect the guitar solo that sounded solid in this song.  It comes out of nowhere.  The guitarists sounds like they’re influenced by Korn.  There’s definitely some strong Korn vibes in the songs Everyone Needs to See, Hypocrite and Soul Ambition.  The riffs sound like Korn riffs, but heavier on those songs and on other songs.  The guitar work sounds super impressive on Down with the Clown, which is an instrumental.  It is not a cover of Insane Clown Posse’s Down with the Clown.  It would be pretty hilarious if they did cover that song.

Bill Jones has a unique sounding voice.  He has good clean vocals.  He does a bit of growling with his vocals.  He sounds pretty rough at times.  His vocals are really good on Eastside Story, Soul Ambition, and Streets.  Streets has the best lyrics.  It’s about how the streets are tough and how the streets have claimed lives.  It’s somewhat of a deep song.  It’s super catchy.  I listened to it a bunch of times.  At times, he sounds like he’s influenced by Jonathan Davis of Korn.  He might be influenced by Corey Taylor of Slipknot.  He’s not trying to emulate any of these vocalists.

How about the bass on this album?  The bass by David Donigan is good.  There’s nothing really noteworthy about it.  You don’t hear the bass that well in any of the songs.  The vocals and other instruments overpower the bass.  How about the drums?  Clint Sabon doesn’t do anything technical nor does he do anything that’s mind-blowing.  He keeps things heavy and simple.  He might be influenced by David Silveria of Korn.  There’s some Korn vibes with the drumming.  Sabon doesn’t go super crazy with the drumming.

I tried to look for more info on Clownhammer and there’s unfortunately not that much info.  Sean Baker has been touted to be this guitar virtuoso, I do remember reading that.  I would say that’s a fair assessment of Baker.  He goes all out at the end of the album.  If you are open to groove metal with nu metal elements, you will probably like this album.  I’m not so big on nu metal, but I was pretty shocked how they blend in nu metal elements with heavy metal and groove metal.  Could they start a new trend?  It’s quite possible.  People in 10 years from now may discover this album by accident and then go for Clownhammer’s sound.

album: Fornetes Folm / His Crown Grows from His Skull
texto:
Úlfarr, maybe the most prominent representatives of the honestly speaking not overly prominent Cumbrian black metal scene, are no friends of regular albums or double full-lengths. Instead, they put a hybrid of album and EP on the table. That’s fine, 48 minutes in total are a good duration and the EP is not just a nice addition. Okay, it’s acoustic intro is completely useless – why does an EP with three songs need an intro? But the following two songs are a total disaster of the best kind. The “Transilvanian Hunger” aesthetics reappear. Massive vehemence, rigorous high speed and a voice which sounds as ugly, raw and non-conform as possible. It’s almost a shame that these two musical atom bombs spread their terror only for five minutes in total. Nevertheless, two things are obvious. The EP follows a remarkably different approach than the first eight songs and their integration enriches the entire output.

“Fornetes Folm”, the regular full-length, sets the focus on more sophisticated song patterns. Unfortunately, the single parts of the tracks do not go hand in hand every now and then. Speedy sections develop a powerful dynamic, but spoken words parts, only accompanied by a few sluggish guitar tones, appear like an alien. Due to the fact that they show up and the beginning (“Alarūna“) or the end (“Hildeleoma”, “Moonskin”, “The Cold Council of Old Shadow”) of the songs, they do not cause too much damage, but the intention behind them remains unclear. On the other hand, the songs are not too complex and whenever the band rushes through the wasteland of terror one can enjoy the dynamic and a solid-to-good (or even very good) quality of the guitar lines. This and the fact that Úlfarr do follow their own formula without copying other band’s style makes “Fornetes Folm” to an album which is definitely worth listening. Of course, the horde does not reinvent the wheel, the way to ignite a fire has also already been discovered and the recipe for a good burger has already been written as well. But there is no role model that the band is obviously leaning on. That’s cool.

Sometimes the utterly throaty vocals appear almost as a parody, sometimes the guitar lines storm forward without a clearly defined aim, but usually the band is able to bring its musical visions into a useful form. Stylistically, it follows on from the last work “Orlegsceaft” and the production also does not differ a lot. The guitars and the voice dominate, the drums are not pappy or feeble per se, but only the snare finds its way to be heard. The bass guitar is – I would almost like to say naturally – is about as present as a bottle of schnapps and two cigarettes at the breakfast of a well-educated upper-class kid. Nobody’s perfect, but the strict, dense and merciless guitars make up for this – in terms of both the mix and the leads. Perhaps it is true that a higher degree of individual features would have been a good idea. On the other hand, the album works as a whole and this is doubtlessly a positive fact. Thus, the band has taken another little step into the right direction. The hybrid release consolidates Úlfarr’s dictatorial, apodictic way of proceeding. Moreover, the material’s quality is slightly better than it was the last time, at least in my humble opinion. Cumbria has very inspiring nature, north-west England is certainly worth a trip. But as long as you or me do not have the money and / or the time for this, we can find solace in the little piece of Cumbria that this full-length / EP offers us.

I am just a casual progressive metal fan, having used to listen to Dream Theater, Queensryche and Blind Guardian many ages ago (15 years ago or so), and my favorite Emperor album is Prometheus…, while also returning to Borknagar from time to time. My issue with this genre is usually in the intensity department, which the extreme metal manages to deliver without problems. However, The Thirteenth Sun is stuck somewhere in between, with hints of harshness and blackened edge, while also having the tendency to remain chill and dreamy. It is an interesting balance, but not without its flaws.

The one aspect I absolutely love about this album is the dynamics factor. Even if the tempo changes are a quintessential trait in progressive metal, these are easy highlights when transitioning from the more calm passages to the blackened tremolo-driven moments, with the double bass accentuating them. The rhythm section is very tight, with the drummer always complementing the atmosphere either with the said fast double bass, or with the heavy use of cymbals. The guitars go from clean, semi-acoustic riffs to palm muting, alarming chords and/or tremolos, always in line with the desired tempo. The result is a clever manipulation of the listener’s moods, going all out with the instrumentation in order to give him specific ones.

How many bands really do that, especially when using minor keys? Of course, the trick cannot work with the same effectiveness every time (it would have been boring otherwise); but when it does, it is a work of art. For me, tracks like Planes of Creation, The Universe Is Burning, and The Fabric of Time have the best dynamics and usage of the bands manipulation skills. The first song actually starts way to pretty for my taste, like an early Rush album, but it actually has a theatrical vocal duel between growler Hupogrammos from Dordeduh and screamer/clean singer Radu Barna, the bands vocalist. The second track mentioned has an even more atmospheric black metal vibe, with an eerie, astral sample, giving the impression not of solar creation, but of the solitude of space (it feels a bit phobic only when thinking about it), while the latter track seems to burst in a blast fest during the second half, even though it just teases with the listener, due to its intense nature.

The rest of the tracks do not cling on the blackened specter that much, being more dreamy and laid back. The intro has this cliché bass intro, which kind of turns me off every time, but as already stated, nothing is what it seems at first glance with this album. The outro in an instrumental that looks like a Borknagar worship track, interesting for its tribute, but quite vintage at the same time. The other two tracks are not as memorable, maybe because I was stolen by the more contrasting and/or familiar aspects from the other ones, and in time, they don’t hold that much. The same goes for the lyrical aspect that, while conceptual, is at worst, an afterthought, and at best, a secondary element, built on the much more developed and interesting instrumental one.

In the end, I truly recommend this album and this band for what Romania and more so, my hometown Brasov, has to offer in the metal department. It was one of the best metal albums from 2017 and it needs more exposure, especially considering the effort put in the songwriting. It isn’t flawless and I am not sure about the direction the band will take, as this album isn’t very clear on this matter (nor the Romanian metal scene in general, for that matter…), but one cannot find himself not enjoying this full length as a metalhead.

Begerith's unabashed lampooning of Behemoth's antediluvian trinkets of terror continues with the pretentiously confounding A.D.A.M. Down to the artwork, which emulates that hand-painted style purported on The Satanist, the comparisons continue, but to be fair these Poles continue to at least competently present this particularly venerable fusion of black and death metal. For sure there is no shortage of obtuse, Martian riffage feeding on atypical channels of dissonance, all rebuffed by the occasional bone-crunching death metal volley.

Speed isn't Begerith's strongest suit, but they instead lock into a stolid upper mid-paced gait that gives the riffs just enough breathing room to do some damage during the blasting intervals, and the occasional use of reasonably tasteful synths adds a flair of triumphant/epic flair befitting of the ancient subject matter presented. The more nimble cuts like "A.D.A.M. II" are real jackhammers, let down only slightly by the marginally muffled production, which while balanced, lacks low end regarding the drums. Guitars hold together during the tremolo bits and raze plenty of real estate when the occasional groove is called for - all perfectly audible and peerlessly performed. If anything, A.D.A.M. trumps its predecessor My Way to the Star... in that it offers more material and somehow feels more focused.

Bushuev's ragged howls are sepulchral and bite deep, espoused in that Nergal-esque choppy intonation we've come to expect. The biggest (and best) surprise for me personally was that the band didn't overplay the Middle-Eastern note progressions that bands aiming for this style so often bleed dry. It oftentimes sounds like a gimmick; a forced attempt at evoking a very particular set of mental images without the composition to actually warrant it - sort of like a way of cutting atmospheric corners.

The heavier, more death-metal influenced sections remind me of Finland's Gloria Morti at times, but with bands occupying such a densely-populated genre crossroads, comparisons rotate repeatedly throughout. Safe to say that Begerith have carved out a decent album with A.D.A.M. - mildly theatrical but never eschewing the basics in the name of pretense. An easy recommendation, especially since it is streaming on Bandcamp. A viable improvement and reason to keep an eye out for these fellas.

I finally pulled myself together to review this album. Live Invasion is Freedom Call's first live album, released in 2004 on SPV. I have all FC albums. Once I loved them a lot. Now I don't listen to them so often, but they are still good. Crystal Empire is my favourite. 

As a live album, the setlist on LI is PERFECT! (See below for a full listing.) OK, almost. I would prefer to trade Land of Light and Eyes of the World for Ages of Power and Over the Rainbow or Tears Falling. But other than that, every one of my favourite FC songs are there (except a few that probably wouldn't work so well live, like Pharao).

The performance is good from all sides (tho not exceptional). Especially kudos to Freedom Call for pulling off the vocal harmonies remarkably well. Backing vocals usually suck on live albums, but they are quite good on this one.

Production is OK. Drums are sort of too loud, and guitars and keyboards are too low. Especially the boards are often inaudible. Length is a very respectable 67 minutes. I dunno which songs to recommend as highlights, tho.

The special edition comes with a 37 minutes bonus disc featuring the entire Taragon EP, a special "story version" of Tears of Taragon and two new covers, namely Doctor Stein by Helloween and a song named Hiroshima that I don't know. 

The Taragon EP has four songs: Warriors of Light, Dancing with Tears in my Eyes, Heart of the Brave and Kingdom Come. DWTIME is a cover (Ultravox, I think), the rest are FC songs. Of all these especially Warriors of Light and Hiroshima are great.

Overall, I'll rate the album 80%. Excellent tracklist and good sound, and great bonus material.

Listening to this album, I expected Ethereal Shroud to be a group of at least three members but to my (very pleasant) surprise ES turns out to be the solo project of one Joe Hawker. For a second album, "They Became the Falling Ash" is a stupendous effort in layered atmospheric depressive blackened doom metal. It has many elements that should make it a great album: a distinctive ghostly ambience that heightens the moods and emotions expressed in the songs; a firm grasp of the types of melodies, riffs and sounds that produce an impending feeling of chaos and hysteria; good use of reverb and other effects; and a style and production that make the music monstrous. It does fall short of being great, and that's a pity - but it's better to strive for greatness, to approach making recordings as if each and every one of them is going to be your last and the only legacy of yours that you leave behind.

All three tracks on this album weigh in at a minimum 10 minutes and two of them reach beyond the 24-minute mark so you have some idea of the heights Hawker has turned his target sights towards. First track "Look Upon the Light" sets the tone for the rest of the recording to follow: it's a roller-coaster ride over hills and through dales of intense heightened emotion, shrill trilling tremolo guitars heralding the way, raging storms of bass grind, percussion ranging from blast-beat super-fast to emphatic crashes, and in the far background gruff crunching-rock vocals growling through lyrics of mass fiery ritual sacrifices. While this is a ginormous epic piece of dense layered guitar-distortion grind, I'd have liked the singing and the lyrics to be clearer, as the imagery in them is so vivid and worth emphasising in their own right. 

"Desperation Hymn" is not much more than an extension of the first track and again the vocals are deeply buried in murky reverb. Being squinched between two monster pieces, both of which bleed into it, and not having much of an identity of its own, this song deserves a different treatment to work as an effective interlude: a sharper sound, less reverberation and a bit less bombast perhaps.

"Echoes in the Snow" is a more melancholic and elegiac doom piece, and there is greater emphasis on melody and less on dense textured fierce tremolo guitar battery. Emotion is much more complex and expressive here. As with the previous two songs, the singing is shrouded in too much reverb though given the song's subject matter and its place in what is essentially a trilogy of songs, the vocals should be very wraith-like. The song's resolution is handled very gradually and delicately as death claims its victims and disperses their material being into dust. After the arduous journey through existential torment, the peace that follows when the album ends is serene indeed.

The whole album is hard-hitting and can be an exhausting experience over one hour but it does need to be heard in one sitting to be fully appreciated for what it is. The twists and turns and the laborious journey from one climax to the next in all three tracks trace the transition experienced as one passes from life through ritual sacrifice to death and dissolution, and the interrogation with God that takes place during that transition. I really would have liked a bit more variation in the instrumentation during the long extended instrumental passages - maybe a cello in one track, more piano in another - to contrast against the guitars-and-drums juggernaut delivery.

Even with its shortcomings, this is a well-crafted opus that deserves a reissue (with the sound cleaned up a bit and the vocals brought further up in the mix) on a specialist BM or doom metal label.

Can we take a minute to acknowledge just how strictly Wytch Hazel has adhered to their formula? In addition to the years spent polishing their signature spiritually charged hard rock, each of their albums has also shown airtight consistency in releasing every couple years with a ten-song total averaging around forty-ish minutes every single time. There’s a fine line between the religious devotion of never missing a Sunday church service and what could be interpreted as dogmatic fanaticism.

With that established, I must admit V: Lamentations seems to fall a little short of the impacts that peaked with 2020’s III: Pentecost and 2023’s IV: Sacrament. The melodies are as jovial as ever but have less of the energetic push that made their last couple outings so explosive, leading to a more easygoing approach with more relaxed playing. It’s not the most dramatically noticeable shift, but it’s hard to pick a finger on why the hooks don’t feel like they stick as much as they should. The speedy charges on the opening one-two “I Lament” and “Run The Race” are missing a certain bite while the mid-tempo anthems like “The Citadel” and “Racing Forwards” gamble on lethargy.

But by virtue of the band’s tight as hell songwriting, this still manages to be a pretty enjoyable listen. Certain tracks are well suited to a more restrained outlook between the almost psych-folk “The Demons Within” and “Heavy Load” as well as the extra pastoral whimsy on the closing “Healing Power.” There’s also room for some simpler hard rock as “Elements” feels like something KISS would do and “Woven” echoes some of the lingering hustle, especially when coming off as a contrast to the acoustic instrumental “Elixir.”

While V: Lamentations shows some diminishing returns in Wytch Hazel’s tried and true classic metal template, there’s still an underlying faith that keeps it at a solid caliber. It’s something of a mixed bag as the hooks don’t have their usual earworm appeal but the mood and song templates feel in character. Part of me wishes they had leaned even more into the mellowness, perhaps hitting even further into folk or heavy psych. As much as I miss their Thin Lizzy worship’s fiery underbelly, this has plenty of comfy sweet spots.

When people think of Quiet Riot they either think of Randy Rhoads or they think of their party-rock anthems "Metal Health" and "Cum On Feel The Noize". This album proves that there is more to the band than those things. Sadly, this is the only time they really stepped up and proved it before vocalist Kevin DuBrow's death the year after this was released.

What makes this album stand out, you ask? Well, plenty of things. The band have done away with their glam rock party sound in favour of more sophisticated blues/hard rock inspired by DuBrow's and drummer Frankie Banali's favourite bands. The musical aspect of this album is golden; all their other albums after Metal Health still sounded quite a lot like Metal Health, but always lacking the same memorability, and sounding more and more dated with every release. This album, however, sees the band reinventing itself, sounding current but having a definite 70s blues vibe. The album is the band's most refreshing listen since Metal Health, hands down.

The vocals are strong. Kevin DuBrow possessed an extremely powerful voice that barely waned with age. He sounds just as strong as the DuBrow that existed in the Metal Health days. There is a guest appearance from the amazing Glenn Hughes on the closing track "Evil Woman" and he has writing credits on some of the songs too. The first track  "Free" is slow but beautifully heavy and melodic. It's a change of pace that should be welcomed by Quiet Riot fans. Other standouts on the album include "Blind Faith", the very bluesy "Old Habits Die Hard" and "Don't Think".

If any song on the album does sound like a "Metal Health" song, that would be "It Sucks To Be You" although, at the same time, it doesn't sound like it's desperately trying to be a hit, and it doesn't drag the album down at all.

Metal Health guitarist and bassist, Carlos Cavazo and Rudy Sarzo respectively, do not appear on this album. Although they appeared on the band's previous two albums before this, there were apparently conflicts between members so it seems like their absences were for the best. The remaining classic members, DuBrow and Banali (who also produced the album themselves), along with guitarist Neil Citron and bassist Tony Franklin (with contributions from touring guitarist Alex Grossi) have done this album for themselves, and obviously had a hell of a time doing it.

Overall, this is an impressive, underrated release from the band. It's clear that by this point, the band were making music they truly enjoyed rather than trying to hold onto the glory days by repeating that glam metal sound any longer. Like I've mentioned, it's a real shame that this is the only album in this style that they did before DuBrow died. The way he died too, seemed in a way, avoidable. He died of a cocaine overdose, and one can only wonder why and how his infamous cocaine habit from the 80s re-emerged. Looking into this also makes the album title seem ironic: if DuBrow had gone into Rehab following his relapse, perhaps he would still be alive and rocking out! But, all we can do is remember him for his life as a rockstar, not remember him from how he died, so R.I.P. DuBrow: you went out with a hell of a bang with this album.

Spanish old school death metal titans Bizarre are summoned for their debut album to be unveiled... So let's get into it!

An eerie introduction begins our descent into the catacombs of Bizarre, effective yet short and to the point. Roaring vocals and dismally dark riffs punch into life with ferocious drums, delivering a swarm of eerie and malevolent death metal with some grandiose synths sat below the depths for a short moment before the storm of Lovecraftian horrors dives into the murk. Vitriolic and scathing, this music is so full of dark energy and tight musicianship that it is impossible to escape the immensity of Bizarre and their odiously atmospheric sounds. Restlessly beating drums give the music a fierce heartbeat as the monolithic riffing contorts into inhuman shapes with ethereal leads further adding dimensions to the unearthly death metal. Vocally, the roars and snarls have a bestial ferocity that suits the unrelenting storms of instrumental violence gloriously. This is not faint or meek music, this is a firestorm of pure sonic devastation.

Venturing further into the deep realms of the abyss, the music has a technical and melodic edge to the otherwise rather old school death metal which is an interesting juxtaposition. Taking a lot of their cues from the Finnish death metal influence they so openly declare as their primary inspiration, “Invocation Codex” puts a more modern yet unapologetically derived spin on this sound which is done so in a very interesting fashion. Some Gothenburg style melodies creep in to give the music some haunting yet catchy moments before diving back into a burst of bestial malice without warning. Production-wise this album has a surprisingly clean sound that allows the sheer sonic diversity to be heard with clarity, while not overly polishing it to the point of sounding clinical. Some of the bass-driven Finnish dirge is lost, but in place we see a more technical flourish, which sometimes works for the best but can also detract occasionally from the atmosphere of the album. This said, it does also give the band a bit more of a unique style to give them character atop their obvious worship of the Finnish gods of the 90s.

Deeper into the depths Bizarre take us ever lower with their sonic upheaval of all things. Catatonic drum grooves and magnificently malicious riffs keep the momentum of the album strong as drawn out snarls superbly deliver their cosmic horror lyrics of dread and otherworldly beings. Delicious is the delivery of this music and its violently restless progressions that harken back to the old school but bring it firmly into the present day. Another interesting element, some of the soloing on this album is so gloriously melodic in a more traditional heavy metal sense of epic shreds, it breathes a different kind of life into the music that is definitely born of talent but also different ways of thinking. As an axe-slinger, this will always appeal to me. Rumbling bass lines break the mould with more intricate rhythmic hooks and overall we see a very thorough record that has been thought out to great extent unfurl into something wonderful.

A unique, labyrinthine and crushing monolith of a debut album. Musically tight with an old school attitude that is somewhat modernised for maximum destruction, this Lovecraftian death metal creeps and lurks into life before taking us into the chasm for an assault of the senses from every angle.

Long have I been a fan of Coventry, England, UK band Cathedral. Introducing myself to their early delights, such as, 'Forest of Equilibrium' & 'The Ethereal Mirror,' it wasn't long before I had everything else the band had released. My love for the band even reached a somewhat ridiculous climax a few years ago when I traveled to England just to see them play live at Bloodstock and even visit their hometown. So, as you can probably imagine hearing the news that the band was splitting up hit me in an odd way. No, I wasn't blubbering out tears and screaming, but you know, when a band you've loved for a long time splits it does rip something out of you. On the other hand, I believe all good things should come to their logical end and having been together since '89 that time had finally come for these doomsters. They'd etched the stone of doom and left their influence infinitely known among all that listen to this sort of music.

Prior to the recording of this album long time bassist Leo Smee left the band and was replaced by Scott Carlson of Repulsion, although Scott had helped Cathedral way back in '94 with a few Black Sabbath cover songs and live work prior to Smee joining the band that same year.

'The Last Spire' may be the bands last record, but in a way its like a journey back to the beginning. Forgoing the long time stoner metal/rock tendencies within their music and the more progressive and even experimental traits of their last record, 'The Guessing Game,' this final effort is pure heavy doom all the way. The atmosphere within the record is often dark and gloomy, the riffs are crushing and oppressive, while the tempo rarely goes faster than a turtles pace and the song writing itself is by far some of the finest they've busted out in years. Lee Dorian's signature voice is as ever strong and potent, as well the guest spots from Rosalie Cunningham (Purson) and Chris Reifert (Autopsy) only make the vocal portions of the album all the more dynamic. Honestly their are some proggy touches to the album, in the form of some moog and synth noodling, although its intermingled with the heavy riffing and hard hitting bass in just the right way that it seems very natural and not out of place at all.

Although I do enjoy this album quite a bit I found that its an album that really requires multiple listens before it really sinks in. I had the same issue with the previous Cathedral album, but this one being more straightforward I figured I'd be alright, yet that wasn't the case. Fortunately once you get to about the third of fourth spin you really take notice of the little things and see the album for what it is - bleak heavy as all get out traditional doom, just the way I like it.

I wont jump to an conclusions and call this the doom album of the century, because it surely is not that. However it is a solid piece of doom and a thrilling final statement from these legends. Surely a must for the long time fans, or even casual listeners of them, 'The Last Spire' may be the end of Cathedral, but I've got ten documents of doom to listen to from them until the day I die. Rest in Peace, Cathedral, the pallbearer is waiting for you.
