The first time I heard the killer main riff to Ozzy Osbourne's overplayed but classic radio hit "Crazy Train" was back in August of 1995, when, after partaking of highly taboo marijuana (also for first time) - or "grass", as Mom calls it - a friend of a friend fired up his amplifier before ripping out those ever recognizable yet memorably scorching notes, in the process flooring me outright and thus cementing a life long Ozzy fascination, one already started long ago with Black Sabbath, but now even more defined and quantifiable. Without delay, I tracked down almost all of his solo albums under the Sun (pun intended).

Although I dig Ozzy's work with Zakk Wylde to a fair extent, predominantly gravitate towards the dove chomper's first four records, starting with rather commercial, if not widely reviled debut, released in 1980 next to Sabb's pioneering Heaven And Hell. Aside from fact the latter half of Side A fails to fully sparkle - as the World can let go of The Beatles-like "Goodbye To Romance" (yet brief, classically inspired instrumental "Dee" is a noble tribute to Randy's dear mother) - and that responsive, ill-advised call-to-action following Stained Class' "Do It" incident, "Suicide Solution", isn't most auspicious song title, they're are some kick-ass, genre and era defining riffs and solos here any six-string aspirant needs to study up on ahead of glorious guitar hero ascension...including those which progress at a snail's pace. 

In a nutshell, the first two tracks, "I Don't Know" and "Crazy Train", are pure textbook Ozzy. (Just ask Yuto Miyazawa...) Despite being played to death everywhere, stuck in a vacuum, it's hard to deny Randy's phenomenally eloquent, hand cramping style. Looking back, I'm grateful to have heard Blizzard Of Ozz in its entirety before being mercilessly assailed by them, as otherwise, might've been compelled to simply take fellow writers' word that it wasn't worth total scrutiny. As for sketchy "Suicide Solution", it's alright (pun number two), sounding like derivative bonus to 1978's Never Say Die, with its loudly bopping bass and Ozzy's telltale falsetto wail. 

Side B rules, no matter what anyone says. Both "Mr. Crowley" (not my tenth grade English teacher) and "Revelation (Mother Earth)" showcase Randy at his most classical, reaching for the  Heavens during his awesome, drawn out leads while former pays tribute to cheesy 1980s horror in same darkly mesmerizing vein as "Believer", from Diary Of A Madman - not "maiden" as often surmised. For my money, the coolest cuts reside towards the back, namely the raunchy honky-tonk crusader against filthy and morally corrupt adult film industry, "No Bone Movies" - whose soul saving directive I wish I'd taken to heart sooner, especially once twenty-first century internet pornification was in full swing - and most favourite, the ingeniously riffed, downright wicked closer "Steal Away (The Night)". 

While you couldn't come up with a sleazier riff for the former, this last encapsulates everything I dig about Randy thanks to its gripping back-and-forth opening riff and cathartic verses, embellished further by seriously intricate guitar moves - particularly, challenging secondary riffs!  Its powerfully transitioning bridge riff is one for the ages. Again, "Steal Away (The Night)" is easily within my top Ozz songs. If anything, Randy's spirit is always present during these comparatively amateurish bouts of tablature bound adulation. At the end of the day, Ozzy's frosty Blizzard is an essential, coming-of-age heavy metal landmark worth sampling every now and then.

Viikate is a strange phenomenon in metal. The band is currently listed as a folk metal band in the Archives, but I have my own serious doubts about the viability of the classification; a fan of Korpiklaani, In Extremo and other such bands will probably be in for a surprise, if they purchase an album by Viikate. A pleasant or a nasty surprise, that depends on how open a mind the folkmetalhead has when he hears the first tracks of any Viikate album.

First of all, their music does not meet the intuitive definition of folk metal. When other folk metal bands are pretty much defined either simply by the use of old instruments, or by the more demanding use of folkish melodies in metal, Viikate does things differently. For the instruments they occasionally use some older types of instruments, but not the medieval flutes, juohikkos or bagpipes; more likely they include a modern accordion or other similar instruments for a bit of mood, or for an instrumental piece among other songs. Their basic sound is that of a classical four man band: drums, bass, two guitars and clean vocals. One of the guitars is strictly a rhythm guitar, while the other one is usually an older kind of hollow-body semi-acoustic one. To describe the sound is a much harder task: they aim for -and achieve- a lightly metallic version of kind of music played by the UK band The Shadows and others from the late 1950's. Imagine the famous song Apache by The Shadows, played with a solid modern rhythm guitar with a metallish sound helping. Remember the original clean lead guitar sound and lots of echo. Then add a carefully restrained, depressed clean baritone voice and melancholic, slow melodies, and you have a pretty good approximation of Viikate. 

The second problem with the folk metal classification are the songs themselves. While some of them are originally traditional songs, the versions by Viikate are closer to such great masters of post-WWII music in Finland as Tapio Rautavaara (I know, this explains nothing to anyone outside Finland, but bear with me). Some are actually traditional folk songs, first modernized by Rautavaara, then covered -or emulated- by Viikate. So, there are no actual folk songs on any of their albums. What there is, is more like old 1930's to 1950's schlagers combined with late 1950's rock'n'roll with early undistorted electric guitars, more specifically "rautalanka" as it was called in Finland; "iron string" would be a direct translation, but once again, the translation loses something essential; we have a strange language. 

So, don't expect to hear merry fluting, goblins pillaging and burning, stories of gallons of mead and folk dancing, tales of heroes beating the crap out of each others with blunt weapons, or anything the term folk metal usually conjures. The lyrics are, if possible, even more depressing than the melodies. They describe alcoholism, death, melancholy, and generally losing and everything changing for the worse. Frost, hunger, loneliness and all-embrazing hopelessness are frequent subjects, and the lyrics are generally reflected in the melodies and sound. The attitude is that of giving up for the last time, with humility and completely without aggression.

Noutajan Valssi (The Reaper's Waltz) is the first full-length album of the band. The preceding EP releases are still quite unknown and difficult to find, but have fortunately been compiled as the Kuutamourakat compilation. Noutajan Valssi pretty much defines the sound and style of Viikate, and the later albums follow it without any deviations from the norm, other than improved production. The album opens with an instrumental, all-accordion piece, aptly named Alkusoitto (Elämä on niin pirun raskas juttu toisinaan), which roughly translates into Prelude (Life can be such a damn heavy burden sometimes). That should give you an idea of the average merriness level of Viikate. The album also ends with an instrumental, and in between there are seven melancholic, depressed, gloomy and generally unhappy songs. The general mood is truly far removed from your average drinking-and-brawling atmosphere of some stereotypical folk metal.

This album started a tradition -or a joke- of Viikate: while in the early 90's the CD releases contained extra tracks compared to the vinyls and cassettes, Viikate usually does the reverse and adds a bonus track to the vinyl version. This is probably due to their very retro image; these albums are magnificent attempts in achieving a 1950's atmosphere, and the mildly pro-vinyl approach is just a small increment to add to that. The bonus track on this vinyl is a really classic song by Tapio Rautavaara.

Unlike the later albums, none of the tracks on Noutajan Valssi really stands out as a hit single, but the whole is very stylish and expresses the main theme, finnish melancholy, with amazing tenderness and respect. Perhaps the more refined sound of the later albums, especially that of Kaajärven Rannat, lose something of the rough down-to-earth expressive strength of Noutajan Valssi. In the world of Viikate, music is listened to with an ancient gramophone in a log cabin, drinking hard liquor and contemplating cooking a soup of poisonous mushroons for the whole family after the crops fail and the only cow dies. Sometimes there's a light at the end of the tunnel, but usually the stories are about the exact moment when the said light finally gets turned off.

The excellence of Viikate may be difficult for a foreigner to understand. The importance of the lyrics (in Finnish), ties to older musical pop culture of Finland, and the way their music has been shaped to describe the local melancholy, all turn Viikate into a band that has quite specifically been designed for local consumption. I still recommend people from other countries to give Viikate a try: just remember the caveats above and shed your folk metal expectations.

Finding the rating is once again a difficult task: the later albums contain more memorable hit songs that have actually gotten some radio time, and the quality of their production makes them slightly more enjoyable than Noutajan Valssi. But in the final analysis I feel that this likely is a more important work, since everything by Viikate after this owes much to this one. Also, the rougher production just adds spice to the songs. I'm going to rate this one as high as I would rate the later releases, as I can't make up my mind on which one is better. And since there's really nothing to compare this to, the rating is rather irrational, and simply conveys my enjoyment of the album, nothing more.

One question remains: how would I classify Viikate after questioning its folk metal status? Honestly: I have no idea. I've never heard any other bands that are even close to Viikate soundwise, and I believe folk metal is the closest established genre there is. So let's leave it the way it is. There's no question about Viikate belonging in the Encyclopaedia, just the genre is obscure and unique.

With the exception of certain intrumental stuff that will never appear on the Metal Archives, Viikate is probably the only band that manages to accomplish the near-impossible: my dad (almost 60 years old) recognises some of the songs AND we both like them. That won't happen again for a while.

Sometimes, all that's needed for a talented and committed act to take the World by firestorm is a brief yet heavy hitting and meaningful EP. This is the case for central Finland's Steel Systems, a young, guitar crazy band comparable to fellow countrymen Lord Fist, and to various degrees, further pioneers of awesome "melodic heavy metal". Obviously, the cover to March's five track extended play, titled Burn To Rock, reeled in faster than deceptive clickbait, but then delivered in aces and spades as soon as the glorious opener, with its clever and slippery riffs, blew my mind.

A big, favorable trait evident out of the gate is the loud and thundering impact of the bass as it plonks along fervently, buoying first anthem "Thicker Than Blood" in such a way that it's a feast for the ears. The drums are light and powerful at the same time, and in general, in regards to the band's overall sound, auspiciously hint of Australia's Johnny Touch due to their metallic fleetful-ness and the vocalist's crystal clear mid-range, as well as Sweden's Screamer in terms of well-placed harmony lines backing the riffs. The very first guitar solo is truly great. 

The opener is basically a quick clothes-hanger meant to strap one in for the ride; ensuing songs are variably longer, as the solemnly paced albeit dizzying, almost Airforce (of Britain) reminiscent "Down In Flames" and initially becalmed but soon upbeat and playful "Seeds Of Hope" crest the horizon ahead of pair of four minute blazers "Nightime" and "Black And White". I'm unsure if the latter aims to be political, but it adequately paints a picture, however blurry or ambiguous, of presently unprecedented times. 

For its part, "Nightime" is a straightforward go-getter, definitely a crowd pleaser thanks to its stirring rhythm and old school, Iron Maiden styled instrumentation. As far as nostalgia goes, this gem's soloing is lifted out of the long gone 1970s, recalling the feel-good likes of Boston even! Another highlight consists of "Black And White", which soars sky-fortress high with its fast and wispy rocker of a main riff and catchy chorus. Sadly, the EP ends all too soon. Sure enough, Steel Systems's Burn To Rock EP makes for a great way to start the day.

Anyone who doubts power metal's storied and unique atmospheric appeal would do well to check out Jokela, Finland's Thaurorod, as the sextet's latest, Coast of Gold, released last month on CD under Drakkar Entertainment, incorporates the very best elements of the genre, be they  majestically sweeping guitar riffs and rapidly fluttering, at times, hummingbird evoking solos, relentless high-velocity blast beats and ephemerally enchanting keys befitting a most charismatic front man who reaches astounding vocal registers (you're forgiven in advance if, as I, you erroneously take him for a woman) while enthusiastically sounding like he's narrating ancient mariner tales  from an old, dusty tome beside a crackling log fire and bear fur rug.  Indeed, these ten emotionally charged and highly expedient tracks readily conjure images of Treasure Island or, for want of a contemporary comparison, the swashbuckling and televised buccaneering odyssey Black Sails - all I need now is a hook, eye patch and wooden peg leg.

Things begin with a stark cannon ball bang on "Power" before yielding bedazzling transcendental rhythms, from the riveting and hard-driving, techno styled "The Commonwealth Lives" to the stoically raw "Illuminati" and irenic, cleanly drifting closer, "Halla". Each track reels you in from the get-go while growing in intensity and mystical flair with each subsequent listen. Also notable are the arching tempos which effortlessly swoon between mellifluously crooning passages and outright ramped up instances of purely soaring and stratospheric, guitars and keys dominated dirges, as on the cryptically illustrious stand-out cut, "24601".  More than just an East Coast zip code or petulant Hollywood teenage drama (!), this radiant and resplendent track, with its orchestral piano touches, sweetly incepting opening lead and overall Cardiant evoking ambiance beautifully unfolds right up to its soul branding chorus and beyond (suffice to say, I can't stop joyfully repeating it as it's stuck fast in my psyche!). 

Further commendable sundries include, but are not limited to, the urgent and dramatically drawn-out neo-classical humdingers which are "Feed the Flame" and  "Into the Flood" - I especially dig their "rocking shred" solo sections, intertwined as they are with all those wickedly whirling keys - and "My Sun Will Rise" thanks to its incredibly tight and razor-sharp bridge riff which grippingly bursts out of nowhere at 02:04.  As inferred, the drums are wound up to the hilt while the bass, despite more or less providing stout, reinforcing accompaniment, prominently resounds throughout "Cannibal Island", another memorable stand-out piece, with its coy little girl introductory chanting followed by an uncharacteristically buoyant pace reminiscent of a Sea bound, gold bullion transporting flotilla flying the royal Spanish flag.  To conclude, I can't recommend this enough, whether you're a seasoned genre aspirant or scoffing skeptic. Should you fail to thoroughly enjoy Thaurorod's Coast of Gold, I promise to reimburse your piece of eight.

Well I just stumbled across Norwegian grindcore band Beaten to Death, and their 2013 album "Dødsfest!" and it's a monster of an album. Full of excellent musicianship, a good deal of humour, and a huge degree of creativity, this is a really unique and brilliant album.

Sure, there are the usual hallmarks of grind, tracks mostly between 1-2 minutes, and a heavy dose of blastbeats, but there's also so much weirdness and creativity on display too, that don't get fooled for a second that this is a typical grind release. The vocals are of the metalcore blueprint, the metalcore grunts and screams aren't my usual preference, but it's done well enough here, and they're vicious enough to rip the flesh from your skull. The bass is staggeringly good on this album, massively groovy, bouncing up and down throughout, in a manner that's simultaneously smile and headbang inducing. The most interesting of all is the guitars. Unlike most grind there's not a heavy crushing distortion on the guitars, rather they're more of a softer post-rock style. Trading off between strummed chords and pretty melodies, which could come out of post-rock music, to some really discordant and technical fretboard wizardry, and some heavy grinding chugs and breakdowns, the guitar performance here is monumental. "True Norwegian Internet Warrior" has these technical riffs at their best, really interesting, while the post-rock melodies of "Døv, Døvere, Død" are a real joy to behold. And with that bouncy bass, blasting drums and vicious vocals it's still a really brutal album at points, there's no danger of the technical and melodic side of their music detracting from Beaten to Death beating your ears to death, especially on the climax to "Aspen Hellweek", one of the best tracks here.

While having the technical grind elements of Gridlink, and the melodic purpose of Deafheaven, Beaten to Death maybe lack some of the refinement of those two bands, but what they lack in refinement they make up for in fun, energy and a sense of humour. Some of the song titles are weird and humorous and some clean "woahs" in the background of "Nazi Slipper" are fun as hell. Throughout the album, in spite of the excellent technical and melodic edge to those guitars, it still remains really fun, humorous and constantly headbang-demanding. Beaten to Death don't take themselves too seriously and the album just oozes fun. Any grindcore fan who wants something really different should give this one a go, this is a really unique album, and one to bring a smile to your face. Beaten to Death's mix of ripping grindcore, technical fretboard wizardry, melodic post-rockisms, and a good deal of fun and humour make Dødsfest! a beast of an album., and one that just DEMANDS back to back listens!

Flowing Tears review for Serpentine

 

 

Flowing Tears is one of a few original Gothic Metal bands wandering the Metal scene today. They're unique take on chord progression and structure coupled with their singers’ very different voice and their usages of samples makes for one melodically bombastic album.

The production is more on par with a debut or a good demo, but its far from bad. The guitars are an interesting mix of Doom and Goth blending an assortment effects and rhythms into an original yet easily digestible soup. There are no solos but the leads are haunting. There are parts of the music that remind one of mid period 'Novembers Doom' and 'Anathema'. Surprisingly however, this band isn't Doom in any way. The songs are about even in their muted to open chord passages.

The bass does some interesting things here and there but mostly follows the guitars. The Drums on the other hand are very well excited and tight. The rhythms they put out are very classy and heavily rooted in old school Doomdeath. 

The keyboards and samples (done by the guitarist) are mostly used for subtle effects and moods. They are never dominate but always present. The vocals are unique, not because they are done by a female, but rather that they are deep and somewhat bass heavy. This is in stark contrast to the legions of Christina and Tarja clones flooding the scene today. While not the best singer, she works well with the songs as a whole.

Over all the songs are a mixture of beauty, silliness and sorrow. The lyrics are kind of strange and the singers grip on English is shaky at best, but this is very different and very good music. There is a energetic vibe that is overlapped by thick layers of regret and teen angst and introspective doubt.

This is something that everyone can get into as they sound like no other. Granted that the middle of the album isn't as interesting as the beginning; there is a lot going on in this fairly simplistic yet very rocking music.

When it comes to rough and violent black metal, you can easily take your pick of the thousands of bands in the style playing anti-religious or war infused riffs to evoke tempered feelings and head banging. When the duo Anaal Nathrakh (consisting of V.I.T.R.I.O.L on vocals and Irrumator on everything else) began, their style on the debut (The Codex Necro) leaned heavily towards that regular, riff-based kind of aggressive black metal, somewhat along the lines of what bands like Watain, newer Mayhem and Gorgoroth were doing in the post-second wave of black metal. So while The Codex Necro was fine by its own merits, Anaal Nathrakh knew their brand of raw black metal needed a pick me up, and so, in 2004 on their sophomore, Domine Non Es Dignus, the duo started sprinkling grindcore elements into their music to create the unique brand of violent black metal, which they continue to play to this day on Venitas.

As I mentioned this is pretty violent black metal, what with grindcore in the shotgun on this one. While black metal on its own can be quite intimidating, here it’s grindcore’s trademarks such as sonic blast beats, slithering, indecipherable barks and screeches, riffs that ignore any rule of melody or speed, and heavy, low-end tremolo picking (bringing out the punch in the more thin, trebly aspect of the black metal elements, sometime even verging more on death metal) that does most of the hard, heavy work. The points in which the two work together are devastating, with their ominous, sinister black metal riffing hitting light speed, hacking and slashing the listener with it’s trebly, rusty tones, and the grindcore heavy low-ends and robotic drumming matching it, one can witness the true extent of the monster these men have made. Although I’m astounded at how coherently the more violent bits were, as I would assume such cacophony would be but a mess of white noise, but instead, ended up coming through.

With all this talk of violence, I should let you know that Anaal Nathrakh knows they can’t just focus on pure, physicality. If anything, I’d say the band’s strongest point are their more melodic aspects that, while still plenty violent at times, really cut through the stress and pulls the listener directly to them. With soaring choruses that utilize VITRIOLS amazing, opera-esque voice, the choruses that are created are actually really well defined, and give songs like Forging Towards the Sunset, In Coelo Quies, You Can’t Save Me, So Stop Fucking Trying and A Metaphor for the Dead,a perfect balance of heaviness and extremely catchy melody, making them extremely memorable. And finally, in the middle ground, the band has absolutely perfected it’s ominous, evil passages, not only in the trebly, cold riffing they owe to their Mayhem influence, but also in the well written lead work which utilizes dual leads (and anti-leads, if you want to call them that) to twist and curdle your mind. The grand, opera vocal work also helps to evoke the feelings of a twisted, Italian opera singer commanding the ravages of hell to, uh, ravage like on the tracks The Blood-Dimmed tide, To Spite the face and Todos somos Humanos.

The only place I can really find the inconsistencies in this bands riffing are with the odd Meshuggah-influences that have an odd moment of spotlight (again, the opening of To Spite The Face) with syncopated, groovy riffs and bombastic breakdowns showing up from time to time. I guess they’re not bad, but just sort of random, and sort of a step towards the exact opposite of the two genres that make up this record. Another odd tidbit I found on this record were the rare moments where industrial elements would be pushed through, such as purposeful, robotic clipping, or blasted, rubber toned sounding drum beats, which were clearly done via programming found on songs like To Spite The Face. From what I know, these bits have been here and there on past releases, but have somewhat diminished here on Venitas, which I’d argue is for the better; but a blackened industrial grindcore just sounds way to weird for me.

For a combination of genre’s that are both synonymous for the words noisy, cluttered and low-fi, Venitas actually does a great job of keeping the chaos controlled. While it’s still a cacophony, one can still hear everything in perfect conjunction, the black metal gets to keep its thin, cold, scratchy riffs and grind keeps the low ends and brutal rhythms, as neither cancel out in the mix.  I’m not sure who did the engineering and sound, but whoever did must be one hell of a wizard. Most of the moods on this record range from sinister, violent, triumphant, stressful and foreboding, mixing together some of the key atmospheric elements of the Norwegian reign, such as the cold and eerier atmosphere of the slower and cleaner parts as well as the more supernatural kind of feelings one doesn’t find in grindcore.

While fans of Anaal Nathrakh were somewhat disappointed in the mildly watered down nature of last year’s Passion, I think a rekindling of everything that makes this band great can be found on Vanitas. It’s not only violent, evil, ominous and energetic, but it’s melodic, catchy and memorable. While the band is clearly rooted in black metal territory, the interesting and creative grindcore elements on this record have surely cemented Anaal Nathrakh with some of the greatest in the UK extreme scene, along with bands like Napalm Death and Carcass; not only do they create something unique, but they also have the pure creative staying power to sustain it.

De Profundis has been on my radar ever since I heard Kingdom of the Blind, an album that is undoubtedly good.  When the first single for this album was released, I got excited.  I gave it a listen, and I was not a huge fan.  I thought it sounded more blackened and less progressive than their 2015 material.  Then I took a look at the album artwork.  It was pretty cool to look at, but it looked like a black metal album cover.  They day it released, I listened to a few tracks out loud, but I lost interest and decided to listen to something else.  I didn’t really give it my full attention until recently, and it’s much better than I expected.

The blackened aspects of their music are more present on this album than on the last, but it always somehow goes unnoticed.  That's probably due to the fact that everything - the technicality, progressiveness, death, and blackened aspects - blends together so well on this release.  It's like they actually know what they're doing!

And that's exactly what's going on!  De Profundis is maturing!  However, they aren't maturing in the way that isn't fun.  It's not like they were partiers before and now they work in a cubicle exchanging lame jokes about staplers to their coworkers.  It's more like they were really annoying before, and now they're starting to understand that it's time for them to change.  Of course, they weren't immature when they wrote Kingdom of the Blind, but they were still in the process of maturing, and this is the final product.  Currently, they are that guy who regulates his party and work life successfully (if there is such a life), so he has his fun, but he's still serious about things.

That being said, the guitar riffs on here are much better, and they are very memorable.  Every time I listen to this album, I specifically remember "War Be Upon Him" and "Beyond Judgement."  These are the most memorable riffs on here for me, but there are others; they just aren't memorable enough for me to point out which track they are.  Like I said before, the riffs are better, well structured, better written, and flashy.

People always say someone blasted through puberty when they go from a short, ugly kid to a tall, handsome gentleman, and De Profundis is no different.  Their doom metal stuff was never the best.  In fact, it wasn't good at all, but their progressive material is good.  However, this album surpasses their other works by a lot.  Kingdom of the Blind is a great album with warming riffs all over the place, but their latest release is the next level up, adding flashy technicality to their style.  The Blinding Light of Faith is by far the best album offered by De Profundis.

Overall Rating: 89%

Grenadier is a Canadian melodic death metal band that was recently formed in 2018. If the name rings a bell, then you know this band is an unapologetic clone of the infamous Arghoslent, a very controversial melodic death metal band that shares members with Grand Belial's Key. There's no need for an introduction with them, so I'll just stick to talking about Grenadier. This band obviously plays in a similar style; the only difference is the subtraction of any vulgar or racial lyrical content. So, if you're a person who cannot look past the controversies of Arghoslent, as well as separate the art from the artist, then you've come to the right place. Grenadier is a fantastic band that copies the band's style extremely well, and their debut album "Trumpets Blare in Blazing Glory" is a very strong start for this band.

Much like with Arghoslent, Grenadier delivers a hostile and tight performance of melodic death metal. With tons of traditional heavy metal influences to go along with it, bands like Running Wild and Mercyful Fate come to mind; this makes for a very interesting and engaging listen. What I like about this style of melodic death metal is that it doesn't sacrifice any brutality. This is still a very aggressive and riff-centric listen that balances the melodies to a tee. The music is triumphant, prideful, yet ungodly vicious and galloping. I also like that even though the band is an obvious Arghoslent worship band, it doesn't sound bland, boring, or repetitive. The band still manages to write catchy hooks and memorable songs.

The fantastic riffs are complemented by a bombastic drum performance. Many of the riffs are propelled by these barbaric but galloping drum beats played in almost a d-beat-like fashion, which gives them a very urgent and violent effect. There's a lot of frantic cymbal crashing along with some very propelling fills that get things moving. I love the usage of the ride cymbal and the constant kick drum rhythms. The drums aren't overly blasty but fit the parts and sections in which they do appear; it shows that the music can be equally intense with or without blasts. I love the overall thrashy and energetic performance, and how the drums flow very well alongside the guitars. The drums showcase a lot of cool transitions while also backing up the melodies.

Now let's talk about the tasteful guitars, which have a lot of character and melodic touches. This is how you write good melodic death metal; the melodies aren't cringey and instead have a triumphant sound. Fitting the music while also keeping things very intense, there are so many catchy rhythms and chuggy riff patterns. I love the very vibrant melodies on songs like "Atrocity Cycle," and how they sound like they're crawling. I really enjoy the cleaner melodic notes that appear in this song as well. There are, of course, tons of great hooks and chugging riffs that get the head banging to the beat. This album is very mid-paced, with slower riffs and more aggressive tempos spliced in. But it doesn't hinder the riffs or music at all, because every song is still very strong. The riffs have some really cool progressions and how they're built upon.

Another thing I really enjoy is the solos and lead work; when they show up, they're colorful and fantastic. That's not to say they're happy, because this is still very intense melodic death metal. Another thing I'd like to point out is, once again, the traditional heavy metal influences. It makes the riffs all the more memorable and catchy; they're also filled with variation and dynamics. It's just a blast to listen to overall; I love the grooves and how the riffs can be melodic yet rip my face apart at the same time. The blackened feel of some of the tremolos on here makes for even cooler moments. If you're looking for melodic death metal that isn't cheesy and doesn't overuse melody, this band is for you.

If you're familiar with Arghoslent's vocal style, then this should feel just as familiar. The vocalist, Adam Sharr, is very obviously trying to sound like Von Demonicus, who was Arghoslent's original vocalist for a long time. Adam does a very solid job of replicating his voice, even managing to add in some black metal-inspired screams. They aren't frequently used, which isn't a gripe whatsoever; what is used frequently is Adam's deep, gritty growls, which have the raspy register that sounds exactly like Von Demonicus. His vocals are abrasive and flow with the music in a pummeling fashion, and I like his overall triumphant and energetic voice that shines across each song.

Finally, let's talk about the production/mix of this record. I really enjoy how this album sounds, especially for a genre like melodic death metal. I love it when this style has a more gritty yet clear sound, and this record is a perfect example. The guitar tone is thick, blunt, and fuzzy as hell, yet it is clear enough that it doesn't drown out the melodic tendencies the riffs have. The drum sound fits this style of death metal well; I love the crunchy snare tone and the crisp cymbal sound. It fits the guitar tone perfectly. The vocals are upfront where they should be, which gives them more attention and command. I would like the bass to be a bit more transparent and clear, but the orgasmic guitar tone makes up for it.

Grenadier's debut full-length is a ferocious yet powerful attack of melodic death metal that follows the formula that Arghoslent excels in while also not sounding like a complete bland copycat. If you want melodic death metal with balls that's constantly in your face while also displaying great riffs, Grenadier is for you. This is my favorite kind of melodic death metal, the kind that rips your face off but also remains heavily brutal and intense. So overall, I say check this out if you're already a fan of bands like Arghoslent. You will be very satisfied with this album.

FFO: Intestine Baalsim, Arghoslent, Grand Belials Key, Ares Kingdom, House of Atreus, Deceased.

Excurses - Devil's Footprints "EP"

Independent Release

While setting the Winnipeg Metal scene ablaze with their outstanding debut, 5-song EP entitled, "Devil's Footprints", Excurses are coming a long way with this record, becoming a household name in the Metal scene... 

Well, from the first listen to this album I was deeply surprised at how talented and precise this band was; their frantic, beat-changing drumming, their technical, metallic riffing, and the fiercely screamed/growled vocals made up for this fantastic mix of fast and technical Death Metal with a melodic edge, and at points, heavy Thrash with unremitting dancy grooves and precise drumming, which are all combined extremely well! Every song is also very creative and different from the last; I love how in every song they change the speed of the music beat; whether it's aggressively fast with blast-beats and chugging, or just very metallically structured and melodic, they come out of nowhere, hitting you hard with the next beat they throw at you. And they do this very precisely as well. This album also has a pretty clear sound to it, and a very nice production, which makes it even more enjoyable to listen to! Now, as I love every song on this album, still, my favorites have to be "Devil's Footprints" and "Ignorance of the lost". The wonderful riffing and drum placements on "Devil's Footprints" are amazing, and they blend everything perfectly! The vocals are also very good and a lot stronger, maybe even a little bit more vibrant sounding than a lot of Metal screams you'll hear. "Ignorance of the Lost" is another amazing track, and it's a little more thrashy sounding with heavy, dancy riffage, fast drumming, and powerfully heavy vocals, with fronting screams and backing growls. The lyrical content on all of the tracks are also pretty boldly written, but they might still need a little work on their lyrical ability in the future; their just not written powerfully enough for me to really get into them. But I could definitely see these guys picking things up very soon in the extreme Metal world, and this EP very well might be their big starting ground.

So, this is definitely a quite exceptional release, and, as of right now, it is one of my favorites too! I highly, highly recommend this CD to anyone who wants some Thrash infused Death Metal with technical, yet melodic elements. They're at the top of their game with their musical abilities, and I definitely hope to see more of them soon!

Finally, fucking finally. A modern deathcore release with riffs. My life is not complete. It has been ages since At Rest last released something, and they seem to have been all but forgotten. When I first heard that they dropped this EP I didn't even know that they had reformed, let alone have anything to release. So I decided to check out their latest EP titled, "The Perversion of Morality." Let me tell you, these guys are really going to do great things with this style and sound they are going for. Its filled with riffs are really is a blast from the past for old school deathcore fans. It still just baffles me that this EP was released in 2017, its like 2007 never ended for these dudes and I am fucking loving it.

I got to say. The riffs are powerful with this EP. They really take a dark melodic influence on the riffs and I cannot get enough of it. They really manage to get you head banging with these riffs they just keep coming at you with. It was honestly extremely weird to type that about a deathcore band. I really think the riffs shine out in this instance of deathcore, keeping brutal yet melodic and beautiful throughout the album. It is really something to mosh to, but also to low-key cry too. It really just gets me going and is extremely memorable. I just need more of this band ASAP. With all this being said, they do have to occasional chug in their songs but it does not consume the entire song. It is mostly just during the breakdowns which is obviously fitting. 

The drums on the album seem so far typical. Not so much in a bad way but they fit with the music. I just don't think I could point out anything special about them. They don't seem to blast beat all the time which is always a plus. Blast beats are annoying in large doses. The china cymbal seems to be frequently used quite a lot in the songs, which does get old but it fits. Just wish the drummers are was not so attracted to that cymbal.

The vocals for the most part are averages, but its nice to hear some normal highs in this modern game. This man does really have some of the best highs in the modern game I got to say. He doesn't do anything crazy like tunnel throats, or such. Just straight fry highs which really sound amazing and I prefer them to tunnels. He just really seemed to stick to the old school deathcore book and not do anything majorly crazy. I just really got to say these highs are something to remember. They fit with the dark gloomy atmosphere that all these songs have and they sound very sinister. It is really a highlight in my opinion on the album. More people should really look up to this guy for high screams. I would enjoy that a lot.

Overall, this is a damn good comeback release. They are bringing back old school deathcore and I just cannot get enough of this EP. After being out of the scene for so long its nice to see these guys have that old school melodic tough. As well as the very dark atmosphere and synths to go along in creating a damn good sinister sounding EP. I highly recommend for fans of old school deathcore. It is really a work of art and so far my favorite release of the year.

The tome opens to little fanfare, but what follows will certainly cause more of an uproar. Little by little the sky turns black and the wind starts to blow. The tips of the grass begin to change color as well. The animals turn their heads and look toward the north horizon, where something that we cannot see is happening. They know what it is even though we do not. All the computers, all the televisions and all our technology begins to malfunction – our ears are annoyed by loud, ringing static from every television. We hear a strange echo in the air, breaking into a melancholy metallic lead guitar. We hear the beginning of Arch Nemesis’s Shadows in the Mirror.

This album is just otherworldly in nature. Even before you listen to it, the strange, dark cover artwork pulls you in like a fish on a hook. The first chords hit you, and they are melodic, dark and emotional. The riffs are crunchy, full of a deep, pounding grind that hits hard despite not being the main focus of the music, and the vocals are a huge, deep wail, sailing over the music with an eerie finesse – as the singer’s ritualistic intonations are often ever so slightly off, subtly off-kilter and strange. They make the listener feel uncomfortable, but not in a way that is detrimental to the music; rather more of an addition to the bizarre atmosphere and hellish feel of the music.

There is a certain theatric quality about this. The band crafts twisted, ominous epics with searing leads abound, pounding through the crushing wall of riffs and the pensive slow sections with power and majesty. They make every song a miniature epic in their own right, and while Shadows in the Mirror might take a while to grow on some listeners, it is incredibly rewarding in the end. Most of this is dark and murky, but sometimes you get a more rambunctious section that comes off as blazing and triumphant. Everything is seamless. Some of my favorite parts of this are when the band lets singer Niclas Thomsen go into an acapella section and build up these cool chanting sing-along parts. How come this trick isn’t more widely used? It works brilliantly. Check out “The Huntress,” in the beginning – there’s this killer, wicked-sounding chant that builds up through a storm of odd, almost narrative lyrics, and it's so damn cool it's hard to describe. Just listen to it if you can.

Through the pounding “Forever,” which is a strangely linear song without any kind of repetition of lyrics, the band introduces the world to their style. Further songs like the epochal “Fatal Victory” and the sinister “Nemesis” expound on this – oblique melodies and subtly, slightly gothic keys clashing to create quite a unique sound that I really dig. I could give this a higher score, but sadly, the album sort of pitters out at the end, with the two longest tracks just not remaining as compelling as what came before it.

So, in essence, the shadows in the mirror sadly only remain as shadows. The band would improve with time, though.

Doom done incredibly! A band located mere hours from me but brought to me from a friend overseas, Witches' Dance are a spectacular act straight outta Jersey that project an incredible idea of what I now anticipate in the future. The template alone is everything that I love about doom. Slow and compelling riffage, channeled through a buffer that takes off any degree of sharpness but doesn't drown it in fuzz like your by-the-numbers stoner metal artist. The vocals actually take a bit of a hit from this, yet they still retain a level of harsh integrity due to the yelling nature. Even better, I can't say any of the sixteen minutes ruins this with poor songwriting.

Even with such a quality, they amazingly do well with fading and suspense. "Mystic Whisper" has to be my favorite track on this because of their precise unloading of the intro. The rest of this one follows up with endless grooves and incredible drumming technique that just force the blunt edges right into your skull. Even the fucking lyrics here have such a ring to them. 

But all four of the songs on Demo 2020 are amazing. I'm probably hyping this up a little bit, and part of this is probably just because of how well the band's first release (and on demo format) roped me in. All I can say is that it provides loads of anticipation for a full-length, so consider my expectations high.

Post-reformation Manilla Road have certainly been something of a curiosity, varying in both style and quality with each release, leaving the listener clueless as to what the next album might hold.  From 2001's shallow, accessible mid-paced thrasher Atlantis Rising, to 2002's incredibly strange, dense and solid heavy/doom/death release Spiral Castle, to 2005's obscure, repetitive, disjointed heavy/power/death album Gates of Fire...which leads us to 2008's Voyager. Making a return appearance from Gates of Fire are singular drummer Cory Christner, whose constant erratic pounding has always seemed fairly charming to me and whose style fits the vast, ancient chaos of Voyager perfectly; as well as the iconic heart, soul, and backbone of Manilla Road, Mark Shelton, who handles the vocal duties exclusively here, since Bryan Patrick, who shared vocal duties on the previous two albums, has taken a temporary leave of absence.  Gone as well is bassist Harvey Patrick, who is now replaced by Vince Golman, who is proficient but does little to mark his style, as Voyager isn't particularly bass-heavy.

The first thing that's unique to Voyager is that it's a concept album, specifically about vikings and their nautical adventures and conquests; as such, I dare say it's Manilla Road's most ambitious album to date.  While individual songs certainly stand out, it is more cohesive as a whole than any other MR album, both sonically and lyrically.  The vast, murky, ancient, chaotic atmosphere is exuded throughout the entire album, evoking perfectly thoughts of blood and death upon the ancient seas.  It is dark and melancholy, alternately brooding and punishingly brutal, with a stronger death metal influence than any of the previous MR albums; Shelton even performs some surprisingly adept death growls in "Return of the Serpent King" and a few other places throughout the album.  Additionally, in the non-ballad songs, the riffing style is very close to death metal, albeit with some heavy and doom influence.  Despite Shelton's clean vocal style for most of the album, I'd be loath to call this anything but epic melodic death metal.

Shelton certainly proves his versatility with epic metal here; he has done everything from death, doom, and thrash to heavy, power, and even hints of NWOBHM (on Crystal Logic).  Regardless of genre, everything Shelton touches seems to turn to sprawling, atmospheric gold.  Of course, with increased atmosphere and increased ambitiousness, comes a further increase in inaccessibility.  For Voyager perhaps more than any other MR album (although Spiral Castle comes close), don't expect to appreciate it on the first few listens.  It took me close to a year to fully understand it in its entirety, and I had already been a MR fan for some time.  However, you will surely be greatly rewarded if you give it the time and effort it deserves. Song-by-song, the album is slightly weaker than it is in its entirety, but every song is at least solid, with the best of them being absolutely breathtaking and incredible.  Overall, this album has more atmosphere than any other MR album; while a few individual songs may stand up to it, as a whole it cannot be beaten in the way it completely immerses you in Shelton's world of death, honor, vikings, and the vastness of the ocean.  It falls only behind The Deluge in consistency, as well, making it one of the finest albums MR have written, for sure.

The album opens with the instrumental "Tomb of the Serpent King", which, similarly to "Gateway to the Sphere" on Spiral Castle, introduces you to the world of Shelton's vikings and immerses you into the album immediately.  While, when listening to the track alone, it can drone on, leaving one desiring to skip it in order to hear "Butchers of the Sea", in the context of the entire album it couldn't be better, providing the perfect backdrop for the album, building an atmosphere of vastness and dread, until it explodes into "Butchers of the Sea". I note here that Shelton's vocals are more aggressive than they have been since Atlantis Rising, his raw, grating roars evoking the band's thrash era, with even a high-pitched clean shriek to boot, something I would have thought Shelton incapable of in 2008, as he hasn't done any since The Courts of Chaos back in 1990!  The soloing here is fantastic as well, complementing the riffs well, building not only an atmospheric masterpiece but a musical one as well.  "Butchers of the Sea" is certainly a highlight of the album, as are the pondering, mystical "Tree of Life", the dark, murky, almost sludgy "Voyager", and the tense, climactic "Totentanz (The Dance of Death)".

Of particular note is "Blood Eagle", which features an organ solo (or rather, a synthetic organ solo) at the beginning - a good fit for the song by the way, although not exactly the best part of the album - and the song "Return of the Serpent King", which wouldn't be too out of place on a standard death metal album.  While not exactly my taste, it's definitely a solid number, with crushing riffs and vocals as well as retaining an epic feeling to it, if perhaps less so than the rest of the album. Overall, the album is incredibly ambitious, atmospheric, and musically enrapturing; with catchy solos, crushing riffs, moving acoustic passages, and heartfelt vocals, what more could one ask for?  Despite Shelton being 50 years old here, not to mention a heavy smoker, he does a more than adequate job with the album, in fact it's possible that he structured it around his vocals; because, though at times he indeed sounds old, it merely sounds like an older viking passing down a story to the younger members of his tribe.  If you're a fan of heavy metal, death metal, epic metal, or Manilla Road, you need to listen to this album, now, before you regret going without it.

Drawing attention with its international members from Switzerland and Greece, Taär makes a strong entrance into the black metal scene with its first full-length album Catharsis Till Dawn, released on April 11, 2024. This quartet, whose members have previously appeared in different projects, comes before us with a legacy whose name we do not know but whose experiences are felt in every note of the songs.

Taär's music blends the dark soul of the 1990s with the production power of today. What is felt throughout the album is a black metal narrative kneaded with longing for the past but strengthened with today's technical sharpness. Catharsis Till Dawn acts as a time capsule for those seeking the nostalgic purity of the genre.

With the opening track "Celestial Carnage", the album captures the listener from the very first second. No comfort, no mercy. Taär drags its listener directly into the heart of darkness. Relentless blastbeats, sharp guitar riffs, and vocals that alternate between screaming and praying are harbingers of the aggressive tone that permeates the entire album. Tracks like “Feathered Echoes of Wrath” and “The Storm of War” have a classic black metal vibe that reminds us of Immortal’s Battles in the North or Watain’s Rabid Death’s Curse; however, Taär makes their own identity clear by presenting these classic tones with a clearer, more powerful, and more contemporary soundscape.

Taär draws attention not only with their speed, but also with their ability to create atmosphere. Tracks like “Perpetual Descent” slow down the tempo to offer both melodic and dark layers. This balance shows that the band can convey not only speed but also emotion. Although the album generally moves at a high speed, such slowdowns allow the listener to breathe—for a short while, of course. “A Depths of Damnation” reinforces the dark atmosphere with its heavy use of bass. Although most of the songs are adorned with anger and darkness, the rhythmic breaks and light melodic transitions placed in between save the album from monotony. In fact, dissonance and melody are skillfully intertwined in some parts.

Taär establishes a solid structure not only technically but also thematically in Catharsis Till Dawn. The last track bearing its name, “Catharsis Till Dawn”, is like a closing prayer. The album, which ends with a meditative snare drum and ceremonial vocals, makes you feel like you are in an endless loop when you rewind.

The fact that the album remains both raw and powerful is directly related to the success of its production quality. This modern but not sterile soundscape brings together the atmospheric darkness of the 90s with the clarity of today.

Conclusion:
Catharsis Till Dawn is perfect for those who miss the nostalgic black metal feeling but want to hear it with modern sounds. This album, which looks back at the early days of bands like Immortal, Marduk and Watain, uses them only as a reference while preserving its originality.

Even on their first album, Taär show that they know what they are doing: Raw, intense, aggressive but controlled. While paying respect to the spirit of old school black metal, they also clearly show their future potential. If you want to relive the spirit of the 90s with a modern explosion, Taär’s Catharsis Till Dawn album will be the ideal journey for you.

Standout tracks: Celestial Carnage, Perpetual Descent, The Storm of War, The Impaler’s Triumph

Germany's Audio Kollaps specialize in an apocalyptic flavor of grindcore informed by crust and a large helping of death metal, which is sure to grab the attention of extreme metal fans that don't normally listen to much grind (such as myself).

The band's riffing style on Ultima Ratio tends to favor menacing death metal tremolo lines for the verse sections, aggressive crust progressions for the choruses and thrash breaks as bridge pieces or intro riffs ("Die Leere"). The guitar tone really works well for the tremolo lines especially, letting them slice right through the mix. Those tremolo riffs have a strong sense of melody to them, but there isn't much in the way of traditional lead guitar, with melodic leads over riffs being practically nonexistent and genuine solos showing up only rarely. This approach makes sense, especially as the band only has one guitarist. Most of the riffs are adequate or good; a few completely destroy, such as the death metal tremolo meets thrashy assault in the middle of "Tief Gesunken." The drums follow the riffing patterns pretty much as you'd expect, with blastbeats or double bass during the tremolo lines, d-beats during the crust riffs and thrash beats during the thrash breaks. Björn is a more than capable drummer, though, so he mixes it up often enough, throws down some interesting fills and transitions between the various styles as if it's second nature to him. The one thing that is disappointingly absent from the album is a noteworthy bass presence. Sometimes it's difficult to tell that it's doing anything other than standard subconscious riff-fattening, but sometimes, especially during the tremolo riffs, you can hear it doing a sort of nondescript, fuzzy rumbling way down in the mix. The one standout exception is in the second half of "Alles Schwindel" where there's a distinct and groovy bass line that snakes along while the guitar focuses on a different riff entirely. It's a missed opportunity to be sure, but not something that actively annoys or really takes away from the experience.

Kai's vocals are quite similar to Karl Willetts' in Bolt Thrower. In fact, the similarity is almost uncanny, with not just the same flavor of growl but also a similar pronunciation. It contributes to the album's death metal flavor, pushing it away from its crust and grind roots. There are also some extremely buried vocals that could very well be sampled from somewhere, but they sort of sound like a man making cat sound effects with a hell of a lot of reverb. They're strange, to be sure, but they're buried enough that they just sort of add a subtle melodicism unless you listen really closely, plus they only show up on a few tracks so aren't too much of a nuisance.

Other than the issue with the bass I mentioned previously, the production on this album is really quite class. The drums are incredibly weighty and the cymbals are nice and crisp, the guitars have a really crunchy bite to them and the vocals roar right through everything. The mix has enough aggression and grittiness to be effective at what it's trying to do but isn't at all muddy or unbalanced. If you like the production on albums like Warmaster or the Sunlight Studios bands (though the guitar tone here isn't quite the same as that, though they aren't completely different either) then you'll probably appreciate how this album sounds.

I find myself enjoying the more overtly death metal tracks on Ultima Ratio a good bit more than the grindier ones, but that most likely reflects my personal tastes moreso than the band's competency at either genre. Even so, the tremolo lines that tend to make up the fastest parts of the album are uniformly solid or better, so there really aren't any sections that have me thinking, "yeah, alright, when is a good riff going to show up?" like a lot of the fast sections in noisy, chaotic grind do. I won't make any claims about being an expert in grindcore, but this does sound quite different from the majority of grind I've heard. Fans of riffier grind like Rotten Sound might really get a kick out of this, but I think it will appeal especially to old school death metal fans like myself who love some nice, headbangable thrashy goodness.

Do you like riffs? Do you like thrash? Do you like riff filled death-thrash insanity? (The correct answer to each of these questions is of course, HELL FUCKING YES!!!!) Then Shrine of Scars is not a band to be missed. Their sound is reminiscent of Schizophrenia and Beneath The Remains-era Sepultura and early Death. Yes, it is that good. The guitar work is similar to what you would hear on Beneath The Remains. Each song has too many riffs and tempo changes to even attempt to count. The vocals are similar to Chuck's on Scream Bloody Gore but they are a little more growled. 

The demo opens with the title track, "Deathbed for a Weakening Spirit" and it absolutely rips! A killer intro riff, great lyrics, in general it is fast paced insanity. The album continues in this vein until track number five, "Ripe." "Ripe" starts out with a slow, crushing riff and an all around depressing sound. Then around the 1:30 mark, the pace picks up and another killer riff comes in and just rips my fucking head off. I really can't explain how much ass this kicks. The only fault I can find is that the album is a little under produced, a little more bass and this album would essentially be flawless. 

Bottom line? Check out Shrine of Scars now! They own you, they own your neck, and they own me. Be careful, extended listening will cause severe whiplash!! Great demo, I look forward to their next release.

The production on the Ascended side of the split is murky and deep, heavy on the low-end. It's a perfect fit for Ascended's more atmospheric brand of death metal -- "Abhorrent Voices, They Whisper" is largely instrumental, yet its jangling bass, repetitious riffing, and eerie horror samples are quite convincing. The vocals near the end rise like a roar from the deep... "Spirits of the Passage" is a mid-paced combination of ultra-deep vox and rousing guitar, suffused with a good dose of doomy Finnish gloom.

In contrast, Helcaraxe's side is nimble and quick, packed with non-stop riffing. As usual, their brand of melodic death metal is also heavy on the bass, and the deep yet understandable vocals also add heft to their sound. "The Morbid Force" is a tribute to the inexorable power of death, utterly void of spirituality or sentimentality; the distinctive chorus plus the triumphant main riff will have this stuck in your head for weeks. "Dark Sorcery"'s groove is memorable, too, so much so it's hard to believe it's only 1:45 long.

This is a top-notch death metal split: I've been flipping it over and over for weeks. The contrast between the two bands is just perfect, and both deliver two excellent tracks. The cover art is also quite exceptional, also -- I like the combination of both bands' aesthetics, and there's plenty of detail to ponder while you're listening! Highly recommended.

Standout tracks: "Spirits of the Passage", "The Morbid Force"
