Ah, early Evergrey. Interesting musicianship, great atmosphere, attention-grabbing singing, and just the right amount of melodrama. Watching how they gradually watered down these elements and spent a good chunk of the following years trying to claw their way back to what once made them great is a compelling journey in itself. Fans of their early years usually single out Recreation Day as the final hurrah of Evergrey’s first phase, before they dove headfirst into the languor of syncopated one-note riffs and schmaltzy lyrics about tasting neverending flavours of sorrow. I beg to differ and cast my vote for the sometimes overlooked In Search of Truth. Beyond faster tempos and livelier guitar work, their first three albums had a unique, haunting atmosphere that they would seldom revisit in later years. "Mark of the Triangle", for instance, is just a few The Sisters of Mercy nods short of being a top-tier gothic metal song. Its eerie intro and ominous outro are far more unsettling than anything your average goth rock band (complete with The Crow cosplay) ever produced. The same can be said of the choral arrangements in "Rulers of the Mind", "Dark Waters", and "Misled", which, when paired with Sven Karlsson’s understated keyboards, coat the entire auditory experience in a beautiful veneer of pervading darkness. That approach is far more agreeable, at least to yours truly, than Evergrey’s later preference for sleek, electronic ambiances.

So yeah, this is a gothic metal album disguised as a dark prog metal one. Oh, and thematically? It’s about some poor schmuck who got abducted by a particularly invasive group of extraterrestrials and… um, “lost his dignity” to his otherworldly captors. As usual, Tom Englund takes themes that are one smirk short of a comedy skit and treats them with the most deadpan seriousness imaginable. His character is an emotional wreck, no longer able to function in society, a paranoid, traumatized shell of a man haunted by shadows of his violators. His sleepless nights are filled with dreadful visions of his torturous experience aboard their ship. Maybe he’s just an unhinged soul trying to rationalize more earthly traumas, or maybe he really was probed halfway to Alpha Centauri and spat back into Nowhere, Kansas without so much as a “whoops, sorry” and a memory wipe. Discredited by loved ones and apparently visited frequently by the aliens, he ends up in an asylum for good measure. Englund frames the entire narrative as the diary of a miserable victim slowly unraveling, and if you can stomach the occasionally kitschy and repetitive prose, it effectively conveys the dimly lit, suffocating musical environment of the album. I, for one, prefer that sort of approach compared to what the band would latch onto later. Sometimes it’s easier to emotionally engage with a focused story, no matter how fantastical or sci-fi it may be, than with dozens of songs about being vaguely distraught for equally vague reasons.

As mentioned earlier, the album also benefits from a stronger focus on guitar work and hooks. The addition of Henrik Danhage did, and still does, wonders for the band. Opening track "The Masterplan" more than makes up for its one-note riffs (damn it, Tom!) with a healthy dose of excellent lead work and a sweeping, inescapable power metal chorus that sticks harder in your mind than the alien torture devices used to crudely shaboink our wretched protagonist. Critics are right to point out that nothing following that track quite matches it, but that’s because it’s the most stylistically distinct song on the album. "Watching the Skies", its not-quite-twin sister, comes close with a sharp power metal tempo, equally tight leads, a better main riff, and an earworm chorus. The rest of the tracks are more contemplative and tamer in terms of speed, but that doesn’t diminish their worth. "Rulers of the Mind" moves between aggressive, staccato-laden verses, busy bridges, dramatic choirs, and a simple but effective chorus that ties it all together in a neat package. "The Encounter" attempts to bridge the band’s two major influences, power metal and sorrowful gothic music, with varying success. Meanwhile, "Mark of the Triangle", one of Evergrey’s darkest tracks, is a tour de force of atmosphere. It leads the listener deep into the protagonist’s fractured mind, where jagged, saw-like riffs evoke memories of the tools used to harm him. The wandering piano, melodic leads, and stirring string section before the final chorus guide us through his moments of solitude and attempted therapy. As the ghostly outro fades rather than resolves, we’re left with the sense that this cycle of mental breakdown will repeat endlessly until the poor soul either loses the last fragments of his sanity or ends his own suffering. None of this is innovative, but it doesn’t need to be. It works, just as all solid musical storytelling should. "Misled" takes a similar approach to bookend Mr. Really Fucking Unlucky’s journey, this time with a sprightlier tempo and an amazing pre-chorus bridge that ramps up the pace and blends harmonized guitars and choirs into what may be the only time you’ll ever headbang to the sound of a psychotic asylum inmate’s cries of despair. Wholesome stuff.

Sure, some moments don’t land. "State of Paralysis" is a meandering, sappy ballad that serves mainly as a preview to the chorus of "The Encounter". "Dark Waters", while containing some cool melodies, desperately needs a stronger hook or a faster section. It drags without earning its runtime. "Different Worlds" tries to be what "State of Paralysis" couldn’t but goes way too far into corniness, with Tom channeling a tired, not-so-bright Stanislavski student while moaning and performing the protagonist’s sorrow. I’ll admit, this kind of thing would be a turn-off for me even if they brought in Daniel Day-Lewis or Anthony Hopkins to deliver it. So yes, I might be biased.

In Search of Truth is Evergrey at their most poignant. It is, at once, brooding and energetic, theatrical but understated, sophisticated yet matter-of-fact. It strikes a balance the band would never quite recapture, but it cemented their ability to craft competent, dark, modern, and commercially viable metal that still holds up two decades later. Its weaker points, namely the soporific ballads and some weightless mixing, aren’t enough to sap its strengths. Check it out if you want to remember what these guys could do before deciding to commit to writing heavy music for bleeding hearts. You won’t be disappointed.

Oh, and please, avoid driving down dark forest roads at night. And whatever you do, don’t watch Fire in the Sky.

The fact that Joe was only a member for a very short time, and he appears on the solo cd series is kind of funny.  Most casual Melvins fans will glance at this release and dismiss it, but within the grooves of this EP contains some of the heaviest drone metal since the band Earth (see track 3, Hands First Flower which takes up 23 of the EP's 27 total minutes) which doesn't seem surprising since Preston was in one of the earliest formations of Earth.  

Starting the disc out is a track called 'The Eagle Has Landed' and is a bizarre sample of a scratchy, jazz record playing while a baby is crying in the background.  This type of thing became a staple for the future Thrones records that use various strange samples from movies and other unknown sources.  A good introduction to Preston's style.

The next track starts and sounds instantly familiar as Preston's own.  'Bricklebrit' lasts only 3 minutes, but sounds like it could be taken from the first Thrones demo tape and is the most easily accessible track on this record.  It is the classic Thrones sound with heavily sludged bass plays over programmed drums.

My personal favorite, the previously mentioned 'Hands First Flower', is a Doom Metal masterpiece that fans of Earth or Sunn O))) will shit their pants over.  Turn it up loud and massage your inner demons.

This album is nowhere near a Melvins album, and will probably be disliked by many Melvins casual fans, but if you liked the Melvins album 'Lysol' (also with Joe Preston) this record is one step beyond into the realm of totally bizarre drone metal.  A great EP that I wish would have been an LP.

album: III: Songs of Happiness... Words of Praise
texto:
When (Dolch) name an album 'Songs Of Happiness... Words Of Praise' when they kick things off “with great fanfare,” when they dedicate 'Track Six' with its devilish reverse vocals and the most disturbing song on the new EP to the “feel-good hormone” serotonin, then you can take all of that literally - but of course you can't. The two Hamburg, Germany, natives are masters of irony and cynicism, existentialists of extremely dark music, taking the genre apart, dissecting it, so to speak, when they play with fake applause and extremely prolonged sustained vibrations. They have now settled comfortably into their niche of a cool, restrained, reduced sound cosmos between ambient loops and viscous black metal eruptions, which is based entirely on repetition, although the word “cozy” would never even cross my mind for a tenth of a second in this context. Uncomfortable, isolated, brittle, fragile is the ground on which they move.

The new songs are even darker, more unwieldy, and more inaccessible than the familiar songs from the first two demos or the latest single releases, often soporifically slow—not much happens here, but this is precisely what has an absolutely hypnotic effect. All the songs function like mantras, sung, but even more often whispered and murmured – like Eurythmics on strong tranquilizers.

The clock is ticking during our brisk ride on 'The River' which is all about life and death, about the space between the two when there isn't enough energy for one or the other. A death- (or life?) weary 'Siren' lulls us to sleep against the backdrop of a slow heartbeat with her longing, painfully echoing, enticing song, until we are virtually overwhelmed by guitars and drums, which are immediately silenced as well. 'Hydroxytryptamine Baby I' takes place entirely in a fog, perhaps in a padded cell, from which gagged whimpers and fragments of voices emerge, while the drums and trumpets bring back obsession and leave us paralyzed. It could hardly be more frightening or ghostly. '100,000 Days'? They just have to overdo it. But even a (Dolch) is just a Tool, and six minutes of fragmentary melodies and ethereal vocals are finally followed by twelve whole minutes of a single, as usual muted feedback oscillation. The suffering, the torment – it just never ends. A showpiece of seemingly endless uniform repetition, most of which happens in the background. And a wonderful song for the distortion noise endless loop at the end of a concert, as already celebrated on their tour with King Dude.

This (Dolch) should only be given to listeners with strong nerves on prescription or at least with a package insert. It should be used regularly, but initially in small doses; as with any other psychotropic drug, the effect will only become noticeable after some time. For risks and side effects, ask your psychiatrist or local shaman.

Originally published on Saitenkult.de

titulo: The name is not the only thing different
album: Ode to the Churning Seas of Nar-Mataru
texto:
To state the obvious at first: the band in question right here is actually named Pyogenesis. For the re-issue of their demo from 1991 the band named themselves differently. There seems to be a legal issue with their former drummer Pit that doesn’t allow the band to use the Pyogenesis moniker for this release. So they went with the name Kabandha which is derived from Hindu mythology describing a carnivorous demon in form of a headless torso. So far so bad-ass. But the name is not the only thing different on this group’s release.

Pyogenesis is a prime example for a band totally subverting its sound and attitude to the point where it is simply unbelievable how they used to sound like when they have started. What they have done on  “Ode to the Churning Seas of Nar-Mataru” is a far stretch away yet from their self-titled EP on which they paid tribute to the so called “Peaceville three”, i.e. Paradise Lost, Anathema and My Dying Bride, serving up finest melancholic death/doom metal. And it is worlds apart from the trendy alternative pop/rock band they have turned into later.

On this demo the listener is confronted with straight death metal with goregrind influences. These goregrind influences may come to no wonder to anyone considering how close the line-up is intertwined with the legendary grind band G.U.T. Its lead vocalist Olli even performs some backing vocals on this demo. It is mostly the vocals in which the goregrind influences emerge. The vocals are mostly an inhumanly sounding guttural growl which is probably pitch-shifted on some songs like it is usual in the goregrind genre. 

However Pyogenesis don’t totally dive into the grind territory with its often silly gestures but performs a really serious and somber kind of death metal. Putting it into the “cavernous” death metal category would go too far either, as this demo sounds not close enough to Incantation, Immolation and others. Still the band achieves to capture some really dark and captivating riffs altogether which brings back memories of 80’s death metal combined with the aforementioned grindcore-ish parts. As this release was recorded in a studio the sound quality is rather good for a demo from 1991. Every instrument is clearly discernable. The guitars have the typical down-tuned but sawing kind of sound whilst the bass sounds great especially due its chunkiness.

Unfortunately there are no lyrics printed in the inlay. Nevertheless the lyrics of the two songs “Rise of the Unholy” (from which the band took the term Kabandha) and “Path Below the Skull” can be retrieved on the Metal Archives due to being re-released on the “Rise of the Unholy” EP in which the lyrics are printed inside. The titles suggest it and the lyrics at hand proof it that the band’s members used be interested in the occult and literature. Terms such as “Nar-Mataru” are probably derived from the faux Necronomicon which used to circulate among those interested in discovering the left hand path. This dark and occult atmosphere surrounds the “Ode…” demo, not only lyrically but also musically as it sounds truly evil. The riffs sometimes remembering of the early works of Morbid Angel and the invocative deep growling voice are able to conjure something really sinister.

Altogether “Ode to the Churning Seas of Nar-Mataru” is a really worthy release and together with Fleshcrawl’s demo among the first actual works of death metal from Germany when this subgenre of metal was still very new in this country. Maybe in the end it has even been the better decision to not having put the Pyogenesis name onto this re-issue as the featured material does not come close to the Pyogenesis of today or their former member Tim’s one-hit-wonder Liquido, but that is a different story…

Review originally posted at http://www.teethofthedivine.com by Erik Thomas

Though some may consider The East coast and Florida the main stays of US death metal, but for the home of technical, brutal death metal, you need to consider that in California there are such amazing death metal acts as Deeds of Flesh, Vile, Brain Drill, Decrepit Birth, Odious Mortem and Severed Savior, who after five years have finally released the follow up to Brutality is Law.

Personally, I thought Brutality Is Law was a pretty standard Unique Leader affair, but on the Willowtip released follow up, Severed Savior have appeared to make a Decrepit Birth like development and evolution in their already technical brutal sound. Like Decrepit Birth, Severed Savior also recruited an Odious Mortem member to help out, vocalsit Anthony Trapani, he along with the addition of Mike Gilbert on Guitars to the core of bassist  Murray Fitzpatrick and drummer Troy Fullerton appears to have added some flare and memorability to Servile Insurrection.

Like Psycroptic’s Ob(Servant) earlier this year, and Decrepit Birth’s Diminishing Between Worlds, Servile Insurrection simply raises the bar for what can be done with technical/brutal death metal nowadays. Stupefying complexity melds with pummeling brutality and even some unexpected tangents (i.e end of opener “Questions”, “Servile Insurrection”). However, while the band has musically evolved and developed some truly jaw dropping music, and even melodies, the lyrics not penned by Trapani appear to revert back to 8th grade (”Fecalphilliac”).  Musically though, the likes of “Inverted and Inserted”, “Rewards of Cruelty”, “Fuck the Humans”, “Acts of Sedition”, “Spoils of War” and the closing title track are at times, simply jaw dropping in their execution, heaviness and complexity. Even interlude “Intervallo del Tradimento” is superbly done. And whereas some of Ob(Servant)’s tracks overstayed their welcome, Severed Savior keep all their assaults in the 3-4 minute range.

The only downside to this spectacular addition to 2008s already superb death metal releases s that, partially to the punishing but familiar Zach Ohren production and the swapping of members, some of these bands sound a little similar, and frankly playing this side by side to say,  Odious Mortem’s Cryptic Implosion, it was difficult to tell which was which.

Not a bad problem to have though….

Jolly little tunes for kindergartners these Finnish guys traffick in - certainly NOT! Second album release "Ritual IX" is a long droning sludge-hammer doom-a-thon: it's just three tracks with minimal lyrics of occult ritual worship and extended passages of glacially paced minimalist bass-heavy drone rumble. Amazing that I've not heard of this band before - hell, even my trusty music supplier Aquarius Records doesn't seem to know these guys - and that the MA website had no reviews of DBR's albums. Apparently the musicians are publicity-shy and don't have a Facebook or other social media page or website. Myself, I stumbled across DBR on Youtube and found some of their songs had been uploaded there.

"Enneargy" gets the, uh, energy going at soporific levels and more or less maintains that for long stretches of time with a cycle of quite simple bass chords descending a short staircase to Sheol. What vocals exist are high and clear if sounding quite distant in the mix. There's also a higher synthesiser accompaniment as a counterpoint to the main riff loop. A sudden convulsion before the halfway mark and the music picks up urgency and pace. It's not all trudging doom though: after the 10th minute, the music becomes jazzy and atmospheric with spacey effects, and it all sounds very psychedelic.

Second track "Enneanacatl" - DBR seem enamoured of words related to the Greek word "ennea-", referring to anything to do with the number nine, as in nine-sided or nine dimensions - is a lighter, speedier track juxtaposing heavy stoner doom, light jazzy elements and a raspy spider voice from the realms of black metal. There are some light psychedelic touches and the music has a good crunchy texture. The track changes to something more retro hard rock in style, the vocals become clean and something of a Latin influence creeps in.

"Enneathan" is a much more stoner-doomy track, very relaxed and in sound milder and appearing stoned. The pace and beat are steady if rather monotonous and the various atmospheric effects, suggestive of alien forest ambience, add to the track's organic development which includes a shrill deranged lead guitar. As the track progresses, it picks up speed, a vocal in a trance emotionlessly intones the lyrics, and lead guitar plays a spindly melody amid the rumbling music which itself seems entranced, going on and on in a hypnotic shambling groove. 

At the 20th minute, the business end of DBR kicks in and God-Almighty doom riffs are chucked at us like lolly-sticks going out of fashion. After the halfway point is reached, the track lapses into quiet stillness, from which an oppressive doom-ambient droning fuzz gradually emerges. The piece becomes a long coda of cold cave-like atmospheric oppression with a malevolent bass drone rising up and down. 

There's enough variety on the album despite the very long and usually repetitive instrumental passages to keep listeners' attention. Perhaps "Enneathon" could have been edited for length in its last 15 minutes but for me as it is, the length seems fine. I wouldn't mind if the coda had been longer actually; the band could have added a slight tension-breaking mini-climax to it. Some listeners may find the coda as is somewhat of an unwanted tag-along. Apart from the length of the final track, the album is very good and followers of Electric Wizard, Sleep and similar bands combining stoner rock, doom metal, space ambience and retro-psychedelic styles should give the work a hearing if and when they come across it.

It’s clearly debatable when some of the original doom/death metal bands started to lose their death ’n doom elements and what they started to sound like instead – which is if you’ve heard plenty of these 90’s kind of albums sometimes hard to describe. In Anathema’s case, you'll still find plenty of ingredients the style would be made of (woe is me kind of lyrics, dramatic clean/harsh vocals and moving guitar leads). As you might see, I’ve excluded the rhythm section because this one differences quite a bit compared to the band’s earlier works. Pentecost III still relied on notes that made one feel doomed, but here Anathema lack the physical weight I often associate with any form of doom metal. Only ‘’Restless Oblivion’’ feels like a slightly exception, with a bulldozer-of-a-riff opening and its brute chorus, but to call The Silent Enigma a proper doom/death metal album might be far-fetched.

It's tricky to describe what Anathema have ended up with instead.  We're not dealing with the melodic guitars on autopilot approach that Katatonia was responsible for with their second album, nor does The Silent Enigma resemble any familiar sounding  transitional gothic metal efforts. Aggression is more so caused by the vocals and not so much by the guitar work itself - as ''The Sunset of Age'' clearly demonstrates; slowly working towards that emotional climax through  juggernaut chords, enigmatic acoustic passages and  and an apocalyptic solo that might end up rather frustrating for those seeking approachable or gruff doom metal variants. 

Having taken over in the vocal department, Vincent Cavanagh sounds like a man who goes on a lonesome journey in search for happiness but ends up spiraling into depression instead. ‘’Shroud of Frost’’ feels like a cry for help where the throaty roars become almost too much to handle (literally perhaps, you can almost hear his voice break in there!) while the introspective ‘’A Dying Wish’’ unfolds itself as an acceptance of an unfortunate fate. While certainly emotionally provoking, The Silent Enigma does also have its clumsy moments that prevents it from falling into the classic category though. Sometimes the guitars aren’t engaging much and the spoken passages become too prominent, which causes certain songs to become somewhat powerless. Take the title track for example, where Cavanagh sounds like a whining tenor who thought Tom Warrior didn’t whine enough in the late 80’s and decided to imitate him. ‘’Cerulean Twilight’’ hints the direction Anathema would take with Eternity; sounding more like autumnal rock than self-pity metal (which includes the majority of these tunes in case you wondered), but with a whispered vocal approach feels like a missed opportunity while ‘’Nocturnal Emission’’ features some distorted spoken notes and someone grasping for air in between (?!) - It’s hard to find any real value in it.  

Saved by its highlights, Anathema still manages to deliver the goods, not to mention opening and closing the album with their best tunes is a solid trick. ‘’Restless Oblivion’’ shows the band at their heaviest and most instant; a spiteful vocal performance howls between the hypnotic verse and shattering chorus. The aforementioned ''Sunset of Age'' has some of the better vocal effects used to lead the verse, while the final verse emerges with enormous emotional power. The gloomy preface of ‘’A Dying Wish’’ is somewhat misleading, as it quickly becomes clear the tune has some real fire to it: an energetic closer with an interesting contrast between the adventurous guitar acrobatics and the vocals that express nothing but regret. It’s the fastest tune on the album and no wonder the band still play this song live (well, sometimes at least).

Anathema would soon lose most of their rough edges, as Eternity showed a new direction of the band. Now I like that album as well, but a part of me wonders what the band could have ended up with, had they worked on the strengths that they demonstrated here. The verdict is rather simple -  The Silent Enigma doesn’t fall in the classic category, but occasionally it's rather great.

I was amazed to see no reviews for any album of this Swedish Horde and that is sad indeed. They date back to 2012 with their debut album and although I myself have not heard it I have heard their last four releases and every one of them is fantastic. This is a truly underrated band and this review hopefully puts them onto your fucking radar. 

I am a massive fan of all things speed in the genre of black metal and the second wave, back in the mid-nineties, is the era I most enjoy. Bands like Thy Primordial, Sorhin and Marduk are some of my all time favorites. Had these maniacs released material like this in the golden age they would have been legends. Sadly its 20 years to late but luckily for you its freely available. The album that could sum up their career most adequately if you are also a worshiper of the second wave scene is Setherial's - Lords of the Night Realm and anyone familiar with that slab of pulverizing brutality knows what a hell ride of satanic glory they are in for on this release from Daemon worship productions. 

The drums are played at maximum speed throughout and are loaded with drum rolls aplenty. The tempo on the skins is at warp speed and hammers away incessantly in a nightmarish whirlpool. The rhythm guitar is laden with tremolo picking and the bands slows things down from time to time just enough before the next onslaught commences. There is almost zero bass guitar to speak of so no comment in that department. The vocals are a touch monotonous and could have been a bit more varied but this is a minor niggle to the bigger picture. Themes and of darkness, death, decay and damnation which is what we all crave anyways.

Obeisance to a witch moon clocks in just under 40 minutes and the general feel is one of razor speed mayhem. This band goes for the jugular and doesn’t let up until the CD comes to a smoking end after track #9, the album titles closer. This band certainly warrants checking out if you are into hyper speed black metal. Satan is pleased and so will you be

Buy or die

When was the last time you could recall staring at the face of hostility, only to be perplexed by the beauty surrounding it? It’s hard really to even conceive such a thought, since those two hardly go hand in hand. But maybe some of us have never been in a situation like that before, and therefore can’t comprehend it as well as another might. For instance, my father, who served in Vietnam, told me about a time that his base was under mortar fire. In-between the mortar rounds and explosions, he claimed that smoke mixed with the morning Vietnamese sun to create an inexplicable surrounding.

But At the Gates seemed to master this effect flawlessly.

“We are blind to the world within us…waiting to be born”

After 32 seconds of industrial noise and effects, those chilling words are passionately and calmly spoken on “Blinded by Fear” before you’re taken down the path of lunacy and depravity. This deranged portrait of life is known as “Slaughter of the Soul”, and you’re stepping square into its asylum. Tomas Lindberg’s seething vocals mixed with Larsson and Björler’s vindictive riffs are enough to make you collapse to the floor. However, with every lyric sung, every riff that is played, there is an undisputed presence of touching melody. The wonderful euphony of “Under a Serpent Sun” is more than a confession to the power of melody that these musicians posses. It’s no question that brutality and grace exist in harmony here, but it’s the brutal aspect that could be the selling points at critical moments. The title track is one of the most rip-roaring tracks on this album, complete with frothing vocals and searing guitars. And composing of one of the most ingenious audio clips ever used, “Suicide Nation” will send a chilling message within the first second as the sound of a shotgun being loaded is blasted into the speakers, only to be followed by maliciously crunched riffs. 

“Children born of sin, tear your soul apart!”

On past albums, Lindberg had a bit more of “Death Growl”, and was certainly deeper. On here, however, his voice is a bit more rasped and stretched, making him seem even more desperate. And when Lindberg snarls, you know his giving it his all. He aims to leave his body void of all energy after every song, and it’s a wonder he got through a whole album with death by the cause of exhaustion. After listening to him put his body to the test on “Blinded by Fear”, he continues on his impressive performance throughout the whole album, notably again on “Cold” and “World of Lies”. Listening to him bark out “Suicide - jaws locked around your spine” on "Suicide Nation" will leave the vision of a man stripped of all hope. 

Combine Lindberg with the experience of the guitar work, and a whole new world is opened. From the unrelenting “Blinded by Fear” to the acoustic based “Into the Dead Sky”, Larsson and Björler effortlessly put forth one of the most stunningly unique Metal albums. While the riffs they fire off on this album are a bit simpler and straight-forward than their past releases, they feel more completely written and thought out. And their solos, while short, are nicotine to the ear. “Cold” features a striking use of effects blended in with raw talent to envelop the listener and stamp its mark on the song. 

While the work here is truly breathtaking, there are a few blemishes. For starters, since this isn’t as technical as their past releases, some of these songs border on being ripped off one another. This surely isn’t a problem in the beginning with the first 7 songs being completely distinguishable, but the last few, like “Nausea” and “Unto Others”, are hard to tell apart. And that being said, “Nausea” is probably the blandest track on here, as it becomes borderline hardcore punk with its overly simple riff base. And besides a shining moment on “Blinded by Fear”, the bass is still virtually non-existent. However, to cancel that out, Adrian Erlandsson does a phenomenal job on his drum parts. While it’s not anything that will drop your jaw, it’s more than solid. Adrian performs with pin-point precession, and never misses a beat. 

This was the last album by At the Gates, and what a way to leave. The compassionate mix of brutality and melody that they created on “Slaughter of the Soul” has still yet to be matched within the Gothenburg genre. And besides a few hiccups here and there, this is their masterpiece. If you call yourself any kind of a metal head, I can’t stress to you enough how much you need this album.

Overall – 4.5/5 (92)

Recommended Tracks
Blinded by Fear
Slaughter of the Soul
Under a Serpent Sun
Suicide Nation

*For a better summary than the last real paragraph above, please obtain the track "Suicide Nation" and listen to the first second. Thank you.

Greek thrashers with a knotty history dating back to 2007, Benefactor Decease have been delayed many times in putting out their second album, beginning the process in 2020, which was already 5 years after their debut full-length. This series of misfortunes includes the news that guitarist Kostas “Sarcastic” left the band after recording Abnormal Attachments. The album itself is quite an achievement, in an avenue of thrash metal not routinely contemplated: that frigid and anti-social corner where Toxik and Voivod sit staring at one another, while Coroner directs the hostility.

The quintet’s interest in bizarre and uncomfortable subjects of modernity finds its parallel in the jarring and technical workouts for all the instrumentalists, flitting between extreme speed attacks that reference Sadus and moments of eerie serenity, such as the interlude ‘Eroticised Felonies’ or the futuristic introduction of ‘Technophobic Syndrome’, the latter set off by a boxy bass solo between the frantic thrashing. Vocally, Panos “Cut-Throat” Toufexidis leans into the unsettling vibe, with some rabid Kreator style work enhanced by pockets of throat-mashing more usually seen in grind. If this sounds a bit unhinged, that impression remains accurate for a sometimes over-stimulating 48 minutes, during which Benefactor Decease pull out full songs of any length between 2 and a half and 7 minutes, not to mention a few interludes that are also prone to atmosphere. As such, the overall feel of Abnormal Attachments hovers on a curious line between old-school thrash metal and the urban menace suggested by American death metal, as well as the sci-fi obscurity of Coroner's themes.

It's entirely possible that you could enjoy certain songs and hate others, but the emphasis during the album remains on sudden and tricky methods of attack, so even if 'Imprisonment Atrocities' feels lopsided and awkward near the beginning of the listen, the title track might hit smoother when over halfway through. The methods on those 2 songs are relatively similar, stitching together riffs for 7 minutes without worrying how often the time signatures alter, and often halting the song entirely to enter a new section. When going flat out, Benefactor Decease can be mistaken for late '80s Sepultura, though this impression never lasts more than about 30 seconds before more chaotic shredding (guitar or vocal) enters the picture - either that or menacing ambience. Here, everything feels sudden and hostile, but without forgetting the art of writing good music.

Now, this band has popped up on my recommendation list for quite a few times now, but I hadn't bother to check them out until this release. Mainly because this was released on the same date as Dreamtale's latest album and I find the Finnish masters' release a bit of a disappointment. And bloody hell, by contrast this made Everlasting Flame sounds even worse even though the two were, stylistically speaking, fundamentally different. And knowing my taste? Of course this one suits me far better.

Though Trick or Treat started originally as a Helloween tribute band, and despite the fact that they'd never totally thrown off that influence ( I mean, which Europower managed that anyways?), this opus is definitely as enjoyable as it can get, and, of course, verily old school. The typical orchestral intros worked well to start that Halloween vibe by repeating the classic rhyme,,Trick or treat, trick or treat, give me something good to eat''. Then the title track jumped on with all the double bass drumming, fast trilling guitar riffs, highly infectious and upbeat chorus you can ask for in the genre. This might as well be released back in the 90s. The resemblance ran all the way from Helloween to Freedom Call. I mean, just listen to that little groovy verse as well as the over-the-top chorus in Crazy. If you don't want to singalong I suggest you try another genre. Now, one of my favorite tracks on the LP is definitely Escape from Reality. When the riff starts with quite the  Eagles Fly Free energy followed by shredding solo, I knew I'm gonna love this one. The banging rhythm doesn't disappoint either. Generally I'm here for the speed, but the mid-paced rockers Peter Pan Syndrome (Keep Alive) and April actually sound quite... touching. Of course, Conti's voice is part of the reason why those two worked for me, but I like the whole swing feeling of the song too. Also, nothing can bring the album round to an nicer end than a bloody 11- min epic with all the energy of a simpler and more vocal-dominate Gamma Ray.

If you prefer Italian symphonic power along the line of Rhapsody then I wouldn't recommend this to you, but if you like the more simple and catchy yet also heavier German side of the genre, then try this by all means.And obviously, I'll stick with the old school stuff and call this a masterpiece. 

Highlights:
Creepy Symphony
Crazy
Escape from Reality
Falling over the Rainbow
The Power of Grayskull

Satan’s Cross is a Mexican black/doom metal band consisting of S. on guitars, bass and vocals and M. on vocals, also known as Sulphur and Mercury when performing with the heavy/doom metal act Violet Magick. The band digitally released their debut EP, the eponymously titled Satan’s Cross, in December 2014, but the German label Dying Victims Productions picked up the two track presentation for an early 2015 seven inch vinyl release.

Satan’s Cross features two tracks, “Sumerian Night” and “The Conjuring”, which combine for a grand total of just over eight minutes of material. The band cites the likes Mortuary Drape, Venom, Bathory, Death SS and Mercyful Fate among their primary influences and, despite the broad swath of metal those acts cover, it really serves as a fine starting point for the sound that the band is going after. Imagine a form of old school, first wave black metal that is dipped in the waters of occult doom and traditional heavy metal and you’ll have a fair idea of what’s to come.

The release starts off with slow plodding, featuring rumbling bass lines and crunchy, crawling power chords while raspy, growled vocals begin setting a rather occult tone, taking nods from the Italian school of doom, notably Death SS and Paul Chain. It shouldn’t come as a surprise, considering their other band, Violet Magick, is firmly rooted in the realms of old school Italian doom. Before you know it, though, the band delves into a faster, blackened metal style, encompassing the pummeling percussion of Hellhammer with a dose of Venom-tinged riffing. Frenetic trem riffs are scattered throughout, adding a slightly second wave tinge to some of the riffs while keeping the presentation rooted in things much older. Rather than stringing together dusty doom and old school black metal into a haphazard amalgamation, Satan’s Cross sandwiches the two separate styles together, resulting in a diverse playback, even if the doom is exhibited far less than the dirty black metal.

It’d be interesting to see if Satan’s Cross allows the doom to shine through more on a full length album, but as it stands, Satan’s Cross is an interesting debut that serves as a preview for this newly formed act. Certainly an act to keep an eye on, this Mexican duo brings a first wave sound that is choked with the dust of occult Italian doom metal. There’s certainly room to grow for the band, but they give an interesting twist on the old school revival.

Written for The Metal Observer.

I cannot really think of too many CDs of my collection coming from Romania but after having discovered Loud Rage Music (a Romanian label concentrating on releasing extreme metal outputs by Romanian bands and musicians) that is going to change. The first example of what the metal heads from that country are able to produce is also the latest release by said label and an extraordinary example of smashing old school death metal presented with modernized sound qualities.

Rancorum is a five piece death metal combo attacking the listener with two guitarists and this greatly pays off. Hard hitting trademark chords are pitched against mesmerizing and at first glance slightly disharmonic-sounding melodies creating an unholy force of destruction. The main chops are mainly reminiscent of the classic US bands like Morbid Angel or Monstrosity but there are also influences from some Swedish heroes (Grave in particular) and a few hints of their Eastern European peers. While most songs are kept in mid-tempo or faster regions Rancorum have not forgotten to include some slower parts in which the music is crawling out of the speakers like a reanimated corpse. In those moments the atmosphere gets very dense and sinister leaving the listener with a slightly uneasy feeling.

The songs are cleverly constructed with the right balance of straight forward and steamrolling parts and some more sophisticated pieces lending each track its own character. Tempo and rhythm changes can be found in each song but they are placed with a great feeling for the timing and the flow of the album. Although the music being quite technical in places there are tons of hooks making “The Vermin Shrine” an album being easily enjoyable for any death metal fan. Longer and shorter solos work as transition between the various parts helping to link the different pieces of each song.

The growling delivered by singer Ravager is deep but he is using his pipes in a way to make the lyrics perfectly understandable. In my books this is always a plus as I am fan of brutal and aggressive yet clearly articulated vocals.

Another big plus of this album is the powerful production. The guitars are crunchy and the drums have an immense punch. The mix is crystal clear making each instrument perfectly audible without sacrificing a certain level of rawness. Each detail can be fully enjoyed making this album an absolute must-have for any collector of great old-school death metal.

Norway’s Massemord has had its share of lineup changes throughout the years. Originally a solo project of Lord Hastur Warmachine (of Sykdom and Svartskogg), the band released a slew of demos and full lengths before Cris Pervertor (of Satanika) joined the band on vocals. It wasn’t long until Barren (also of Satanika) joined the band to provide additional guitars. Somewhere along the way Lord Hastur Warmachine, the founder of the band, left and Barren took over as the resident multi-instrumentalist. Convoluted slightly?

Stay Fucking Necro was released by the band independently in 2013 and was recently reissued by Cold Raw Records on CD. While the album was released in 2013 it features material that was recorded by the band in 2004. Some of the tracks were released on 2008′s split with The Frost and Valdur and the rest of the tracks were originally released under the Svartskogg moniker (one of Lord Hastur Warmachine’s other projects) in 2004 because the label rejected the tracks. So basically, they were Massemord tracks released under another name and Stay Fucking Necro finally issued these songs under the correct name. It’s things like that this that seem to define the type of rocky career and instability suffered by the band over the years.

All of the material on Stay Fucking Necro was recorded with Lord Hastur Warmachine on instruments and Barren on vocals (credited as Der Henker here). The music focuses on cold black metal and is packed full of minor key movements, melodic trem riffing and extremely catchy, sweeping chord progressions. The songwriting is solid, allowing the album’s thirty-three minutes to fly past comfortably. The percussion is chunky, with lots of blasts and loudly resonating cymbal crashes, but it fits well with the raw yet melodic style at play. There are a few moments that teeter on the brink of blackened rock riffing, but it still manages to retain an authentic feel. Massemord’s sound can be likened to any number of second wave acts, but then again, Massemord was a part of the second wave explosion.

While the band is fairly well known in underground circles, it’s amazing that the band never really reached a wider audience. Fans of the second wave should find some enjoyment here. It’s not the most polished record on earth, but it’s pretty damn good. Lord Hastur Warmachine may no longer be the main songwriter and instrumentalist, but these tracks show just how capable of a riff writer he was. The newest incarnation of the band, with Barren and Chris Pervertor, show no signs of slowing down, so here’s to hoping this reissue gets the band to remember their roots a bit.

titulo: i have no fucking clue what this is
texto:
I really have no idea what to make of this.  Two-piece band from some shithole in Arizona, one full-length (on Redrum, no less), zero attention from anyone, music that doesn't quite sound like anything else in the world.  I think I like it?  I'm not entirely sure.

I'm at a loss as to what the influences here might be.  I'm thinking... Repulsion, old Cryptopsy (and I mean old old, like 'Blasphemy Made Flesh'), possibly some Swedish shit in the groovier moments.  What this really comes off as, though, is people from a crossover band playing death metal.  I get a certain punk vibe from this album, though it's not immediately apparent in the riffing or drumming apart from the occasional strummed, punky riff or thrash beat here and there.  There's something about the offhand feel of the music in general as well as some of the truly bizarre musical decisions at play that suggests it to me.

Actually, while listening to it, I think I know what one of the major aspects to this album's weirdness is: the drummer rarely uses his double bass pedal.  There's definitely one there, but it's very rarely used: blast beats are replaced by weird half blasts where 16th notes are bashed out on the snare but a simple quarter note bass drum beat is kept, like it's Kataklysm or something.  Moreover, all the riffs seem so fucking weird, a blend of Repulsion type oldschool grind and some Swedeath influence that makes it all feel incredibly off-kilter and deranged.  You know what this really sounds like?  A real band made out of a Chainsaw Dissection-style project.  It still has all the weird repetition of certain passages, the short, looping riffs, and the almost incoherent song structures where passages just slam into each other with no real sense.

But then I could write an essay on what makes this album weird as shit, like the strained, grunting vocals, the lack of a bass guitar, or the weird, directionless nature of the songs, but I think it's easier to accept that I just don't really get it.  It's not very catchy or especially well composed, but the sheer weirdness and impropriety of the music makes me enjoy it on a strange level.  What's with all the doomy riffs that sound like they're from an Incantation album or the absurdly nervous, weird drumming which makes it sound like Smokedog was recording his shit with a gun to his head?  I don't know, man.  This is a weird release.

I wouldn't call this GOOD in the way you ordinarily would, but it's almost absurdly interesting and sounds like nothing else out there.  Pick this up if you're a curiosity seeker like me, but 'normal' death metal fans should definitely pass this up.  Redrum was doing some weird shit back in the day.  By day I mean six years ago.

titulo: It is and yet it isn't
texto:
This album represents everything what Krypteria is about. We have fast and modern tracks like "Scream", catchy commercial and chorus based symphonic tracks like "The Promise" as well as epic tracks with a lot of classic influences like "At The Gates Of Retribution". With the energizing opener "All system go", the slightly experimental and psychedelic single "Time to bring the pain", the more commercial gothic pop single "Somebody Save Me", the calm and hypnotizing "Dream Yourself Far Away" and the powerful "Sweet Revenge" that mixes the band's classic roots and inspirations with a modern and sharp sound, we have five potential hits on the record. 

We also have many great orchestral passages and epic choirs in the choruses. We have a couple of sharp riffs and solid guitar solos. We have a great female vocalist with diversified influences that is the beautiful Cho Ji-In. This album could be described as the quintessence of Krypteria's sound. This is the heart of Krypteria. This album presents us everything what Krypteria is all about and if you had just to chose one single album from the band I would recommend you this one. 

But nevertheless, something is missing and there are also many negative sides. It is and it isn't at the same time. There is too much routine but there are no truly surprising elements on this record with a few mellow exceptions like the strong bass guitar lines in "I Can't Breathe".

The main problem is that there are way too many filler songs on the record that all sound rather similar and can't impress. After a while, the simplistic riffs bore to death. The omnipresent choirs in the choruses become repetitive and stereotypical. After a couple of tracks, Cho Ji-In has shown all of her talent and just keeps on repeating doing the same three different styles. The first four tracks are interesting and introduce to the band's style and the last three epic or catchy tracks are also well done but the weakest tracks are surely in the middle of the album that is way too long with over an hour of running time. 

The album opens and finishes on a high note but the middle part is really weak. "Lost" or "Out Of Tears" sound completely redundant and are terrible fillers. Tracks like "The Night All Angels Cry" add simply too much kitsch, too many orchestral passages and too many choirs into one single song and deliver too much of the same.

That's why a lot of talent and many interesting and authentic approaches are ultimately ruined by a couple of big stinkers in the middle of the record that rate this album down. It's still a decent effort and fresh output of its genre but the band lacks of focus, passion and creativity after a while. Most of the songs are much more energizing and emotional when they are played live but sound somewhat dull, static and repetitive on this record. The songs sound too cold and don't breathe the passion and energy they could. A part of the track list choice and the length of the album it's the production that is the third negative element in here.

In the end, I would still recommend this very representative record of a band with a lot of skills and talent that may one day get the breakthrough they would deserve. They just need a better production, a little bit more courage and a little bit more focus to make not only a good or decent record like this but a true highlight of its genre. I still believe in the three sympathetic guys and the charismatic woman and will follow their way for sure.

If you’re familiar with bands like Mortician, samples at the beginning of songs is not something new, but while Mortician uses samples from old horror movies, Fluids step it up a notch and uses samples from gore videos online and mockumentaries. The opener ‘Caught’ starts off with audio of a man being tortured, most likely cartel related. This along with foreboding synths makes you feel on edge right from the beginning. The sample makes you feel uncomfortable, and makes the music hit that much harder once it kicks in.

A deep guttural proclamation announces the beginning of the actual music, and is followed up by thick, massive guitars and pounding drums. From the moment you are able to hear the guitars, it becomes apparent that the similarities to Mortician don’t just end at the samples. The guitar tone is very similar to that of Mortician, with distortion so heavy and palpable it becomes crushing. Fluids once again takes it to the next level, with the guitar tone being even thicker and heavier than that of Mortician’s.

My immediate thoughts upon listening to Fluids was also just that, a Mortician clone that tries to be more extreme than the band they’re also trying to replicate. The more I listened to the album, the more it grew into something of its own, instead of just being a Mortician rip-off.

Although this musical style isn’t something new, Fluids manage to perfect it with this record. This type of death metal is already incredibly heavy, but this album takes it to the extreme, and manages to create something heavier than anything anyone who has tried to make music along the same vein as Mortician. The album is just sheer brutality from beginning to end, all while remaining memorable, and never becoming monotonous. Every track stands out and has something to offer, which is quite hard to do when making this form of music.

Tracks like Hauled offer slam-like riffing near the end of the song, while other tracks even contain some melodic elements. Dumped is definitely the peak of the album. It is heavy and groovy, and slows down midways through with a melodic doomy section. This transitions into a heavy section with guitars once again reminiscent of slam. This is paired with the best vocal performance on the entire album, and makes for a nasty groove. The album ends rather in quite an odd way when the rest of the album is taken into consideration. The outro track, ‘Scattered’ is a melodic instrumental piece, which feels oddly cathartic. The album before it has introduced us to humanity at its most vile and ruthless, and the closer feels as if it’s reflecting upon the horrors we have just witnessed.

Exploitative Practices is a record that pulls out all the stops, relentlessly crushing you with filthy riff upon filthy riff, taking what Mortician great and turning it more extreme. I think this album even manages to surpass its primary inspiration and becomes something even better than what it tries to replicate.

Highlight tracks: Dumped, Shot, Scattered

titulo: The Sound of A Band Ripping Itself Apart at the Seams
texto:
Pantera's 8th album (and fourth since their sonic transformation on "Cowboys From Hell") is an album that personifies the sound of interpersonal conflict. At this point in the Pantera camp, there was a clear divide in the members and the good times were gone. Addiction, anger, and frustration with each other fuelled the songwriting on "The Great Southern Trendkill." For that reason, this album is my favourite in Pantera's whole discography. 

I'll be the first to admit Pantera is not my favourite band in the world. I enjoy "Power Metal" from time to time (reissue this one already guys!), enjoy some songs off "Cowboys From Hell" and "Vulgar Display of Power," and think "Far Beyond Driven" is their next best effort, but even that one has some pretty notable flaws. I like a couple songs off "Reinventing the Steel" as well, but it's not a highlight of the band's discography. 

What I love about "The Great Southern Trendkill" is that the pretence is gone. On the previous few albums, many of the songs were about being tough, being violent, and was very much along the lines of the band as a unified front against the world. On this album, the sights of the band turned inward as they self-destructed. Phil Anselmo (not my favourite person in the world on the best of days) howls like a wounded animal on this album, and Seth Putnam chips in. Gone is the macho-man vibe. In its place comes a raw, unhinged stream of consciousness for 53 minutes. Phil wrestles with himself on here, from songs like "Suicide Note" (both parts), "13 Steps To Nowhere" and more. These songs are rife with vitriol and venom for anybody and everybody. Given the content of these songs, I understand why Phil had to record his vocals separate from the rest of the band.

Again, I've never been bold enough to call myself a Pantera "fan," but I always thought their most important contribution to metal was using their semi-mainstream status to play with heavier, more underground bands like Morbid Angel, Satyricon, Neurosis, Sepultura, Crowbar, Sacred Reich, Trouble, and more. This was a great way to introduce newcomers to heavier bands, and I wish older legacy acts would do this more often. This album is a gateway in of itself to the heavier side of metal.

This album is not a death metal album, but it definitely feels like the most extreme Pantera ever got. Unlike the previous albums, there's no obvious hit like "Cemetery Gates," "5 Minutes Alone," "This Love," "Walk," or "I'm Broken." There was little in the way of commercial aspiration on this album. In its place, the band needed to exorcise some demons by etching them in wax. It's also Pantera at their most experimental, as songs like "Living Through Me (Hell's Wrath)" get into some industrial territory halfway through the song, "Suicide Note Part 1" has some eerie synths, and vocal effects alongside the 12-string acoustic guitar, and "The Underground in America" gets into noise territory near the end. This is by no stretch of the imagination a Justin Broadrick project, but for a mainstream metal band to delve into these kinds of sounds, it's a step outside the mainstream and pushes against any attempts at streamlining.

As a drummer, I believe this to be Vinnie Paul's greatest performance. He has always been a hard-hitter, but beyond punishing his drumheads, he gets incredibly creative with his drum parts.  Songs like "13 Steps to Nowhere," and "War Nerve" are highlights. He rarely keeps rhythms simple, but never overplays. If Gene Hoglan was the drumming equivalent to an angry ballerina (graceful but impactful), Vinnie Paul was like Mike Tyson, as he hammers the listener over the head, but slips and weaves too. 

I've always thought Dimebag Darrell was a very good guitarist, but I've never understood the need to deify him. However, on this album, he finds the perfect balance of guitar pyrotechnics and bludgeoning. There are less guitar solos that balloon into the highlight of the song (like the solo in "Domination"), but they're consistently interesting to listen to. "Floods" has the biggest exception to this statement, and I always wished that outro went a bit longer. I also believe that "Floods" could have been the closer to this album, but the pacing of the album as is still works great. 

When it comes to heaviness in metal, there's always some subjectiveness involved. Archspire might have the fastest blasts, Sleep or Electric Wizard may level buildings with their walls of sound, Vital Remains might sing the most about Satan, and Portal, Mitochondrion, Infernal Coil or Oranssi Pazuzu might go the most dissonant, and Pissgrave might have the most gruesome album art. I love all of these bands (except for Archspire), but I don't see heaviness as the be-all end-all for metal. Heaviness is a thing I can enjoy, but bands like Diamond Head on "Lightning to the Nations" managed to write riffs that are still crushingly heavy to this day, and Gorguts writes twisting, dissonant tunes with the best of them, but neither of them had "heavy" as the end goal. It was a byproduct. I often think this is the best approach for metal bands. This race to the bottom for heaviness as the end-goal is how we see breakdown-after-breakdown deathcore bands get popular. There is a point to this digression: "The Great Southern Trendkill" doesn't feel like the band said "ok guys, let's get heavier than ever before" on this album. Instead, it feels like the culmination of years of infighting and personal issues. The heaviness was a byproduct. Type O Negative's "World Coming Down" is another example of how this can happen. 

Pantera's legacy in the metal world is one that's always shifting. Unlike other major names, they didn't go to influence other phenomenal bands in the same way that Metallica, Slayer, Iron Maiden, Judas Priest or Death did. As well, the bitterness between members and the circumstances surrounding a reunion lingering for as long as they did until Vinnie Paul's death made the "reunion" possible was the legend of metal websites for much of my life. If you strip away all the posturing, chest-puffing, and artificial push for heaviness seen in the previous 3 Pantera albums, you get "The Great Southern Trendkill." Vulnerability and introspection made for the heaviest album of Pantera's career. They never topped it, and never will, and that's okay.

texto:
It was really hard to decide how much i liked this CD. I feel i have to be in a certain mood to really enjoy it, but there's never a time where i really hate it. There are a lot of people out there that are going to love this music, or hate this music. Myself, on the other hand, i find it somewhere in the above average category. Its somewhat great, but it does have its bad points. Sometimes, Opeth is just heavy as hell and banging out the low, creepy riffs, while other times theyre just going into a melodic breakdown of acoustic guitar and a crooning voice that you would never guess would come out of the vocalists mouth. 

Pretty much every song does the "Opeth breakdown," and most of them contain the thrash-like riffs that are hard and kickass, with the death vocals that are quite excellent. I don't find this album very different than any others in terms of vocals, and guitar parts. I think speaking guitar-wise, this is probably the best of them, for i find that the melodic stuff is quite pretty and its really worth the time to listen to. The thing that was done the best on this album was the bass. Sometimes basses just aren't heard very much throughout albums, but Opeth is one of those bands that wants their beats heard. It works very nicely with the guitars, on all parts of the song. You wouldnt think of it, but it adds a lot to the album and the sound quality of each song. 

One thing that you can expect from Opeth, is long songs. They are a band known for extremely long songs, that have many different beats hidden inside them. The longest track is somewhere around 13 minutes, but something i notice, is that the tracks don't grow old. They do enough switching of their stuff in one song that i find i can listen to the entire thing without ever being tempted to press the skip button and carry the CD to the next song. 

All in all, if you can handle something that has just such an abundant load to offer, this is the CD for you. If youre looking for straight-up metal and nothing but that, don't get this CD because youll be too disappointed with all the acoustic parts they go into. Highlights are "The Leper Affinity," "The Drapery Falls," and "Patterns in the Ivy."

In my opinion the Slovaks have built one of the most impressive local scenes over the past years and there are no signs of them slowing things down anytime soon. Thanks to quite a few connections between bands, labels and musicians from the country I keep stumbling upon more great stuff, so I am not afraid of running out of top quality music within the foreseeable future. One of my latest finds are Krajiny Hmly who released their second full length “Poza ćierne hory” only a few weeks ago. Their style of atmospheric black metal with pagan roots fits nicely into stuff that has been produced by some of their fellow countrymen and as all of the members are seasoned musicians you can expect a highly professional and expertly performed piece of black metal art.

When broken down into detail it could be stated that this is mainly second wave black metal, honest and true. With a production that combines the best of underground aesthetics with clarity of delivery, the band’s sound is just as stunning as the album’s artwork. One thing that I really love about this album is that every track features a unique characteristic, and while Krajiny Hmly have produced one stringent piece of music by staying true to their formula over the whole 40 minutes there is a lot to discover. The mood of savage enjoyment provided by cold riff magic will keep the listener intrigued for several consecutive spins.

Sweeping and epic in scope, yet possessing a raging heart of pure fire and fury, songs like the mighty opener “Vo Svetle Rannej Hviezdy” will immediately get the blood pumping. The band make very good use of dark melodies, seemingly teasing them into existence out of the grim haze of the guitars with loving attention to detail. These sit alongside some well-composed riffs and blackened grooves, forming the bulk of the songs with great passion and care. The band sound sharp and motivated, totally dedicated to their material, while still injecting it with an enthusiastic energy. 

There is nothing truly new or innovative to be found here, but this is anyway not what Krajiny Hmly have in mind. However, the songwriting is top notch and delivers some of the most competently crafted classic black metal tunes I have heard within the past few months – and this is saying something. Most tracks keep providing the listener with substantive, memorable, and surprisingly catchy content form the very beginning of the album until the closing moments of the nearly seven minutes long epos “O Skalach, Burke a Vecnom Plameni”, one of my favorites here. In its middle part things are slowed down for a while, with a calm guitar melody delivering some atmospheric moments, before the final attack starts.

The vocals by singer Wyrd are howled in classic fashion. Of course I do not understand one word, but the Slovak language seems perfectly suited to express what bands like Krajiny Hmly seek to transport. The same can be said about the production, as “Poza ćierne hory” comes with a sound that is very organic, yet dynamic and diversified at the same time. Overall this album is a strong statement by a band that should be checked out by any fan of traditional yet fresh sounding old school black metal, and for me personally a strong contender for my year end list 2021. This is quality stuff and I for one will check out their previous releases as well.

When I first heard Children of Bodom, the style blew me away -- it was a very progressive styles done in a very aggressive manner. The fact that most of them were about 18 years old when this was done was far more impressive. Most of the best electric guitarists of all time out there either are faded into obscuraty in their 40s, dead, or sold out, and kids today need someone other than Korn, Tool, Creed, Slipknot, and new Metallica to look up to as the pinnacle of guitar ability.

This album has slight black metal influences, and the vocals are somewhat raspy in their harshness, but it has absolutely nothing to do with the genre at all. It's also obviously not the most serious work out there, but 

Deadnight Warrior just leaps out of the thunder with a fast, memorable introduction of complimentary keyboards and guitars. Alexi's harsh, screamed, unintelligible vocals punctures the song, keeping is rapid pace and providing contrast and conflict to the melodies. The all too brief sweep-picking solo on this song is killer.

In the Shadows begins with utter fury, with polyrythms creating chaos among the quasi-evil riffs. The song continues to speed up and slow down, but remains intense even with all the neoclassical work.

Red Light in My Eyes Pt. 1 begins with a harpsichord of dissonance, and slows down into some really off-key, funny growling, which soon picks up and just as quickly returns to its neoclassical nature. The funny vocals return, but before you can laugh, you are twisted upside down again with a furious barrage of drums and diminished riffs. The too-brief solo is amazingly fast, though.

Red Light Part 2 begins with a Malmsteen-style flourish and continues in much of the neoclassical style, reaching a crescendo of the scream of "FIRE!" The melodic guitar and keyboard work through this whole song is excellent, as intense as it stays.

Lake Bodom begins with a legendary intro of dueling keyboards and guitars, and would make almost any guitarist want to grab his axe and try to imitate it right away. The main song is intense and complex as usual, which only whets your appetite for a return of the intro. The guitar and keyboard solos are excellent rapid-speed, and help reach the pinnacle.

The Nail continues with the intense fusion of neoclassical styles and eclectic thrash/speed styling. Though it's heavy and fast to begin with, it gradually grows faster and reaches a climax of melodic fury after inventive riffs that showcase just how good the children in CoB really are.

Touch Like Angel of Death finishes the album with a simple rythm upon ghostly keyboards, slows down, and picks right up with an excellent high-speed melody and a very catchy (although typical CoB stupid/funny in lyrical content) and crushing chorus. The skilled and fast solo fits exactly right as usual. The only thing I don't like is the silence and the little keyboard thing at the end.

I'm giving this album a 90 because it's not perfect and it's a bit too short, but it's is damned good. It ushers in something new which I actually happen to like for a change, and those kids can play their instruments with amazing ability, know their music theory, and know how to make something memorable out of it.

(Note: Originally written for Amazon.com on 3/6/2005.)

I'm not saying this is a bad CD, not at all. I guess it's just the fact that a lot of pressure was put on the band to make a suitable follow-up to 2002's colossal "Versus the World", thus making the song structures seem a bit forced and uninspired. A lot of "hype" was put behind this CD, (most likely due to Metal Blade's ravenous marketing strategies to make the band more popular and mainstream) and that's where this CD falls a bit short. Yeah, it's Amon Amarth, the typical formula of booming drums, soaring guitar melodies, etc; but two huge  things are missing; ATTITUDE and FEROCITY, among other things which aren't uncommon to be seen in AA's music. The whole album just feels worn-down, tired, uninspired, and lacking any genuine feeling or effort. The music has slowed down a lot, which leaves more room for songwriting, but the songwriting, too, has simplified to accessible verse-chorus structures, and the drums have lost that unpredictable "octopus" style edge to them, exception of the first track, and often result in boring mid-paced tempos with little fills or variety. Speaking of variety, that's another weak point here. Whereas "Versus the World" had both slow, epic songs, and the thrashy face-rippers, the majority of the album (if not all) is mid-tempo, creating a large dirge of redundancy. 

Some previous underground bands that went mainstream have gotten better to me, such as Soilwork or Mayhem. But the fact is, AA don't make commercially accessible music, and that's what is attempted here, and it just comes off as weak. There is no fist-clenched, teeth-gritting, pound-your-face-in type of AA to be found... This is definitely the "grimmest" of AA's albums though, and that's something I'll easily admit.

However, this isn't to say this CD is "bad", just disappointing. And don't tell me I need to listen to this more just to "get it". I've had this album since the day it came out, and I have listened to it time and time again to let it grow on me, and never once has anything really stuck to me. Soilwork pulled off going mainstream going well because of their diversity in the music, and AA did the exact opposite. You would swear sometimes that you wouldn't know when the song changed. Despite all of my complaining, there are still some good songs, mainly the title track, the catchy "The Pursuit of Vikings" and the haunting "Where Death Seems to Dwell". But the thing is, there aren't many things here that stick in your head unlike previous AA material. There are no "bad" tracks per se, but nothing really sticks out. The whole album just kind of plods along at one pace, falling into boredom. Simply put, it just seems like a filler CD put out to satisfy public opinion and the record compaany. 

I hope this only happens one time to these guys...AA are far too talented to make music like this and fall so low. A bit of a disappointment... Maybe they just hit a rough spot, but who knows... Only time will tell.

titulo: A very good offering of Greek black metal
texto:
Insanity Cult is a Greek black metal band that has just released their 4th full-length album, “Κάθοδος”, which means “Cathode”, and I thought it was a curious title for an album if it was referring to physics. I just did some research, and I found out that the Greek word Κάθοδος is translated as “downward path”, and then it makes more sense…

The overall sound of these songs is like a descent to the darkest emotions.

After two minutes of an ambient intro, pretty mysterious and unsettling, “Travelogue in Nightmares” kicks in, it’s one of the longest tracks, 11 minutes and a half. It is composed of two parts separated by a soft passage where the drums disappear, the guitars play a dark melody with plucked notes and the addition of a distorted sound, the bass rumbles with its low notes, the sound of a drop falling rhythmically as in a puddle inside a cave makes your breathing slow down, to then speed up when the second part of this song strikes. Greek lyrics are not a problem for me to feel the cold, sorrow and despair, which is a great combination.

The main sensation when I’m listening to “Κάθοδος” is that I’m dragged to a dark hole where light never enters, and I feel surrounded by a thick and sorrowful atmosphere. I’m touched by grief, I’m in solitude, mourning about an unspecific loss, and knowing that I won’t leave this place ‘cause even if it makes me feel sore and sad, here is where I belong.

Vocals are like screams of anger, agony and despair all mixed together, but in a too repetitive tone overall, at least for my taste, with few exceptions like the spoken part in the closing track “Into a Fathomless Dawn”.

There’s an abundance of tremolo riffs, dark melodies and hypnotic loops; sometimes guitars are playing an obsessive tremolo passage and then another guitar is added to convey an unsettling feeling that dominates the listener. And the bass, it has a strong presence, not a mere filler, and it’s highly responsible for the dark and sorrowful tone of this album.

Drums are playing different patterns that go from mid-tempos to blast beats, I also can listen a lot of cymbals being smashed all the time, I’m specially hooked with the drummer’s performance at “Whispering Depths”, mesmerized with the maintained fast tempo and the varied use of all elements to create an immersive and captivating sound.

This is a very good offering of Greek black metal, with a quite neat production, punching sound and a gloomy atmosphere. 7,5/10

I think we have a bone to pick with Canada. Our buds North of the Border have given us musical garbage like Celine Dion, Rush (I'll save a review of my disdain for those prog-composing wienies for another day), and arguably that most awful of back bacon-spawned horror, the monumental tool that is Justin Bi...b..b...b; you know, I won't waste another keystroke on that pussy-ass mutant freak. I can forgive all this and more from a nation who will legalize marriage between a man and a car, thanks to Exciter.

Exciter released this, their first album, way back in the gritty and loud early years of heavy metal in 1983. This was also one of the first true speed metal albums to pop up, with some elements of thrash, evoking a sign of things to come. Exciter here has a raw, almost Motorhead-like sound, made up of unrelenting speed and machine gun-fire riffing. The three bandmates also rule. Here we have Dan Beehler on both drums AND vocals; a mix that one won't find often. His drumwork is pounding and very thrash-like (but with some melody), and his vocals are strong and angry, with lots of piss-and-vinegar shrieks and mostly decent mid-paced yelling. Then we have John Ricci on guitars. He too can riff like no one's business, loud and again almost thrash-like. Alan Johnson rounds it out with the bass, and while he's good, his work is nothing to brag about.

The songs have that nasty habit that many a metal albums have in that they tend to run together a bit thanks to repetitiveness. It's basically "fast, fast, fast, some mid-paced, fast, fast". But hey, this is Exciter. If I really wanted variety, I'd listen to a Symphony X album. This is one of the first speed metal bands, baby, and I'll be damned if no song on here sucks! Though a bit similar again thanks to the speed and raw sounds, they all kick ass anyway. The killer title track delivers awesome shredding guitars and some cool, sleazy synth riffs in the pre-chorus. The short but sweet "Stand Up And Fight" will have you doing just that with more shredding, pounding drums and all-out speed. And don't even get me started on mid-paced crushers like "Iron Dogs" and the dark, near-epic "Black Witch".  

Overall, while the songs run together a little thanks to similar sounds and speed, this is still Exciter, people. Check out this classic for its raw speed and riff after unrelenting riff.

titulo: This is Honestly Kind of Grating
texto:
Yawn, let’s see where the hype train is at in 2019. Of course we have Idle hands, who have found remarkable success mixing Metalhead Approved™ music with more traditional metal. Their album got less interesting with each listen, and once the novelty wore off it became apparent that they’re not particularly remarkable at either metal or goth rock. The latest example I’ve been seeing a lot of is Minnesota Emperor-core sextet False (their name would have been a lot funnier if they sounded like Liturgy or something). They play maximalist atmospheric black metal, if that makes any sense. If that sounds like a weird fit, that’s because it is. While I can see the appeal of the sound in theory, the constant bombast makes this grating and the riffs simply aren’t strong enough to make up for the fact their atmosphere fails to deliver. 

Emperor is far and away the most apt reference point for False. This isn’t to knock Emperor themselves, but they kind of created a monster in the way the encouraged grandiosity in black metal. False’s music is imbued with an immense amount of pomp, there’s big spooky keyboards over everything and their style is incredibly busy. One reason this doesn’t hit me the right way is actually one of the reasons a lot of europower doesn’t jive with me. The ever-present bombast gets grating after a while. The busyness and the bombast could have ended up creating a super jarring claustrophobic sound when paired with black metal, but False’s remarkably polished and clean production doesn’t allow that to happen. 

The riffs here are a mixed bag. They try a bunch of different black metal styles out to varying success. A lot of the bombastic waves of tremolo aren’t very interesting at all, but I found myself enjoying some of the more melodic riffs played on the higher strings. The keyboards are fine in and of themselves, but too ever-present. The drumming is one of the biggest problems with this album. The guy is very technically adept, but you might as well call him Sonic, because his instinct is always gotta go fast. In “Rime on the Song of Returning” the groggy arpeggios would have served as a great opportunity for breathing room, but the dude just keeps blasting away like he’s still backing a full-speed-ahead trem fest. I’ve seen a fairly big deal being made about the vocalist being a woman, which almost seems kind of patronizing since her gender has no bearing on what her rasps sound like – they sound exactly the same as the next black metal band. 

At the end of the day False aren’t bad. They’re just another case of the hype parade backing the wrong horse. Portent ends up feeling cluttered and vaguely headache inducing. Their attempts to merge maximalism and atmosphere just doesn’t work. The admittedly very good outro “Postlude” is the only genuine breathing room the album has and it’s very much too little, too late. Overall, False aren’t any worse than the next black metal band.
