titulo: Didn't Live Up To My Hopes
texto:
I picked up this rather hard to find EP from In Thy Dreams at a concert.  No, it wasn’t a concert with them actually in it, which would have been awesome, but from some people who were selling some back collection of cd’s from some out of business distro.  Having heard (and loving) ‘Highest Beauty’, I snatched this up as quickly as I could.

Too bad it wasn’t as good as I thought it would be.  While the cd is a solid release, it isn’t the no nonsense death metal masterpiece that ‘Highest Beauty’ is.  This album, though good for a first effort, is rather bland.  I had a hard time distinguishing the songs from one another until it became a kind of  ‘death metal white noise’ in the background.  After a few listens the problem only got slightly better.  All the songs sounded basically the same.  No matter how good it is no one wants to hear the same basic song five times.

Lyrically they could use some work too.  It’s apparent here that English was not their first language, as some of the grammar is more clunky and awkward than usual in a death metal song.

All in all I’d say the purchase was worth it, if for nothing else than to sate my curiosity as to what they were before ‘Highest Beauty’.  Now I only need to find myself a copy of ‘Gates of Pleasure’ and I’m set.

My first exposure to Autumn Aria was seeing them open for legendary death metal band Vader, playing a version of standard old school death metal with several newer aged melodic moments, at least on the demo I received from one of the band members. On the four songs, there is a force of killer death metal riffs that range from frantic and furious to mid tempo and irresistibly headbangable. The growls are low and reminiscent of those of maybe John Tardy of Obituary or probably more harsher and in the vein of Suffocation's Frank Mullen. I find Autumn Aria's vocalist, Kiker to be a very fluid and worthy growler showing much talent and combined with the back up shrieks of the other band members make for quite an experience.

The other members of the band all are very competent and know what they are doing. The bass is there, like in all death metal it does its job accompanying the music for rhythm and such, doing it's job and same with the drumming. The drumming here is quite varied, ranging from blast beats to standard death kit banging, which is enjoyable and fits the music. The guitarists are equally as talented, from shredding solos as seen in King of Fools to the badass riffing in None Shall Amend (which is possibly one of the most fun songs to headbang to I've heard in a while punishing your neck and a mid-tempo riff also with a short and sweet solo). The riffing here is done in a similar style to that of bands maybe of Amon Amarth or Dark Tranquillity so which it can still be a mid-tempo riff and still be crushing and powerful even as if it were flying by at blistering speeds; quality headbanging material here.

The only downside of this demo is probably the added use of the clean vocals as a back up in two songs. While I certainly love clean vocals, I really do not think it fits into their overall sound, which is a brutal yet melodic version of death metal. Especially in The Raping of Lavinia do I see that the clean vocals stick out, it isn't necessarily a huge deal because it barely comes up for a brief amount of time but otherwise that song speeds along with the fast riffing so you won't even know it was there. Autumn Aria haven't made a full length album and probably won't make a name for themselves until they do so, but I will be waiting for their full length with high hopes after enjoying them live and enjoying this demo and I await the next release.

titulo: The First (But Not Last) Step In Technicality
texto:
So, when people talk of technical and or progressive death metal, one of the first bands to slip out of your mouth would probably be Cynic, or Atheist.

Now, what does the title have to do with this? This album is where technical metal should've stopped evolving. Starting out as a great behemoth of confusing melodies and jazz-fusion tendencies, technical death metal was the forefront of unusual music. Then, by the late 90's, we had bands like Cryptopsy that saw it necessary to play scales and diminished runs for near an hour with jazzy drumming and growling.

Anyways, onto the album.

The first thing that will surprise the listener, is the production. Clear, yet an unusually fuzzy guitar tone, loud, and very thick, although every instrument is more than clear. 

The next is the vocals, a combination of death growls (performed by keyboardist/producer Tony Teegarden) and a "robotic voice" which is performed by singing in a falsetto voice through a vocoder. 

The guitars. These guitars are why this album is the supreme in terms of technical metal. There are probably only one or two parts in a Cynic song where both guitars play the same thing. Almost every riff consists of a strange intertwining melodious riff that is quickly picked, ending in the occaisional complex chord under heavy distortion. The clean parts are fantastically played smooth-jazz fusion, and Textures (the song) is a culmination of Cynic's collective talent. 

The bass is monumental. Sure, Atheist and Pestilence had great bassists, but when Sean Malone decided to lay down some lines, everything changed. Twiddling with a fretless bass and a synthetic MIDI pickup, through some slight distortion, we have the soudn of this album. Just like the guitars, there is a rare one or two riffs per song that the bass follows the guitar on. 

And, the drumming. The drumming! Sean Reinert, childhood friend of bandleader/guitarist/vocalist Paul Masvidal, is the drummer for technical music. Combining a taste of latin/fusion licks and a heavy sense of accents and rhythm, this album is flowing with energy becuase Sean knows when to play some calm (yet aggressive, somehow) beat, and then follow-up with some ridiculous fill pattern that a drum machine would stutter with.

The songwriting is a pretty damn important aspect of this album. When you hear the genre name "Technical Progressive Death/Fusion" you might cringe, or you might jump into it with an erection. Either way, the perfect fusion of jazz and death metal (no pun intended) on this album is what puts ahead of the others (namely: Atheist). The riffing on this album is fairly consistent in terms of techniques, but even then the guitars never feel dull or boring because of the insane amount of melodic harmonization, and the meticulous detail about it.

The only thing that is even remarkable wrong with this album is the lack of songs. Even just one more song, preferably another full-on jazz instrumental like Textures, would have made this album jump up to a flat 99.

I recommend this to anyone who hasn't listened to it. The vocals may take a bit to get used to, but when they sink in, this album is virtually flawless.

My first listen through this album, I couldn't help but feel pure excitement that the album sounded as good as it did. From the first few seconds, I knew this felt like Northland. The very folk-focused instrumentation and ambient natural sounds make a beautiful introduction to the album's tone and message, and instantly get you in the mood. Right from the start, the music sounds like a very refined and polished version of their first album, with much more focus and direction. The production value is noticeably higher, not necessarily in the quality of the recording, but in the mixing and the fine tuning of each individual instrument and sound. 

	The guitars are just as good as always, with even more focus on matching the melodies to those of the flutes and strings. But it never gets too overpowered by these, and is constantly setting the pace, often mimicking a horse gallop. The drumming feels much more precise and progressive, which is a welcomed change in the typical folk metal scene. It is not overpowering, but not underwhelming, and sits at just the right place. Even the use of synth and folk instruments has been improved on, which is hard to believe considering their prominence on the previous album. They feel natural, unforced, and completely believable.

	Lyrically, the album has a pretty interesting story. To make things brief, it talks about how humanity has failed the natural world and needs to be wiped out and restarted. While it sounds like a very corny and cliche theme, it actually works very well with the Northland sound, especially considering they have folk instruments and natural ambient sounds that are more prominent than the guitars at times. While listening to the lyrics, you are fully transported to the world that the album creates, and you can fully feel the message behind each line. The incredible vocal work plays a huge role in this.

	In the previous album, the vocal style was quite varied, but in this one, that variation is increased massively and done in a much more musically tasteful way. My main issue with the previous was the clean vocals, which sounded very off. It is clear that they have had some practice since then, because the clean vocals in this album are some of the best in all of folk metal. From death metal styled grunting, black metal screams, and folk metal chanting, this album features it all. At one point, only clean vocals and acoustic instruments are used, swapping between male and female vocals. It leaves a beautiful break during the climax of the action that sounds like something Howard Shore would write. This vocal dexterity is what honestly sets the album apart from other folk metal releases of the last few years. 

	To sum it all up, this album is exactly the album that it should have been; and more. I went into it blindly, not sure what to expect. The previous album was great, but felt slightly off, so I was hoping this one would fix that. Boy, did it ever. It completely flipped my expectations and instantly became one of my favorite albums of the year, perhaps even the last five. If you liked the first album, you will love this. If you like heartfelt and genuine folk metal, you will love this. Even people who hate this sub-genre will likely be able to enjoy what  Downfall and Rebirth  has to offer. If this band doesn't hit the big time and become the next Ensiferum after this one, I won't know what to think, because this was one hell of a joy ride.

Baphomet's first self-titled single, released in 1990, shows the death metal band with almost a completely new lineup, with only guitarist Steve Rzepka and bassist Gary Schipani remaining. New vocalist Tom Frost is presented, having a fairly different style from previous vocalist Mark Paravolos. I am happy to have continued my listening of Baphomet chronologically, as the early demo a year later was an effort in extremely low fi death metal with not quite as much structure and more of what could have been, instead now on this single, Baphomet have become more of a matured and full on death metal outfit.

First off, the biggest change is having a legitimate production where everything is much more clear and has a better overall sound; no static fuzz! The vocals are more of a grunt and harsher growl instead of the early extreme metal raspy yell that Paravolos used. Frost exhibits a more guttural grunt that is typical of a lot of death metal bands. What I find to be the best here are the riffs, the good use of mid tempo riffing that is simply heavy as fuck as well as the faster rhythm riffs of course. This whole demo is practically a journey of nonstop bludgeoning death metal, unrelenting and harsh.

Spectral Maniac starts off with the ominous bass leading into low growls and fast riffing, death metal, duh! There is a certain air of technicality to be found here, I don't know if it's just the simple fact that they're from New York or what but Baphomet displays it nicely. The riffing to be found is solid and worthy of snapping necks. This is a nice change of pace from the previous demo with the barely distinguishable riffs. Torn Soul starts right from the get go with frantic death metal insanity, and nice to hear that chaotic solo work from Rzepka again; none to be found on Spectral Maniac. Torn Soul is just a relentless riff-fest and Frost does his best long held growl. 

So with Baphomet's first single, it shows a nice progression with a better usage of distinguishable and better riffs but at the same time a lack of the fun lead work that was found previously. This is still overall better, but almost like 2 steps forward, 1 step back. I don't mind the vocals as well but it's definitely a change of pace and almost like, more of the same. This is still a decent outing and great as a classic early death metal single.

One of the most magical, most captivating aspects of the most beloved music genre on this earth is that there is so much absolutely phenomenal material waiting to be discovered that can completely mesmerize you for a long, long time to come. Sometimes that long time can be pretty much until the end of one’s life (whenever that may come for each one of us) when you have been blown away by a record on so many levels so deeply that you simply know you will be returning to it time and again with that elevated feeling of pure and unshatterable joy. This is the case for MetalBear with Valhalore‘s sophomore release “Beyond The Stars”. Just two months ago MetalBear hadn’t even heard of the band. Now I am sitting in this blissful state of full transcendence evoked by Valhalore’s newest release giving it a 5 out 5 rating with the fullest of confidence. This is truly the beauty of metal. Let’s find out what has moved MetalBear to such degrees to reward for the first time so far “The Eternal Masterpiece (Album of the Century contestant type of material)” rating in such definite manner by taking you on a transcendent journey throughout this celestial gem of an album.

The leap from 2017’s Voyage Into Eternity to this is nothing short of astounding. That debut was full of promise – sprawling, ambitious, and emotionally honest. But Beyond The Stars is a true masterwork, honed with precision and poured from the heart. It’s the kind of record where everything just clicks – pacing, production, songwriting, emotion – and not a single track, not a single moment is wasted. Even the instrumental interludes don’t just connect the chapters — they kind of illuminate them in a way that makes every moment on this record a pure bliss. Take for example the way the hauntingly beautiful instrumental interlude "Dusk" sets the stage for the epochal ballad "Wayfinder".

With this in mind, what sets Beyond The Stars apart isn’t just its songs - it’s the journey they create when experienced together. The pacing is impeccable: the album knows exactly when to strike, when to hold, when to let you soar, and when to let you rest.  The balance between fury and feeling, between riff and rest, is almost otherworldly in its precision, as evident on tracks such as "The Storm", "Within The Fire", "Horizon" and "The World Between". The decision to also feature a guest vocalist (Anna Murphy - ex-Eluveitie; Cellar Darling) on the album's lengthiest track - “Heart of the Sea” - is fantastic and one proving the band's astounding songwriting maturity. Muphy's voice intertwines with Lachlan’s in a duet that is both haunting and heavenly – an inspired choice that elevates an already masterful composition and that serves as a testament of the record's brilliant cohesion - one that often takes decades to master.

Beyond The Stars is a timeless achievement. It’s an epic folk metal odyssey that extremely masterfully also ventures out to melodeath, prog and power and does so in a way that manages to feel both intimate and massive, rooted in storytelling yet unafraid to reach for the infinite. Every track – every single one – is a highlight. The interludes are sublime. The emotional peaks are staggering. And the overall effect is not just one of musical satisfaction, but of sheer transcendence.

To MetalBear this is not just a great album. It the kind of release that defines a band’s legacy. And it is one of the finest metal albums of the decade. Valhalore has not just reached the stars – they’ve become one with this magnificent release.

--- Originally written for 1MetalBear.com

There's very little music that I seriously can't handle to listen to for a long time. I can't listen to harsh noise for more than, say, 45 minutes at a time; my ears just can't handle the abuse for that long. One of the other things I can't listen to for a long time is Dragonforce. Listening to 'Inhuman Rampage' is like running a goddamn marathon for me. I have to take a nap after it's over.

Actually, maybe it's more akin to someone sitting you down in front of a massive bowl of delicious candy, saying that you can't get up until you're done eating every piece. It's wonderful for a while, particularly when you're hungry, delighting in each piece's sweet and flavorful fun. After about a third of the way into the bowl, though, you start to not want to eat candy anymore. But it's not really an option, is it? He's not OFFERING you all the candy you can eat, he's making DAMN WELL SURE you eat every piece. So you persist. The unwrapping of each candy becomes more laborious, your tongue becomes sore from the constant sugar's tastebud-bludgeoning hammer, and your stomach swells painfully as you pack more and more candy down your gullet. You keep eating, and it becomes more and more exquisitely painful with every piece. And after a while, you notice that you no longer taste sweetness, but just a hot, salty flavor. Do you know what you're tasting?

It's your tears. Your tears.

Okay, so I can't deny that I love Dragonforce. They are, like candy, delicious and sweet. I don't give a shit that they're uncreative and only have one song, because that one song is fantastic. They're incredibly fast, catchy, and fun to listen to alone or with friends. They're great driving music. They're INCREDIBLY shallow and disposable, but they are perhaps the best trash that metal has ever come up with. Most importantly, it's EXCITING music: it has a constantly driving intensity to it that really forces you to enjoy it. Constant melodic riffs and solos and soaring vocals over a bed of nonstop double bass and blast beats? Yeah, I'm game for that.

The real problem comes when I try to listen to a whole album. It's almost physically painful. I can handle 25 minutes, maybe a half hour of this insanely melodic, hyperspeed power metal before my brain just shuts down. It's just too much. For some reason I can listen to hours of brutal death, grind, or ultra-raw black metal, but for some reason, this little band is somehow too much for me. Maybe it's just the number of notes is too much for my primitive, slam-oriented brain to handle and were it only that Dragonforce had more breakdowns I'd be able to get through a whole album. But as it stands, I'm put into a coma for six months when I listen to the whole thing, which is really quite a terrible thing.

That being said, those first 25 or 30 minutes are pretty divine. Dragonforce is one of those bands which really does make me overtly cheerful and want to play air guitar. The music is pop in metal drag, obviously, but it's stunningly well composed pop that never gets boring or trite. I'd imagine they're a fantastic band live, and that hearing this while surrounded by thousands of other equally nerdy individuals is a lot like visiting Mecca. But it's almost as good all alone in your room and does make you feel like you can jump over a mountain using your cock as a pogo stick. In short, it's heroic and catchy and perhaps some of the best pop music out there today. I love it.

It's the sort of thing where you almost appreciate its shallowness. It's music that will not stand the test of time, but it's not meant to. It's an outburst of flamboyantly cheerful youthful enthusiasm, and while you could criticize it for that very reason, the band really sees that outpouring of feeling as reason enough to make its music. It's decidedly immature and decidedly inartistic, but perhaps the willingness to abandon more erudite values is what makes it so charming. You can find worth in a lot of things, you know. Because the fact is, though it has no value, we all demand a little candy at one point or another.

In a way, this EP is a huge mistake. It's title track is lumped in with what is essentially the “leftovers” from other recordings. That's not to slight the four other tracks on their own, but they pale in comparison to the scope and songwriting brilliance of it's epic title track. This EP is hardly known, and hard to find; I think the band did an enormous disservice to the 15 minute epic by grouping it with acoustic tracks, a re-recording and a cover. It should have been the anchor to a full length album, with all new material.

Since it's only 5 tracks, I think I can do a quick track-by-track rundown; every track is very unique anyway. Earth Pus is a re-recording of a song on their debut album, which is definitely the most straightforward, though still sufficiently groovy death metal, with this band's usual kiss of jazz and metric modulation. Blackout is an acoustic version of the song from Leading Vision, done in a sort of flamenco style. The 3rd track is a Cynic cover, very fusion jazzy, and tonally abnormal – not enough metal for my tastes. The 4th track is another flamenco, Phrygian-Dominant style acoustic track that takes a bit more liberties with the source material adding in little chimes and overlaying guitar harmonies.

The final track is what you're really here for – whether you know it or not. Frankly, you'd be forgiven for being unimpressed by the first couple minutes. The song opens with a kind of andante groovy riff, moving into a bridging section with relaxed swinging drum beats, and distortion skimmed off the guitars with ... singing – yes, singing. When I first heard this track I was put off; the singing's not great, and it's a little tough-guy for my tastes, but it slowly folds in the harsh vocals, and the song proceeds, as the guitars bring the distortion back in and play increasingly busy riffs. When this first section is done, it makes what follows all the heavier. Just before the 3 minute mark, we're back to all-out syncopated death metal and signature melodic, jazz-tinted Gorod leads. Pretty soon we get the first solo which is one of the finest the band has done, with a great swinging and active drum beat complimenting it so well. Here is where the song really picks up – the transitions are so seamless, guitar harmonies swoop in to lift the song into a new part, drum beats are used so well to facilitate the ebb and subsequent flow of each new idea. By the 6 minute mark, we're up to blast beats with rapidly shifting guitar leads, jumping right to left in a staggered fashion, and a tense build-up resolves into a super choppy, but gorgeous guitar melody playing alone – just once - before the drums drop in to punctuate every note of this supreme riff. This transition is very unexpected, and executed with virtual perfection. The song moves into more solos and revisits it's opening riff. At this point, the song opens up a bit, and relaxes; lulling you into thinking the twists and surprises are over with. It has some great, choppy, disjointed rhythmic leads and another really unpredictable transition, before finishing with the an embellished reprise of the aforementioned supreme riff.

Every transition in this song is so well done. Of the ones you can see coming, they're done seamlessly; of the ones you can't, they blindside you, or promises you something, and gives you the bait-and-switch. This is how you keep someone's attention for 15 minutes.

Scoring this and putting my final thoughts to it are a bit tricky because I absolutely love the title track, but tracks 2 – 4 are just mildly entertaining at best and the opening track is fairly good. All things considered, I would say the title track pretty easily tips the scale in favor of this being a worthwhile release. I think the title track alone makes hunting this down worth it, I really do think it's that strong of a track.

Few stylistic movements in the classic era of speed metal are as packed with inspiration as the piercing, bloody-eared reign of power/thrash that hit an incredible peak of progressive interest as the late 80’s ensued. Long in development and truly ambitious the hardest workers yielded the most intentional and amazing works and their names still ring the hallowed halls of heavy metal: Helstar, Agent Steel, Artillery, Fates Warning among others had risen to the highest standards by ~1988 and unexpected influential side-bars from Angel Dust, Crimson Glory and Liege Lord doubled down on the rise of 80’s US power metal with intense results. This refinement of technical thrashing ability, soaring and dramatic vocal performance informed by progressive rock song structures continues to inspire underground modernists in power, thrash, and even death metal to some degree. Few of these modern day arrive with such willing engagement than Athens, Greece thrashers Sacral Rage who have undergone a similar 1984-1988 progression from ‘Fear of Tomorrow’-esque speed metal towards ‘Master Project Genesis’ heights.

‘Beyond Celestial Echoes’ is a grand ‘ante up’ with consideration for their already huge leap in concept and overall quality that came with ‘Illusions in Infinite Void’ (2015). That full-length debut was a monster with a dramatic arc and thrashing riff-work worthy of albums like Messiah Force‘s underrated ‘The Last Day’ and Helstar‘s ‘A Distant Thunder’ where complex rhythms and sharper guitar work begins to edge out purist hits of heavy metal. It seems the band would agree that it was a massive record in terms of both capturing a really incredible sound without relying on retro-recreation because they made to sure take their time and at the very least rise to that high-set bar. Where I felt they could improve was largely the thrash metal side of things in terms of managing those Coroner and Watchtower influences to make better sense in the bigger picture. In tweaking their approach further towards technical thrash metal composers Marios Petropoulos (Necrovorous) and Spyros S. (ex-Mentally Defiled) ensure a more cohesive whole this time around.

Though the moving-parts of the Sacral Rage machine is the ultimate majesty the exploding star creating necessary fission for life has to be vocalist Dimitris K. whose dramatic King Diamond and Agent Steel style cadence and range provide limitless expressive dramatics (see: “Samsara (L.C.E.)” immediately) to emphasize the more ambitious points of composition; He acts as a wild but purposeful narrative instrument that hugely defines ‘Beyond Celestial Echoes’ transcendent proggy power/tech-thrash presence. This extra push for refinement really does reach the level of classics like Fates Warning‘s ‘Awaken the Guardian’ and capitalizes on some of the missed opportunities of classic-but-forgotten gems like Angel Dust‘s  ‘To Dust You Will Decay’ and Target‘s ‘Master Project Genesis’ all of which balanced similar elements. The band surely achieved the intended balance of European and North American power/thrash metal influences and avoid any redundancies with the previous album.

A sucker for the high-drama of a space operatic theme and an outspoken fan of twisted sci-fi technical thrash metal riffing ‘Beyond Celestial Echoes’ cut off my head and screamed down into my lungs from first riff. Sacral Rage have gone well beyond ‘retro’ appeal with their intense and attention-grabbing sound thanks a sharp balance of undeniable thrash rhythmic appeal given detail with enough progressive flourish to enrich across multiple listens. It feels a bit like discovering the first Annihilator album back in the day and just ‘needing more shit like this’ because the big four just felt flaccid afterwards.

My listening experience can be summed up with yet another simile in that it resembled reading a great novel and wanting a sequel right away; I came back to the album for weeks analyzing, comparing, and above all mentally juicing its grand musical statement. It wasn’t that I was captivated or spellbound as I often am with thrash records but that I felt myself ‘edged along’ enjoying every moment thanks to a sense of narrative provided by the vocals. This experience suggest an appropriately high recommendation from me and in preview I’d say the duo of “Suspended Privileges” and “Samsara (L.C.E.)” offers immediate thrash riffs and peak range in terms of vocals. If you’re somehow still on the fence what pushed me into the stratosphere were my favorite tracks;  The Watchtower-esque “Vaguely Decoded” and the insane 14+ minute epic closer “The Glass”.

titulo: Not really my cup of tea...
texto:
Sanguineous plays Brutal Death Metal and I’m not the fittest person to review this demo, since I’m not into this style of music, but I’ll try. This totally pro tape looks and sounds very professionally done. The sound is good, all the instruments can be heard really well and create a a very massive wall of sonic brutality, especially thanks to the hyper-fast and brutal as fuck sounding drum machine, which nevertheless doesn’t sound too annoying and plastic. 

Most of the time it’s played on very high temp with quite rare slowed down parts, followed by great very deep growling vocals and ov korpse – very intense guitar riffs. The only exception is the last, 4th track, which sounds rather doomy and slow. I really have no idea which well known bands in the genre to compare them too, but if you like your DM sounding like a never resting machine-gun – you’ll probably enjoy it. 

The negative side of this release is the fact that apart for the last song. it sounds like a 20 minutes long one monotonous song, since even after listening to this tape very carefully a few times – I noticed that one or another track was finished only because of the silence between the tracks. Personally I got very bored despite the aggressiveness of the songs, but if you like Brutal Death – better check this band out yourself.

The jury has been out for some time regarding whether Magic Kingdom or Iron Mask would have the distinction of being Belgian guitarist/songwriter Dushan Petrossi's principle project, though circa 2011 it seemed that things were leaning a bit more in the latter's direction. It's important to note that while the two projects have been fairly similar, by the time Metallic Tragedy was unleashed, Petrossi's original project appeared to be the more adventurous and experimental of the two, relatively speaking. On the other hand, since the release of Shadow Of The Red Baron, it became clear that Iron Mask was a project that was also somewhat conducive to a darker sound, though it would still remain the safer of the two respective projects. Black As Death, which sees a couple substantial shifts in the band's line up, generally maintains this trend into darker yet still largely familiar territory, all the while continuing to showcase Petrossi's ongoing loyalty to the Malmsteen model of meshing Baroque and early Classical era musical cliches with fast paced power metal.

To dispense with the obvious, the recent recruitment of former Malmsteen vocalist Mark Boals does much to further the suspicions of some that Petrossi may be fielding a tribute band of sorts here, though the end result musically is a bit less overt than one might suspect. The introductory instrumental "From Light Into The Dark" is actually a substantial departure into a dreary atmospheric place that rests somewhere between a dark progressive prelude or what often adorned the beginning of a number of sinister sounding thrash metal albums. It paves the way for the 7 minute title song "Black As Death", which is generally a heavier, more down-tempo bruiser that accents Dushan's ongoing fascination with melding darker aesthetics with power metal generally melodic and triumphant character, though it ends up in an ironically up beat sounding chorus. A similar musical situation occurs with the somewhat more church-sounding nod to medieval lore "God Punishes, I Kill", mixing in some sampled Gregorian chants and featuring Boals' signature high notes.

As things progress, a smattering of musically eclectic elements and a fairly familiar inclination towards mid to late 80s Rising Force territory tends to take over the album. Not one to be tied down solely to western common practice era music, a rather interesting amalgamation of traditional Chinese musical sounds and a slow paced, thudding groove in "Genghis Khan" occurs to mix things up a bit, along with a rather oddly folksy nod to Celtic music in the bonus track "Sons Of The Sun", complete with roaring bagpipes. On the other end of the stylistic spectrum are more predictable nods to old school heavy metal in the Odyssey brand of arena fair such as "Broken Hero" and "The Absence", riding mostly on melody and pretty well loaded with keyboard detailing courtesy of Mats Olausson, yet another musician that has previously worked with Malmsteen. On the faster side of things and carrying the usual bag of precedents set by Malmsteen on Trilogy is "Feel The Fire", though Iron Mask breaks the mold with a towering storm of ferocity that rivals Dragonforce in "Blizzard Of Doom" and a dark, Gothic and occasionally extreme speeder dedicated to every creature of the night in "Nosferatu" that's also a bit more frenzied, multifaceted and dangerous than anything out of the Malmsteen brand.

If nothing else, the sentiments among some that Iron Mask was becoming more of a primary venture for Petrossi compared to Magic Kingdom were definitely warranted by this point, as Black As Death accomplished the rare feat of all but matching Metallic Tragedy qualitatively, and also pulling Mark Boals back into the power metal world after a series of hard rock and progressive stints that were solid, but maybe not quite his bread and butter. In a sense it reaffirms that fact that neither person has really strayed too far from Yngwie's kingdom, though they've definitely managed to carve out a rather impressive fiefdom for themselves. It's also interesting to note fellow former Malmsteen vocalist Goran Edman also makes an appearance on this album as a guest, albeit doing a ballad that is suited to his smoother, crooning vocal approach. It's a nice slice of sugary, solo rich power metal cake with a darker chocolate texture, and it's another winner for anybody looking for a good set of hooks mixed with some occasional additives that are a tad less conventional.

titulo: New vocalist saves a lot here
texto:
Italy and thrash metal. I've got a lot of that lately, thanks to Punishment 18 Records sending me promos of their ever-growing catalog. And once again, it was my first contact with a new band. 'Dragged' is Ground Control's sophomore album after the 2006 debut 'Insanity'.

I also checked out older songs by the band, and thank god (take your pick) they have a new vocalist! While the music is built from the same elements as their older stuff, insanely bad screaming vocalist is no more. The elements that make Ground Control's music are old school thrash metal, more rocking groove and good old heavy metal. Sounds like modern? Yeah it does, but still Ground Control must not be confused as a nu-metal band or something like that. Ground Control manage to sound at least a bit original. This is because they use special vocal melodies that do not directly remind me of any band, but the voice surely has some Hetfield-ism to it. The vocals are clean singing with some streetwise attitude on them. Music-wise they sit next to early 1990s Metallica and Annihilator, knitting together more darker feelings with energetic rocking. However, still the band are incapable in offering a varying album.

This album was played with intensity. Powerful and nicely clean sound is really striking and organic, not having any kind of digital feel to it. If the sound is good, the covers and booklet are some of the worst ever, with ugly color scheme and failed outcome of concept.

'Dragged' does not crash land. It has enough of power to keep it flying, even though the unvarying contents can be quite a ballast at times. Rocking thrash with balls if you want some, just nothing outstanding.

(originally written for ArchaicMetallurgy.com in 2010)

I'm going to be honest with you; I haven't bought a My Dying Bride album in 8 years, and I never had that many of their albums to begin with. They were one of the first metal bands I discovered, but I guess I just got bored with their sound and started getting into other things. But when I heard about this, it intrigued me. I listened to some of their samples and went for it. I guess I just like radical departures from bands sometimes, even if many others don't. It also has sparked my interest in the band again, and I am certainly going to go back through their catalog and catch up on some of the better albums I've missed.

Yes, this album is perhaps on the opposite side of the metal spectrum. There isn't really a hint of metal here at all, but this album perhaps showcases their darkwave/gothic themes with a neoclassical twist. There is heavy keyboard, piano, and violin use, along with spoken word and some opera vocals. The music is very sparse - perhaps a bit too sparse at times, without kicking up much of an atmosphere. In fact, several parts of it are just downright boring. There are many sections of this album that I really enjoy, especially the gentle, trickling piano melodies heard throughout, but all of them seem to be tied together so loosely and indolently that it doesn't really form anything solid. Maybe it's because all the parts are derived from past songs, jumbled up and regurgitated into new compositions. Maybe totally new material would have been more complete sounding, who knows, but that wouldn't have been very fitting for a special 20th anniversary of the band.

Obviously, this album is extremely long - the triple album is over two hours (even though it could have fit on 2 discs... hmm). Still, it's certainly one of the longest albums I own, and the sparseness makes it seem much, much longer than that. Listening to the whole thing at once almost requires some sort of mental preparation and special attention if you expect to get anything out of it. Keep in mind that disc 3 does not come with all versions - might have to buy the one that says "box set." 

My biggest complaint is the vocals. I'm not a huge fan of the opera vocals, and I'm not a huge fan of the spoken word thing either. It's OK, but it seems to break the ambiance too much, even though the ambiance is usually pretty boring. Sometimes the music almost halts completely to showcase some of these vocals. While the opera singer is definitely talented in her respective field, I'm not sure those kind of vocals really belong here too much. Maybe a few here and there would have been nice, but they are pretty much in the spotlight. Also, Aaron's "spoken word" is something he has done on many MDB albums, but it just seems to fit with a metal atmosphere much better than this.

My favorite track is probably "The Distance, Busy with Shadows," which features a gorgeous piano melody dancing quaintly with several different synth melodies, the track constantly swirling and transforming with a simple elegance to it. Sounds like it could almost be a ballet score. The best part is there are barely any vocals; in fact, I wish there were none at all. Another favorite is the second half of "And Then You Go," consisting of eerily gorgeous keyboard harmonies with some feathery opera vocals that I actually enjoy, creating some of the most layered and soothing parts of the album. The atmosphere here continues into the next track, "A Hand of Awful Rewards," which is perhaps the most ambient and minimal tracks here. The third disc has a bit more variety, "The Burning Coast of Regnum Italicum" being another one of my favorites, going through many different movements, including tender piano melodies, ambient keyboard harmonies, and even sounds of a thunderstorm.

Even though I see the many flaws in this album, it is something I keep going back to, which tells me it's either growing on me or certain parts are just strangely addicting. The whole album is still very intriguing to me, probably because it's just so different from anything I own. I kind of wish I could give it a better score, and maybe if all the best parts of this album were smashed down into one hour, I would, but in its current state, this is the best I can do.

Before I actually heard this EP this band already was starting to make some waves in the underground. To begin with more people than you would expect for such a newcomer were wearing a t-shirts of theirs at gigs I attended. So while my interest was peaked because of such things I did initially keep on forgetting to check them out. Part of the reason why is because I kind of expected them to just be another rethrash band, something I do not really need. Eventually I did and sure did not regret it.

This EP RIPS. I can not really think of much worthwhile speed metal coming out over the last few years. However this EP makes everything about that alright.  There is one simple reason why. This is speed metal to the max. There are fast killer ripping riffs all over the place, great catchy songs, and high pitched classic 80's style metal vocals. The performances of everyone on this are tight too. There is really nothing else I want on a speed metal release. The fact that they actually also slow down occasionally and play some sweet solos is like a big middle finger to all those shitty thrash bands who are just stuck in one mode. The last thing that makes them great is that they already on this EP have a fully developed own sound. So many bands do not manage to get this far in a 30 year career and they just do it casually like it is nothing. No this does not mean that this is innovative bullshit either. JUST KILLER SPEED METAL.

I love this EP and I urge you the reader to get it in some form or another. Maybe one or two of you guys might not like the classic 80's styled vocals but I do not care about you. RIFFS that is what I care about.

titulo: Occision - One of AZʻs Best Kept Brutal secrets
texto:
A few of us remember seeing these guys play live from 1994 onward. The first thing that most of us folks noticed that blew people the fuck away, was when young Jesse Johnson was doing his double bass work live.! He was an extremely tight drummer for being a high school age guy, and blew people out of the water with his musicianship. Overall, their playing very tight as a whole, but the drumming stood out then and it stands out now on this later release. One who had been an earlier fan would have caught some of their best tracks such as "Public Execution" and "Oblivious Recall" live. 
 
The new release has taken the melody, brutality, harmony, and technicality to higher levels as expected. The new line up has added some former Nuctemeron (AZ) members such as Richard Medina on vocals which, made their sound more brutal than ever. His deep and guttural vocals really stepped them up quite a bit in the game as did the increase in everyones technicality within ten years since their inception. Tiffany Woods, the former bassist of Nuctemeron (AZ), also stepped up her game with the melodies she provided when she switched to guitar and dual jammed with Charles Watson.  Charlesʻ brother Byron Watson has been the bassist in their line up since the beginning. Overall, when I hear this release, it is above and beyond a majority of the mediocre crap I hear in the AZ scene or for that matter America as of late. This kills the boring and lame Deathcore and Emo Metal poser crap that can only offer the same Pantera type breakdowns in riffing. And their newer stuff, although, no longer featuring Tiffany, is top of the line as it gets. This release was a sign of the insane gravity blasts attacks to come on their later releases. There are some grindier elements with precision  executed with their extremely technical and brutal onslaught of Death Metal done only the way these Jedis could do it! Do yourself a favor and buy this release! No true Death Metal freak could be disappointed by this or their later material at all. Occision is true AZ Death Metal and they fucking rule!

This album is a relentless aural assault that begins its venture with "Fall of the Human Empire" in brutal riffs and dirges unto "Hunger of the Night Feeder", and continues with its perverse overtones on the middle track of "Throne of the Pedophile".  It then continues onward in the assault with "Lying Bleeding at My Feet" while never relenting or diminishing the brutality of this CD release while  transcending unto the last two songs. "Within My Grip" and "No Motive" are everything that can be expected of a Brutal Arizona death metal band of this caliber.  There is no question that the precision, integrity, and gruesome attacks never falter on this excellent "Killing is Instinct, the Pleasure Lies in Murder" LP. They achieve being one of the kings of Arizona Death Metal through this release!  Their continued progressions into releasing formidable music of this destructive nature make this a quality release that no true Death Metal fanatic can afford to keep from their collection!

titulo: Mozart and Beethoven Would Have Been Proud
texto:
Helstar were evolving gradually, but surely, adding new ingredients with each subsequent album (power metal (“Burning Star”); speed/power metal (“Remnants of War”); speed/thrash (“Distant Thunder”); technical speed/thrash (“Nosferatu”)) to their arsenal, logicaly reaching their creative peak near the genre’s zenith period. Unlike other bands, who reached their pinnacle at a very early stage (Mercyful Fate, Agent Steel, Metal Church, Paradox, etc.), which led to the bands splitting up, or experiencing major line-up changes, James Rivera and Co. were moving towards the culmination of their career step by step in a well measured, sure-handed, pace. And what a culmination it was… “Distant Thunder” was already a pretty strong album, but even its most inspired moments were not even remotely hinting at the overwhelming listening experience which “Nosferatu” would be.

   This album is the perfect metal analogue to a classical symphony, a triumphant technical speed/thrash opera, never achieved before or after. From the complex multi-faced song-structures, to the classically-inspired guitar duels, to the lyrical concept behind the music, to the direct nod to their inspiration (the 2-min instrumental “Von Am Lebem Desto Strum”): everything at display was intended as a tribute to the classical musical heritage, an ambitious undertaking which arguably produced the finest fruit of the whole 80’s American power/speed/thrash metal scene. 

   What also made this album even more compelling at the time was the fact that it provided a more digestible form of technical metal, as opposed to the ultra-complex, hectic style of Watchtower and the very characteristic, abstract/spacey delivery of Voivod. The technical side of the genre had already reached its summit in Europe (Deathrow, Mekong Delta, Target, Sieges Even, Living Death, etc.) a year earlier, and the other side of the Atlantic was sadly falling behind (Savage Steel’s “Do or Die” being the “lonely warrior” on the battlefield). “Nosferatu” did a lot to bring America back in the competition, along with same year’s Watchtower’s ‘Control & Resistance”, Nasty Savage's "Penetration Point", Toxik's "Think This", and Annihilator’s “Alice in Hell”.

   Andre Corbin had joined the band one year earlier for “Distant Thunder”, lifting the musical proficiency quite a few notches up, testimony for which was the excellent instrumental “(The) Whore of Babylon”, among other niceties scattered throughout. But he was yet to perfect his interaction with Larry Branagan which found its full realisation less than a year later. A warning sign for some may have been the closing of the regular 2-year gap left between albums, but very soon it became evident that the guys’ creative genius couldn’t possibly wait for so long to be unleashed upon the scene, to the fans’ utter delight. 

   The dramatic thundering riffage on the opening “Rhapsody in Black” already suggests at great things to come, and the standout performance of everyone involved more than fulfills all the promises. The Branagan/Corbin duo cooperation is extraordinary, and these guys should be mentioned right beside Downing/Tipton, the Schenker brothers, Murray/Smith, and Denner/Laroque. They literally cross out the entire Shrapnel catalogue with just a few songs down the line with the puzzling execution of some of the most intricate guitar "duels" to ever grace the scene. There is hardly a single moment which would not make you gape in wonder at the genuine brilliance and the effortless swing of creativity at large here. Rivera’s performance is traditionally standout, the man emitting passion, dramatism, and authority in various degrees throughout the album, following the music's mood swings unerringly. “Perseverance and Desperation" should not be left unmentioned as well: one of the five best instrumentals in metal history, a gorgeous classical piece, which Yngwie Malmsteen is yet to come up with. To add other song-titles here, however, would be mind-stretching and unnecessary: every composition is a gem in a perfectly constructed piece of art which would hopefully never be stained with a belated follow-up (remember "Abigail 2", "Keeper of the Seven Keys- The Legacy", etc.); so praise the band for having become a full-blooded aggressive thrash metal act in the new millennium!

   This colossal effort, for obvious reasons, remained underappreciated by the fans in the late-80's due to its complex, conceptual manner of execution (at the time the fanbase was still adjusting to Queensryche's "Operation Mindcrime") which was not a very common phenomenon on the scene back in those days. But, judging by the raving reviews which this album has started receiving more recently, now one can only be glad that the metal brotherhood has eventually acknowledged its immortal status, like it always happens with the true genuis. But I would suggest we stop rambling and simply quote Mr. Bram Stoker in the end; the man had said it so well in the distant past: "One man (album) undead... Nosferatu". 

Unrest in peace...

Murder Squad are a woefully under-appreciated supergroup featuring then-members of Entombed and Dismember, notably Uffe Cederlund on guitar and Matti Karki on vocals. The whole point of this project was to pay homage via outright worship of one of the major influences on the old swedeath scene: the mighty Autopsy. The band has even enlisted the help of the man himself, Chris Reifert, to provide drums on two tracks as well as backing vocals for this album. The funny thing is, no matter how hard they try to blatantly ape Autopsy, by this point in time the musicians involved were too deeply entrenched in the Swedish sound they spearheaded to totally divorce it from Murder Squad's music.

Matti Karki does his best Reifert impersonation, trying his best to pour on the slop and filth, but the man is famous for a reason and so his vocals come across as a combination of Reifert's gory gurgles and Karki's own growling roar. The result is some of the most inspired vocal work I've heard, serving as a perfect way to narrate these ghastly proceedings. It's actually quite telling to hear Reifert's monologue spewed all over “Disturbing the Freaks” alternate with Karki's bellowing, which further highlights the idiosyncrasies of both vocalists.

The guitar playing follows the same paradigm, the Autopsy-ish doomy crawls and grindy leanings getting spiced up with liberal doses of undeniably Swedish tremolo riffs. The intro to “Spunkslut”? C'mon guys, it's like you aren't even trying to hide the fact that you're from Stockholm. If Autopsy hadn't been such an important influence on Entombed/Carnage/Dismember in the first place this would probably sound a million times more disjointed than it does. Actually, that's not true – multiplying by zero tends to still result in zero, because the way the two styles meld is like death metal heaven. Shit, even the fucking guitar tone sounds like Uffe couldn't figure out how to physically remove the HM-2 from his effects chain while he was trying to make his rig sound like Mental Funeral. Not quite as chainsaw as the classic Entombed/Dismember records but not as analog as early Autopsy either, this finds a perfect middle ground and revels in it. Though the guitar solos are sometimes as ugly as the leads on those early Autopsy albums (“Born in Sewage, Bred in Bile”) other times Uffe definitely takes a cue from Dismember and adds loads of melody and heavy metal to his to his lead playing.

Peter Stjärnvind actually sounds like he's having fun drumming on this album, finally playing what he thought he was signing up for when he joined Entombed in 1997 but wound up drumming on Same Difference. Maybe he was inspired by Reifert's playing on “Spunkslut” and “Masterpiece in Morbidity” because the way his double bass sputters all over the place as he hammers the beats home is practically revelatory. Listen to the pounding percussion in “Rising from the Ashes” and tell me that's not a guy with a huge grin on his face bashing away at that kit.

More than anything, this album is a hell of a lot of fun. It's no wonder it appeared at a time when the members' main projects were themselves getting their shit together and effectively “getting back to their roots” after experiencing mid-career nadirs. This material is also the heaviest shit some of these guys had played on in years. I mean, just listen to the grindy, obliterating “Homocide” and tell me that wouldn't kick you in the nuts and tell you to get back to playing some fucking death metal, huh?

Reifert's direct involvement and the consistent strength of this material makes this an absolute must-own for Autopsy fanatics. It's miles ahead of Entombed's then-contemporary work, as well, and shits all over Hate Campaign. Swedeath fans who write this off as typical non-essential supergroup circle jerking are doing themselves a huge disservice by not giving Ravenous, Murderous a listen. One can only hope that these guys wander back to a recording studio sometime, especially now that Autopsy itself has come back in full force. Maybe it'll even spark a Dismember reunion!

titulo: Feel free to come back again whenever you want!
texto:
It's always a curious and complicated feeling to hear something new from Bulldozer. I've already touched upon how the band was one of the main chapters of the Italian metal history, yet not many seem to remember that they also managed to get rid of their own heavy Venom influence and carve their own sound, which culminated in their gloomy swansong Neurodeliri (1988), both the perfect epitaph for the band and possibly a seminal work for certain fringes of the thrash genre in the years to come. Like many of their peers, they reunited at the dawn of the thrash resurgence of the 2000s, yet they chose to stay in a state of deep slumber, broken only by selected live appearances and their only 'new' full-length (Unexpected Fate, 2009) as well. The album itself was a successful synthesis of their old sound with new sensibilities, but their almost complete stillness surely was a remarkable patience test for us fans. Frontman AC Wild himself stated: "...I made a calculation: we took 10 years to release one single. If we plan to complete one album with eight more songs, we could finish and release our next album in 2101". Well, with such signs of almost creative bankruptcy (or just a lot of relaxing on their part), we're left torn between taking every little thing they put out as a miracle, and just giving up on a band which is clearly out of ideas and will, who leaves some 'ear candy' from time to time, but without much effort.

You know, if every little thing they put out is just like Heretic!, you'll be scourging yourself night and day for ever thinking about the latter option. It's that good.

Okay, it arguably doesn't qualify as a 'miracle', but Bulldozer managed to surprise me once more, by changing exactly zero things about their style. Either they rehearse in Dragon Ball's Hyperbolic Time Chamber, or I don't know how else to explain it. Heretic! unites the best of IX and Unexpected Fate in a single package just longer than 3 minutes. The sound is amazing, especially considering that Unexpected Fate's mixing never left me fully satisfied, there's even time for an ominous keyboards break leading to the melodic solo, and I'd also dare saying that AC sounds better here, even if the track was actually recorded before his health problems and (luckily) temporary retirement in 2019. You can really feel this man doesn't exactly like religion. The song is an ode to famous heretic (hence the title) Giordano Bruno and less-known fellow Pomponio Algerio, both victims of the Inquisition, used as a means to hint that, even if the procedures are different, in some ways the church hasn't changed that much since then. The song was also accompanied by the band's first-ever video, with Death SS's Steve Sylvester acting as Bruno, really worth watching. Highlight? The 'Burn in flames!' pre-chorus. AC is absolutely on fire here, and the Neurodeliri-esque keys are the icing on the cake.

If we'll ever get a new Bulldozer album, I'm pretty sure it will be unlikely to hear other 8 songs just like Heretic!. But hey, in the case it'll happen, you won't hear a single complain from this mouth.

"Perchance you who pronounce my sentence are in greater fear than I who receive it" (G. Bruno)
