titulo: Don't be fooled by the name..
texto:
I came across this band only today when I saw they contributed to the soundtrack of possibly the greatest metal documentary ever made, Get Thrashed (See this. If you have not then as Paul Baloff says,” DIE”). Not that I hadn’t seen the documentary earlier it was the first time I really paid attention to the music played in the background and boy did it slay.

I came to know about the band through the Get Thrashed My Space page and ran over here to MA to get all details possible. Seeing this EP I got my hands on it as soon as possible and it does not disappoint.

Don’t be fooled by the rather lame EP name, Dudes of Darkness (Dudes!!? WTF!!!?), Because man does this consist some of the best modern day thrash material available today. The band contributed 2 tracks, Can U not Talk and The Law – Anthem to the aforesaid documentary. Both of these tracks are not surprisingly the best ones here.

The leads are something expected off of a 80’s thrash band in full flow. A shred fest, this EP contains a ton of riffs and the occasional, in your face, and face melting solo. The vocals are not the usual thrash type, but similar to that of Joey Belladona of Anthrax fame, Tobias Jansson reaches those high notes with no effort what so ever. The drums are a great here too. Aggressive, not hogging the limelight and a great talent is Johan Rudberg the drummer. The bass playing consists mainly of playing along with the guitar but once in a while comes in the bass slap and boy it’s heard.

The production is pretty awesome and it’s too hard to believe that it’s self-produced. Fuck record labels they say, let’s produce our own stuff and let us make it sound way better is their motto it seems.

So, if you yearn for underground, heavy as fuck old school thrash metal, then start hunting for this EP. It is one of te very few good thrash bands today.

One of the most important and well-known bands in the thrash metal panorama, even if they are not part of the Big Four: Testament. Their debut, entitled The Legacy, from the previous name of the band, is to be considered a masterpiece of the thrash genre and of the whole metal, together with their second album, The New Order (which I consider even superior, despite the level being more than valuable either way, but that's just my opinion).

Returning to The Legacy, it is a fundamental album, in which the heavy and fast guitar riffs of Eric Peterson combine perfectly with the solo parts of the other phenomenal guitarist of Testament, Alex Skolnick, coming from the same guitar school of Kirk Hammett. The powerful voice of the great Chuck Billy, whose talents are universally recognized within the metal world, dominates throughout the record, his vocal performance on The Legacy is truly excellent. Also noteworthy is the work of Greg Christian on bass and Louie Clemente on drums who, within a monstrous formation like that of Testament, risk going unnoticed, but who nevertheless give their contribution, in some cases also in songwriting.

As for the album itself, it contains nine tracks, which are truly one better than the other. To be clear: only masterpieces or very good songs. Among the masterpieces we must absolutely include the opener Over The Wall, with which Testament present themselves to the whole world, a song with a very heavy riff and an excellent refrain, with Chuck Billy's voice recognizable among thousands; needless to mention the solo, which is also beautiful and characterized by truly inspired melodic cues. Another excellent piece built on Skolnick's solo skills is Burnt Offerings, another spearhead of the album, a perfect example of what we ideally call melodic thrash metal. Then we have another classic: First Strike is Deadly, characterized by heavy riffs and with the voice of an absolutely fit Chuck Billy, but Skolnick is again at the forefront, as the author of a memorable solo, to say the least, something exciting. Do Or Die is no less, very heavy, with a truly exceptional refrain. Impossible not to spend a few words on the last two tracks, namely Alone In The Dark and Apocalyptic City, two masterpieces in which the soul of Testament is completely laid bare, which corresponds to the desire to combine power and speed with melody. Two masterpieces full of enthralling riffs, exalting solos, refrains that you can't help but sing, full of pathos (almost as if you were talking about power, not thrash metal) and which give a charge never seen before. Although it is not up to these masterpieces, C.O.T.L.O.D (Curse of the Legions of Death) should also be mentioned, a splinter (just over two minutes long) of uncompromising thrash metal.

In short, a fundamental, beautiful album: a classic. A work that is very much influenced by Metallica, especially in the insertion of more than significant melodic inserts. A record to have, for those who love thrash and metal in general. The production could make someone turn up their noses, being quite crude, but when the quality is what it is, the problem doesn't even arise.

Bathory is widely known as a pioneer of two genres of music: black metal and Viking metal. He released his first album in 1984 which I consider to be the absolute first black metal album and, four years later in 1988, he released a prototype to the Viking metal genre with "Blood Fire Death". This album contained the first Viking metal tracks to ever be recorded but was still firmly rooted in black metal at the same time. It wouldn't be until 1990 with the album "Hammerheart" that Quarthon finally transitioned Bathory fully into the Viking metal sound and created something truly breathtaking that would be completely perfected with the final album in Bathory's "Viking" trilogy, "Twilight of the Gods". This give new meaning to the word "epic". This is usually seen as the lesser of the three albums by many and while I still hold "Blood Fire Death" and "Hammerheart" in the highest of regards, "Twilight of the Gods" is the epitome of Viking-era Bathory, and probably Bathory overall.

This album begins with the title-track of "Twilight of the Gods", and clocks in at 14 minutes in length. The song follows a slower pace, similar to that of "Hammerheart" with songs like "Shores in Flames", and choir vocals soar like a Valkyrie readying for The Wild Hunt. This is the longest track on the album and the most epic. Why wouldn't it be? It bears the name of the album itself. The acoustic guitars are absolutely magnificent and add to the heroic atmosphere, combining beauty with epic metal. The solo in this song doesn't flaunt its technicality, rather boasting an elegant atmospheric beauty that became synonymous with Quorthon's Viking metal albums. 

Although the title track opens up this album perfectly, both in the overall theme and musical structure, it is not my favorite song on the album. "Through Blood by Thunder" and "Blood and Iron" both tie for that honor. They both open up with the exact same guitar riff, although the one in "Through Blood by Thunder" features an undistorted electric guitar, while "Blood and Iron" utilizes an acoustic guitar. Both of these songs execute their respective styles beautifully. "Blood and Iron" is the longer of the two and thus, it sounds a bit more epic. The pace remains slow and hypnotic by showcasing an evident influence of epic doom metal. This seems to be a central musical idea throughout the album, of course. This is the least black metal-sounding Viking album Quorthon had produced at this time. The drumming is especially simple and focuses on overall groove rather than technicality. This is the case with all of the songs throughout the album and while it doesn't change much, it really doesn't lessen the quality of the music. 

It seems that Quorthon's clean vocals had improved a bit from "Hammerheart", to my ears, anyway. He sounds more heroic and comfortable with his vocals. However, it also seems that his performance here has been panned by quite a few listeners, as well. I guess different people have different opinions. I've never thought he was a particularly great singer anyway but here, he sounds more natural and comfortable, and less awkward, not that he was bad to begin with, of course. The lyrics to this album are also top notch and themes of epic tales of battle, nature, and Viking mythology are perfected here. The lyrics aren't necessarily complex in syntax, as Qurothon is Swedish and English would be a second language, but they still evoke the heroic atmosphere:

"Though death may await me on the battlefield
I die to go on but by the great hail I will go,
I am marching under the runes"

See? They're simple but still follow the epic themes and we can understand them clearly due to his improved clean singing being the primary vocal style throughout the album.

While Bathory has always had a strong discography disregarding the second album of his fairly watered-down thrash metal era, "Twilight of the Gods" remains his strongest original Viking-era album and may be his strongest overall. I'd rate this among the best albums of all time and every time I listen to it I get the same feeling I have always gotten, and images of epic battles in the North.

Back in October two very unique extreme metal entities released a split album via 20 Buck Spin. On one side we have Dream Unending, whose otherworldly and ethereal gothic death/doom takes us through ponderous portals while the flip-side contains atmospherically charged black metal sepulchre and mystical wisdom from Worm. Let us embark on this adventure together.

Dream Unending

Dreary guitars and vocals come in with a mountainous heaviness coupled with the body of acoustic guitar and slow drum work. The sleepy nature and stunning production of the music blend the more ambient end of extreme metal with a sublimely enriched performance that does not take long to shine through in the form of intricate guitars that pluckily divert from the more typical notions of the genre. With a mournfully harrowing vocal performance, the growls and drums really drag out across those resplendent guitar notes to give us a truly sombre soundscape full of dynamics and nuance, sparse in their mix so as not to overshadow each other. Enchanting instruments and mixed clean and harsh vocals give us a constant flow of natural and organic compositional progressions while the mood of the songs is never lost or jarring. It feels like Dream Unending are very content in their own little part of the wider Heavy Metal spectrum and they are occupying it with some great songs.

Spectrally soft and yet crushingly intense, the qualities of Dream Unending’s prior works are present here tenfold, indeed this is something unearthly and special. Of course the Peaceville trio spring to mind, as do some death-doom pioneers, but equally there are notes of jazz and progressive rock to be found in this music. Furthermore it might be a little far-out for some fans, which I think is a valid response to music as unusual as this in the metallic underground. That said, I think equally people will be attracted to the rich palette of musical prowess that Dream Unending offer which propagates the sensibilities of Paradise Lost, Opeth, Sentenced, Thergothon and more into something quite wonderful. Impeccable grooves and atmospherics dance in a slumbering yet engaging fashion to create formless and yet driven, timeless and grieving soundscapes from start to end.

Worm

Crystalline guitar and synths ride waves of thundering double kicks and malicious vocals, that spooky Worm vibe coming in strong from the very onset. Admittedly I have sometimes lamented the loss of their grotesque death-doom past as heard on “Gloomlord” and “Foreverglade”, but their ability to execute spellbinding black metal rife with melody and tasteful synths akin to early Dimmu Borgir, Emperor, Obtained Enslavement and the like is certainly impressive. More so the lead guitar work is insane, as we have heard before, taking some ferocious shred elements into a genre that typically lacks solos. Speaking of the crazy musicianship, the drumming is fantastically varied and sharp while the bass lines contort into inhuman shapes superbly. The keyboard use plays perfectly around the melodies and the vocals are raw and raspy as they should be to fit such a sound. Interestingly, the sodden dungeon-lurking atmosphere may feel like inhaling dusty cobwebs until the aorta turns to parchment, but contrastingly there are these epic, soaring moments that take those glacial icicles and spearhead them through your chest.

Worm may have sacrificed some grit, but equally have ushered in a lot of emotive, introspective and mysterious elements to their craft. This feels like a very modern continuation of the Scandinavian Black Metal scene of the mid to late 90s. In a world where many bands attempt to be old school to varying levels of success (and don’t get me wrong, many of my favourites fall into this category), Worm do the opposite and attain a very current sound with extremely clean mixing to give us a shiny package. Somehow, this inexplicably feels like a mysterious chest found deep in a castle keep that has not been touched for centuries, in spite of its up-to-date methods. Whether you prefer or disdain this, it must be commended that Worm have not simply followed the masses. All of this enforces the magical nature of their side and one’s ability to be utterly lost in its transcendental tranquility. Chilling, wintery Black Metal that is vibrant, diverse and bewitching, another triumphant new chapter in Worm’s discography which seems to never hit the same spot twice.

Conclusion

This split is clearly meant to be something very unique, in which it is profoundly successful. Both bands bring an obscure and often overlooked take on extreme metal’s past into the modern day without rehashing any of their forebears. Both have a modern, dreamy, otherworldly and yet still metallic approach that oozes musicality and variety in so many forms. As much as I often despair overtly progressive Heavy Metal, this is one of those rare gems where it does something cool without losing that essential core the genre must uphold. “Starpath” is an extraordinary journey of secretive and yet sublimely heartfelt music where each band has gorgeous new pieces to offer and fits the other without occupying any of the same spaces. Explore…

Written for  Nattskog

Note: This is a review of the CD re-release of the demo, with the 3 extra demo tracks from Gauderon Dherg's 3-track demo added at the end.

Crebain is one of the tragically overlooked figures of USBM, lurking in the shadow of such giants as the wildly popular Leviathan and Xasthur. Indeed, were it not for Aquarius Record's praise of this album, I probably would never have heard of Crebain, unless I magically got my hands on his split with Leviathan (which is another must-own album, as all of Leviathan's output it) However, unlike many frostbitten, Californian contemporaries, Crebain does not ply the slower, more atmospheric realm of suicidal black metal, despite the rather cliche image put forth on the demo (numbered in blood, ooh, so grim and kvlt). Rather, Crebain goes the far more vicious route of straight-ahead, riff-centric black metal.

And boy, are those riffs massive. From the opening blast of "Night of the Stormcrow" (after the short, obligatory intro of crows cawing), one can plainly see Ancalagon the Black (seriously?) is a master of the guitar. Riffs slice and dice just like the best black metal of old, and AtB's skill is evident in the variety of riffs he manages to dish out. Like the other review noted, quite often there is a thrashy feel to the music, laid down mostly by the guitar. However, this album is not speed all the way through; AtB knows when to slow things down and let the music breathe a little (again, the opener is a good example of this).  Also, amazingly, the drum machine on this album is not particularly annoying, since AtB clearly put some effort into the drum programming (take note, all you endless Xasthur clones). Vocals are distorted to hell, but actually sound fairly interesting, and are thankfully somewhat buried in the mix - one of the greatest and most common mishaps in black metal is mixing the vocals way up front in the mix, which basically ruins any attempts at atmosphere. Production is pretty much spot on for black metal...lots of distortion, everything can actually be heard, and it is still raw as all hell. Even the early demo tracks don't sound atrocious...not nearly as good as the main portion of the album, obviously, but instruments are still audible and the "wall of noise" effect is thankfully not present.

Standout track "By Our Talons Heaven Shall Fall" (great song title!) has an amazing intro riff that gradually morphs back and forth throughout the song, with a great bridge at around the 3 minute mark. AtB is also quite capable of slower, more menacing songs, with "Darkness Be My Bride" being a prime example. Amazingly, the 3 demo tracks tacked on at the end hold up just as well (although the first is simply an older version of "By Our Talons Heaven Shall Fall," so of course it was going to be good). Riffs will typically be repeated over and over for a hypnotic feel, and then either another layer of melodic tremolo picking will be placed over it ("Cries of My Motherland"), or the riff will gradually morph as it burrows into your head. 

This demo is certainly not without faults - the atrocious opening to "Time To Die," which I can only guess is some attempt at humor, being the most egregious, though the actual song is absolutely devastating - the sheer power of the riffs and AtB's mastery of black metal songwriting cover up most of the shortcomings. I'd appreciate a real drummer on future recordings (the drum machine is not bad by any means, but we all know live drums are better), but other than that, Crebain has released an absolutely killer collection of fast, thrashing black metal songs that will please any fan of the faster end of black metal. Let's hope Crebain can emerge from the shadow of his suicidal brethren and rightly take it's place as one of the most respected members of the USBM community.

titulo: Portrait of anti-hero consumed by anguish
texto:
From noisy raw atmospheric BM beginnings on debut EP "A Frigid Spectre", Missouri-based project Ascalapha follows a more melodic, conventional song-based path on first album "Somber Vampyric Night". While the EP dealt with loss, abandonment and lack of hope and purpose, here the album revolves around a vampiric creature, tormented by anger, despair and guilt, and in thrall to appetites and instincts it cannot control in an unending and dreary life.  The protagonist is driven by instinct to seek out and take the lives and blood of those who remind him of the life he once had – or might have had, had he not become a vampire. In nine songs, most of which feature lyrics, we gain an insight into the unending existential pain and anguish experienced by the vampire, and perhaps by others of his kind, in flowing raw music of fury, darkness and intense feeling that emphasise the vampire's inner turmoil.

The first few songs on the album from "Dark Moon" through "Ceaseless Drought" and "Nameless Path" to the title track carve out a standard melodic 1990s-era second-wave BM path with sometimes distinct riffs, rapid-fire blast-beat percussion and strong raspy vocals whose range travels from snarls and growls to groans and screams. There's a lot of repetition in the music, especially in the title track where the tension and underlying ferocity build up to almost unbearable levels and an early, bloody climax can be anticipated. It's on the title track that the vocals really start to shine, dripping as they do with a mix of sheer venom and relish, horror and revulsion, and madness and confusion as our anti-hero is compelled to follow the voices in his head. 

"Our Lives Intertwined" brings some instrumental ambient relief in a simple yet darkly evocative track of repetitive riff loop / synth tone-poem minimalism, and leads us into another phase in which Burzumesque black metal and synth melodies are mixed into music that can be muscular and powerful yet still melancholy and regretful. "Noche sombria" ("Sombre night") runs from sadness to anger and savagery in music that constantly shifts and rarely repeats itself, echoing the complex emotions and memories of its protagonist. In its variety, urgency and rugged energy, this song is the major highlight of the album. "Una Vida Que No Es Mia" ("A Life that is not mine") is a more despondent, all instrumental piece commenting perhaps on "Noche sombria", its jangly tones reflecting regret and sorrow for what has been lost and what cannot be changed. The album comes to a resolution in "Remorse", in which the protagonist takes leave of us to continue on the path he chose and for which he accepts responsibility for, even as it fills him with self-loathing and hatred. We are left with a deep feeling of emptiness and sadness for a being labouring under an eternal curse, for whom immortality is punishment. 

The musical and thematic direction Ascalapha has taken on "Somber Vampyric Night" may have been trodden by a thousand million other BM acts, though the raw and aggressive style of music shows plenty of spirit and ferocity still in the classic 1990s melodic black metal of bands like Darkthrone, Emperor, Immortal and Burzum. Using a minimalist approach emphasising melody and repetition, with just a small set of instruments (guitars, synths, piano and percussion), Ascalapha musicians Monstro and Nikola Dušmanić describe in depth a tale of a dark being in thrall to savage appetites and instincts which repel him and cause him anguish and self-loathing, yet which paradoxically lead him to commit more and greater acts of violence and blood-shedding depravity.  The tools and methods used may be familiar to MA fans to the point of being banal, but the portrait so painted is not so easily forgotten.

banda: but this is a nice creek
texto:
Giant Squid have made quite a big name for themselves considering they only have two full lengths, one of which is restricted to just one thousand printings, but their reputation of being a refreshing change to the post-rock/post-metal/progressive rock scene has helped them garner almost unanimous praise from fans of the style. For whatever reason, likely the obscurity, the first EP is largely unheard of. It's a pity because this is some extremely interesting and unique music, but it certainly lacks the out of the box charm that the full lengths boast. The music is mellowed out beyond belief, and having multiple keyboardists totally change the way the band go about things; it's about as far away from metal as you can get for most of the duration, almost feeling like a post-rock influenced jazz band, but it is just as engaging as the more famous releases. 

This first EP is so totally different from what came after, it's totally different to anything I've heard period. It's hard to pinpoint a single biggest change in the band as the vocals are different, the production is different, the songwriting is different, even the instruments are different, but overall it typically comes together pretty well.

All the vocal approaches any listener of the band knows are here, the nasal vocals and the harsher screams of Aaron Gregory are more or less as they would later be, if scarcer in quantity, The female vocals are handled by Aurielle Zeitler instead of the usual female vocalist Jackie Gratz. She has a pretty similar voice to Gratz, if a bit more underdeveloped technically speaking. She is kind of shrill and irritating but nothing bad enough to detract from the music much. She is also utilized a lot more than Gratz is on the full lengths as the more laid back music lends itself to her voice a little more, it's just a pity her performance isn't quite up to the standards the band would later have. Joining the usual three pronged vocal approach are a couple of different voices. One is the non-nasal clean voice of keyboardist Andy Southard who is sadly missing from later releases, the style is most prominent on the exquisite "Dead Man's Fog". Like all the band's vocalists, he's still a long shot off technical perfection, but he sounds excellent. Along with this Aurielle uses a lower pitched voice at times, it's only rare, but it complements her higher tones excellently when they are used..

The production on Monster in the Creek is notable as the music was recorded live with the vocals dubbed over later. Despite the haphazard method of recording the sound is excellent. The low end has a fantastic sound with the thick drums and bass flowing together smoothly while the clarity on the keys, guitars and vocals is impressive. The big difference in the production is the mixing though. Where in later, much more metallic releases, the sludgy, meaty guitars served a purpose of delivering crushing blows; here they are of little consequence. This is keyboard driven music and the mix reflects that. Even in the three middle songs with extra guitar presence they provide nothing more than a backdrop to the attention grabbing keyboard work. The only song to be released elsewhere, Throwing a Donner Party at sea shows how big this difference is, on The Ichthyologist the song is a ripping, violent metal track with lots of energy and anger. On here the energy remains, as it is the only song with tempo or sludge guitars at the start, but the riffs are not a focus at all, instead that memorable riff is performed on keys and surprisingly it works quite well. Instead of an out and out metal track the song feels almost like a post-metal version of the Cardiacs, and I love it.

The band has always done keyboard driven music pretty well, which is why this debut EP's heavy progressive leanings shouldn't be seen as a negative, but the problem comes in the actual keyboard sound. It's oddly campy for a band which has usually used it for genuinely atmospheric purposes. It's oddly compressed and midi sounding. It's a real pity the only element of the sound that doesn't sound excellent is the one most of the music is based around.

This keyboard focus is one of the major differences in songwriting compared to their more famous works. It's not that keys are something lost to the band, but of the 5 songs here, two of them never touch a metal riff, and two of them only break into sludge mode in the last minute of music. This is a totally different beast. The EP title itself seems to allude to this somewhat, while the later releases spoke of the deep sea and ocean monsters this one simply mentions a creek. Indeed this music sounds perfect for lounging about a rural creek side; it's just so laid back. This is a mixed blessing, the music sounds extremely unique, even more progressive and free flowing than the full lengths but is kind of dry at times. The title track is pretty uneventful and the awful keyboard sound is at its worst, and 'Age of Accountability' tends to linger on the softer side of things for longer than the song’s limited ideas really deserve. However the upshot to all of the lazy vibes is the song 'Dead man's Fog'. It's entirely soft, but the beautiful keyboard melody, background guitar effects and excellent vocals all come together to create what may be the bands single best song and it doesn't even have any metal on it. If they re-record any other songs off this EP in the future hopefully this one is right up near the top of the list. 

The reason for all of this is likely the lineup, there are two keyboardists here and their interaction creates a whole different dynamic for the band. With the band achieving some kind of stability in recent times it's unlikely this sort of sound will be attempted again. This is the likely major appeal of this EP; it represents a chapter of the band that we probably won't hear again.  

For all its charm and unique appeal this isn't as good as the albums. The first song is undeniably weak, the keyboard tone is pretty annoying at times, the closer is poor, and the EP is just a little bit too focussed on the softer side of things and lacks some of the dynamic that the band uses so well. With that said, 'Dead Man's Fog' and the interesting original version of 'Throwing a Donner Party at Sea' make Monster in the Creek well worth tracking down just on their own. This album is a unique step in a unique band's history, well worth any fans time.

Stratovarius used to be one of the best Power Metal bands around, but after the sublime Destiny, they sank rapidly in quality, and although they would have worse moments on future albums, it is Infinite in particular that is the only one that seems to be consistently mediocre and useless, having no special reason to exist and being a generally uninspired, lifeless chunk of fluffy crap that I don't see why anyone is buying into at all.

There is one very good song here, titled "Hunting High and Low," which is a brainless, fast and catchy Power Metal number that pretty much anyone can enjoy, and it is damn good at being a brainless, fast and catchy Power Metal song. Sure, it isn't timeless or anything, but it does have a great hook and one of the best choruses the band ever wrote. The melodies are fun and will never leave your head, the vocals are peppy and powerful and the guitars and keys duel like Tazmanian devils on crack, and this song just rocks without pretension. "A Million Light Years Away" is not a bad song, with a cool little main melody, but it is pretty substandard, too.

The rest, though? Total dung, all of it. "Mother Gaia," Tolkki? Are you serious? This is some of the most contrived, half-assed garbage I have ever heard, and from Timo Tolkki? That's saying a lot. Just listen to the ridiculous part where the song drops out for this polka-like melody and Timo Koltipelto singing like a lounge singer. Interesting in theory, yes, but very, very poorly written, and it never gets any better, either. This is probably the worst song Stratovarius ever wrote until their self titled album, completely irredeemable. The title track doesn't sound so bad at first, and it has a few good parts, but a few minutes in and I already don't ever want to hear it again. Totally insufferable; if this band wants to make the world a better place (as the lyrics say), they should just eradicate all copies of this album instead. "Freedom" is as boring as a Stratovarius song gets without being on the self titled album, "Phoenix" is perhaps the most derivative and cliche song they have ever recorded and "Millennium" is just bland, bland, bland. And how about "Glory of the World," which manages to both rip off "Will the Sun Rise?" and be as stupidly catchy and shallow as metal can be? Annoying!

Aside from all of that, I just don't like the general mood this album seems to have been based on, this condescending assumption that listeners are morons that need everything spelled out for them. The hooks here are very blatant, as I mentioned above, with no subtlety or staying power at all (well, alright, "Hunting High and Low" is good enough in my books, you've got me there). They're all cleanly defined as if to say HEY! LOOK AT ME! I'M A CATCHY HOOK! ENJOY ME!, as if we wouldn't be able to enjoy the songs otherwise. As if this band wasn't making thoughtful AND catchy metal music just years before this. Look at the aforementioned "Glory of the World" - it's really ridiculous how far this band went to create "catchy" songs; there is really nothing here aside from a flashy hook. And "Millennium," too; just listen to that shallow "heavy" riffage. About as subtle as a bowling ball thrown at full force to the face.

The melodies are the same; very elementary and basic with little innovation or even subtlety and thought put into them at all. I think Stratovarius's problems can be summed up in two ways, with the first one being the longer of the two: the band was just half-assing this one and dumbing down their songwriting for an audience that didn't need it. The second is a bit more simple, and I can tell you what it is in two words: Timo. Tolkki. I've ranted about him before, but basically he just kept getting more and more strange, bland and nonsensical with his songwriting over the years as his mind decayed, and I think this was the exact point where you can see his drop off of the sane realm of metal songwriters. "Mother Gaia" would be the specific point where his brains began to slowly leak out of his ears. I just don't understand why this album even exists. It's a complete non-sequitur to the universe why anyone would ever want to listen to this album over anything else that is better and more relevant, including this band's previous four releases. Stratovarius were already pretty poppy and accessible, even in their more erudite moments, so...why?

This kind of blunt, unambitious slush is just inexcusable. All of these songs are just silly and boring, sounding stilted and incomplete, as if the band wasn't really finished writing them. There is no urgency, no energy, no passion to anything on this album at all. You ask, aren't you being a bit harsh on this? Yes, maybe, but then again, why shouldn't I be harsher on this? This is pretty, flashy and listenable, but really, it's about as deep as a fucking kiddy pool, and you should stay away from it if you don't like getting your intelligence insulted.

Albums like these end up being insanely fun to listen to. In the endless sea of Darkclones being pumped out into the fringes of the metal community day by day, it can be an absolute godsend to stumble across a band that doesn't sacrifice the ethos or principal sound of a scene without falling into all of the traps that fail to make them stand out. Indeed, retaining an aura of individuality in an already oversaturated brand of black metal is a true feat in this day and age, and Craft is more than a worthy collective capable of accomplishing this task. 

This orthodox group, no strangers to the black metal scene at large, resides in south central Sweden, and their particular sound deviates from the all-out assault that contemporaries such as Marduk, Watain, Funeral Mist, and Dark Funeral are so heavily known for. Instead of opting for an all-out sonic assault full of cartoony ties to theistic Satanism and blast beats so fast that they could beat Noah Lyles in a 100m sprint, Craft opt for a much more restrained approach that reminds me of bands like Armagedda and Ondskapt. I say this because this sound reeks of Darkthrone (and by extension, Celtic Frost) inspiration; bands like these wear their influences proudly on their sleeve, but there's a certain je ne sais quoi in the way that they mix pained black metal howls and rasps with all kinds of dissonant swagger. 

Musically speaking, all of the major elements you'd come to expect from an early 2000s group of this ilk are here: Speaking of swagger, Craft opt for persistent midtempo groove sections that make for a conducive headbanging experience as a whole. There's never a moment where I don't make some kind of stink face, espeically in the tracks "Reaktor 4" and "False Orders Begone." When it comes to black metal, these Swedes don't resort to exceptionally slow dirge-like passages a la Nortt or Lurker of Chalice, nor is this atmospheric and ethereal in any sense of the definition; it's just a solid example of pure filth in a deliciously digestible format. 

There are some moments where the mean, nasty grooves make way for some energetic double-time tremolos, primarily in "N.D.P", but the name of the game is all about sass and hateful bombast. While not the kind of apocalyptic torment that maybe a band like Katharsis could happily claim, nor is it an emotionally crushing experience capable of leaving you bedridden for days, Craft present a master class of making no-frills material sound fresh and engaging. The buzz that they received back in the early 2000s, looking back from a removed persepctive, made a lot of sense as black metal was diversifying and getting sucked into the tractor beam of mainstream metal publications. Fans thought that a return to the unrefined, filthy flair for the old school was just what the scene needed, and th such a compelling

For those looking for pure, uncut black metal far removed from melodic, atmospheric, or post-rocky flairs, check this out immediately.

titulo: Isn't it cheating if you're taller than the maze?
texto:
Not a hell of a lot of metal bands got to sign with huge labels like Atlantic in the 80s, and surely it was a testament (pun intended) to the trajectory of your career to count yourself among them. Or was it? Well, in the case of Maryland's Wrathchild America, who added the national suffix so they wouldn't dare be confused with a crappy UK band, it certainly seemed like they were going to be huge. Back in the close of that great decade, this was one of those bands that even your normal high school friends had heard about, you know, the cliquey types who liked Metallica, Ozzy, Megadeth and Anthrax but couldn't be bothered to ever delve further into the underground or even consider themselves 'metal heads' publicly for fear of losing job prospects or not getting laid by the good girls.

Yes, Wrathchild America had a lot going for them, but I'm not it had truly manifest in the debut Climbin' the Walls, with its iconic hesher in a maze cover artwork. Though the band would later develop into a more interesting hybrid of progressive thrash with a few jazz aesthetics, this is more like a mixture of Metallica's 1984-86 period with some traditional British heavy metal, not terribly unlike another hopeful band, Powermad. You've got some decent enough songs here like "Climbin' the Walls" itself which has a few decent, ripping guitar riffs and stupid but fun lyrics; the driving, melodic "Day of the Thunder"; the goofy but endearing vampire epic "London After Midnight"; or "Silent Darkness (Smothered Life)", a hymn to being buried alive with a nice melodic guitar line in the chorus. But then you've got garbage like the bluesy hard rock & roll of "No Deposit, No Return" which might have fit better with their UK counterpart, or "Candy from a Madman", which is hard not to laugh at despite an acceptable riff or two.

Then there's the cover of Pink Floyd's "Time", which you might not expect on an album like this, and well, it's "Time". While a band like Voivod would manage to convert an experience like "Astronomy Domine" into something relevant and even poignant on the mesmeric Nothingface this very same year, it just doesn't seem that it belongs with Wrathchild America. Granted, it's not the worst cover out there, but it's not doing Climbin' the Walls any favors. Otherwise, this is just not all that great of an effort. Catchy enough perhaps to get a few people to notice, with decent guitars and drumming. The production was sufficient enough to match label mates like the comparable Savatage, but in the end, this album would be greatly outclassed by its follow up, and I very rarely find any compulsion to go back and listen aside from maybe two songs.

titulo: Mom! Help! The KKK is naked in my bed!!!
texto:
Somewhere in the land of metal archetypes is a railway whereupon runs the conspiracy theory train; it's been in service for several decades and is regarded by some as a convenient means of travel, whereas many see it as a noisy nuisance that is in dire need of being decommissioned for smoother modes of travel. In contrast to other modes of expression, this one is largely a lyrical pursuit that tends to lend itself to just about every sub-genre resting under the metal umbrella, and even those who crave a world of only the status quo can't help but like a few bands that dabble in tin-foil hat poetry. Thanks in large part to the relatively consistent output of this locomotive's aging engineer Dave Mustaine, younger bands have been showing up of late to purchase their tickets, although the same train's goofy conductor Al Jourgensen hasn't been doing this mode of travel any favors of late with his recent auditory hallucinations under the guise of albums containing music, let alone the questionable friends that he's been giving free passes on board of late to reminisce over his glory days of snorting heroin and insisting the world not think him a moron for doing so. 

Whatever level of musical aptitude that existed in Ministry's arsenal following the 1990s died when the band first folded tent in 2008, and the world would not be any different if they'd been content to stay buried. The twisted, incoherent collage of sound resting on top varying drum lines that may as well be looped that is AmeriKKKant is the testament to a zombified corpse that can't even muster the strength to bite into living flesh, let alone catch up with any prospective victim under the age of 90. All of the tired musical ideas that were marched out on Ministry's early industrial metal output and generally mirrored on Fear Factory's Soul Of A New Machine and Sepultura's Chaos A.D. are retreaded in the most banal of fashions, largely at a plodding tempo, and saturated with sampled and manipulated spoken passages from various television and cinematic publications to the point that songs trade blows within themselves between inducing boredom and insufferable annoyance, not to mention the flirtations of nu-metal via the frequent use of DJ record scratches, as if the world needs another formerly respected band swapping bodily fluids with Limp Bizkit.

Deconstructing the moving parts of this thing is a task comparable to sifting through a confetti mixture of rat, hamster and chinchilla turds of various shades and textures in an effort to find a pattern. Occasional chime-in parts by Uncle Al's aged, haggard gruff shouts provide little in the way of anchoring things, and play second fiddle to a host of randomly selected samples and canned instrument sounds that supposedly form the cadence points. Generally the longer things go, the more incoherent they become, though the album's nails on a chalkboard opener "I Know Words" is moderate in scope and takes the cake for incongruousness with an endless, unorganized stream of sampled violin notes with no discernible melody and a royally annoying assortment of manipulated voice samples from the current President of the United States. Nevertheless, plodding slabs of stool-smeared toast like "Twilight Zone" with its bizarre blues harmonica passages and the hyper-redundant "Wargasm" run a pretty close second in terms of turning minutes into hours with hypnotic riff fragments and drum grooves laced with even more redundant spoken samples.

Perhaps one might chalk it up to the pitfall of trying to blend the minimalist tendencies of industrial music with a conceptual album format, but even when discounting the lack of any real hooks or even signs of progression, the atmosphere isn't really utilized effectively, and moments of ball-crushing heaviness are basically non-existent. The closest things get to a full on metallic attempt is the woefully dumbed down two-riff pony "We're Tired Of It", which is basically a processed rehash of an up tempo Nailbomb song with hip hop trimmings on the side and a gimped out series of gang vocals out of a geriatric Machine Head fan boy's convention, or for those who like to keep their descriptions brief, a parody of the thrash metal style. However, the true coup de grace is this album's first promotional single and homage to America's latest domestic terrorist group "Antifa". Half the time this thing makes extremely sloppy attempts at assimilating Tony Iommi's doom riffing style into their mechanistic formula, whereas the remnant attempts to keep older fans in line with mid-paced retread riffs that ΚΕΦΑΛΗΞΘ borrowed from The Black Album. Though it's a foregone conclusion that this song received a fair bit of hate since its release on the internet a few months back from bereaved fans of Taake and free speech enthusiasts alike, most of it came from this song being an rancid pile of auditory dung that was clearly trying to pander to a highly visible demographic for those NWO approved dead presidents.

The only real way that politically-charged art can be made distinct from commercialized propaganda is if the art itself can stand even when stripped of its lyrical message, and this is the ultimate downfall of AmeriKKKant. Whether one falls under what Ennio Flaiano rightly observed as the two camps of Fascism (Fascism and Anti-Fascism), one would be totally remiss to say that any enjoyment could be had listening to these smatterings of random, disjointed fragments of sound save in the context of some rally by a group of like-minded people who couldn't give a shit about metal or even music in general. There are plenty of extremely well executed right-wing and left-wing albums out there in a whole slew of metal sub-genres that could be enjoyed by anyone who likes good music, this one simply opts to go a very different route and simultaneously smears it in the listener's face. Speaking plainly on the matter, I'd personally prefer a good Hydrochloric enema over having my eardrums raped by this album again.

Having bought, played and enjoyed to bits their prior DVD, entitled ''The DVD'', I went for this one blindly, thinking since it was a more modern, digitally filmed gig, in widescreen, with 5.1 sound and whatnot, it was going to dance all over the older one. Man was I wrong! Does it mean this is a bad one? Obviously from the 85% rating I gave it, no, it is fantastic. But it is the performance alone that saves the day here, not the picture and sound quality, mind you. The product comes attractively packaged, with great artwork and a thick booklet with a ton of info, printed in thick, glossy paper.

Filmed at a little venue called Ulu, in the UK, the gig finds our deathgrind monsters -and inventors of both grindcore and subsequently deathgrind- crammed in a tiny stage where there is no space to move around, so every musician is locked in place, with Shane obstructed from view by Jesse, and only Barney being able to perform his hectic stage antics somewhat during the performance. He had just cut his hair, so no hair swinging around during headbanging, which is at the same time funny and sad.

As mentioned early, the performance is unsurpassable; this has to be their best ever, and certainly way better than the ones I attended, when they were down to just Mitch Harris' guitar, after the demise of Jesse. On the older DVD, the bottom end was loud and boomy, yet reducing bass with my bass control cured the problem 100%. This time you press play, in  stereo mode (I don't own a home theater setup, but an audiophile stereo rig) and there is no bottom end all, with guitars coming across as screechy and overtrebly; just cranking my bass control quite a bit cured both problems to an acceptable extent.

Picture, despite this being a double-layer DVD, is allotted a surprisingly low bitrate, which, together with the bad authoring and mastering, makes for a noisy picture, with the occasional cublocking here and there during complex scenes with busy strobe lighting or rapid movement, though nothing major; I managed to iron out most of the flaws with the video noise reduction, smoothing, and detail enhancement options of my Blu-ray player. Maybe the blame partially lies on the ton of extras included, easter egg and whatnot included, in typical turn-of-the-century fashion, at which DVDs were not as good as they are today, with honorable exceptions; got a lot of those, so I should know.

To the marrow now: once everything was corrected to the best of my possibilities, I started enjoying the whooping 83' Ulu gig. The combo blazes through a tightly packed, wisely-chosen selection from all of their discography, from Scum to Enemy Of The Music Bussiness. Not many from FETO are included, but the band, as any fan knows, evolved from pure grindcore to a more death-metal oriented style after that album, so those versions, are, well ''deathier'', if you allow me the neologism, and a welcome variation from the originals, in the more modern style. I HATE when a band performs their songs just as on their records, favoring variation and experimentation instead. Versions of all song are wilder, faster, and fiercer than on the CDs, and even the Florida death metal-influenced ones, which snooze me out of my wits, made me headbang till my neck was in pain. Sadly only one song, Hung, from my all-time favorite, Fear Emptiness Despair, was played, but that is understandable due to the unpopularity the album has, considered by most punters,  reviewers, and even Shane Embury, as their Cold Lake, Celtic Frost's ''worst'' album, which I love as well. Guess I am a sucker for lost causes?

Guitar interplay between Jesse and Mitch is otherwordly, one on each stereo channel, with plenty of parts played with a generous use of volume pedals, esp during the solos. Jesse is way louder on the left side, so I evened him out with my balance control, but probably most people won't care or notice. At the reference volume levels I use, leaving such an imbalance unattended can deafen you on one ear. Snares are luckily loudly mixed in, making the grindcore parts sound like they should, yet the kicks, tom, and bass guitar need the aforementioned boost to come alive. Shane picks his bass at the neck of his instrument for maximum boom, and that is not quite evident here, as is the top end, featuring quiet cymbals; not a problem if you have any kind of equalizer. The band is so tight it squeaks, and the 83' seem like half an hour  when the gig is over.

Extras are in abundance, and mostly all of them are of enough quality to be enjoyable. Wonder where the easter egg is at? Go for the dolls' eyes until they light up and press enter; you are in for a huge surprise.

The incredibly good: THE PERFORMANCE

The not so good: overall picture and sound mix

The ugly: nothing really

I understand the 5.1 mix has gobs of bass, so if you have that option, experiment. This is a must-have for any ND fan, unless you hate live DVDs, or do not have the equipment to compensate for its flaws. A solid 85%, that would have been a 100% if not for those.

titulo: To Walk the Extra Green Mile and Climb Mount Doom
texto:
End of Green appeared in the midst of the doom/gothic metal wave which was the only genre to viciously oppose to the grunge/groovy/industrial hordes that were largely dominating the scene during the-90’s. Some of the band members were also occupied with another doom metal formation, Mirror of Deception, at around the same time, but expect no elegiac epic hymns along the lines of that other act here. In fact, the guys had managed to achieve a fairly unique, interesting symbiosis between classic doom, gothic, and hardcore the latter giving the music a somewhat uncanny modern-ish feel. Not to worry as there are no detrimental additives whatsoever; it’s just that this “core” motif gives the album reviewed here a fairly characteristic aura.

The band have defined their style as “depressive subcore” which strangely hits the mark although I would personally replace the “sub” part with “doom” since this is first and foremost a doom metal recording before anything else… with a twist. That twist is perhaps not that audible on the opening “Left My Way” which is vintage doom also introducing the excellent, slightly hoarse soulful clean vocals; at this early stage the approach is clearly on the traditional side along the lines of Pentagram, Saint Vitus and The Obsessed. “Away” tries to run away from this pattern with speedier more dynamic rhythms which recall the faster-paced moments from the Crowbar exploits; and this is where the “core” connection becomes evident, to these ears for the better. Nothing of the kind, though, on “Seasons of Black” which is a short depressive doomster; and on the title-track, a melancholic elegy of the balladic, tear-jerking variety.

“Tomorrow not Today” starts moving around with more vivid riffage although it remains pretty much within the doom metal confines with very good emotional vocal performance. “Sleep” is not exactly a sleeper, but is a dynamic depressive epicer with jumpy guitars, and “You” brings back the shadow of Crowbar with another more aggressive stroke, but it’s the catchy alternative quirks ala Therapy and Alice on Chains that steal the show here. “Nice Day to Die” is not recommended for the suicide-prone although both the music and the vocals sound strangely uplifting, perhaps intentionally, to contrast with the depressing lyrical content. “No More Pressure” is trad doom at its finest taken straight from the early Black Sabbath efforts, and to some this may be the finest track here excluding the several more brutal quarrelsome vocal insertions. 

The band continued with this fascinating mixture on the sophomore “Believe, My Friend…” (1998) which was still a more doom-soaked saga; but on “Songs for a Dying World” (2002) things started shifting towards more dynamic, less sombre ways of expression with more overt gothic rock leanings akin to those on Paradise Lost’s “One Second”. By the time of “Last Night on Earth” a year later the transition was completed, and there was very little doom or core left on it the fans enjoying a full-fledged gothic rock feast still ornate by a (un)healthy doze of depression and pessimism. The latter shades are not that strongly present on the other outfit the guys got involved with, the more classic-sounding doom metallers Voodooshock, with whom they give more freedom to their passion for all things Sabbath-esque. All good on all fronts, no signs of slowing down, especially when Mount Doom can already be seen looming on the horizon… there’s very little left before it can be reached and ultimately conquered.

titulo: Why the Fuck Wasn't the Whole Album Like This?
texto:
Annihilator's third album, Set the World On Fire, would be the first of their albums to be really panned, mostly due to the increased amount of mainstream/glam/pop metal influences that frontman Jeff Waters attempted to blend into the band's (formerly) tech-thrash sound. What to some might seem as a shame ends up being a total tragedy after hearing what might have been. If the StWoF album would have just stuck to the formula set up by the StWoF single and not juggled styles as it did, that album would certainly not be seen in the generally negative light that it often is today.

This single features what would be known as two of the best songs off of the full-length. "Set the World On Fire" isn't an all out thrash assault, but it features one hell of a cool main riff and a great sense of melody (though the lyrics are a bit contrived). Shame there weren't more songs like this on the album. The other is "Knight Jumps Queen," the bass-oriented groover (quite reminiscent of Testament's "Trial by Fire" at times, though not as thrashy) with the clever lyrics about a chess match. Again, not a true thrasher, but the type of song that the full-length really could have used more of. While these two songs would go on to appear on said full-length, it is the third, rarest track that is most interesting. This lineup's rendition of "Hell Bent for Leather" is fucking awesome. It channel's the incredible energy and catchiness of the original while making it heavier and adding Annihilator's unique style to it. Think that solo couldn't get any better? Listen to Neil Goldberg's sweep-arpeggiated variation and think again. This is also Aaron Randall's finest vocal performance in Annihilator, hitting all the highs and lows without strain.

Even if you already have Set the World on Fire, this is worth getting for that great fucking cover. Too bad it wasn't included on their greatest hits or the rarities album, as this is not easy to find.

titulo: S.D.I. and The Megamosh Sign a Peace Treaty
texto:
Part III from the S.D.I./The Megamosh franchise so far although our three friends from Osnabruck in Lower Saxony have gotten together again recently, hopefully working on the fourth instalment… and it had better be better than the one reviewed here since it, despite its several more or less overt merits, left quite a bit to be desired some 37 years ago.

How time flies, god damn it… it was like yesterday when I was in the studio some time in 1989, only to see the new S.D.I. opus there… waiting for me. A complete surprise appeared just a few months after I had gotten a hold of its extraordinary predecessor. Couldn’t wait to go back home and give it a listen, hoping for another grand ode to The Megamosh.

How could I have known that the guys and said beast had signed a peace treaty shortly before this album’s release… there was no Internet at the time, metal magazines were a rarity in Bulgaria, and save for the most renowned acts on the field there were hardly any pieces of news spread around the metal fandom. But back to this treaty supposedly signed in some dark dungeon deep Down Below: to put it short, the speed, thrash, crossover noise generated on the first two showings was more than enough, and after Satan was raped and dealt with quite nicely with the sophomore, there was no need for the guys to continue in the same direction. It was the late-80’s, for crying out loud, the audience’s tastes were changing, “I Wanna Fuck You”-propagating hymns were a thing of the lusty, uncouth past; sophistication and intellectualism were swiftly becoming the order of the day…

and the guys obeyed, to the fans’ utter chagrin and to The Megamosh’s ultimate delight, by shooting this album which is built around more complex, more thought-out and much less horny compositions regardless of the naughty, or perhaps mistreated,-looking girl on the cover. The shift in execution is obvious from the get-go with the more entangled riff-patterns on “The Deal” which deals uplifting power/speedy cards with quite a few interesting melodic twists and turns including a short acoustic balladic etude. Kruse shouts quite a bit here sounding less restrained, but strangely fitting the optimistic merry-go-round-esque attitude that goes one jolly notch up on “Night of Tears”, a rousing melo-speed metal fiesta that sounds closer to the Scanner shenanigans from around the same time than to anything the band have composed earlier. Not bad by any standards although it becomes clear only too soon that thrash won’t play any role here with “Violence” looking at the stripped-down speed/crossover feats on the debut, and “We Want More” introducing a heavy, steam-rolling approach spiced with sudden fast-paced outbursts and a cool memorable chorus.

Mentioning choruses, “Kiss Ass” takes first prize in this department after overcoming a goofy acoustic intro, and although the dominant aura is one of nonchalant crossover demeanour ala Suicidal Tendencies, the band still manage to acquit themselves with several noteworthy speed metal-ish “windmills” which sound more convincing than the overflow of ideas in the second half those unnecessarily complicating the environment on an otherwise frivolous, air-headed cut. No such films on “Never”, another carefree speed metal anthem with very good guitar work and Kruse’s bass pirouettes finally featured more prominently; and on “Mother” which combines power and speed in an intriguing, Scanner-esque again, fashion standing for the highlight here, an eventful, proficiently-executed number the title-track following a similar pattern, closing this opus with style and a marginally friendlier flair, with sprightly bouncy rhythms and another catchy chorus.

There are a few moments that suggest more elaborate, nearly progressive, layouts, but the jolly good mood is just too big for those to develop fully. Besides, with thrash completely missing from the equation it’s hard to view this album as an attempt from the band to jump the same wagon as Mekong Delta, Sieges Even, and Deathrow. Yes, the songs have been elongated, the ways of expression have become more diverse, but these new ingredients are hardly an exhibition of unheard of creative flair as the guys used to achieve leaps and bounds of striking musicianship previously without them. The longer tracks sound like more or less finalized copies of the monumental “Coming Again” from “Sign of the Wicked”, seldom generating a very high level of excitement; fortunately, the shorter material nicely balances things out, carrying the carefree speed metal spirit with which the band’s repertoire has become synonymous. 

That same spirit seems to have possessed the guys, or rather guy since from the initial line-up it’s only Kruse that has left, after the reformation as evident from the freshly released 3-track “Ballrun” demo which is again on the borderline between speed metal and crossover, nothing too complex, just the good old school metal played for the fun of it. No signs of The Megamosh at this stage… I guess the best… sorry, beast has given up mistreating the three artists here who, who knows, may as well do fine without his (un)wanted interference.

For those curious about the Japanese sludge doom metal band Corrupted but who were put off listening to their albums because they'd heard that essential recordings like "Llenandose de Gusanos" and "El Mundo Frio" were very, very long and had the nature of endurance tests, you need not fear: throughout their career Corrupted released several EPs of manageable length. some of them less than 20 minutes in length. One day these EPs should all be gathered up and released on the one compilation album, that would be good for those people who aren't able to buy the music separately but can get it if it were all together in one product. "La victima es tu mismo" could qualify as singles material as its A-side is the title track and the B-side is a shorter song, less than half the length of the title track. The whole thing runs to just under 19 minutes.

As the shorter track, "Los Colores del Cielo" might be minor but it's still grand: noisy, oily guitars like pouring metallic rain and slightly floppy yet hard percussion accompany Hevi's gruff ranting. The music initially is no more than backdrop for the vocals but after the second minute the guitars start piling on the pressure and listeners feel the tension increase almost imperceptibly but steadily. The drums continue to lumber on as before. The continuous run of guitars, almost throbbing though actually not, has a deranged edge after some time. While I would have liked something dramatic and explosive to end the track, going out in a pyrotechnics display isn't Corrupted's style and the track leaves me feeling strung up high and struggling to come back down. I suspect I'll just have to cut loose and plummet down.

The title piece is slightly more varied and has at least definite though very slow and miasma-like rhythms and chugging riffs. It's more like a song than most other Corrupted pieces I've heard, with alternations between instrumental passages where effects and melodies may play and parts where Hevi croaks out lyrics, during which the music merely keeps time and rhythm. The instrumental parts sometimes feature very prolonged, high-pitched guitar feedback squeals set far back in the mix. After some time, the shrill parts dominate the track before fading out. Later the song changes to a more flowing and noisy metal shower with steady if perhaps monotonous drumming. Hevi's voice rarely changes from near-animalistic groaning and growling while the music becomes frantic and quite edgy and frazzled. Again, I find the ending not to my taste: I always feel with something this intense, suggestive of anger on the edge of explosion, that there's got to be some kind of release and resolution, even if not a very good one or one that satisfies most listeners.

The music is very much what Corrupted usually delivers: hard-hitting, no-frills sludge doom metal with plenty of crust and a pessimistic view of human frailty and corrupt politics and culture. These guys don't perform songs that most people would recognise as songs; Corrupted's songs are more like poetry readings or long declamations that happen to have a doom metal backing and an angry attitude born perhaps of idealism and yearning for a better world turned into despair and cynicism over the extent and depths of human depravity and corruption. The cover artwork of a silhouetted person looking out over a bleak and ruined urban landscape suggests something of that outlook.

Morbid Landscape are from Serbia and play Death Metal, which is influenced by various bands; especially early Morbid Angel has had an impact on the process of song-writing. The demo consists of eight tracks, but the style is not limited to one particular facet of the Death Metal scene alone, as the vocals show an occasionally resemblance to the grindcore scene. The music is not too technical in its design, but drifts away into this region now and then without ever loosing itself in it; furthermore do these bursts not appear on every song. In respect to the tempo should be mentioned that Morbid Landscape tries to vary it between the songs and therefore are blastbeat part of them as well as slow ones have been woven into the compositions. 

Into the New Eon needs some to evolve in the head of the listener. The tracks are quite complex and full of ideas, which the band was able to combine in a neat way. A factor that has a positive effect on the music is the skilled production. Little is to complain about it and their part enabled the band to prove their quality in their early state already. Each instrument has a good deal of power and can be examined clearly. 

This is certainly an interesting demo which is offered by the band, now for free, but before that distributed on a CD, and the quality is also on a good level. Nevertheless is the resemblance to Morbid Angel there and to those familiar with their early releases, this fact will be revealed very quickly. It is not necessarily bad to present music that enables the listener to figure out what the influences of this band has been and how they have dealt with it while writing their music. Yet it should not be stretched to excess and the bottom line on how to do it can be perceived on this demo.

titulo: The Unsung Frontiersmen of the Death Metal Genre
texto:
Incubus is in all probability one of the first wave of extreme metal bands in the 80s who were responsible in influencing numerous bands who innovated the death metal genre. Now don't be surprise if you might not get as many information about the band if you don't do your own deep research, as they have flew off the radar of most fans of the genre these days due to the lack of exposure. If in some way you have heard about the band, or even got a hold of their materials, then you already know that these fellas are top-notch talents from the old days that are way ahead of their time.

Serpent Temptation is the debut record from these Louisiana-based (originally from the thrash Valhalla of Brazil) death/thrash metal maniacs, and it is an album that contains 8 murky, hasty, and one of the most fervent death/thrash metal tunes ever recorded in the history of the genre. Every bit of the songs in here are catchy and memorable. Each track carries killer lightning speed and beefy thrashy riffs,a unique vocal approach (as Scott's technique appears shouted, but at the same time growled), and flat out blazing drumming.

One of the highlights that is extremely noticeable in Serpent Temptation is the very well structured and very tight rendered guitar riffings. Each one of the songs has a level on elaborateness in them that gives them their own way of catching the audiences ears. When Francis (the band's axeman) plays at slower tempos, he can materialize with some of the heaviest riffs plausible, and simultaneously, the fella can instantly shift to frantic supersonic tremolo riffing at a moment's notice. But it is the drum work in all of the tracks in here that holds the true stupefaction of the record. Moyses (the band's drummer) displayed a very unique style of producing the blast in this album. The method that he used here is very conventional to the thrash metal genre. The thing is, the drummer slugs the drums like the usual technique that thrash drummers does it, but the dude does it so fast in a lightning speed tempo that it could match a full blast beat style used in the death metal domain.

The raw and dirty production of the album also complements the content and intensity of the whole output of the band. The evilness and cruel atmosphere of the unprocessed style of mixing and presentation really brings out the real grandeur of this offering. I also love the art work of the album, as they kept it plain and simple, yet it instantly reveals to the listeners and the fans the horrors that is upon them once they give the record a spin.

Altogether, this debut studio record is an utterly superlative classic masterpiece. This chef-d'œuvre of an album should be respected as such the connoisseurs of the death metal and thrash metal genre respects the early albums of old Sepultura, Death, early Kreator, Morbid Angel, and Dark Angel. I highly recommend this magnum opus to all fans of the mentioned genre and those who collect gems from the old days of the extreme metal music archives.

Brought to me by a trusted friend, California's Voidhämmer gives a sensation of anything but the warm California sun. Swinging into the new year with their first and only release, Noxious Emissions is one of those 4-track death metal EPs that quickly eludes to a promising future. While not much to go off of yet, the band secures their ability to write crushing, murky rhythms under a fierce umbrella with thick gutturals to match the even thicker sludge of the atmosphere. The drums especially stand out, working double-time to ensure crushing blasts that grab the listener while also coating the bottom layer in thick muck to match everything else.

Diving into the filth factor right away, "Rotting In Excrement" wastes no time getting to the point, even laying down some almost technical chops amidst the more straightforward yet marshy rhythms. "Cadaveric Bloat" more or less follows suit, leading into "Phosphatized," probably my favorite track due to the punkish vibes let in by an even sharper guitar tone. If that isn't enough, the bass on this one stomps everything in its trail, before screeching into the closing "Coffin Leakage," smothering the listener with tough stomps.

Obviously Voidhämmer are still in their infancy, but if Noxious Emissions is anything to go off of, it's a pretty safe bet that they're capable of crafting a fucking stellar full-length. Do not sleep on this.

Thyrfing is your typical Viking metal band with some harsh vocals. But what makes them stand out from the rest (and what makes them good) are the synthesizers played by Peter Lof. 

The music itself is very predictable. It’s mostly mid-paced, although the openings to some songs are slow due to the synthesizes and the outro bass part in “Going Berserk” is also on the slow side, although “Vargavinter” is fast throughout the song. The guitar is played using the same rhythm part over and over; only it’s played fast linking it together. What sucks about it is that it’s the exact same lead on every song. Every song has the same tune of the guitar, and the only difference is the speed of the guitarist. Bass part is what you would expect, following the guitar, although there are some quick solos in most of the songs, and the bass does the ending for the song “Going Berserk”. 

Nothing new or exciting comes out of the vocals. This is one of the albums with Thomas Väänänen doing the vocal part, and he does an ok job. He’s just average, doing nothing spectacular or amazing on this album. His harsh croaky voice fits with the rest of the music, and goes well with the synthesizers. 

Like I said, the synthesizers are what make this band unique. Almost every song opens with them and they play throughout the songs. It’s played usually mid tempo like the rest of the work on here but it’s really fast in “Vargavinter”.

This is a pretty decent album. It can be predictable and get a bit repetitive but other than that this is a strong album. Fans of Viking metal should look for it.

Portugal's Atomik Destruktor play conventional thrash metal with a good mix of fast and groovy riffs. This album Unnatural Disorder is the only full-length they released during their period of activity, and it accomplishes a lot of things, but definitely falls flat at others. The best parts on the album are its fastest and most technical parts. For this reason I think the album spends a bit too much time lingering on uneventful riffs, but the groovier riffs are undoubtedly catchy and enjoyable to some degree.

I also think the album is slightly lacking in the production department; the guitars don't pack as much of a punch as I'd like them to, and this unfortunately detracts from some of the album's best riffs. The beginning of the title track, for example, has a really awesome opening, it kind of reminds me of the riff in Metallica's 'Fight Fire with Fire', but the guitars sound a lot flatter than they need to for an album that came out in 2015, and it makes the whole thing sound a lot less sinister than it otherwise could have.

Complaints about the instrumentals aside, the songwriting on the album is very decent. There's more than enough variety in the tracklist, so it never feels like you're listening to a song for the second or third time. For a thrash metal album especially, this is big; songwriting is of utmost importance in this genre, and Atomik Destruktor definitely nail it.

The vocals follow the typical style of thrash with lines that are yelled in a very raspy fashion. The vocalist does a good job, but I find it very difficult to understand the lyrics at most points. For example, in the song 'Phantom City', before looking at the title, the chorus sounded more like it said 'Shredding at Sea' or something like that. This wouldn't bother me if this were a death or black metal album—for a thrash metal album it does. 

I think, based on the cover art, I went into this album expecting the music to sound a lot darker than it did. Unnatural Disorder is a pretty groovy album, but that's not inherently a bad thing. The band undoubtedly do a good job of turning catchy riffs into catchy songs, and that's something I can't complain about. Unnatural Disorder is a respectable contribution to an underappreciated scene.

Henriëtta, strange name for a metal band if you ask me.  It kinda reminds me of an aging woman who thinks she's still thirty-four and wears too much make-up and perfume to be taken seriously by the rest of the sane world.  On the other hand, you can easily remember that name, and quite frankly, you should.  If you're an old school metalhead, you definitely should remember Hernriëtta, because she rocks!

There was a time when Henriëtta was named Exhilaration and before that they were named Smekmuk.  With each name change came a line-up change.  In fact, the band have been looking for a solid line-up ever since their inception in 2011 and only now seem to have found it.  The new name is a tribute to the 'Evil Dead' movies, and so is the album title.  Yep, this is horror-induced death thrash.  

The album opens quite silly with a bizarre electronic intro, something between the Pong game and old school EBM.  However, after a few seconds, the song 'Henriëtta' kicks in and we're slashing our way through a bunch of freakish zombies.  From then on, the listener is being drenched in a twisted cesspool of old school thrash metal and evil growls.  The whole reminds me of something between Megadeth and Autopsy.  

What I like about the album is the uncomplicated nature of the songs.  They make pretty damn good headbanging material  In a way, they're quite simple, maybe even I can play some of these if I practiced a little more.  Either that or these guys make it sound simple because they're geniuses.  Yet, it gives the whole a vintage old school atmosphere, where even old school Sepultura often comes to mind.

That being said, don't take these guys too lightly.  They know quite well how to come up with excellent songs in perfect thrash tradition, complete with flashing solos.  Some of these, including the awesome track 'Cry For Heaven's Gate', could easily become fan favorites.  'Midnight Neutering' can effortlessly start moshpits (yes, I know that title is hilarious too) and 'Apparitions In The Fog' will make many Iced Earth fans drool.

In recent years I've seen Dutch and Belgian bands come up with stunning old school inspired material. You could even say that there's somewhat of a revival going on these days.  In that 'new wave of Lowlands metal', Henriëtta certainly deserve their place.  Soon, these guys will make their way to the bigger stages and to metal festivals all around.  I just hope nobody comes up with the brilliant idea to show up at one of those gigs, wielding a chainsaw to massacre everyone in attendance. 

Serge Timmers

Proving that it is still possible to do it yourself, Dead to Rights bring us an incredibly solid independently produced album. Although younglings of today’s mathcore and deathcore movements might find the sound a little too “old school”, anyone with knowledge of metal history will acknowledge the organic brutality of this recording. It hits you right between the eyes but you can also tell that the instruments are being played by men and not machines.

Simply labelling Dead to Rights as thrash or death metal would be somewhat limiting. There are sprinkles of progressive and doom elements throughout their music that blend with the aggressive forefront and create an inventive, original sound.

Blind Hate is composed of songs that achieve a good middle ground of complexity and the desired head-banging catchiness. In an age where every band seems to have six members, Dead to Rights remind us, as Pantera did, that good songwriting can often outshine layering. Brian Wall holds up the guitar fort all by himself with clear and precise riffs. There is no jumble of notes here; although brutal the guitar parts are perfectly decipherable. Graham Malloch’s drums provide a rock-solid foundation which is polished to splendour by Christopher Pacey’s fretless bass lines. Pacey also delivers a roaring and brutal vocal delivery, which in the end is the deciding factor that leans Dead to Rights more into the death metal camp.

The only bothersome point about this album is its short playing time. Clocking in at 31:30, it leaves me wanting a few more songs. Perhaps for the next release Dead to Rights will treat us to an instrumental intro or outro, marked by some of that lead bass we all know Pacey is capable off?

Either way, I can’t wait to see what else this band has in store for us.

titulo: Beyond The Black - Lost In Forever
texto:
Beyond The Black are busy these days. They started up in 2014, and have since played Wacken twice and now managed to put a second album. So, since they’re young and hungry and ready to show the world what they can do, I’ve built up quite a bit of hype for the sophomore effort, Lost In Forever. The position they’re in, they have to balance this album so that it hits just the right amount of experimentation and sticking to the sound they started on debut album Songs Of Love And Death (2015), which was far from flawless. Making another SOLAD would also be a big mistake; they need to move forward.
